Ultimate General is an easy to get into wargame which is great fun. The pacing of the game is great. Individual firefights can last a long time which I mean as a compliment compared to some other "wargames" where everyone rushes in and one side dies very quickly. There is plenty do (adjusting your men, trying to flank, bringing up reserrves etc) and I never felt the need for an accelerate time button. After each battle there is a brief summary of how then battle went and depending on the outcome you get to decide a broad strategy for the next battle which can vary the map and placement of units. I found the end of battle summary text a little disconnected from the battle that I thought I had fought but this is a small gripe. I suspect the replayability is not as high as I would like as it is based around one major battle. However, I am guessing there will be many mods or battle packs in the future.

I really like this game.
At this point I don't know whether I have it in me to ever complete the game. But I keep coming back, trying to scratch my way forward every now and again.
It's a really minimalist twin-stick shooter, where in each level, you dodge, and you shoot. When you are not shooting, you move slightly faster. And you need to shoot all the level's enemies until they become black holes into space... and the enemies are just as deadly when black, but move faster. Every four levels, the game's mechanics change. The enemies change their patterns, or abilities.
The aesthetic, as you will see on the game's store page, is very sparse. It's difficult to think of anything that could be clearer; there is your ship, there are your bullets, and just about everything else will probably kill you. That's pretty straightforward. It's all in a colour palette which reminds me of the Atari 2600. If I'm wrong and it's not precisely... there's definitely something late-1970s about it all.
The sound is... unsettling. Really unsettling. And each level is unsettling in a fiercely new way.
As still images, you can't see the incredible intensity of the game. But it's an endless dance of dodge, shoot and dodge, win or die.
But it's one of those games where I try and play it to the next checkpoint (around 10 - 15 minutes) then stop, exhausted. It's not that it's super fast or there's a ton to visually process, it's that it's really intense.
I've only got 12 levels to go, I think. Wish me luck!

Shovel Knight is a REALLY fun game.
Everything from it's level design, to it's unique and challenging boss fights. It may be a platformer that takes less then a GB to download, but it still delivers a more enjoyable experience than some AAA games I have played in recent memory (in my opinion).
Even though it emulates the NES look from the 80's, Shovel Knight has a really appealing art style, with it's very colourful backgrounds and really nice looking sprites. This in turn makes each level very unique to play, whilst never really recycling anything from it's previous levels, introducing at least two or three new enemies to contend with in each new area. Add alongside that some secret areas to uncover for musical notes, which can be played by a bard at the village hub.
And of course to go along with this is a fantastic soundtrack that really fits each area you play, with no song feeling out of place and just feeling really catchy. It's just great.
You'll also come across a decent amount of interesting characters who each have their own humorous flavour, but some characters, (especially the wandering travellers) really could have done with a fleshed out backstory, but they don't have one. This really hurts the characters as they each have a unique style and boss battle, which really makes you want to know more about them.
Now, while Shovel Knight as a whole isn't that terribly interesting, his dream sequences, whilst just being the same thing every time, do flesh out his drive a bit, giving you more feeling for his motivation.
And when it comes to gameplay, Shovel Knight controls absolutely fine, with each movement feeling very precise and on point. I never once felt like the controls were fighting me, and there was never a cheap death, as it was all just my fault at the end of the day, for not paying enough attention.
Now that's not saying the game is hard. It's definitely a casual ride from start to finish, but it still maintains a level of challenge that's really appreciated. There's always that one part where it feels really difficult to navigate (cough flying stage cough) and even when those parts got very frustrating, with me dying over and over, losing pretty much all of my valuable gold, there was always a checkpoint that would welcome me back at just the right area. And when reaching the next checkpoint after beating aforementioned tough area, it just adds a nice level of satisfaction. And of course, if you feel like it's too much handholding, you can always destroy any checkpoints you encounter for a bit of gold, rasing the stakes considerably.
When it comes to the relics you will purchase for your playthrough, none of them ever felt overpowered, as most have different uses for different situations. There was always a boss who was really challenging to fight, but with a certain relic at my disposal, it did make my fight a bit easier. What's great is you don't have to use these either, so if you feel like it makes the game too easy, just don't use them.
And that brings us to the health and magic system. Relics will require magic to be used and will quickly use up your magic metre if you haven't invested enough points into it, and health is self explanatory. In order to upgrade these two you will need to spend a pretty decent amount of gold in order to upgrade by at least one point, and it's definitely in your best interests to upgrade your health first as there's pretty much no boss fight where you'll pass through without taking at least one point of damage. There's also a one-use goblet which contains a temporary power up of your choice, with the health restore being the most useful by FAR.
Now when discussing the boss fights I won't say too much, but I will say that each boss is entirely different from one another, challenging, and fun to fight. Minor spoiler crucial to this review:
Now, in conclusion, with all this being said, Shovel Knight is a highly enjoyable game, definitely worthy of your time. It's just such a colourful and charming platformer that really makes me cherish the experience I had with it, and the extra challenge modes and the free expansion is just icing on the top of this 8-bit cake. Go play it.

Coin Crypt is a nice fun game to play a few minutes (or hours) at a time.
Yeah.
That's it. Not much to it.
It's just a fun game to play, easy to pick up, and just takes up a lot of your time. Every run is different, level-wise. You probably won't get the same exact run two times in a row. You can do a lot of things. You can donate to only one god in one run, you can try only using certain coins in another run. You can just joke around and choose a card at random if you want. As you play this game, you can choose whether you want to save up your coins for a god, or to save that one key for a chest or another location that's blocked off. The whole game is full of these situations between your fights against others only using these coins. The further you get into the game, the more characters you can unlock. Each character has different abilities, or stats that make each of them unique. Go try to do runs with different characters if you want.
Yeah, that's it. Yeh. Yeah. Yee.

is a multi-chapter story, the first part of which is free and the remainder is paid DLC.  I recommend it based on that consumer-friendly policy: if you are at all interested, you should download it and try it out.
That said, I won't be buying the rest of the story.  There are several problematic elements of this visual novel.  To start with, I'm surprised that this is listed as only available in English, as to me it reads like a bad translation.  There's a lot of clunky grammar and weird word choices.  Character moods are expressed awkwardly, and more often than not are telling rather than showing.  This all makes it hard to emphasise with the main character, or fully immerse into the world.
The plot has promise, but is poorly executed.  There are plausible ideas about near-future technology and the intersection of power and information, but they are clumsily presented.  It's a shame, as there are a couple of moments when everything really comes together: the music, the art, even the dialogue perfectly building the mood.  But those are islands of quality in an unimpressive sea,

What Is Life? is a 1944 science book written for the lay reader by physicist Erwin Schrödinger. The book was based on a course of public lectures delivered by Schrödinger in February 1943, under the auspices of the Dublin Institute for Advanced Studies at Trinity College, Dublin. The lectures attracted an audience of about 400, who were warned "that the subject-matter was a difficult one and that the lectures could not be termed popular, even though the physicist’s most dreaded weapon, mathematical deduction, would hardly be utilized."[1] Schrödinger's lecture focused on one important question: "how can the events in space and time which take place within the spatial boundary of a living organism be accounted for by physics and chemistry?"[1]
In the book, Schrödinger introduced the idea of an "aperiodic crystal" that contained genetic information in its configuration of covalent chemical bonds. In the 1950s, this idea stimulated enthusiasm for discovering the genetic molecule. Although the existence of DNA had been known since 1869, its role in reproduction and its helical shape were still unknown at the time of Schrödinger's lecture. Pirate Pop Plus, besides being a very fun alliteration to say, is a game where a pirate shoots anchors to pop bubbles.
It's a very simple concept, one that could get boring very quickly. So how does this game vary it up? Power ups ofcourse! Which I counted about... 6 power ups. That's it.
Well what else does it do then?
It changes the gravity!
And how does that effect the gamplay?
You're now on a different side of the square!
Oh.
You still have to dodge the bubbles when you're falling though, right?
Nope, you bounce off of them if you land on the top of a bubble.
Oh.
I remember playing these sorts of games on buses and cars, games where there's a simple mechanic and power ups to balance the ever increasing gameplay, and having grand old time with them, but this game lacks a key mechanic that the other games had, progression.
In tetris, the blocks get faster and faster when you reach different levels. In this game, the bubbles have the same slow pace it had from the start, they just chuck more bubbles at you, which is a little bit of a lazy design choice  if you ask me.
While this does make the game more challenging, it also makes it absolutely impossible. There was an instance where two bubbles bounced in the same place, at different times, so all I could do was stand there and slowly wait to be killed.
Which could have been easily fixed if I had a jump button.
While this may seem like a minor gripe I have for the game, it's absence restricts the developers from filling the screen with bubbles, and allowing faster gamplay and more split second desicions
After I played normal mode and found these problems, I switched to hyper mode to see if it were any different, maybe the bubbles actually moved faster than normal mode. But, I was disappointed to see that the only changed they had made was give you one life instead of three. Instead of increasing the chaos, it just made me angrier when I found myself in a situation where it was impossible to escape.
So far the problems I've risen are rather large, so why am I recommending it you ask?
Because the power ups do
enough to vary the game up, and bouncing off bubbles while falling is an interesting mechanic that does improve the gameplay.
It's a decent game that's definitely worth the price, but it could've been so much better than it is right now if they make these minor changes that will remove the major problems.

My thumbs were aching slightly after an hour of playing THOTH. Look for an angle, look for a way around, try not to smash into a moving obstacle, and then “bam!” you are toast. It is a one hit instant death and back to the start of the level set. Undeterred, I went back at it repeatedly until I finally made some headway. One thing is for sure, THOTH is more than a challenging game. It’s made of bare-knuckled tension with the full intent of breaking your game-fail tolerance.
From the beginning of the game, you are presented with a sparse minimalist screen with the title name in white and some electronic beats grooving lightly. Once you select a level, the music changes tone with a slightly ominous chord and a movie sound-effect similar to walking into a room filled with xenomorphs. When I first began playing I had absolutely no idea what type of game this was. Suddenly, I was a little circle moving around and avoiding a sinister looking set of squares that obviously had it out for me. Geometric rivalries are real here, shoot first and ask later. Very quickly, I discovered exactly what style of game this is.
It’s a twin stick shooter, folks; a fairly intense one at that.
Now, for me this felt daunting because my experience with twin stick shooters is minimal at best. I’ll have to review this from the viewpoint of someone who doesn’t have reflexes of steel. Think reflexes made of marshmallows with rainbow colored coconut flakes on top. Perhaps melt them into cookies for good measure. There, now you’ve got it. Take a deep breath and let it out before watching me get stumped playing a twin stick.
I won’t lie. It took me a number of attempts to even get to the first level save. You must complete four levels to get a save point within the game. There are 64 levels - 16 level sets - of nerve wracking enjoyment. In order to get very far, you’ve got to be experienced with using both left and right joysticks on a controller in a coordinated effort. Frankly, that’s not me. For the most part, I use the right joystick to change camera angles or aim badly while playing a shooter. Yet, I wasn’t beat-down. I play a fair amount of platformers and fighters so I can manage to aim and fly at the same time. My first reaction after multiple deaths was mild rage. If you have a rage issue, I don’t recommend this game. The first three level sets are not impossible, but level set 4 may induce controller throwing fits if you have trouble keeping a cool demeanor. You have to dig deep from your inner patience to play THOTH. After awhile, the zen sets in and you keep at it doggedly like any good challenge inspires.
For those without a controller, there are keyboard and mouse controls. To my surprise, these are actually good controls and you may even have an advantage playing with a mouse and WASD if you primarily play that way. I preferred a controller myself.
So, what sets THOTH apart from the other reflex games? A few things stand out to me. First and foremost, once you shoot out the color from an enemy it does not die. Instead, it attacks you at a faster rate and with acceleration. Yes, those dead blocks are not only chasing you around, they are accelerating towards you at a very fast pace. Several of them can gang up and attack like a school of piranhas making a lunch of you. With the one hit deaths, THOTH comes at you with teeth snarling.
It’s not just the enemies out to get you because the environment can kill you as well. Death walls may disappear or revolve around you. Sometimes, they can alternate as deadly or neutral every time you shoot a block out. Even the enemies may change, where you have to keep an eye on them from destroying not just you but the whole game space like a bomb ready to blow.
A crucial bit of information is that when you shoot, it slows down your movement. This single property is essential to how you maneuver through the levels. Often you must dodge before shooting, or carefully move out of the way and line up a shot because they’ll form a line of death if you don’t leave a way out somewhere. You can’t just roll in, guns blazing, or you’ll die in seconds.
Each level set is a different puzzle, a slightly new strategy. It’s this puzzly attribute that makes the game substantially more intricate than a game based solely on dodging and attacking. It’s an unpredictability that echoes of playing Asteroids on a CRT screen at an arcade. You are looking forward to seeing if you can make it out or get boxed into an oncoming attack.
There is a definite reliance of color scheme and balance with the game environment. You won’t see amazing detailed landscapes or breathtaking graphic imagery. Instead, THOTH, places you in a color saturated pantheon of line art. The emphasis is on the gameplay, not the images. However, there is very careful attention to the overall look and presentation of each level. It’s sort of like playing a nice art-deco game from 1983.
The background sound is more a series of alien tones and sound effects. It’s as if the sound designer from a science fiction movie put all the movie sound effect samples into one track and handed it over for use on THOTH. While not aggravating, the sound does not exactly do much to keep the gamer from getting frustrated.
The gameplay in THOTH never changes, only the level consistency changes around. From what I played, there were no power-ups or added bonus weapons. I won’t deny that an argument could be made that THOTH is somewhat lackluster. However, that’s ignoring one prevalent game trait; the level patterns are unpredictable. Variation is key with a completely static set of movements and attacks. It gives the game a bit of a rogue-like feel, even though it’s not rogue-like in format. THOTH is about using your honed skill set. Imagine a real life WWI pilot. You can’t upgrade your plane or buy weapons in mid-air, it’s just you and the plane. If you get shot down, you die. Much of the same feel of that gritty situation is in THOTH.
While I enjoy the game, and plan on keeping it installed for a while as I whittle away at some of the level sets, it is definitely repetitive. It is also not a game for everyone. Some people may find it too boring or too tedious. It’s just not a game I would brag about to all my friends with excitement. Mostly, it’s a game I would show to my friends and see how far they can get. There is a co-op option, but I was unable to convince anyone at home to play with me if that gives you any idea.
For me, it’s a great way to get my twin stick skills sharpened. I found it a nice challenge since the game is quite easy to pick up and I’ve become a little closer to my controller because of it. For a zen experience of twin stick goodness where you constantly evolve your game strategy like a cat chasing a running mouse, THOTH delivers.

Despite being a game that gave me 5 days of continuous fun, it still isn't worth buying, especially at it's original price, that is more expensive than CS:GO and Supreme Commander 2.
The positive things about it are that :
-It has a conquest mode(Singleplayer), which doesn't let you be bored while waiting for your friends to join you in MP.
-The designs and concepts, special attributes for each faction are kind of unique and enjoyable
-Units are very well balanced(you can defeat a colossus with a few divisions of infantry if you do it right)
At least the majority of the other things are perfectly balanced too, by the way.
-Modelling is very detailed and properly done
-Lots, lots and lots of ways to win a match
For example, you can either slowly grow your army and make it powerful, then split infantry and vehicles to surround the enemy base through the forests/ruins and open areas together.
You can make your enemy waste all of their resources by counter-attacking them every assault
Or you can completely fortify yourself and focus on building orbital cannons to eventually destroy the enemy fleet, and there's way more than just that. Including making an army of colossi and completely wiping everything off on your way to the enemy HQ or (teleporting/transporting with dropships) your army of infantry straight to the enemy palace.
-It has a few unique features, such as dynamic weather events that can destroy you or aid you in your battle.
As for the negative things though...
-It lacks content, although it has every unit specialized for everything.
(and it has 24 maps, only 6 of which can be played 2v2, also approximately 22(at least for Intar) units for each faction)
-No mod support
-Random crashing after battles(only during 1st session and then super rarely) and a few corrupt, unedited files
-A few annoying glitches, such as being unable to kick players from your lobby if they joined while you were ready, unless you manually fix that by swapping the player's place with someone else.
-Semi-poor tutorial that still leaves a lot of content in the game unexplained.
-Impossible to cancel connection, forcing host and other players to wait for someone to disconnect because someone crashed(or is lagging)
-Doesn't display the latency of other players,.. At all.
-The AI is very stupid and annoying, completely focused on rushing. First it goes with a weak bunch of infantry units straight to your HQ, then it keeps pounding you with tanks and slowly expands while you already probably took over 75% of the map. Keeps repeating assaults(sometimes organized ones though) until you completely demolish them with something strong, like 2 war colossi with a support vehicle, covered in shields.
-The OST gets repetitive after a while, but you won't notice it much because you'll be focused on figuring out how to get rid of the rushing enemies most of the time.
And by the way, the "Air Fortress" thing isn't really a fortress, it's just 2 bulky-looking dropship-like bombers with lots of health. 10/10 would get disappointed again. If you want to see a real aerial fortress, play Supreme Commander|Forged Alliance with mods or Supreme Commander 2.
Sorry, I honestly can't recommend this game, it's only enjoyable while it's free to play or super cheap, as long as it doesn't support community mods.

Shovel Knight Campaign:
Wow, this game is great. It took the good parts of retro gaming and threw away the bad. Let's get into pros and cons, shall we?
Pros:
-Fun gameplay, with intense platforming and pogo-ing
-A good deal of difficulty, for those who like a challenge
-A lack of "Dead Rising"-esque "fake difficulty", in which the game forces you into a situation where you have to cheese your way out.
-Fun bosses, entertaining characters, and an endearing story.
-Epic plot twists.
-Addictive gameplay.
-The fact that Shovel Knight, the main character, is a knight who wields a shovel.
-Cool character design.
-Cool visual effects, even for a retraux game.
-Some seriously cool characters. Special mention goes to Specter Knight, Black Knight, Propeller Knight, and the Phantom Striker, all of which have awesome duels and are fun to fight.
Cons:
-Flying Machine, Propeller Knight's stage, is kinda cheap. Still no fake difficulty, but the level is pretty much outright designed where one change in variable would make it hard but tolerable, whereas all variables are against you. It's both an intense, awesome challenge, and MIND-NUMBINGLY FRUSTRATING. If you don't like extreme difficulty, don't buy this game.
-Lack of post-battle dialogue most of the time. This leaves no context to what happens after the battles. Thankfully, there are exceptions, but not that many. A few words added after the Order members' defeats would make the story far more coherent.
-The endearing cheesiness faded away in battles like Specter Knight and Plague Knight, but the story becomes cheesy and goofy again in fights like Propeller Knight or Polar Knight. This can be a bit of whiplash, especially if you fight Specter Knight before King Knight.
-A bit too much pogo-ing. Sometimes, you can cheat through boss fights by tracing the boss's location, and this removes the intensity.
Overall, 8.9/10. For all who like retro-style games, buy this. For all like me who haven't had a taste of what retro gaming was like, buy this. For those who can't deal with the difficulty, I don't blame you. Still, buy it anyway, just to try.

An Absolute Classic. Many great memories with this game. Sid Meier's Civilization IV is a cult classic, and for good reason. Fun, fast paced gameplay, extensive research trees, interesting tech that completely changes the landscape of the playing field. Being over a decade old, the visual aspect of the game is understandably lacking nowadays, but you see everything you need to. The extensive choice of rulers and perks that come with different civs is commendable. It provides the player with the feeling that they have much more control over the course of their civilization, and this gives a unique depth to the world. As is the standard with Sid Meier's video games, the player truly feels like they are discovering something never before seen when they trek the vast expanse of water in their Caravan for the first time. Multiplayer mechanic is a perfect platform for competitive players or cocky friends to challenge each other to a great, long run of civ and gives way to an incredible, unique experience that no other game can quite achieve. A truly unique game that spans across generations, and will surely be remembered for its incredible run as the go-to RTS game. I speak with a heavy dose of bias, and the game does suffer a bit from graphical glitches, bugs, the occasional crash, etc., but it's an experience everybody deserves to have at least once.

You know what? I'm going to recommend this, even though I hate it, because it's clearly a clever game that would be absolutely PERFECT for someone who is not at all like me.
It's a minimalistic twin-stick shooter where you shoot at blocks, except there's strategy to it: as you shoot the blocks, they become progressively more full of vacuum, and the more vacuum that's in the block, the faster it moves. When a block is all vacuum, it ZOOMS, and goes faster than you and it kills you dead, and then you have to restart a SERIES of levels. So you have to shoot at all the blocks, but you can't get too unfocused, because it's not like these things have a set number of hit points or whatever. The vacuum gradually fills back up with color if you're not shooting at it, so you have to figure out how to balance all your shooting perfectly.
Yes, I only played this game for six minutes, and no, I didn't enjoy them, and no, I'll never play it again, but this game is OBVIOUSLY VERY SMART.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

After playing it during this July's free week (2015), I've decided to purchase this game, and here's why:
1. A galactic battle map aside from the planetary tactical battle map adds a layer of strategy.
2. Gameplay mechanics focussing on resource management makes a tank rush strategy virtually impossible and thus, fun.
3. The purchasing and selling of base upgrades allows for strategy changes mid-game and thus adds to fluidity of battle.
4. The ability to look up at the sky and see orbital battle between fleets while conducting ground combat gives off an epic feeling.
That being said, there are some caveats:
1. The game crashes quite a bit. This can be frustrating in the heat of battle.
2. The AI could sometimes be quite dumb.
All in all, I like this game.
This game is recommended if you like the Tiberian series as well as Dawn of War II.

I would highly recommend this game to others, especially since it brings strategic and tactical elements that a player has to consider and react to which are rarely (if ever) found in other games. Flanking plays a big part in this game, both in trying to flank the ememy while being very aware of being flanked yourself.
This game also forces you to consider issues of concentration of force- you want to exert enough force at a point to make a difference, but not so much where the high density of troops causes more casualties because of cannon fire.
Last, this game really forces you to consider the placement and use of your troops. Do you move more troops to point A to try to gain a strategic point? And if so, where do you pull them from? If you pull them from point B, you may become very vunerable to an unforseen attack in that area. If you use your reserve troops from another area  in the attack, you won't have any fresh troops to stem the ememy attack in another area later in the game.
To sum it up, this game presents the gamer with a lot of strategic issues that you have to resolve. Do well, and you live to see another day. Otherwise....

Simply a fabulous game.  Had lots of time in, so it's not an opinion with zero merit.  Cannot understand the negative reviews here.  This ought to be a self-selecting audience. Anyone playing this likes Civil War History, and/or strategy games.  For those seeking some hysterically complex game with 70,000 hexes and 500,000 units, I would say you won't find it here.  But if you are looking for a great, fast-paced, fun to play strategy game, this fills the bill perfectly.  There are plenty of units, great animations, and the field of dead is rewarding, at the end of a battle.  There are a few tweaks necessary for line of sight stuff, but often your own troops and geographic features are legitimately blocking the artillery - usually can be remedied by moving it around.  When you DO find a good spot for your artillery, it is devastatingly effective.  I just had a great game, with an 'Epic Victory' at Cemetery Hill.  As the Confederates, I won the high ground on Culps Hill and a Hill just south of the battle area, and moved my artillery up fast.  The battle ended with me having 6500 dead to the Union 10,000 dead, and I had Cemetery Hill.  It was glorious.  My only real complaint is that it is difficult sometimes to perceive your position on a hill, relative to the enemy (and between your own units).  A rotating oblique view/camera might help address the positioning issues.  I am not sure if the developer reads these reviews, but I would love to have a replay feature.  Not sure if it would be too much of a nod/copy of SMG, but a replay feature would be great, or some mechanism to review one's performance after a battle.  The battles are tense, and demand some concentration. There is not really time to look around (except a snapshot on pause), and it would be great to review how things went, at a more leisurely pace when the battle is done.  I have played through a dozen or two full campaigns of several battles, and find it interesting and engaging each time.  The ground is familar, but trying new tactics or taking different chances keeps things perpetually fresh.  Great game.

so after a hiatus from FCE i've managed to rack up another 25 hours in the last 3 days, suffice it to say this game has improved signifigantly since i last played (around the time my first review was written)
my previous review was full of candor, i was only trying to point some the holes in the progression.
i would like to add, for anyone who had read my previous review ... i went into the game expecting a different game experience and it relfected that disappointment in my review.
in any case i was happily surprised when i started up a new world again. before the game was simply too easy, 1 million+ piece ore veins and no hostile mobs were my biggest issues. the tech tree progression is a lot smoother now and makes more sense.
Pros:
-extensive tech tree progression ( lots of new higher tier machines)
-survival is more apparent now
-unique mobs
-early game progression is much more balanced
-more building blocks added (windows and a few others)
-very few bugs/glitches ... reletively polished
-new base defense system .. awesome :)
Cons:
-still some unfinished UI elements, nothing gamebreaking
-no penalty for death
-still no compass or map feature of any kind  .. lost your base? easy, dieing is the fastest way to find your base :)
-the giant Spider bot like to step all over you a lot :P (doesn't affect gameplay but is annoying when trying to see something its standing on lol)
now knowing what to expect from FCE has been a better experience for myself, so if you resource/power management and logistics and really strange mobs trying to hinder your progess constantly then grab this game.
side note: the Developer seems to be a lone wolf on this game so dont' expect a lot of new content to be added on a schedule like other games. updates a little slower for this game but the dev is working his tail off to produce this game :)

What about Darsiders? : Darsiders is an Action Adventure Fantasy with a pinch of RPG but mainly Hack&Slash game.
You are WAR, one of the 4 Horsemen of the Apocalypse and you have answered the call of the 7 seals bringing Chaos and Destruction on Earth. Brought to the Council, you have been accused of breaking the Truce between Hell and Heaven and started the War which see the Destruction of Earth. Stripped off your Powers, you are send back to Earth to uncover the truth and those responsible the treachery and seek Revenge.
The plot as you can see is interresting and keep you going as you can't wait to find out who's behind all this, the graphics are really good and most of all even if it was a console port, the Devs have made an effort to optimise Keyboards and Mouse users, and i really appreciate that.

There are also some RPG ingredients and you can upgrade your character with more powerfull gears and items, souls of your victims are used as currency so the more you kill the richer you get yeah that's evil :D.

I generally don't get the appeal of non-pornographic visual novels. They don't reach the visual level of comics, the writing of novels and their actual gameplay percentage fluctuates between 0% and 1% so they are not actual games either.
However, even by the low standards of visual novels this was underwhelming. Everything about Invisible Apartment is amateurish from the subpar writing to the generic japanime-style graphics.
On the topic of story-writing: can we get a single cyberpunk story that isn't about hackers and AI? Yes, Neuromancer was great, we all loved it but that was more than 30 years ago and maybe we could find a different kind of story for once?
Yes, I'm under no obligation to play this but with all of its obvious flaws and shortcomings I'm not obligated to give it a pass either just because it's for free (the first fun-sized chunk at least). I pretty much spent my time after work pretty much finishing this after putting it off for like months.
Got into it a lot because this was something I've been looking to play: An adventure game, similar to Metroid/Zelda, but that's like fun on combat. And it was what I wanted.
Now I when I say similar to Metroid/Zelda I mean this game has very STRONG influences of those games. Which, as you progress through the game, you find yourself equipped with more gear than you can shake a demon at and you start to get that little thought: "Hey! I saw that very same thing back when I started! Maybe I can go back there now!"
And it's basically that.
Not to mention, there's all these puzzles in each dungeon that involves using that Dungeon's main item and NOT TO MENTION using that very same weapon you got IN that dungeon to defeat the Miniboss/Boss. Also, very much LIKE Zelda, you get a nifty Lifestone each Boss you wipe off the husk of a planet.
So this game has very very STRONG Zelda influences.
And Metroid.
And...surprisingly Portal? (You'll see what I mean when you get there)
So this game of various influences actually manages it to make it work, which for me, seems hard to do.
SO!
- Combat is Brutal (you'll be enjoying ripping apart Angels, Demons and other things easily.
- VERY VERY Strong Zelda Influences (If you're into those type of games)
- It's
. Honestly, this game was pretty much a total timewaster after work and I enjoyed it.
- I think Mark Hamill voiced this...not really sure, but you can tell he's using his Joker voice.
- Metroidvania influences as well, it's really quite satisfying to get into a place you couldnt before.
- Ending was good. Was totes excited.
- Drags on. War's a big bulky guy so he can't really...walk fast. He can trundle, though. Not to mention you get his Horse like halfway through the game and you can only use him in certain areas.
- Collectables out the♥♥♥♥♥ If you're not looking for little Artifacts, you're looking for Lifestone Shards and Wrath Shards.
- Music is boring. Just a lot of drums and gregorian chanting.
- Combat relies a lot sometimes on reflexes and timing.
- Weapon EXP, as you level weapons up, it takes INCREASINGLY LONGER amounts.
So in total, I liked it!

The original Civilization is among the most enjoyable, influential games of all time. Its sequels have sought to build upon the basic model by adding greater levels of complexity and streamlining the interface. And though the sequels were definitely great games, they were still rooted in an interface and gameplay style that had changed very little since the original was released in 1991.
That's not the case with Civilization IV. It reenergizes the core concepts of the series, staying faithful to what fans expect while also creating a wholly original game. While the game hasn't lost any depth or detail, every aspect of the design has been streamlined to make it easier for new players to jump in and less monotonous for veterans. Die-hard fans will definitely find that the game offers up so much more variety this time around. The shape of each game is quite different, from the ways you build up your empire to the ways you tear down the empires of others.
Sadly, even the most comprehensive reviews of Civilization IV can't discuss every aspect of the game. There's just so much to experience in this game that you can't possibly hope to cover every topic. While I'd love to tell you all about the other joys and secrets here, Dan and I have to go and teach the Greeks a lesson

Action games from Czech Bohemia Interactive have always been games for masochists. And in the series Operation Flashpoint, and in the ArmA series for the sake of realistic wounds, correct ballistics, kilometer races on armored troop carriers and other purely male joys, players had to endure a badly optimized engine, weak graphics, numerous bugs and frankly over-complicated management. At one time it seemed that in ArmA 3 the situation would change, but in the end we got almost everything the same thing - except for except that bugs.
Stability Islands
For almost 15 years, Czechs have been doing virtually the same game. And although in ArmA 3 the action has moved for 30 years into the future, and instead of the actual technique used its futuristic analogs, the essence remains the same. Before us again a huge battlefield - this time it's two islands, copied from the Greek Lemnos and Ayios-Efstratios, - where brave NATO soldiers are fighting with the next bad guys. Previously, the bad guys were Russians, and now the Czechs have written a story about the rapidly growing Iran, which took a fancy at the islands that had recently separated from Greece. Here, under the feet of the local guerrillas, militiamen, bandit formations and remnants of the regular Greek army are confused - some of them support NATO, some - Iranians.
Despite the updated setting, the ArmA 3 story differs little from the plot of the very first Operation Flashpoint. Brief information about the game. Playing for one of the American peacekeepers, we first lose almost all fellow soldiers, hide in the woods, then find our own, and gradually building up firepower, go to the counteroffensive. At the same time, we have to fight against all the same Russian equipment - for example, the T-90 tank was renamed the OB-T-100 "Badger".
The gameplay has also changed little. It's the same hardcore military simulator where the impact of wind and gravity is calculated for bullet trajectories, a single shot can be fatal, fatigue and body position affect the accuracy of the shooting, and wounded soldiers are bleeding. The schedule of leisure is also known for several years. We are fighting as part of a combat unit or commanding subordinates, indicating where to flee and to whom to shoot. We coordinate the actions of several types of troops - for example, you need to suppress air defense mortar calculations, then call the aircraft, and then send the infantry to deal with the survivors. We storm or defend villages and airfields, and also organize sabotage behind enemy lines, take part in tank battles and combat sorties.
In ArmA 3, water procedures were added to this: for the first time in the series, we were allowed to dive underwater in order to secretly penetrate enemy bases, neutralize or install mines, drown surface ships and walk on a submarine. There were even shootings under the water, where the shells again behave realistically and fly to the addressee, as if in a mode of delayed action. Another notable innovation is the ability to remotely control drones-drones, for example, to fly a few kilometers from its position, turn on the thermal imager and reveal the location of enemy mortar calculation.
Difficult and painful
However, for newcomers or simply people who are not used to patience, unquestioning obedience and well-coordinated work, all this military field charm is still a seven-headed monster, to which one simply does not know how to approach.
When you're half an hour shaking in the back of a truck, just to die from a single, no one knows where the shot came from; When right during the battle you are forced to dance on the keyboard on the multistage context menu to just shout "I'm wounded!"; When to activate the sniper scope you need to press a few buttons (!), And every second flight by helicopter or plane ends with a drop in a kilometer from the airfield - at such moments the admiration for realism gives way to a dull annoyance.
This is especially true in a network game, where coherence and mutual understanding are important as nowhere else. There you can wait for twenty minutes, when the players get on board the turntable, then fly for a long time and without a single shot disgracefully disappear in the sea abyss, becoming a victim of an inept or simply bored with such dynamics of the pilot's events.
Of course, beginners and idiots can be found in any network game. It's unclear why the developers are stubbornly clinging to these blatant anachronisms in their gaming system. If they made the tactical management of the detachment less bulky, and the story campaign more dynamic and modern, ArmA 3 would immediately push the boundaries of its audience and even could go to the territory where Battlefield and Call of Duty now dominate.
But no. Tactical management remains as openly obsolete, confused and over-complicated. Half of its functions are unavailable for most of the game, and such elementary things as the ability to tell the fighters the behavior mode (to act silently or aggressively) are completely absent. The plot is the same as in ArmA 2 Brief information about the game generally degraded. Not only that for some reason he was divided into downloadable episodes, so also the very first of them, "Survival", as if specifically designed to scare away as many people as possible from the game: practically throughout its entire length, we simply run somewhere, occasionally distracted by Short skirmishes and talks on the radio.
Of course, the authors did some work on the errors. Entered a detailed manual available directly in the main menu. Improved graphics, optimized the engine, got rid of a huge number of bugs. Even slightly improved AI - transport is now less likely to be confused in the three pines, companions are more intelligent, although the enemies still can not respond to direct hits or not to see the enemy five meters away. But this is not enough for the game to cease to be a purely niche product.
* * *
ArmA 3 remains a hardcore entertainment "for their own", where the main focus is on folk art. Of course, these virtual 900 km2 forests, fields, villages and villages are a fertile field for fans who have already flooded Steam's shop with a huge number of mods, conversions and new campaigns. But in this case ArmA 3 is more like a set of tools equipped with teaching missions than a full-fledged game.

This is a game that I am extremely conflicted about. It has a clear focus and theme, which it executes well. I believe that it does something very special and rare, which is that it is able to communicate its ideas effortlessly and intuitively without words and with minimal text.  It is an extremely simple game, which allows for a very pure showcase of ideas, and that is something that often gets lost by developers under layers of systems and complications.
This game has a very basic graphical style and a singular theme which it sticks to throughout. It is stylish and it works. There are some games, like Limbo, which try to do one thing and do it really well, and this is one of those kinds of games. The shooting feels good, the controls are responsive and work.  Halfway through my play through, they added mouse and keyboard support, and I switched from a controller to M&K, and I found the added precision in shooting helpful but didn't make the game that much easier, as I felt that I was trading off some movement control for shooting control, and both aspects feel balanced fairly.
This is a challenging game, it is a test of reflex and some pattern recognition. It is also very short. It is the twin stick shooter equivalent of Super Meat Boy, or, if you are feeling generous, Dark Souls.  However, it is in this structure that I inevitably became bored and frustrated with THOTH.  The game is a collection of short levels in which you must shoot all of the enemies to progress. The game gives you check points every 4 levels. Being touched by any enemy is always a one hit kill and you will be returned to your last check-pointed level. This seems fine at first, and even adds some tension and meaning to the game’s progression. However, it quickly becomes clear that you will spent a lot of time replaying the same levels. The game does a good job of fast restarts and this is why it feels like Super Meat Boy. It also sometimes has the feeling of beating your head against the same boss that Dark Souls did. However, unlike those games there is significantly less depth to this game. Not that it is totally void of mechanics, but there is basically shooting and moving, and if you aren’t shooting, you will move quicker.
But the simplicity that is it’s brilliance is also it’s downfall. In Dark Souls, if you are stuck, there are other things you can do, like grind out souls to become more powerful, or go to a different area. In Meat Boy, you can switch your character, or go to the dark world and try a different level. In THOTH, you can’t, other than replaying older levels (which gives you no additional bonus), if you are stuck and you want to keep playing, then you have to keep repeating the same sequence of levels and hope that this time you are able to avoid the hazards or shoot better. In Dark Souls, even in the sessions when you make no in game progress (or even lose progress), there is at least a feeling of learning. In THOTH, there is often not even that. Even when I had learned the strategy to successfully pass through each level, I was forced to repeat that same action and hope I didn’t make a mistake, and if I didn’t make any progress in terms of level progression, then it really felt like wasted time.
I only got stuck a handful of times, and only twice really badly. The first was around level 36 and the second time, and more significantly, was the level 16 checkpoint, specifically level 13. I was stuck on this series of levels for roughly an hour, which is significant when you consider I beat the game in under 3 hours. This means that I spent somewhere between a half to a third of my time with this game repeating the same two or three levels, in the hopes that I could get to the fourth, then dying quickly and doing it again.
This is made worse by the structure of the level series. Generally, the first level will show you the new mechanic, and then the subsequent levels will build on that concept and increase the challenge. This means that a large part of what I was doing was replaying the “tutorial” levels. However, they were not without challenge, and the fact that things could go badly so quickly meant that it was not a guarantee that I would get to the place where I was stuck each time. Needless to say, this made for some frustrating moments. Quite frankly, if I was not so close to the end of the game at that point, I would have stopped playing, because a lot of the enjoyment I got from the game was gone by then.  Even once I got through and found myself progressing at a reasonable rate through the end of the game, I was maddened each time I had to replay content. The mechanic had gotten under my skin and my tolerance for it had basically vanished.
Once you complete the last numbered level, you are given a series of challenges. They are numbered as 8, 16, 24, 32.  These are a randomized collection of level that you need to complete in a row (the first being eight levels, then sixteen, and so on).  This actually solves a lot of the problems I had with the repetition of the game, but it highlights another issue, which is the extreme difficulty level. I may be able to complete 8 or possibly 16 levels in a row, but I will never get to 32, so I am not even going to bother trying.
You may find this criticism to be more on me than on the game, maybe you think the failure is my inability to be “good” at video games, and that difficult games should be, well, difficult and punishing. However, for me, the lack of depth and variety in the game, and having to replay the same content made me wish that there was some middle road, such as, if you beat a level more than 100 times, you don’t have to play it again. Because, at times, I felt that my time wasn’t being respected and that sucked away a lot of the enjoyment and enthusiasm that I had at the start of my play through.
Ultimately, I am recommending this game, because I think for the cost and the actual time you have to put into it, it has enough interesting ideas and a good enough style to carry it and make it worth experiencing. It is a great example of how you don’t need a big budget or expensive graphics to make something fun and engaging. However, it is also an example of how a design decision can destroy an experience. If you don’t like twin stick shooters, or you don’t have a tolerance for grinding without progress, then this is an easy pass.

TL;DR: THOTH has fresh new gameplay that tests your skill, and the sound design is top notch. Solid 9/10 - points off for lack of online multiplayer, lack of volume control, and erratic cubes.
Jeppe has yet again created a game that is a truly unique experience, something that many game developers wish to obtain.
Similar to 140, this game's minimalist design is deceptive. It's a fast-paced twin-stick shooter that has a brutal difficulty. The puzzle aspects of THOTH make it an exciting blend of wits and speed, and the constant barrage of new and exciting level designs keeps you on your toes.
Speaking on the art and music of the game, it has similarities to 140 with the minimalist design, but instead contrasts the bright color palettes of the levels with dark, droning music that is almost sinister in a way. The chaotic tone of the music and sound design matches up perfectly with the game, with each level creating a new way to torture your mind and your reflexes.
The one thing that bothers me is the random bouncing of many of the cubes, which can make it difficult to predict where to move. Although this does force you to keep contstant focus on the level as a whole, it can be a bit infuriating when a bad bounce catches you off guard.
The lack of options (especially volume) doesn't bother me very much. The default volume is at such a level where it isn't too loud for me. While having to control the game volume from the system volume is a bit of an annoyance, it's not major issue that ruins the game.
Its really a fun game but I get crashes often. I don't know if that's just me or its the game.

+ Incredibly nostalgic retro vibe.  The sidebars look a lot like a gamebouy advance or DS with a D-pad and action button that actually moves with your inputs. The game itself has "high resolution 4 color pixelart" which will certainly give you the sense that you are back in the 90's playing on the original gameboy.
+ The gameplay is surprisingly fun. It's more or less a sequel to Super Buster Bros (AKA Super Pang) which originally came out in 1990. You shoot out hook and chains to pop bubbles while trying to avoid them from hitting you. At the same time the gravity frequently changes which forces you to play sideways and even upside down.
+ Variety of weapon power ups
+ A shop where you can spend coins to buy a variety of cosmetics to customize your game along with unlock new soundtracks and characters. (this increases the replayability considerably)
- Since the game uses minimal colors, it can sometimes be hard to see the small bubbles against the background, especially when there are power-ups, coins, and other pickups dropping all over.

Etherium is an interesting Sci-Fi, Real Time Strategy game. It feels like a lot of other RTS's out there and doesn't seem to bring anything new to the table. It has a playable tutorial which makes the commands and controls easy to learn. The story in Etherium doesn't really shine through in the tutorial and seems fairly generic. It isn't a bad game, it just feels like a lot of other RTS's lately. I would have liked to see more base building in this game and felt that aspect was very limited. It didn't seem like there was a big difference between the different factions, but there were special abilities you could unlock once you expanded a colony with the technology center, and those were sort of neat.
All in all, I think the game could have been a lot better if they had some diversity with the factions, and allowed the bases to be more expandabe. The game does offer single-player campaigns for each faction, as well as Skirmish mode, and Multiplayer Mode, but there appear to be long waits for some of the Multiplayer games. Graphically speaking the game is bland. My advice, Etherium isn't a bad game, but you can probably do better.

Written as of Alpha 1.11 (or 1.13c multiplayer, whichever you prefer). I have not played a lot, but from the meager 2 hours there are a lot of things that, unfortunately, made this a waste of money for now. The price tag would be justified if the game weren't the mess it is now. There are ofc a lot of pros to it but the amount of cons, and the form they take, is just a little too much. Also, as much as people would love to say it is a Minecraft clone, the similarities end at "block based building" and "mining". You could just as well place Space Engineers in the same category then.
Pros:
- Infinite worlds, a la Minecraft (better than the 256 block height it has anyways)
- Good potential for a crafting system, unlike any other Minecraft-ish game
- Research, blueprints, power system, different mining modes
- Much more realistic processing and production, with ore smelting, refining, and producing items and gear
- "Health" system with temperature, power levels and hypothermia
Cons:
- Buggy UI and menus, to the point it becomes very annoying
- Lack of a proper tutorial (there is one but it's messy and sometimes unclear)
- Buggy creative multiplayer with no proper netcode or player sync
- Extremely buggy survival multiplayer (lots of ore duping without even trying and more)
- Very odd color scheme and graphical design choices for blocks and machinery (more of a personal opinion, but ir sure seems off)

When they say "infinite worlds" they really mean it!  I decided to test this and built a structure going from the surface (Y:0) and built all the way up to 3,254...  I could have kept going, but let's be honest, that would have been pointless.  So then I decided to find the floor of the world, and dug down to 9,153...  And I could have kept going.  Minecraft's 256 block height limit is put to absolute shame, as this game shows its beefy and well-constructed voxel engine.  I'll admit, I'm going to use Minecraft as my comparison here, because Minecraft is the definitive voxel game to compare to.
The game's view distance is comparable to that of Minecraft's 15 chunk view distance, which means you can see a lot.  In Minecraft there's a survival situation which revolves around food.  Currently in FortressCraft Evolved the survival situation revolves around body heat.  You're in a constant struggle to keep yourself cool enough and warm enough at the same time.  Standing in fire makes your body overheat, draining your power cells, and will kill you of heat exhaustion.  Staying underground or out in the elements at night can cause you to begin to freeze, and you can die of hypothermia as well.
The game is looking good already in its pre-alpha state, and I absolutely can't wait for the full release.  Normally I'd say "don't buy this early access unless you're ready to deal with bugs," but in this case, the sooner you get it, the less you'll end up paying in the end.  So it's at your discretion, buy now and save, or buy later for peace of mind.
Some of the features work, some of them don't, but you'll still find plenty to do in this game.  Better pack yourself a lunch, because you're going to be playing this for long hours.

Which, as you progress through the game, you find yourself equipped with more gear than you can shake a demon at and you start to get that little thought: "Hey! I saw that very same thing back when I started! Maybe I can go back there now!"

Not to mention, there's all these puzzles in each dungeon that involves using that Dungeon's main item and NOT TO MENTION using that very same weapon you got IN that dungeon to defeat the Miniboss/Boss. Also, very much LIKE Zelda, you get a nifty Lifestone each Boss you wipe off the husk of a planet.
So this game has very very STRONG Zelda influences.
And Metroid.
And...surprisingly Portal? (You'll see what I mean when you get there)
So this game of various influences actually manages it to make it work, which for me, seems hard to do.
SO!
- Combat is Brutal (you'll be enjoying ripping apart Angels, Demons and other things easily.
- VERY VERY Strong Zelda Influences (If you're into those type of games)
- It's
. Honestly, this game was pretty much a total timewaster after work and I enjoyed it.
- I think Mark Hamill voiced this...not really sure, but you can tell he's using his Joker voice.

- Music is boring. Just a lot of drums and gregorian chanting.

This game is one of the most finely crafted platformers I've seen in some time. The music is classic and fun, the graphics are retro but not boring and muddy, but the gameplay is where this Shovel-themed adventure really makes waves. The jump arc, the shoveling mechanics, finding tons of gold and treasures to upgrade your Knight with, and even some awesome extra campaigns! (Plague Knight is available at the time of this review, and Specter Knight will soon follow) The levels are well thought out and unique, and the bosses are enough of a challenge the first couple times to be satisfying to beat. You get tons of sub-items to play with, altering your play style and giving you new attack and movement options. The Wii U and 3DS versions have extra stuff if you get the Amiibo, but you hardly need them to enjoy this masterpiece.
Do yourself a favor and give Shovel Knight a try. Some games are fun, but this game has fun in spades.

It's good so far, and it uses the Unity Engine, which means it's not a big corporate game, etc. A few things to note: This game is not complete, not by a long shot. I've already run into a LOT of bugs within my playtime already, below is a list of them.
-- The 64-Bit Version may crash upon Quitting the game to desktop.
-- Having more than one ore type in your inventory will confuse the smelter's "Feed Ores" button. (You cannot make a storage system without multiple ores.)
-- The A.R.T.H.U.R or whatever it is called, requires a Power Core to be crafted for it to work proper again. However, you do not know this recipe, even after researching the black box and power suit upgrades.
-- Right-Clicking items in your hot bar (using the mouse-enabled HUD) removes them from your inventory, forever. You cannot collect more of the item, you cannot see the item when using scroll wheel, etc. It's gone, forever.
-- Using your mining laser on coal ore (or any ore) constantly will seem to continue mining the ore incredibly faster than an ore extractor, this is not the case, the blocks that appear dropped are ghost ore item drops.
-- Game on "Fabulous" has issues with block animations, etc. The loading screen also freezes on that setting, even though the computer can handle said setting over 60 FPS (IE: Getting screen-tear since my computer can process faster even on Fabulous.) The setting can also lag computers that are far, far above the recommended requirements.
-- The spider mech enemy does nothing.
-- Your gun cannot hurt the spider mech enemy. (IE: The spider mech has no hitbox.)
-- Sometimes, during the day, the solar cell on the suit does not work.
-- Sometimes, even if you have enough power and research points, some research items will say they can't be researched.
-- The world select button on the Escape menu does nothing.
-- When creating a world with a custom name, the world's name reverts to "World" on game reload.

If you're more into smashing your enemies as in vanilla Total War then you may as well skip this or buy it when it's £1.99 or less.

Observations on the gameplay:
Pros:
- Satisfies my need for a Civil War Strategy Game.
- Strategic Factor is there, if you don't pay attention to your lines, the AI takes full advantage of that.
- In between battles overview strategy is very neat, I think if you pick the wrong "approach" you can really put yourself in a bind.
Cons:
- Once encircling the enemy and routing them, the AI acts goofy, tends to drive the AI into my lines which... end up routing too? I don't complete understand that yet but I'm assuming its not just 100% coded yet.
- Eliminating Units proves very difficult, I literally had to chase down a brigade of Snipers with 4 brigades in order to complete eliminate them.
- The AI seems to be able to "stall" the ending of the game when they have a chance to conquer my land. When trying to do the same on the offensive, the timer runs out like telling me "You suck". It costed me a pivotable battle.
I'll recommend this game to anyone who enjoys strategic/tactical games. There is a lot of "multi" managing going on, similar to Total War but at least you don't pay the price like you would in Total War, your units 95% of the time come back into the field of action.
None the less, I rate it 7/10, good value for the $10 dollars.

Pros...
-Big world to roam around and explore
-A lot of quests; main storyline and side quests to keep you busy
-Armour and weapons have their own designs (RPG rules dictate more skin = more defense,)
-Gorgeous graphics
-Campy, self-aware humor in the form of intentionally bad writing, voice acting and dialogue
-Always stuff to slay and make you feel tough like the big, bad, skimpy Seraphim you are
-Class customization with special traits, perks and four skill/ability trees for each class
Neutral?...
-A lot of quests are just "go here and kill X" or "go there and gather X". It generally works but can get tedious having to fight your skimpy butt through half of the continent to loot a stone or something and then sprint your skimpy butt way all the way back for an often mediocre reward.
-Character "classes" are gender locked. I didn't care about this, but I recall it being a common complaint from critics.
-Too easy. Bosses basically have a lot of HP. Just slash away.
Cons...
-The camera is atrocious. Good lord.
-The AI is abysmal. Escort missions suck; for example, I had to escort a villager to his sister. He would dart clear across the map, aggro a bunch of crap, runs in another direction, aggroing MORE stuff, by the time I finally FOUND him, he was dead and I failed the quest. Don't expect other escort missions to be better.
-No Steam Cloud support
Overall, it's an enjoyable hack n' slash and worth picking up, but I would recommend doing so on a sale.

This game is one of the most finely crafted platformers I've seen in some time. The music is classic and fun, the graphics are retro but not boring and muddy, but the gameplay is where this Shovel-themed adventure really makes waves. ** ATTENTION ALL NARUTO FANS AND PLAYERS ALIKE **
This review may contain spoilers and comparison information regarding other similar games to this one. Read at your own discretion...Now, under normal circumstances, I don't review single-player games unless...1: They are absolutely awesome or terrible (Glitches notwithstanding) or...2: I can compare them to an identical or similar multiplayer game I have played or also actively play. This being said, NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM Revolution will be compared and contrasted from/to...1: NARUTO Online. 2: NARUTO Saga/NARUTO Spirit. So here goes...
NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM Revolution quite possibly has the best graphics and most playable characters out of any NARUTO game I've ever played. It is also VERY IMPORTANT for one to remember this is a FIGHTING GAME, so exploration of many areas is going to be quite limited, unlike in the game NARUTO Online, where there are several notable areas of the shinobi world one can freely explore in spite of the simpler (But well-done) graphics. Nevertheless, you are able to run around and even jump up to/down from higher or lower places at your leisure. The fighting here is also going to be fast-paced; be aware of this and be prepared to change your battle tactics (And perhaps your control configurations) in order to suit your foes' weaknesses.
Unlockable characters include...1: At least a few of the Kage. 2: Several variations of Naruto and other notable ninja, including most members of the Akatsuki, and even Madara Uchiha! There are also a few different modes, including the notable Ninja Escapades, which play out much like a typical NARUTO Arc. The downside of this (And every game has a downside) is the inability to explore different areas during the Escapades. In fact, the last Escapade is only a cut-scene with no player interaction whatsoever. The mode which actually DOES allow for some exploration is the Mecha-Naruto Story, which isn't as fun, because of the inability to select your characters as you see fit. And speaking of which...You cannot create your own characters either; you have to make use of the ones provided and unlock additional characters as you progress through the game. Kind of disappointing, but again, similar to NARUTO Online. On there, you CAN sort-of create your own character and shape him or her pretty-much to your liking. One can do the same with NARUTO Saga/NARUTO Spirit, however, I would NOT recommend playing NARUTO Saga/NARUTO Spirit AT ALL!! The story and graphics on there are VERY POORLY DONE; you have to shell out real money to gain access to Naruto himself; the Hidden Leaf Village looks NOTHING like it should; and, to top it all off, the Ninja you DO gain access to are nothing but enemies to Team 7!! Why would anyone want Mizuki on their team!? Come on!! Anyway, I would recommend NARUTO SHIPPUDEN: Ultimate Ninja STORM Revolution for the Ninja Escapades, if nothing else. Otherwise, good luck unlocking all those talented ninja. You'll need it! ;-)

Thoth is a nice little twin stick shooter with some interesting mechanics, but I cannot in all good conscience recommend this game at it's current price. The game revolves around the player having to fight 3-dimensional cubes in a 2 dimensional plane. Because the cubes are 3 dimensional, they can behave quite eratically, which in a 2d plane causes you to die a lot from unexpected movement of the cube. The tracking of the cubes also feels off and because they behave differently when "killed" as compared to when "alive" you can sometimes get punished for killing a cube. All in all these mechanics aren't too bad once you get used to it, but it can cause a lot of frustration. The biggest problem I face though is the absence of an escape key, or at least none that I can find, meaning in order to close the game I have to alt tab and close it through the windows bottom bar. All in all with how the game is done, it feels a lot more like a flash game one would expect to see on Kongregate for free, or maybe for 1 or 2 euro's. but the 10 euro price tag for me means that I cannot recommend this game at all, except maybe for when it's on sale.

Abstract:
I received this game as a part of a Monthly Humble Bundle, and after beating the original portion, I can say that this game was very addicting and very challenging.
Summary:
This game does a fantastic job of balancing its difficulty. For the basic campaign (as I'm calling it), four levels are grouped together, through mechanics or a combination of mechanics. If you die anywhere in those four levels, you reset to the beginning of the first one. However, once you beat these four levels, you enter the next set of four levels, meaning your progress has now saved. This allows for intense moments and avoids major frustrations.
The levels themselves can be very challenging, and some take over fifty tries to defeat (but oh, how satisfying it is to beat those stupid squares). This level of difficulty in combination with its brilliant grouping of levels creates for some addicting, one-more-try gameplay.
Other than that, the simplistic and beautiful graphics, along with its captivating soundtrack, makes for a memorable experience, and the challenges after defeating the "main campaign" makes this game have a great replay value. The very straightforward gameplay ("shoot the things, don't let the things touch you") makes the game very fun, and the implementation of various mechanics constantly spice up the challenge.
The only negative thing I can say is that I believe the game is slightly overpriced.
But if this game is on sale for any value, DEFINITELY pick up this game if you like simple yet challenging games that will capture your interest for a few great hours.
Note: Do not play around significant others, as you will pay more attention to this game than them. They will not like it.

Full disclosure: I got this from a free key.
While Thoth appears to be an arcadey twin-stick shooter at first glance, it's actually significantly different.  The levels are all hand-designed to be small puzzles, where the timing, placement, and order of enemies you defeat are essential parts of your strategy. You also can't move very quickly while firing, and enemies that are "killed' don't actually go away. Any hits will send you back to the last checkpoint, which occur every 4 levels.
The whole thing is extremely intense and satisfying, but it's very tough. It also only took me about an hour to clear the initial 64 levels if that's a deal-breaker for you. If you like the sound of a stylish and cerebral TSS, and those downsides don't scare you off, I highly recommend this.

Installing and running this game takes a little bit of tweaking as it will not run with later versions of PhysX. It's simple though, uninstall PhysX in Control Panel>Add/Remove Programs, then use the PhysX install file which is in the game folder, or download legacy drivers from Nvidia.
I also have it running in WinXP SP3 mode, though I did this before reconfiguring PhysX so not sure if necessary.
**The camera on default settings is annoying! Others have pointed this out but it's easy fixed. It moves for you at the worst angles. Don't worry though, three clicks in settings under Camera (untick them all) and you can control the camera angle yourself using A and D keys, and mouse wheel to zoom.
Having said that, for 5 minutes of tweaking, this game is totally worth it. If you like Diablo, The Elder Scrolls, played the first Sacred or simply love RPG type "kill, level, loot" games, you will love this.
The map is huge and free to roam at your Leisure. Everywhere you go there is something to battle and loot. You barely need to buy armour or anything because you can loot everything you need, unless buying something specific.
So many hours of gameplay, side quests, main story quests, random exploration, whatever you want. Choose your character based roughly on the type of game you would like to play, for example, follow the "light" or "dark" path, choose a character based on their fighting styles, once in game the skills you give your character can complement the base skills you have or you can train something totally unique.
I could go on, but, just buy it. It's cheap and with so much to do and so many ways to do it, you will get your moneys worth. I would go so far to say this game is essential for RPG lovers. Yes I would.

This game is amazing.
It's not particularly complex, nor is it graphically or technically groundbreaking (heh), but in my opinion it gets everything right.
The story is basic, the kind of thing you'd see in an old NES game; but the charcters are quite well written, and each and every one oozes personality. In regards to this aspect the first DLC character (as of writing this review, the other have not been released), Plague Knight tops the original in leaps and bounds. The story of Plague Knight and Mona is so well written, and I just love all the subtle things they dropped in.
In terms of gameplay both the main campain and the first DLC are very very solid. Responsive, fluid, and effective. Whenever you die in the game, it's almost always your fault.
The level design is also brilliant, with well thought out puzzles and tests of skill. The game also features abundant secrets, with many collectables and secret areas filled with loot. There's enough that you feel encouraged to seek them, but spread out enough that they always feel special.
In conclusion, this game is just simply fun. Extremely well thought out, and extremely well executed. It's a game that will always hold a special place on my list of favourite games.
