I played FortressCraft on the 360 quite a bit, enjoying the hunt for all those hidden little tools you could use to make playing the game more interesting. I especially enjoyed the idea of creating zed spawners. I must have created thousands of those things...
But anyway, on with THIS game.
I had to say this: it's not easy starting out. I had little time to read the help and starting tips before I realized that my suit energy was dropping fairly quickly. To top it off, I had to also wrestle with the controls before I was able to make my way to my crash site.
But once I managed to get the controls down, I was able to start mining for resources. I got lucky and found a tin and coal vein inside the mountain I set up camp on, and eventually found iron and copper (though they were a long climb down into the earth.
I think the suit energy idea is a good idea. It's going to keep you alive, and it allows you to stay out in the cold a while longer before you need to recharge. And the scanner idea was nice as well, though I think I know a tree when I see one. Unless it suddenly grows tentacles and tries to eat me. Then I'm just being eaten.
And the new entities in the the game have given me more questions than answers. There are these flying robots that, when I kill them, drop ruined stingers. Not sure what to do with those, or what they are suppose to do for the bots, but it's interesting. And let's not forget the wacky-looking spider thing I found stuck on the mountain. That thing wouldn't die, nor would it move. I'm curious as to how all of those things got there.
While this game is pretty fun to play, and the creative mode is a blast to mess with, I did have some general issues, ones that I'm sure some or most players will have run into.
1. Resource Management.
While I can understand that resources are going to be important for your survival, it just seems kind of ridiculous to have to travel hundreds of blocks away in order to find even basic resources (it took me over an hour to just find copper). And the majority of the time, my energy is being used to keep my few ore extractors going, or scanning for more areas to mine new resources. I've yet to find anything new.
2. Control Layout.
This is one of my biggest beefs, and for a good reason. As I said before, I had to fight with the controls for a minute before I could get moving, though it took me even longer to learn how to switch back to my scanner from my gathering tool. It also feel a little clunky, having to reach across the keyboard to hit a certain hotkey. I know the keys can be rebound, but I tend not to mess with that. Maybe a few minor rethinkings of the layout would be nice. Or controller support! I'm honestly one for full controller support, so maybe that could be a future addition.
3. Crafting.
The crafting system is relatively straight forward, which is nice, but requires resources that could take a lot of time to find, and even more time to gather. And even with the resources that are almost immediately found, the process requires more time and more resources. To illustrate my issue:
8 iron=1 iron bar, 15 iron bars=1 ore extractor.
It just seems a little tedious.
4. Environmetal Hazards.
Now, honestly, this is a cool feature, but one that needs some working. Heat keeps you from freezing to death, obviously. But what makes me a little irritated is the fact that you can't make heated rooms. It just seems like one of those things that you'd think would have been implemented a while back to help players better manage themselves. I'm really hoping it's added in a future update, though. Cold nights would be so much more pleasant.
5. Terrain.
This one is just something small, nothing major. But I feel like it's something that could be implemented at some point in even a minor update.
Having to jump to go up another block gets a little tedious, not to mention it's a little hard on the spacebar (at least mine, anyway). Maybe the option of automatically climbing up one block could make an appearance in a future update.
But other than that, this game is looking pretty good! I'm looking forward to seeing what the Devs have in store for futue updates, as well as what other players will suggest adding to it. This is a game that certainly has evolved from it's console predecessor, and it's done so pretty well.

One of the most innovative and easy accessible strategy games that I have seen in years. Ultimate General: Gettysburg is great mix of realism and fun, combined with a user friendly interface and simple, but perfect, game mechanics.
The Battle of Gettysburg
The setting of the game is centered, as the name implies, around only one battle: the battle of Gettysburg. One of the pivotal moments of American Civil War history.
This was the battle in which General Robert E. Lee of the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia, after a series of victories over the northern armies launched his second attack/invasion in Union territory. All preparations had been made to assemble as many men as the south could muster to decisively defeat the Union army in the north on their own soil just prior to the US presidential elections. The rationale behind this invasion of the south was to destroy Union morale and cause President Abraham Lincoln to not be re-elected for another term, opening the door for peace. Alternatively, if things would go extremely well, the objective would be to take Washington D.C. and thereby end the war almost immediately.
On the 1st of July 1863, the Confederate Army of Northern Virginia and the Union Army of the Potomac met each other near the town of Gettysburg. The battle that would follow would be the largest of the entire conflict, ultimately resulting in a decisive Union victory. The game puts you in charge of the entire Union or Confederate Army from the earliest moments of the first day right through the entire multi-day battle that would be Gettysburg.
First Impressions
From the start you can choose to fight as the Confederates or as the Union, you start from the 1st of July when the first elements of both armies met each other at McPherson's Ridge. From then on it is you, the player, who decides how the battle will progress. The battle map has a unique art style that is very appealing to the eye. People that familiar to for example Total War games might feel that the graphics of this game are inferior. The difference is that where Total war puts emphasis on graphics and more lighter, arcadish entertainment, this game puts more emphasis on the more realistic tactical and strategic part of a battle. The graphics are therefore of lesser importance, but that does not mean that they are bad. As a matter of fact I very much liked these graphics as I think they are functional and allow the player to have a good impression on what is happening on the battlefield.
Battle Phases and Map
The aim of the entire game is of course to win the battle, either as the Confederates or the Union. However, in order to win, the entire battle is divided in a number of days/phases as are many battles throughout history. You start out on day 1 with mostly a skirmish between the elements of both armies for control of the western ridges of the town of Gettysburg. On the map each objective has victory points. These are the points one needs to capture in order to win that phase of the battle. The amount of time in which you can achieve this is limited usually to half a day, which progresses quite slow in comparison to other games on the market. This game therefore actually feels much more realistic and gives you way more time to think over your tactical strategies. During each phase you might get reinforcements as they approached the field at certain time during the real battle. Your handling of the situation finally determines the how the battle will progress. For example, if you capture more key objectives, such as Cemetery Hill and Culp's Hill as the Conferates, during the first day of the battle this might result in an early victory. Between each phase of the battle you will have multiple tactical decisional options available that can be historical or not, depending on how the battle went thus far. Units that were in battle earlier and  that suffered losses or are on low morale or exhausted, which is abstracted by a unit morale and condition parameter, will inherit this status to the next phase. This gives much more tactical depth to your decisions. Do you push hard and capture key objectives early on with many losses or play more conservative with the risk of losing momentum? Do not forget: enemy reinforcements could still turn the battle even when you are already celebrating victory or in despair. It is these details that make this game stand out from many other strategy games I have played over the years.
Units
Unit commands are simple, yet effective. You simply click a unit and drag and drop a line along which they can move. You can also group multiple units and move them together and units will automatically form up formations depending on how far they need to move. If they need to march a long distance they form a column and form a line when getting closer to combat or their final destination. You can have units walk or run, though running will reduce their condition, thereby making them less effective in a fight and letting them rout more easy. Also units can be forced to hold, which will force them to stay at their location and only move then either ordered or routed. Objects on the map, such as woods, houses or stone walls will give units cover, which is calculated by the cover parameter. High cover reduces the chance of getting hit, which can be vital to give your units the edge over the enemy in firefights. Units can also be ordered to charge, though the outcome can be unpredictable. Charging towards cannister shot loaded cannons might not be such a smart thing. However charging with rested troops into weakened enemy troops holding a position can be a great way to quickly take an objective and gain ground. Here the key is to do the right stuff at the right time and moment. An all out charge with all troops will likely result in a defeat, so picking your battles even within a battle is vital to success.
The AI
When you start a new game you can choose the opposing general's attitude. You can pick many different attitudes, which are distributed in two ways: difficulty and aggressiveness. You can thus have for example a difficult defensive opponent or a balanced one. On the field you can notice the difference between these attitudes. This therefore means that the Union will not always be on the defense only, as was mostly the case in the historical battle under the risk-avoiding Union general Meade. The same goes if playing for the Union, though the Confederates will always attack on the first days, the attitude can matter on how aggressive an opponent is. More difficult opponents tend to flank more and more aggressive opponents tend to charge more often or place their guns closer to the front line. The AI is therefore a welcome surprise and you will find the AI not a pushover, though as a human I must admit I tend to finally win, though individual phases of the battle can be lost.
Closing Comments
Ultimate General: Gettysburg, is a great game that is still being developed as we speak. It combines excellent tactical decision making with realism all coated with decent graphics and art. The sound effects of the game are functional, but not special. The simple handling of units works well and the slower pace of the this game compared to other tactical war games allows for easy control of the units and a very to-the-point system. The AI is good and the different attitudes that can be set, combined with your own different handling of the battle, gives the game more replayability. The multiple battle phases/days and dynamic tactical options between each phase allows for more freedom of choice and again adds to replayabilty and depth to the game.
Though only as of now, one battle, this battle was been implemented the most user friendly and best way I have ever seen from a game. I hope the team that makes this game will continue to add battles in future. I would say for strategy fans, this game is a must buy.

Nevertheless, the trust between our two current characters moves too fast: over just 2 dialogues. Introduction purposes and free game or not, the characters needed more development and "fleshing out", and if the trust development issue couldn't be worked on in part 1, maybe the creator should've found circumstances that forced the characters to work together, even if reluctantly.
I didn't really see a necessity for Bunny to tell "the man" as much as she did, and if making certain choices, she didn't even have the need to see him again. Also, he mostly had nothing to contribute to her objective at that moment. Still, the other episodes could have a lot to offer concerning character development, more information on the game's world, and, of course its future as well as our leads.
Also worth mentioning are the beautiful ost and the pretty artwork, specially the ost: such a pleasant surprise. Thomas Krze's songs really struck me as the greatest part, their beauty is undeniable. I am writing this review to the sound of his "It's not easy to say goodbye". The game has a lot of text, it is the sort of read & make choices game some of us mostly call visual novels xD If you don't enjoy lots of text, this isn't for you.
Seeing as I haven't played the other episodes, I can't really promise you they'll make amends for this lacking introduction. But I have seen really positive feedback concerning the 2nd part, for instance. Check out what other users say about them and the info on them - they're paid though and supposedly longer than this, for obvious reasons - and if you feel like they're worth your time... I enjoyed this short visual novel a lot. The characters are interesting and likeable, though only the protagonist is fully fleshed out. The near future setting is well presented and believable, not overly dystopian as is sometimes the case. The story is good and intriguing, though short, as it continues in the sequel. The music is fantastic and does a lot to set the mood of the game. I think the art is beautiful.
This is not a novel where you steer the story by your choices. There is only a handful of choices, and some of them lead to the story ending early. (You should save occasionally). The choices are more about understanding what the protagonist could and would do in some scenarios. She is talented and capable but also vulnerable. She is not an action hero and has to prioritize self preservation in her choices. The choices are there to emphasize that aspect of the character, and they work well in that regard.
On the negative side, the dialogue writing is merely OK, but not bad enough to distract from the good parts. The characters except the protagonist are not fully developed and their motivations are not quite clear, hopefully this is expanded upon in the sequel. There is also a small number of typos, not nearly enough to affect the experience.
This novel can easily be finished in one sitting, in under an hour. It has good story, art and music. I heartily recommend it.

I haven’t read Robinson Crusoe, so I’m not familiar with the story. That means, I can only judge the game in itself and not so much the story. (If the short version is related to the book though, I got a rough idea what it’s about and that is nice.)
About the game: It is a typical HOG for me, with some nice puzzle elements thrown in.
I choose the „difficult“ mode, so I had limited hints available and only 60 minutes to complete the game – that worked out fine for me, although I was kinda worried it might not be enough. It was enough. Even with one riddle, where you used up seconds to get hints. Still enough left. But with the difficult mode you probably shouldn’t idle around :D
The adventures of Robinson Crusoe was one of these HOGs with kind of blurry graphics, so I sometimes had trouble finding the objects. But that was probably intended :D
And as usual with these games, I sometimes had to really think about what a word looks like. But that really is normal for me, since I ALWAYS play HOG in English and not in German. Even if I could. I think it is a nice challenge to check the meaning of words – and my vocabulary in a way :D
Sometimes it is even worse playing it in German anyway, since for most words there is more than one word and it is actually wrong translated, so you have to translate it back to English to figure out what it should mean. English is easier. For me :D
The most difficult thing for me was this one riddle (mentioned above) where you had to guess words. You get little bits of a picture and have to figure out what it is. AND then you have to write it down. I guess in this case it was a bit more difficult to play it not in mother tongue, but I managed.
Something that really confused me, and always does: Dove and Pigeon. For me it just seems to be the same thing, but… dunno o.o
So, music was alright, drawing was alright, story alright, HOG alright.
All in all the game was a short and nice distraction :)

Even if anyone isn't completely familiar with the story of Robinson Crusoe, the
castaway who was getting lost at sea long before Tom Hanks made is fashionable, I'm sure most will have a vague idea of the general gist of it and what to expect with anything baring the name. There's a great game to be made from that age old tale, but unfortunately, this isn't it.
In this particular outing, Robbie C plays a bunch of hidden object games to find parts for a ship to sail back home. It only takes the lazy pr*ck twenty years to do it, but hey, who's counting? Although maybe he would've done it a lot quicker if it wasn't for the cr*ppy resolution that spoils everything? It's just all so grainy and indistinct that at times it's almost a hit and miss affair trying to find anything. In fact, I'd frequently hear him muttering out his mantra every few minutes of "Well, I don't know what it is, but let's click on it anyway and see what happens", the poor sod.
It doesn't help either that the descriptions can be so woefully unhelpful sometimes. Given the instruction to find a certain number of items, but only getting the vaguest of guidelines for what you're looking for when half the things filling the screen could potentially fit the bill, almost feels like you're being trolled rather than challenged. Hell, with the number of nooses littered around almost every other hidden object scene, I'm amazed Robbo doesn't just grab one of those and end it all. I know I bloody well would have.
While it is predominately made up of hidden object scenes, there are a smattering of puzzles, as well - like some spot the difference pictures or a couple of audio puzzles - but, while one or two are interesting and new to me at least, quite a lot are just annoying in one way or another. They're either really slow or taking the p*ss a bit in what I feel it expects of you. It isn't a real issue to begin with, but the further on you go, the more difficult and annoying everything becomes. It's not even like it's rewarding to complete some of the later scenes and puzzles, and on more than one occasion I could clearly hear old Crusie, The Crusatron, Crusin' USA, yell out "For f*ck sake! Seriously?!" upon finding the last object that he'd spent the past ten minutes searching for. I really don't blame him either, given how vague and heavily obscured some of them are.
While it's not a total train wreck, with so many countless other amazing games in the genre, unless you're completely in love with them and have to play them all, or you simply have more time and patience than you know what to do with, then you're better off avoiding this. Or better yet, go get yourself stranded on a real tropical island. You'll probably get less hassle and have more fun there than you will with this.

What hurt my experience in Arma 3 was in the way the developers advertise their DLC in-game. For those who might not be able to afford all the DLC and only bought the base-game (like me), not having all the DLC means that as you play, the game spams you with advertisements, and they've integrated it in a way that you can't avoid.
Like a lot of people, I play KOTH because it offers progression for players. Your character earns money and experience as your perform certain actions for your team. Money is required to buy anything from weapons/launcher/vehicles/perk slots. Experience unlocks what you are able to buy.
Now, servers provide items from all DLC, even to players who don't own specific content. They will simply have limited access when using the items, and cannot pick up certain content for example, off dead soldiers. They won't be able to enter vehicles they didn't buy, and if you end up purchasing DLC content with in-game credits, the game will place an advertisement in the side of your screen urging you to pay for it. That stays there until you drop the content. At some point, the game will cover your screen with a watermark.
Here is an example:
Fair enough, I don't mind not being able to use weapons or items that are DLC exclusive, but the game doesn't disclose which items are meant to be unavailable when selecting your weapons, equipment, or vehicles.
So if you've saved up thousands of credits to permanently own a weapon, you'll realize after spending all your in-game credits that it's "premium." Which essentially means you've wasted your time and resources on something you can't fundamentally use. Why not simply disclose what is and isn't available to players, instead of lure and tempt people into using your content, and then harass them like they've somehow stolen it from you.
Label weapons, vehicles and other items by DLC owned, so people see what they can and can't use.
I don't personally see any reason to buy DLC unless you're playing in Multiplayer because maybe the weapons, vehicles, and other stuff give you a better advantage in-game but besides that, there isn't a reason to buy it. Especially when mods give you infinitely more weapons, vehicles, models, content, and pretty much anything that the DLC can give you, but doesn't charge you 40 bucks. Modders don't harrass you either. See where I'm gettin at?

initial impressions:
This game is almost ok at best. in the begining you'll find it quite amusing if you play single palyer but the feeling wears off fast.
DLC:
Arma 3 as im sure you know is a military simulator. A military simulaor that relise hevily on DLC and you are more likley to die of old age before you find a good server that only requires the base game. The DLC is disgracefully over priced, with the APEX DLC costing £24.99 ($31.64 thanks brexit) for only a semi-decent map, a new faction, 13 new weapons, some uniforms, some gear, 10 vehicles that add little to the game and co-op campagn, also End game multiplayer. now that seems decent but for that price its not worth it. as im writing this its 66% of and its just not event worth that in my opinion. the other DLCs are a clear money grab, making you pay for vehicles and some guns, the individual DLCs are overpriced even on sale and the bundle doesnt even save you £1 ($1.27)

if you install the a3 Launcher people say its very simple, well im my experience its not, I go to download the mods from it that I need for the server i want to play and it doesnt even do it. nothing. I don't recommend this game - not because it's a bad game, on the contrary, it's a decent game - but because it isn't what it tries to be. And that game it's desperately trying to be is Sid Meier's Gettysburg, the old and apparently peerless classic. Unfortunately, where Sid Meier's game shone, this game seems lackluster.
The pacing of Ultimate General is too fast, depriving the battles of any kind of tension as crises are resolved too quickly one way or another. Where SMG was a rising crescendo of fury, with pitched battles raging back and forth as you and the AI threw more and more regiments into the fray, UGG is a sharp, brief clash where one side suddenly buckles under fire and before you can say "boo!" all of the losing troops are on the run. What could be a slow, considered, developing battle is instead turned into a click-fest as you scramble back and forth between the two wings of your line pushing bridages back into formations.
The developer claims to have an advanced, challenging AI, which is patently untrue. At no point in any of the battles (and I've played the game on highest difficulty from both sides) had I felt that the fight was going to turn dangerously against me. He is easy to outmaneuver, nor does he guard flanks or give up a forward position to establish better lines with reserves farther back. Only the speed of the game manages to mask the inabilities of the AI, as most breakthroughs occur because you were busy managing your line elsewhere. This isn't AI brilliance, it's just frustrating. One brigade will fall back 50 yards out of range of fire, while the adjoining brigades stay online and get hammered for their trouble. If you don't catch your unit falling back and hold them by the hand and drag them back into line, your line is liable to fail.
What the game does get right is the "individual battles within a battle" method of progressing Gettysburg (which, I might add, is straight out of SMG) through the 3 days of fighting. It provides a realistic ebb and flow of combat as the sides rest and resupply between phases of battle. Where UGG misses on this count, however, is that you can give the Yankees a crushing defeat, taking Seminary, Oak, and Cemetary Ridges all in the same battle, and with the blue-bellies routing before you and victory in sight, the battle will end and in the next phase you find yourself fighting over the same piece of battlefield. It makes you wonder why you even bothered fighting so hard. On the other side of the coin, a brilliant defense on the first day as the Union will still see you inexplicably falling back to Cemetary Hill.
The big #1 miss of this entire game is that there in no multiplayer support. The fairly even-strength fighting in this battle is perfectly suited for multiplayer action. There is no current comperable title to UGG. Another ACW offering, Gettysburg: Scourge of War has a multiplay option, but the game is incredibly dense and sports a learning curve that means new players will be massacred failry easily. UGG's simple, elegant design lends itself easily to buy-and-play multiplay where a new player will be competent in a few sessions. Without any similiar offerings on Steam, UGG could potentially corner the American Civil War mulitplayer market - and it would be a great multiplayer game.
Final words: UGG is an okay game - almost a tablet game in the way it looks and handles. If you're into face-value easy to play, easy to master RTS, this game could your next favourite. If you're more like me and you prefer deep strategy like Hearts of Iron, Europa Universalis and so on, you might want to give this one a miss.

I do not see why people do not like this game.
pros
-weather: a very interesting addition that can wipe out entire armies and change the tide of battles
-zone-based bases: an uncommon approach to rts games. You capture zones and use them to house certain extensions that can bring down troops, repair them, or even make your legendary units more powerful.
-command points: use these to call down orbital barrages, spy on the enemy, or even make your units more powerful.
-Squad-based "divisions": The units are organized into divisions which are grouped together in groups of either 10, 5, 2, or 1. These divisions can level up Halo Wars style and even become legendary, which gives a massive increase to accuracy, dodge, and health.
-Colossi: Colossi are massive walkers capable of levelling entire bases or armies. They are the super-weapons of this game, and are certainly cool.
-Multiple ways to win: you can win by destroying the enemy's base or their fleet with orbital cannons.
-Fleet gameplay: A fun, fleshed out experience in conquest mode.
-Secondary factions: Sway these powerful factions into your favor and you may just get some sweet allies.
Cons
-Multiplayer: The userbase is rather small, and therefore, the multiplayer is usually hard to find matches on.
-Crashes: This game sometimes crashes after certain battles, and you may have to replay them.
-the different factions are rather ssimilar
TL;DR
This game is fun and rather well made. It has some refreshing ideas, but the multiplayer and crashes are definitely disheartening. This game is a very fun game. I highly recommend this.

Saying this game is 'like' Geometry Wars is unfair to both games, but if you liked Geo Wars, then there's a good chance you'll like this one too.
It's a twin stick shooter where you are shooting at a high rate of fire at colorful shapes.  But the levels are more like challenges, almost puzzles, instead of just full throttle kill em all.  Unlike GW, when you destroy an enemy, they aren't removed from the board - instead, they go into a 'shadow' mode, where they go faster and are more aggressive, but you can shoot through them.  Most levels have 3-6 enemies, and every few levels is a boss/checkpoint (it plays a little sound so you know).  If you die before completing the boss/checkpoint, you go back to the previous checkpoint - so be prepared to play levels over again when you die on a harder one.  At each checkpoint, the game usually adds or changes a game mechanic, and that will be the mechanic until the next checkpoint.  While they differ wildly, none really change the idea of shooting the enemy, but instead usually involve behavior of the enemy or the environment.  For example, one mechanic used is a 'wall' that you toggle on/off every time you kill an enemy; another is the enemy spitting a shadow block at you when defeated.
The art style differs significantly from GW - personally, I think for the better, though it is definitly less graphically impressive.  It uses pastels, on top of a space field, and the enemies have the color get blasted out of them as they are defeated.  The enemies regen health, and later in the game, have an obnoxious amount of health.  This is to prevent you from basically flying around chipping away health, but later in the game can become incredibly frustrating - an almost defeated enemy will drift behind another enemy, and fully regain health before you can angle around the blocker.  The game starts pretty easy, and for me, didn't get too tough until the last 20 levels or so - I beat the main game in around 95 minutes, though there is co-op and a few other things to beat (only have 5/12 achievements).
tl;dr: fun game that is sort of like Geometry Wars - if you like twin stick shooters with a pastel puzzle kick, you'll get an enjoyable 1-3 hours out of this

Adventures of Robinson Crusoe was likely a fun hidden object game in 2009, but nowadays probably not even old-school HOG fans would enjoy it too much.
Hidden object gamers most likely know MagicIndie as the studio that made one of the best HOGs of all time,
And while it is commendable to show where they started at in 2009 with this genre, the decision to sell it on Steam is questionable at best.
I’m saying this because Adventures of Robinson Crusoe is not a good HOG. Not because the developers were bad but because it is ancient by this genre’s standards: made in mid-2009, when games had nothing but hidden object scenes in their low-resolution, space-saving pixelated glory. Nowadays it just cannot cut it unless you are an old and nostalgic HOG player.
And even then, this game is nothing spectacular. Sure, it has some plot (very loosely based on the title material), the scenery looks nice, the hidden object scenes are fun enough for their age, and there is variation in them… but that is not enough to warrant a purchase.

Play as Robinson Crusoe during his time on an island, after a shipwreck: find items to build a boat, meet Friday... and escape  cannibals!
Adventures of Robinson Crusoe is what I would call an "old" game. Indeed, you don't have any story in it apart being Robinson Crusoe during his 20 years of stay on a lost island. You'll begin on the ship after the accident, then explore the island, then build your house, etc..
The game is a pure hidden objects game: nearly each location begin by finding X times the same item, then you get a list of objects. Some are hard to find, mainly because of a little problem with graphics and because it was like that back then: items were often hidden behind another or being the same color as the background, etc.. Some locations are puzzles: differences, play the right tune, jigsaws, etc.. You even have a guessing game, which is not easy if you're not skilled in English. However, the game isn't punishing you for that, you can give up and you'll go to the next word.
As I've said, I've a problem with the graphics. Indeed, for recent monitors, the game isn't adapting to it. The game was reduced at 1/3 of it and the result was that I was under the impression that it got badly reduced. It can also have played in my impression of not seeing the objects. Apart that, they were pretty acceptable, even if you can say that they're outdated. You have some bright landscapes before getting in a much somber atmosphere with the cannibals part.
The soundtrack was also acceptable, though I didn't have really time to listen to it as I had to play it with the music low for not disturbing my mother, that was watching TV (I could have taken my headphones but I was too lazy to get them).
If you're in for some good old hidden objects games, Adventures of Robinson Crusoe is a nice game, though I would prefer largerly Mystery P.I., Escape the Museum, Mystery Case Files or Hidden Expedition. If you prefer to look for a casual game, you'll better check Artifex Mundi's or Alawar's.

Sacred 2 Gold is a pretty generic hack'n'slash RPG in the vein of Diablo or Titan Quest, only with a more open-world approach. I have about 50 hours played (Steam didn't record some of my game time for some reason, probably related to one of the many, many crashes.)
Pros:
+ Lots of loot.
+ Lots of ways to customize your character's build.
+ Graphics can be pretty sometimes, considering the game's age.
+ Some of the mounts are pretty cool looking.
Cons:
- Game crashes or freezes frequently because of terrible memory management code.
- The main story is so forgettable and pointless that after 50 hours I couldn't even tell you what it was about.
- The world could easily be called "generic fantasy world". There is nothing outstanding about it.
- The voice acting and writing is among the worst in any game. Ever. Seriously.
- The "funny" quests and dialogue are... not funny. The tone of the game is all over the place.
- No respeccing. Want to try another build? Roll a new character.
- The camera is abysmal, even when you disable the autofollow and control it yourself.
- The world is far too big and often feels "copied and pasted". Not nearly enough true variety.
- Fast travel options are weirdly placed, which means you end up running around the same areas a lot.
- All quests are of the "go here, kill these, bring these back" type.
- Almost no interactivity in the environment.
- Music is short and repetitive. You'll hear the same music all the time.
- Despite the plethora of skills and abilities, combat just isn't that fun.
Total Dealbreakers:
- The death penalty in this game is the resetting of a stat called "
" which takes hours and hours of combat to raise. If you die it goes back to zero and you have to build it up again from scratch. This stat is one of the most important stats in the game, and affects all your attributes. It's one of the most brutal death penalties in a game of this type that I've ever seen.
Basically, this game could have been great, but the dev team made some really strange design decisions. Here's how I would have fixed it:
+ Rewrite the main quest so it makes sense and they player feels included.
+ Rewrite all dialogue. All of it.
+ Reduce the world to about 50% of the size.
+ Remove the most tedious sidequests (which is most of them, tbh)
+ Add more enemy types and more interesting enemy behaviour.
+ Allow respeccing through gold or a quest.
+ Remove the voice acting entirely. Yes, it's that bad.
+ Change the camera target and FoV. In fact, redo the entire visibility system.
+ Allow the player to teleport to any resurrection station they have discovered, rather than just portals.
+ Make survival bonus recoverable in a few hours, rather than days!
+Place some stuff in dungeons other than monsters (secret passages, hidden buttons, etc.)
+ Make Riding a "special" skill available to all builds, independent of other skills.
+ Fix the damn crashing bugs!
I uninstalled this game without finishing the main quest, because honestly I was simply bored and frustrated playing it. There are LOADS of far, far better hack'n'slash games out there. Play them instead.

This game is priced appropriately, if not slightly to the purchaser's advantage.
For what you pay for and what the dev delivers, you get a pretty darn sweet little game.  The game's menus are simplistic and easily read and understood.  The graphics are simple, yet clean and fitting for a game like this.  Terrain plays a proper factor in battle.  Troop movement, for the most part, works how it should, and tactical decisions seem to have an impact on the battle.
On the other hand this game has a few flaws.  Ive been able to completely push Union forces beyond the edges of the map without having a quicker, more decisive victory.  I have to maintain a certain distance from the edge of the map, in order to kill the forces more effectively.  Also the Confederate troops seem to retreat an awful lot in close quarters and during charges, despite having greater numbers than the defending units being fought.  General Davis' troops, in particular, seem to retreat almost every time I send them into battle.
Overall the game is great, but with a few various AI flaws.  The dev is, however, actively developing this game and updating it regularly, so I am quite happy with this purchase, and do suggest purchasing this game before the price increases.

From here on out is just a slow climb to gather resources like coal , iron and so on to get upgrades and eventually some sort of automation of ore harvesting and smelting.
There are some interesting features like the ore scanner which scans blocks and is further identified at your reasearch station . It also lets you scan for things that you have not identified, useful for finding new ores or for ones you have previously found. There are a few useful features that are thoughtful and useful and they blend in with game mechanics as to not seem overpowered.
This game is not without its flaws. There are a number of bugs I've encountered.
-When your ship crashes you cannot relocate your starting area without some sort of tool later in the game but it glitched and I accidently had it placed far from my base and I couldnt basically continue reasonably.
-Saving your world and continuing later seems to initiate that crash scene again and again, destroying everything I've built that was in its crash radius, though it left me with 2 starting areas. I lost everything in my inventory though.
The menus are convoluted and half of the buttons seem to work correctly. For example when crafting there are arrows that let you change the quantity of the batch but the arrows dont change anything as if they are just apart of the graphics.
All in all if you like these types of creative games. I would get it on sale as this game has great potential but dont want to risk much more as we all know early access has just become a legal excuse to sell an unfinished product.

I would consider this to be one of the best purchases I have ever made on steam. Be warned as this game does have a few bugs, since it is still in early access after all. When I first bought it my graphics card was not supported by the game and after a few emails with the support team I could tell that they were willing to help me with my problem instead of giving me some cookie cutter awnser like some major games would. But in the newest update they added a new alternative renderer which allowed me to play the game. My first impression looking at was that everything from the menu to the small details on the map had a very comfortable feel to it. The gameplay itself has a few things that may need to be worked on just to bring the game to its full potential. Just a few of these may be a about face command. While it doesn't take much time to order your regiment to about face using movement commands, It still would be a more useful feature for those late game situations where timing can make or break a battle. Also I would love to point out the interested difficulty settings for the game. Instead of just Easy, Medium or Hard, You can choose how aggresive the AI is aswell. So you could have a Aggressive enemy with little idea about tactics or a brilliant tactician who rather defends than attack.
To summarize that whole things
+ Great graphics on menus and ingame
+ Good variety of difficulty settings
+ Good AI (Kinda expected from the creator DarthMod
+ Helpful support team
- Still has its bugs
- Lack of important movement commands (About Face, Wheels, Formations)
- Can be hard to select units at times
Things I would like to see in future
- Other important battles from civil war era ( Yes i know that game is focused on Gettysburg but could be fun DLC for future)
- Some form of Multiplayer ( Either Total War-esque with unit selection or Scenarion specific army compositions)
- Make it easier for modders ( Nick Thomadis of all people should understand how important mods could be to the shelf life of a game)
This game is worth the price.

Demon is hilarious - you're basically inserting curse cards like in Dominion into their deck until it drowns them. The graphics etc are nothing special, but that isn't the point of a game like this. It's fun, deep, replayable, and worth giving a shot.

Writing this review in 'Operation Health'. 04.08.2017-Date of writing/review.
At the moment,the game is holding really good in terms of player base and popularity. If You hear someone saying 'R6S iS dYiNg' Dont listen to him and just purchase the game and have fun (If not,You can refund it you kno). This isn't case (At the moment with the 30Hz Tick Rate servers). 50% or even more of the time,Your headshots might not count because the server didnt registered them and as a result You will most likely be dead. Here is the moment to mention that Ubisoft are going to upgrade the servers to 60Hz Tick rate and soon they will be here.(Maybe 1-2 Weeks from day current 04.08.2017). There are some minor bugs that can be frustrating from time to time,but other than that the game hold very very good and it's awesome when it plays the way it's meant to be. Recently,Ubisoft changed the Matchmaking system to 'One Step Matchmaking system) Which is very good compared to the previous one and lets You find a match for about 30-60 Seconds (Depends on Your rank). They also added Alpha Packs or Loot packs,however You want to call them. Basically,After every match You have a chance to drop one of thoose and then open it for FREE. ABSOLUTELY FREE.<---That's right. There may be Weapon skins or any cosmetics in general. Dont worry about the DLC policy of this game because it's not going to force You to purchase any DLC's (Cuz they are FREE. ABSOLUTELY FREE). I have to be honest tho. There is a decent grind in the game (You have to purchase every operator with in-game currency which You get after every match called 'Renown') It can take You up to 1-5 Months to purchase every single operator depending how much time You spend on the game. What hurt my experience in Arma 3 was in the way the developers advertise their DLC in-game. For those who might not be able to afford all the DLC and only bought the base-game (like me), not having all the DLC means that as you play, the game spams you with advertisements, and they've integrated it in a way that you can't avoid.
Like a lot of people, I play KOTH because it offers progression for players. Your character earns money and experience as your perform certain actions for your team. Money is required to buy anything from weapons/launcher/vehicles/perk slots. Experience unlocks what you are able to buy.
Now, servers provide items from all DLC, even to players who don't own specific content. They will simply have limited access when using the items, and cannot pick up certain content for example, off dead soldiers. They won't be able to enter vehicles they didn't buy, and if you end up purchasing DLC content with in-game credits, the game will place an advertisement in the side of your screen urging you to pay for it. That stays there until you drop the content. At some point, the game will cover your screen with a watermark.
Here is an example:
Fair enough, I don't mind not being able to use weapons or items that are DLC exclusive, but the game doesn't disclose which items are meant to be unavailable when selecting your weapons, equipment, or vehicles.
So if you've saved up thousands of credits to permanently own a weapon, you'll realize after spending all your in-game credits that it's "premium." Which essentially means you've wasted your time and resources on something you can't fundamentally use. Why not simply disclose what is and isn't available to players, instead of lure and tempt people into using your content, and then harass them like they've somehow stolen it from you.
Label weapons, vehicles and other items by DLC owned, so people see what they can and can't use.
I don't personally see any reason to buy DLC unless you're playing in Multiplayer because maybe the weapons, vehicles, and other stuff give you a better advantage in-game but besides that, there isn't a reason to buy it. Especially when mods give you infinitely more weapons, vehicles, models, content, and pretty much anything that the DLC can give you, but doesn't charge you 40 bucks. Modders don't harrass you either. See where I'm gettin at?

I highly recommend Civ 4 for one of the best mods I played. Fall from Heaven 2. A mod that adds so much to the game that the vanilla game is like a mud hut next to Taj Mahal.
The mod is set in a dark fantasy world, recently waken up from a long period of winter due to the god of winter reigned unopposed until a hero emerged and slew him. This new world has decimated the old civilizations and sent them into a tribal life, struggling to survive. And here you come in. In short order, the mod adds a bunch of new civilizations, very different from each others. Orcs sucks at science, but can produce 2 units at the same time. The Khazad (dwarfs) rely on their stockpile of gold for prosperity, the elven civs can build improvements on forest tiles, etc. Religions added. Civilization alignment from good to evil. An armageddon count which turns the world into fiery hell terrain as it climbs closer to doom. Lairs and dungeons to explore. A ton of story, more or less every unit and hero (did I mention heroes?) have a backstory. Magic. So much magic. It fixed a bunch of issues with the older Civ games, like when the computer civs just zergs down everything, in FfH2, you can combat that, you have mages that can aoe blast a pile, cast fear and break up the stack, use Blind and lock them up, and if you are the one attacking a strong base which contains those mages, you could use assassins which has the promotion that enables them to start attacking the weakest unit in the stack.
And if you get tired of this, there is modmods and modmodmods with a dedicated community who worked to keep enhancing and expanding the game.

This is a great game, well worth the $10 to purchase it.  As someone who has nearly passed the Gettysburg Liscensed Battlefield Guide exam, missing the cut by three quetions, I can say that this game is a real treat for the historian as well as a casual gamer.  This game mixes historically accurate scenarios with the always wonderful what ifs.  The playing field is wonderfully detailed, included much lesser known landmarks than your traditional game would have included.  Ultimate General Gettysburg takes me back to the days of playing Sid Meirer's Gettysburg.  The two have quite a lot of similarities, so if you are familiar with Sid's version you can see how this game plays.  The only draw backs to this game that I have come across are two things.  One: you only get brigade command and not individual regimental commands, so the tactical command in battle is kind of simplistic.  Two: the brigades aren't historically accurate to the condition of the troops.  In several scenarios, Brockenbrough's brigade, which in real life was poorly lead and filled with lesser quality troops, but in this game they will stand and fight almost to the last man; meanwhile crack units will retreat after the first volley they receive.  Other than those picky critiques this game in extremely entertaining and is a pleasure to play.

That sounds like such a magazine quote, I'm the worst. Listen, the most important things about a game that goes for simplicity and minimalism in its design is that (1) the abstract symbols are easy to read, and (2) each level brings a new idea. And THOTH does both really well. When you see a line of dots, you'll always know what it means based on where the dots are arranged. You'll know what a square inside of a square means.
When I played through the campaign, I thought, "this is pretty rad but I feel like it would be even better if the levels were chosen at random rather than linearly". Good news! When you beat the game (which will only take an hour), you unlock a random-level mode. Not random as in roguelike, just random as in "we're jumbling up the order of levels and also putting a few new ones in." Much like SuperHOT, I feel like the real game begins here.
Simplicity extends to the controls. Left stick moves, right stick shoots. You move faster when not shooting. Patience is key to the gameplay, but the music is so stifling and unsettling that it is difficult to hold on to your nerves as 6 or 7 boxes are chasing you.

I was interested to play this game after noticing the newest game to the series just came out. So i thought before i spend money on it, i'll play the first game so i know what is going on and with all the positive reviews, i thought this was going to be a good series i could fall inlove with. And it just so happens to be free. But even if its a free game to play, it doesn't make it a good game. As you can see, this is a visual novel which has choices you can make. But the choices in this game are dead end choices where you must pick the right one to continue onward. That was a huge disappointment to me because i kept picking the ones that got me caught. Linear novels with no tweaks for pick your own path really bother me because i felt duped in a way. And for whatever reason the "quicksave" button would not let me save at my current point. So i had to start from the very beginning which was frustrating till i found out if you go into the menu and hit "Save" it will work. When you make a visual novel, you want the reader to fall inlove with the plot, the characters and to pull them in. But i was somewhat lost by this novel. When you first start, the game puts you right in the middle of something that you won't understand and does not explain very well later on. And right off the bat you can tell this game felt rushed a bit or was mainly just a project to see if someone could actually make a visual novel. However, even if the art style and charming music were a nice touch which are positive things to note, the scene's did not flow well at all and made you felt like the developers didn't care if the dialog flew from one end of the town to a apartment or a rooftop without warning. I just couldn't understand it. The writing isn't good either but i kept playing it because i really want in my heart to like this so i can try out the 2nd game. So i pushed on, in hopes it would get better. But after reading more of the story, the main character Bunny started to make me mad. It was hard to tell that she was talking to the AI "Mask" and not at the other character she was interacting with in the physical world. But it wasn't just that, it was her personality as well. She seemed to act like a child, not a skilled hacker. I just resented the character even further than i did in the beginning. And also what i noticed is how this novel lacks any descriptive details about the places bunny travels too. *Shes in a park* Well what did the park look like? *shes in a hospital* Well, can we get some more details please instead of bunny constantly talking? I love visual novels so much when the story comes to life, but i cannot recommend this to any of my friends and advise you to look elsewhere. But hey at least this game was free so no one had to waste anything but their time.

Coin Crypt is a pretty fun game.
At this point, i've played over 2 hours and beaten the game once.
Story is short, the intro almost put me to sleep.
Graphics aren't fantastic, the coins are well really done but everything else is a literal rectangle and eventually becomes an eyesore.
Audio is okay. Music's starting to get repetitive, and i'm sure in a few more hours, it'll get unbearable.
Gameplay is this game's saving grace. Pretty sure I haven't seen a tutorial, but it's pretty straightforward. It has turn-based card-style gameplay, but with a timer. The timer isn't there to pressure you into taking your turn, it's there because every coin played takes a certain amount of time to be "cast". Add in the mix of rather unique perma-buff/debuffs in the form of classes and unique coin effects -- it makes for a really different playthrough each time in terms of speed, strategy, and overall "game feel"... That is, if you choose so.
If you're familiar with rouge-likes and turn-based games, you'll probably enjoy what Coin Crypt has to offer -- A comfortable pace of progression with a battle system that'll keep you on your toes, even when you're not fighting.
P.S. The game could use a little bit of clarification when it comes to effects. i.e. "Is the debuff happening to me or the enemy?" It might ruin a short run or two, but if you use context, i'm sure you'll be able to figure it out.

It’s sometimes hard to talk about a Visual Novel because their really isn’t much game play to be had. The story this one has is a bit confusing as you can’t understand fully the world it is set in. It’s a futuristic world where the government keeps tabs on everyone. Our main character is a girl hacker with a ‘awakened AI’ that helps her out in whatever she wants to do. One day while trying to hack something, she gets caught by a guy and ends up wanting to see him. It follows her and him through this maze of mystery into conspiracies about the place New Jessica.
What is interesting is the version I played was free. It also felt more like just the opening to a game. Mostly your clicking to scroll through the text and then when left with a decision, you pick what you want. Some will make the game end rather fast, the others will let you keep going. I went through all of the different branches in the story and they had a really interesting amount of dialog to go with it. The characters personalities’ sort of change depending on which way you go but it’s not a very big change. Bunny is pretty much like a tomboy in how she acts; a real risk taker that could get her into trouble. Her AI Mask seems to be like her physiologist in some ways, over analyzing things she does or the people around him. He acts a bit human in fact especially on his constant want to stay alive and not be deleted. He doesn’t really make jokes, might not even know how to actually, so most of the time he is very serious and stiff. Alex on the other hand is very laid back. He ends up being really caring even to someone he has only just met and will do pretty much anything to protect them. For this beginning to a story, they are the only characters that I can really talk about.
The artwork is so amazing but I can chock that up to it being still images. It’s very bright and actually feels sterile, much like the idea of the future. The people are very anime style especially with the main character having pink hair and then blue. By the way, I really want the thing she uses to change her hair. Anyway, Bunny looks as though she is a lot younger then what I would think; she is more like high school age and yet how she talks seems more like someone in their twenties. Alex looks pretty much like a geeky/cool guy. He’s tall, and always looks like he is leaning slightly back in his artwork.
The music is amazing! It’s rather soft and very mysterious. The music doesn’t seem to overtake the scenes it’s in and there are a couple different songs that go along with the artwork. Most of them are instrumental but there is I think one song that has vocals. The vocals are rather soft again, and they don’t mess with the overall feeling. I couldn’t hear much of what it was singing, so it doesn’t get in the way of trying to read the text.
Overall this is a really good start of the game. It’s not a full version, just feels a bit like a demo but it’s a solid demo. The story seems well put together from what I could see of it, and I really do what to know what’s coming next so if I do end up getting the game, I will let you guys know more about it.

The writing's amateurish and requires proof-reading.  Some of this I'll attribute to the creators being Italian; the issue might be the translation only.  Characters as a whole feel as if they're built slim; they lack a unique voice to the point I had trouble telling the characters' dialogue apart.  The traits also seem misapplied.  Our protagonist is a hacker who doesn't play a role in a hack other than walking around.  Her A.I. companion does all the digital work, yet fails to spot an obvious missing link in a database join.  And in order to make certain a scene happens the mysterious guy she meets turns out to be a stalker if the right choice is made, before the point he would have any motivation to do so.
There's funny dialogue, some of which are spoiled by translation issues, and there's rudimentary scene-setting moments.  The character growth I saw mentioned in a couple reviews, and the reason I'm trying it out, isn't there.  In a half hour's worth of reading, about 3-4 days pass plus indeterminable time while Bunny's unconcious.  The "growth" between the protagonist and maybe love interest is boiled down to about half an hour of conversation split between a few days.  She goes from scared of him to wary of him to trusting within a five minute conversation.
Beyond writing:
This teaser only has 2-3 choices in total.  Basic mechanics are fine.  The artwork is probably the best reason to play the game, and I expect is the main reason for many good reviews.  Setting is a bit glitchy if you have any knowledge of IT; the setting as a whole could've used more setting up.

Invisible Apartment seems to have a decent premise. A young girl is followed while hacking into a bank system, causing the authorities to be alerted to their presence. So, they try to find the other hacker... for some reason.
It's not really explained why the girl and her AI go look for the person who followed her instead of looking for another way to hack into the bank system aside from basic human curiosity. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but when thought about from a logical persepective, it doesn't really make sense, especially when the game itself basically states "we only know they followed you, probably because they were curious why you were breaking into the system." They try to give another reason later, but to be honest, it's pretty weak.
Aside from that, the characters are introduced at break-neck speeds, unless the author doesn't want you to learn their names, in which case it's very drawn out. The names are not the only thing that are whiplash inducing. Scenes flash by with maybe two or three boxes of dialogue and then will transport you with no warning to another area with another couple boxes of dialogue. There was even one scene that was basically the main character making a short "I am who I am" speech that really had no reason to be there, and much like the earlier scenes, cut into that scene, said it's part, and cut out of the scene into the next one.
The art is well done, and I really can't fault it for that. The characters have sort of a moe vibe where everything is a bit shiny, but again, there's nothing wrong with it, and I actually rather enjoy that kind of character design. The backgrounds are mostly simple painted lineart pieces, but it makes sense when the focus is on the dialogue boxes and characters. They also go really well with the cyberpunk theme.
The setting makes sense but the author tries to make some use of what a cyberpunk future would look like and some of the scenes don't always work or seem forced in.
Most of the game seems rather forced, actually. Some of the choices are overreactions or would be illogical in the situation, but are the only "sane" choice and are therefore only there to move the story along. The story itself is pretty short, a half hour play time to go through all of the options and learn a little bit more about the main character. It's a nice touch, but when it leads to the same ending, you almost think "what's the point?"
Originally I thought the game was a demo, and would have recommended it. That not being the case, I cannot, in good conscience, recommend it, though it's honestly more of a neatral rating than it is a negative one. It's half an hour of foreplay for no significant end result, even though there is currently a prequel and soon-to-be sequel. We'll see if the sequel is any better--I certainly hope it is.

7.75/10 - It's The Hero Shooter That's Not Really A Hero Shooter
Game has issues, that's clear, here's the negatives:
-Game didn't quite deliver on what Ubisoft promised at multiple press events.
-No dedicated server support (fixing this alone would move it to a 8-9/10)
-Relies on NAT! (seriously? it's 2017 and we're still ♥♥♥♥ing with our routers to get a game working?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?!?! this isn't console, it's PC huehuehuehuehue)
-The UPlay client is buggy, and matchmaking overall needs a lot of work (enjoy occasionally getting paired with BR as a US/CA/EU).
-Very few game modes (some could see as a plus, but only defuse and hostage, and not including Terrorist Hunt (PvE) or training missions).
-Rather high system requirements.
-Not enough reporting tools (such as being able to report players for being caustic).
-None of the Season Pass characters have introduction videos (I know, it's a small thing, but it helps flesh things out, it'd been worth the effort had they done it).
On the upside though, which there are quite a few very crucial ones:
-Excellent gameplay/gunplay (game feels amazing, providing you can run it).
-Lots of variety, at least in casual, with no real "meta" (besides not using Fuze on Hostage, and even that's negotiable).
-Loot crates are a FREE bonus (as of right now, you CANNOT buy them with cash, you can only earn them by playing, and they give out all items, including "paid only" items AFAIK). You can buy them with Renown, but you can't buy renown with real cash.
-Rounds are short, and rewarding. So saving up renown doesn't take long.
-Additionally, due to the shortness of matches, you don't have to worry about getting your face stomped in for 20-30 minutes straight.
-Only takes getting to level 20 to play ranked (2 solid nights of play), and no stupid cooldowns on doing ranked matches.
-Ranked match leavers are punished HARSH AF (temp ban, renown cost, and instant loss possibly resulting in lowered ranking).
-Oddly very few caustic players, even in ranked, by comparison to other games despite not having reporting tools.
-Despite it being Ubisoft, and this is the most important thing so I'm putting it at the bottom, the dev team for this game is EXTREMELY devoted, even going as far as forgoeing production of DLC in favor of fixing the gameplay (latency/hit detection issues, performance issues, etc.) with "Operation Health" as they're putting it. This game released in a rather... special (read: horrid) state and has started to come a long way since. With issues such as SLI being supported, then not supported, and then supported again with even better results.
Honestly, give this game a try. A long way from perfect, but bashing headfirst through every obstacle in the hopes of getting there. I know, it's Ubisoft and they can suck a fat one in many instances where they've mislead or discontinued support or used horrid DRM, but this one feels and is a bit different, even after well over a year.

After the first level, I can say that it has DOOM like qualitites, and the main character is super funny to listen to.
I have finished the newest DOOM and from the first level comparison, Shadow Warrior 2 has a more enjoyable first level then DOOM, and the development team for Shadow Warrior 2 had a lot more fun with the tutorial then the DOOM team did.
I would not go as far to say it is better, it is similiar in some ways but DOOM is a more serious game that takes place in the future, while Shadow Warrior is more modern and comedic.
If you enjoyed playing DOOM, you will enjoy this game.
After playing more of the game, I came to relize that this game is more like a combination of Borderlands game style, with DOOM violence.
To be more specific on the Borderlands aspect:
There Is a leveling system when you can equip items based on your level, there are attachments that you can buy with in game currency or get from a drop of an enemy, items have rarity, you can change out which weapons are equipped, and the quest system has the main question, and many side quests that you can do whenever you want.
If your are familiar to the DOOMGUY weapon choice option, it has a circle with guns you can choose from, there is that system in Shadow Warrior 2 but you can have any weapons you want, you could have only swords, or shotguns, or a variety of weapons equipped at any time.
Also if your not really into story listening because of boring or dull dialogue, the dialogue in this game is comedic and very sarcastic. But you can skip it if you want to still.
Overall it is a great game so far.

Rome: Total War is the Third game in the Total War series, released in 2004. Being 11-years old, as well as having several newer titles in the Total War series, Rome: Total War considerably shows it's age; However, with that being said it is still a fun, interesting game in the overall series. The game takes place prior to the middle ages, After the fall of the Roman Republic, during the Early Roman Empire. As is typical with the Total War series, You start off with a small number of player factions to choose, in this case 3, and unlock additional factions as playable once you conquer them.
Also as is typical of a Total War game, gameplay is divided between the real-time battles when in combat, and the turn-based actions of exploration, nation-building, and diplomacy. The game that launch the Total War series towards heights that it could've never dreamed of. This game is a turn-based strategy game where you take command the various factions during the Roman Era as you command, build, govern and attack Rome's enemies.
The battle system unlike the system you will see in the modern day versions of the game is really simplistic. Sort of like an almost modern update of Imperial Glory. Now of course, the usual complaint would be "OMG the game is too hard" or "OMG the online players are wrecking me" Luckily the game has an in-depth tutorial plus you have all the time in the world as this game offers various combat both historical and custom made as you polish your skills in battle. The advisor system is really helpful as they give advice towards the player. DO NOT turn it off if your new. Keep that option for advisor input set to "High". Plus the User Interface for manging your territory and what not is simplistic as well.

For some of them it's a simple click of the "zoom in towards target location" while others it's "Find this city" and your just like "Um okay...WHERE?!" some of these tasks are important as it may further your position in the Roman government.
If you still want a simplistic Total War game this is for you.

I cannot stress enough as to how great a masterpiece Amnesia: The Dark Descent is. At times deeply disturbing, at other times adrenaline-pumping. Bold in its design, and nearly flawless in its execution. This game's hype promises pure horror and it certainly delivers.
Amnesia's initial masterstroke is to make the player completely defenceless. One is forced to run or hide from the game's monsters. It did however become apparent to me after the first couple of deaths that running must very much be the player's last resort. You can't outrun your enemies, as they're faster than you, and the game's control scheme makes it nearly impossible to slam doors behind you during a chase (very much unlike Outlast, a game which cannot help but be compared to, and contrasted with, Amnesia). Therefore, hiding becomes your only real survival option.
This is Amnesia's second stroke of genius. The player must hide from the monsters in the dark, behind objects, and sometimes even inside wardrobes. However, to stand in the dark, the player begins to lower their sanity meter, until the character goes insane. Sanity can also be lost by looking at monsters and by being chased by them, and by witnessing supernatural occurences. When one becomes completely insane, weird visual effects impede gameplay, and the player becomes more visible to monsters while in this state. To regain sanity, one must make progress through tasks, or stand in light areas.
Now the third stroke of genius: light is very often a limited commodity in Amnesia. Their are some natural lights, and pre-lit torches and candles, but the majority of light sources must be lit using tinderboxes. Tinderboxes are a limited commodity (however, they are surprisingly common - if you search a room thoroughly, you're likely to find at least one tinderbox), so managing which torches you light is crucial if one is to maintain sanity. The alternative to using tinderboxes is to use a lamp which you carry, however to use this requires lamp oil. This is not only far less common than tinderboxes, but also depletes very rapidly. I also found that the torch did not refill my sanity meter like other lights (or at least it didn't do it very quickly).
Amnesia's monsters are another aspect of the game's horror. They are thoroughly disturbing precisely because they lie in the "uncanny valley" - meaning they are humanoid, but not quite human. They possess disfigured faces and skulk around as if in pain, warning the player of their presence by letting out inhuman groans. Sound is also used to alert players to the presence of the "water monster". Hearing the sound of approaching splashing forces the player to find the nearest object to leap to to get out of the water.
Scares in Amnesia can also stem from very subtle things. For example, I returned to a room I'd visited earlier, which had empty gibbet cages hanging from the ceiling. When I returned, I saw a dead body in one of the cages. I inspected it, thinking it hadn't been there before, but dismissed it and walked away. However, when I turned around, the cage was empty again. I can't help but think there were other similar scares I missed earlier in Amnesia due to their subtlety. Moments such as these create an unnatural atmosphere present throughout the game.
Amnesia's story is, simply put, fantastical in a kind of silly way. But it is a testament to the skill of how this story is told and revealed to the player that one ends up completely buying into it. As the protagonist, Daniel, is suffering from Amnesia, the game weaves its narrative through flashbacks, letters, diaries, and even by what can only be described as telepathy. This telepathy ultimately made me question whether I was playing as Daniel, or was in fact playing as the game's villain, Alexander, and using Daniel in order to achieve his own ends. This question of agency is ultimately resolved by whichever ending the player eventually comes to. The story touches rather cleverly on other complex themes, such as crime and punishment, and the existence of pure good and pure evil.
Perhaps my only quarrel with this game is with its puzzles. I sometimes found them incredibly difficult to work out, although it did feel good not to have a game oversimplifying everything. I also occasionally didn't know why I was doing puzzles, except in order to progress. In other words, the puzzles were sometimes not well integrated into the story. But on the whole, the game did try to explain why I needed to find or assemble certain objects.
What can I say that I haven't already? You will be on edge. You will be scared. You will be enthralled. Amnesia: The Dark Descent is an incredible horror game. An incredible game full stop.

I'm gushing with good feelings about this game. It is so well designed, I bet it's the best twin stick shooter design in ages. All game designers should be jealous of it.
It's all in the details:
4 level challenges give you a rewarding sense and forces you to play well. Great pacing.
Enemies are faster when they're dead, which makes you question when to kill them and where to position yourself.
You have to choose when to fire carefully because you move much faster when you're not shooting.
Similar smart mechanics that always force you to think while you're killing. This makes the game better than most shooters around.
There are some very original mechanics that surprised me quite a bit through the middle of the game.
No filler. All levels matter.
Normally when you have a minimalist visual style, it means that the developer has decided to make all game elements clear and there's no space for visual confusion. I think this game does this well AND still looks great.
Procedural levels will keep me playing this game.
Coop mode is fun
Gripes:
I would not mind some music with beats in the background. Generally not a huge fan of the sound design, although it gets the job done. I have to admit that the current mood helps the game to feel original.
I think it'd possible to have a decent control mechanism with WASD + mouse so that players without controllers would be able to play. Not ideal, but better than nothing. The game can still say "controllers are strongly recommended" and that'd be alright.
No options menu whatsoever. Game is fullscreen, forever.
I think the player's collider size could be smaller for the player. Dodging stuff is very hard.
Since the game design philosophy behind this game is strictly minimalist, the small gripes I have with the game are all caused by the decisions made with this philosophy in mind. But I still have almost nothing bad to say about the actual gameplay, which says a lot about how much I like the game.
Absolutely recommended.

Hey everybody and welcome to a
minimal review of THOTH!
You shoot colored squares, they become hollow, empty space. You still can't touch them, but this is where the mechanics will build from. Later, there will be things like chains you can't touch connecting the squares you can break by destroying said squares and ever expanding black holes. The game knows this, too, slowly building on the mechanics and introducing them to you by showing, not telling. This is a great choice for people who like a game where it feels like the environment is dynamic, and pursues and reacts to you. THOTH has elements of platforming and puzzle solving, as well, with barriers that switch on and off as you kill enemies.
That's about it, really, it's a very minimal twin stick shooter, but very hard, very engaging, and very fun and satisfying to progress in.
Minimal, but an ever-changing color palette makes the graphics feel fresh while giving the level sets a sense of identity and individuality that allows them to be memorable and also compartmentalized in a 'thank god I beat that' vault all the same.
In an interesting twist, the audio in THOTH mostly revolves around sound effects, that phase together to create something resembling music. If you're not shooting or killing enemies, you mostly get an ambient rumbling bass. It has a space horror movie kind of feel to me, especially with the 'silent not-quite-a-scream sound' or harsh crashing sound the enemies make upon dying.
THOTH might be minimal in nature, but the execution makes everything feel vibrant and alive. It is challenging, but fun, and makes you want to play just to play the game, progress, and conquer.
I recommend THOTH at:
Full price.
