Etherium plays like a slower paced RTS-lite with a focus on resource management and control in conjunction with unit management. There are three interesting and visually varied races with their own uses of the resource, and the units, structures, assets and graphics in general are pleasant to look at, but combat is mediocre, gameplay is bland and gets very boring very fast and when considering the frequent crashes and problems, this might well be worth completely passing by. I feel like the developers have tried to emphasize the battlefield as a whole and the player choices and routes to different areas, and have tried to strip the standard building/production mechanics down to a minimum so that the players' focus is more general and overviewish like in, for example, Supreme Commander, but it hasn't worked very well and honestly results in the game feeling bland as a whole.
There is no focus on single-player other than a very lacklustre vs A.I. Skirmish series which doesn't offer any story or anything you'd expect from the big players like the Age of Empires', the Starcrafts, etc. I understand that it's a smaller title with a lower budget, but the lack of single-player element really is a big turn off.
So then the focus is on the multiplayer, which has its own problems. All there is to let you know how you're doing overall is a rank in the top left, and with no stats or information on your matches or even your games as a whole, it's basically a matter of finding and playing games for their own sake, which sounds fine in theory, but in reality is another bland, boring aspect of this game.
That's not even mentioning the fact that multiplayer is essentially dead. It took me 12+ minutes to find a game, during the free trial no less, and there was no alert or notification that I'd joined a game, but that didn't matter because my opponent was apparently afk anyway. For a game focused entirely on multiplayer to have so few players and nothing to encourage team-building, tournaments or improvement is simply an appalling failure.
The visual styling and art styles of each of the three races are mildly interesting and generally pretty good. The maps are all fairly varied and the map assets are interesting. In general, all the visual elements are fairly good in Etherium.
Node management is very smooth and quick. The ability to replace or move a Spaceport across the map for example, takes just two clicks and 2 seconds.
* Despite the games many design issues, the gameplay as a whole can be fairly fun when against evenly matched opponents.
* The different routes to victory are interesting and add a little depth that could've otherwise been missed.
The main problem with Etherium, at least at the time of review, is technical. Unexplained and seemingly random crashes are very frequent and even completing the tutorial for me involved 3 crashes and re-openings of the game. With no patch notes from the developers this is simply unforgivable and means buying this game is a risk. Though there are user suggested fixes in community posts. There are also a number of smaller problems that bring this title down.
* Units are very basic, and provide hard counters to other units. There is no real depth of combat strategy, it's more about area and resource management, which is fine, but something more than rock/paper/scissors would've been appreciated.
* The U.I. is very unintuitive at first, and takes too long to figure out, and the tutorial, while polished, does a poor job of keeping things simple, especially when continually crashing.
I've given this a fairly hard time, but at the end of the day the game would actually be an average to above average RTS title if the Multiplayer existed. Unfortunately the genre has far better options at better prices, and for £14.99/19.99€/$19.99 at the time of review, it's just not worth it unless you're an RTS fiend. Had the multiplayer been a success, this would've been a fair choice and average+ game but for now, there are better options on Steam and elsewhere and you're better served passing this by.

Story and enemy design is astoundingly boring, and combat is just mashing the attack button, occasionally using a magic spell if you get surrounded or turning into an invincible badass for 15 seconds once you build up enough charge.   Every once in a while things are made interesting with getting a horse or a huge cannon for a bit, and exploring hard to find areas is fun.

Disclaimer: I received this game for free since I was one of the game's beta testers.
After the amazing minimalistic rhythm platformer 140, THOTH is an even more minimalistic twin stick shooter. Easy to learn, hard to master. Very hard for certain stages. The controls are self explanatory, one stick moves your avatar, the other stick makes it shoot. But don't press start because that will instantly end the game.
Aesthetically, the game is true to its gameplay philisiophy, just like 140. Minimalistic, with just a buch of colors and geometrical scales. However, the graphical effects are also very nice to look at. The Audio design is excellent and while the music is almost the opposite of 140, since there's no beat or clear melody to listen to, it is an essential part of the gameplay experience and adapts to your progress.
Once you've beaten the main 64 stages, there's extra game modes to unlock. This is where things get really wild. If you're brave enough to make it through the 16 randomly selected levels, the ultimate challenge awaits. But you can always grab a friend for some coop action. Levels in coop will be exactly the same as in single player, however your avatars are both a bit nerfed and if one of you dies, they'll become a zombie that follows the surviving player in the hardest possible pattern. So, if you want to get a little extra challenge, just play coop mode - without a friend.
Mastering this game feels a lot like Super Hexagon. You could beat the game in a very short amount of time, theoretically, but you need to get the right mind set for it. But once you're in for it, you're hypnotized. And finally beating this challenge feels just so damn good.
The price tag might seem a bit high and I do understand how somebody doesn't want to spend 10$ on a simplistic twin stick shooter. But it's not just a bunch of levels and tons of fun, the whole gameplay experience is extremely polished - something you don't see often anymore with thousands of crapware titles making it past Steam Greenlight that look, sound and play like crap.
The only downsides I can think if right now is that you NEED to have a specific kind of controller (Update: Not anymore! As of the last update, WASD+Mouse controls have been added) for it (it won't work with all models out there, due to restrictions of Unity) and that you can accidentally abort a great playthrough by just a press of the button Start. Otherwise, I have no reason to not recommend this game, beta tester or not.

Puts the survival aspect back into the Horror genre and does a damn good job at it too. Hiding for the sake of your life and sanity is the playstyle here during enemy encounters instead of shootin' 'em up like a bad motha*****.  You're  goin' get terrified, and your heart's goin' race at times...no exceptions. I thought the developers were sadistic with the way they were toying with my expectations and making me feel paranoid nearly the entire game...truth is, they're just competent.
The only downside to this game were the puzzles. For a survival horror game, the puzzles were pretty weak in the sense that they were fairly easy to figure out instead offering a good intellectual challenge. There was also nothing disturbing or terrifying about them. Thus, I found that the puzzles were interrupting the flow of the game. Examples of great puzzles done in horror games can be found in Silent Hill. You had to decipher hard, disturbing riddles written in blood for example. Compare that to tinkering with levers and engines in Amnesia. Yeah...
The story while not great, is servicable. It's fed to you in bits as you pick up notes and as the protaganist experiences flashbacks.  You also have multiple endings here as typical in survival horror games and, again, they're servicable but don't leave an impact on you after it's all over. At least it didn't for me.
Fortunately, the good by far outweighs the bad in Amnesia. When you play, follow the game's advice and concentrate on immersing yourself within the atmosphere because that is the main selling point of the game.
I recommend this game to survival horror fans and gamers who want a thrilling, terrifying experience that doesn't rely on predictable, cheesy jump scares.

Ultimate General: Gettysburg is a game that successfully manage to recreate a realistic, plausible and logical line battle experience at the right pace.
It divide the battle of Gettysburg into difference phase where either side has a chance to either attack or defend against larger or smaller forces that are persistent from one battle phase to the other.
After each phase you have sometime the opportunity to make some strategic choice as to where you would like to position your forces in order to attack the other side or wait for reinforcements, leading to some variations as to where your campaign is fought.
You also have to possibility to choose a good variety of AI behavior in the way it fight leading to potentially some replayability.
Visually speaking the game has a colorfull apperance that make you confortable and happy to play it.
When it comes to the UI it's very simple to click and drag your units arround the place and you have ultimatly more options to control your units than you would have in any Total War game resulting in a much more realistic battle of movements.
Movement in the game is key to victory and using the terrain is also very important every position with cover preserve your units from getting killed as well as being targeted, leading to a refined war of movement as well as the necessity to building up forces on a specific location to chase away well positionned forces by breaking their moral.
The moral in the game is an important element as it was during the real line battle. The game make the moral very sensitive and that can take a short while to get used to, while feeling believable. Very few troops will stay in line, while half of there man are dying, in the middle of a field under musket and artilery fire as it should be.
This game current flaw is that it's very focused in terms of campaign to Gettysburg. Since Gettysburg is the entire point of the game, it's justifiably so. On the other hand, if the battle system of this game was mixed with a grand scale strategy game such as Victoria II or even something as simple as Risk with a multiplayer element added as well. This game, game mechanic would have an enormous potential of endless entertainement.
We can only hope that this is a prototype game that will lead to the developpement of something greater in the future.
So I indeed recommend peoples to buy this game, it's a lot of fun for a low price and it will make you happy for a while.

The music is great in some places, good in the rest; the environments are creative and laid out in a way so that it's meaningful to come back to them later. The art is distinctive and the story is a compelling new take on the Christian mythos.
There are some parts that are repetitive or perhaps slightly convoluted, but every puzzle had its own feeling of satisfaction when you finally completed it. The combat definitely had a tactical side of it that I enjoyed, but a more involved combo system might have kept me entertained for longer. I got a little tired of the click-and-hold-to-win sword combo you get once you unlock all the ground moves + flipsaw; luckily the boss and miniboss battles each have their own unique mechanics that make them something to look forward to.

Thoroughly mediocre. I didn't really have any idea what to expect, but even then I wasn't prepared for the complete lack of polish in this game.
The art is decent, but too often it's wasted on quick, throwaway shots that don't make good use of the time it took to produce it. Sprites suffer from a lack of transitions, the default, boring textbox makes it hard to read the text at times, and by the point I had to give up on this game, every major speaking character had the same color name, making it a chore to keep track of conversations. In a medium that focuses largely on dialogue, those are pretty huge mistakes.
Use of sound effects was sparse, while the music was generally lacking. The game opens with a public domain piece, and at one point there's a song that's literally five seconds long and badly looped over and over. Add to that what appears to be a complete lack of any kind of options screen or main menu, plus absolutely wooden writing that has about as much style and substance as a bowl of tapioca, and you have a recipe for... well, something that's just not any good.
It looks like this game was used as a springboard to gain interest (and funding) for future games by these developers, and while there's a good chance their other games are better than this one, I wouldn't pay to find out. Sorry.

A pretty simple but fun dungeon-crawler. Graphics and music are fine, there's no real story. You move room-to-room in a dungeon, collect coins (via chests and battles), spend coins (as attacks in battle, for powerups or more coins), and battle using the coin attacks. Floors are time-limited: if you spend too much time exploring, you'll start to drop coins until you leave.
The god-tribute system isn't explained so I had to search the forums to have an idea what the point was. You can donate coins to gods and in return you'll randomly find bonus coins in chests and debuffed enemies in future levels. If you neglect gods, they'll power up enemies and potentially fight you at the end.
There's a good amount of luck involved in this game (as is inherent in all card games) but there are some things that influence what is drawn. If you don't get the right coins in chests or draw the right coins in battle, you'll lose through no fault of your own. All you can do is try to maximize your chances and hope you get useful coins from chests.
Worth a try if you think you'd like the game mechanics and are fine with losing and replaying it until you get a good run of luck to get to the end.

Sacred 2 is an action role playing game part of the Sacred series. The PC version of the game was released in 2008. This was my first experience with the sacred series, having not played the original release either. I went into the game expecting it to be a little like Dungeon Keeper or Diablo.
The gameplay is top-down style, clicking on the world where to move and the traditional left and right click attacks. This to me is one of the best control systems out there as it is easy to grasp and you are able to do everything you need to do with just your mouse.  Sadly a lot of Sacred's 2 important menus are not bound to keys so you have to click on your UI in order to bring them up, such as inventory etc.  I also did not like the fact there was hardly any tutorial to the game; you get told how to move and attack; that's it.
Upon starting the game for the first time and creating your character, you are greeted with a humongous amount of information straight away. Although the game tries to explain what everything does, I found it a little overwhelming that I was being fed this amount of information on the first screen.
The graphics are dated since this game came out in 2008, you can easily see polygons and sharp edges on everything in the world.  There is a small amount of voice acting in the game too which is done very well, would of made the experience even better if all NPCs had it though.
I have been playing Sacred for about seven hours now; and I am barely even scratching the surface on the amount of content in this game. I am seeing sources online telling me there are about thirty four hours worth of content on offer here which is a huge amount. There are around 100 quests to complete in the main campaign as well as plenty of caves and dungeons to explore, there are said to be about 600 side quests out there too.
I am having a number of technical issues in my playthrough so far. The main one is that my UI will randomly disappear at points, which is extremely difficult to work around as I am not able to see my health or use potions etc. The only way I found to fix this was for you to either die, or reload the game. Sadly this one becomes very annoying very fast. Secondly there is quite a few areas which cause lag spikes and stuttering. I should not be playing a game that is almost seven years old and experience stuttering at all.
Do I recommend Sacred 2? Personally I think I may of been spoiled by recent RPG games. Back in the day I would bet my life on Sacred 2 being game of the year material; but compared to current and recent day RPG games, it just isn't the same. People who have played the game will probably disagree, but since I didn't grow up playing this game when I was younger I can only go off my first experience playing it.  So for me I won't recommend it since I am not having as much fun on this as I do other games. Old school gamers which love having tons of information to immerse and delve themselves into will love this game, it's just not for me.

I played this game a hell lot before it was on steam and recently bought the gold edition during the sale and enjoyed it once more. If you are burned out from other Action RPG games such as Diablo 3, this game will definitely be fun for you. I recommend getting the community patch to fix some crucial bugs as this game is not supported by the developer anymore. Online gameplay has been taken down some years ago aswell, but LAN is still possible obviously.
However, if you reach level 50+ in this game (usually by the time you finish the campaign for the first time on silver difficulty), xp gain really slows down a hell lot, so I recommend tweaking balance.txt xp gain by x10 multiplier to keep the game somewhat motivating.
Other than that it's a well designed game, the classes are very different from each other and deliver extremly solid character development and the loot system is very rewarding and motivating, even if the sets don't change from level 15 to 200 (max) they just gain higher stats which makes a 2nd, respectively third playthrough rather obsolete. The sound / voice acting in this game is brilliant and the enemies have some humourous / hillarious lines whenever you encounter / beat them. The heroes itself have witty and cheesy lines upon accepting quests / defeating bosses / hordes of mobs.
Although the quests are as simple as they could be (fetch me X of Y, go talk to Z) and the story being basically only a plot device to advance through the land, the world is very big and you can explore a hell lot of content.
I do recommend buying this game, if you want a fun timesink and like tinkering around with builds and combat arts (plenty of them available).

THOTH is a visually and sonically oppressive game with incredible balancing and ludicrously fun challenge.
The game uses simple geometric shapes all over the place, but the creepy movement and undulating shapeshifting is, by itself, enough to be stress inducing. Add to that the HORRIFYING soundtrack by Cristian Vogel & SØS Gunver Rybergand you have something that's going to give you a heart attack only a few levels in. I'd almost classify it as a horror game.
The gameplay is simple: use your joysticks to move and shoot at enemies as they barrel towards you.
. Beat four levels and that's a checkpoint. The game does a phenomenal job of teaching you through well-paced trial and error what everything does and how precisely it's going to kill you.
I love THOTH. It's brilliant. It should be played by anyone who wants a good challenge and a terrifying experience.

This game can be a bit buggy, but I've loved playing it. While it has its flaws, it also has a dev who is quick to respond to those issues and communicates with the players to find and fix the problems present, or just to implement good suggestions for the gameplay. I found the mechanics to be rather interesting and unique and had a lot of fun looking for the best combinations of coins.
A great aspect of the game are the classes you unlock as you play. Each class is distinct, and will heavily influence your gameplay. While there are your basic class differences, such as, "Bonus to damage, weaker healing." There are also classes who constantly lose coins. Or who put self damaging coins into your opponent's bag. Or are weakened by how many coins they have in their bag. This ensures that you'll have to come up with a variety of strategies and playstyles to play the game to its fullest extent.

It bothers me not recommending this game. You can clearly see that the developers invested a huge amount of time and love to make this game.
The world is huge, with no loading times except when entering specific dungeons. There are deserts, greenlands, mountains, swamps, jungles, pretty much a full global ecosystem. There are so many different kinds of creatures that I dare say this is the ARPG with the greatest foe variety ever made. Everything from huge, oldschool dragons to advanced robots imbued with magic will stand in your path. Talking about path, you can play either the good or evil campaing, with objectives, characters and locations varying for each one of the paths you choose. Every character class has its own huge set of habilities, starting place, mount and equipment type. There is enough customization to get you theorycrafting for quite a while when building your character. The story isn't the best around, but it gets you going. A sidequest chain in the first area of the game features the members of the band Blind Guardian, which will be a pleasant surprise if you dig the band. There's even a music video of the band playing to a bunch of monsters if you complete the chain quest, I should also add that one of the band's songs feature in the game's soundtrack.There was effort and love in this game's development, you can notice it. Everything is well though and has its own place in the world.
Despite all this, there are also terrible mistakes. Getting the game to run for the first time will be a logistical nightmare. Depending on your rig, the game might run anything ranging from "okay" to "unplayable". It requires a lot more processing power than the graphics make you believe it will, using the Steam Overlay feature will be close to impossible and there will be crashes. Be prepared to redo parts of the game due to losing progress on crashes. No game should be released with these kinds of issues and I cannot recommend a game that comes out like this unless the rest of the game is flawlessly good, which Sacred 2 certainly isn't.
I feel the need to say that, if you like ARPGs, you might still enjoy the game very much despite everything, as I did. Take a good look at some gameplay videos and try it out if you want, but be aware of what you'll be getting yourself into.

This is probably my all-time favorite Isometric loot Pinata Action RPG (i.e "Diablo clone" - you can see now why most people prefer that term).   Set in a huge, beautiful Elder Scrolls-like open world, it is immediately set apart from its contemporaries in other ways as well - some good, some bad, some simply arbitrary.
The Good - The character customization/development is second to none compared to others in the genre, the loot/gear is extensive (the armor sets look incredible for the most part) and the art style is impeccable.  The world is varied and interesting, really a joy to explore as it is handcrafted with all kinds of cool side areas and vignettes waiting to be discovered.
As far as I know this is the only game in its genre to have mounts, and they are badass.  Starting off, every class has access to various types of horse, but soon can acquire unique class mounts (like the Seraphim's Tiger or the Dryad's Lizard) and later several advanced horse-types (flaming horse, unicorn, war horse) to ride and fight on.  Did I say fight on? Yes - this game has mounted combat and it's really not much different from the usual bipedal mob-mowing method. In fact, my shadow warrior fights exclusively on his Hellhound (while in the overworld, at least - in dungeons and other subterranean locales you have to hoof it the old fashioned way)

The Bad - It suffers in a few areas that may matter more to others than myself - such as the writing - and although many quests are genuinely interesting, no one reads text any more. The actual "plot" is fairly abysmal and sparse but hey, this is a Diablo clone - we just want to click and kill and get loot.  Many game mechanics are not explained properly in-game so research or an experienced friend are recommended.
The "Could go Either Way" - While the classes are, as always, unique and cool - they are still gender locked (as Sacred 1 was).  I personally hate this approach to class design but I put up with it because these games are so damned great.  The classes aren't as appealing to me as Sacred's were (where's the vampiress? she was awesome)  Also the voice work is inconsistent - but that is merely a minor complaint.  The game is a bit "old school" with a lack of respec and the ability to totally bork your character development, so lots of rerolls are in store for a new player.
The usual Diablo-type mechanics are also thrown a bit on their heads in some cases, which may discomfort those taking the 'clone' portion of the genre name for granted.  There are no skill trees, but a set of skills you can learn from a pool (and put points into every level, up to 200 or so i think) that provide passive bonuses.  This is the open-ended aspect of character development here, taking a cue from the elder scrolls series; which skills you select and level shape your toon's flavor.
The "active' skills, called Combat Arts or CAs; come as runes, loot that drops from enemies that you can 'eat' to improve each one's power. They can range from healing spells to gap closers to AOE attacks, etc. All the usual abilities we are accustomed to in ARPGs.  Like sacred 1, eating lots of runes increases not only their power but their cooldown time as well (which can be countered in many ways including the aforementioned skills) so there is a balancing game with power vs spammability.  Path of Exile took a version of this concept for use in their gem-based skill system, highlighting Sacred's influence and innovation.
The Lowdown - Although the multiplayer servers were shut down, one can still play through a tunnelling service such as hamachi or Tunngle and I suggest someone try to utilize these as I'm looking for people to play with!  Despite its age I still feel like the graphics are among best in class for the Diablo Clone/loot ARPG genre.  The soundtrack (done by the band Blind Guardian) is a bit different for the genre - a power metal vibe to it, also giving you gentle pastoral pieces that help keep the fantasy cohesion intact.  Also each character class has its own flavor of battle music!  There are so many little details- evidence of the developer love that was put into this game - that it breaks my heart it never caught on as much as some other, less-deserving titles have.
Also to note - for some reason, the screenshots in the steam store page are all stretched-out looking and strange.  The game looks way better than that in motion lol.  I recommend the community patch (now v.0105 or something) and the camera mod if that is not already included, but otherwise I use no other mods.

TL;DR - If you want a finished, bug-free game don't buy it, if you like Minecraft-style games and don't mind waiting for new content and patches buy it. Frustrating at first, but already the developers have made it much better.
I've never played Minecraft but have always wanted to, but when I went to their website and would have had to sign up for an account before I could even see how much the stupid game cost, I became annoyed. I read on another site it was $30 (which I'm not sure is true or not, regardless I became more annoyed). Lo and behold, that same day on the front page of Steam I see FortressCraft for $4. Needless to say I got it.
The first hour was an incredibly frustrating experience because I had absolutely no idea what I was doing and the help menu wasn't helpful at all. Thankfully they have made it much more in-depth, so new users shouldn't have nearly as much trouble as I did. I read a guide and got into it, having quite a bit more fun even though finding ore was tough at first (they have also made this easier, using one key and scrolling to find the ping you want, whereas before there was a key combination for each ping type).
Now that I'm getting my base set up and things automated, I'm having a lot of fun! It's always cool to see your progress so clearly.
There are some bugs which is to be expected since it's an early-access game. Most annoying is that the x64 executable likes to go missing, so I've been playing with x32. There are infrequent crashes, and if you quit when anything is in your smelter the items get lost. Not a bug but slightly annoying when I first started playing: menus that don't completely work. Now that I know the features haven't been implemented it's fine, but before I was clicking and totally confused as to why nothing was happening.
The roadmap the developers have is great, and they seem to be very active here on Steam. Nice to know they're listening! Things I would like to see added are some ideas or guides for power plants and things like that, more detailed graphics (though I'm fine playing with the current ones), and maybe trees that regrow themselves. That would be cool. Seeds and stuff would be neat too.
Anyways, it's a great game and awesome for the price and all the stuff they have planned.

I received the starter edition of R6 as a gift for my birthday last year, and I never expected to end up with nearly 400 hours (and climbing). I've never been too into more "mainstream" shooters, so my obsession with this game came as a complete surprise. Make no mistake: R6 still has an IMMENSE amount of bugs that can be frustrating to play through, but when the game goes right it goes SO right.
The highly destructible environments make for a constantly shifting and dynamic battleground, and it's insanely satisfying to use it to your advantage on both attack and defense. Mira can cleverly neglect to reinforce specific walls and watch through her one-way window gadget to go for surprise wallbangs on unsuspecting attackers. Ash can set a breaching charge on a random window barricade and then use her breaching round gadget to blow up ANOTHER window and rush in while the defenders are still unsure of what approach the attackers are taking with the multiple disorienting explosions. This brings us to the "tactical shooter / intel" aspect of the game, which is another big part of its appeal. While sometimes iffy, the sound in the game can often be just as valuable as the visuals. You can hear the attackers running around on the roof, or blowing up a wall, or sending a drone in to gather intel, and in turn plan your course of action whether it be rushing a busy attacker or simply feeding your teammates information so they can ready themselves for a push by the enemies.
On top of the incredibly fun and (mostly) skill-based gameplay, Ubisoft does a surprisingly fantastic job of updating the game both for balance of existing content and addition of new content. All non-cosmetic additions (operators and their weapon attachments) can be unlocked pretty easily by just playing the game and earning renown to purchase them, and all new maps are available to all players when they are added. Even most of the cosmetics (with the exception of digital content bundles and some select headgears) can be pretty easily unlocked with earned renown, without ever forcing you to purchase the game's premium currency. Every few months there is a new "season" that adds two new unique operators, a bunch of cosmetics, and a brand new map. In the middle of each season they push midseason reinforcements, which are sets of balance changes and reworks based on operator usage statistics and community feedback.
TL;DR: The game really is, despite its flaws, an absolutely fantastic online shooter, and I can't recommend enough that you pick it up and play it with a few friends. Rainbow Six Siege is easily a 9/10 game and the best online shooter to come out of the 2010s, rivaling even the likes of CS:GO in its continued playability and competitive balance.

From Kickstarter, to Greenlight, to eventual release, there was no indication at all that the story of this game was going to be a blatant and hamfisted parable to biblical tales.
A simple note or tag of "religious themes" would have been a lot more sincere, and enough to prepare me for the kind of story I was getting into. Given that this content is THE ENTIRETY OF THE STORY, it seems like a MASSIVE oversight to not mention it at all. I gave it an honest run and plenty of time to prove itself, but by the end of it I felt like I was sitting in a theatre being preached at by the brainwashed children of a religious cult (which is a real and unfortunate experience I've actually had before, and thus not a comparison I make lightly).
As for the actual gameplay, for the most part it's childishly simple and tedious, but occasionally utterly confusing and unintuitive. 2016 has been a big year for games, and one of the most welcome trends in my book is the transition of FPS games back to their speed infused arena roots. Whether it’s Overwatch‘s Team Fortress 2 inspirations or DOOM‘s strict adherence to old school sensibilities, shooters in 2016 are picking up where they left off in the early 90s, right around the release of the original Shadow Warrior. How fitting then that 2013’s Shadow Warrior was one of the first titles to quietly lead the charge in this shift. Flying Wild Hog reignited this style of FPS design three years ago, and 2016 sees the team attempting to use this influence to move the genre forward. Borrowing the best ideas from many recent shooter hits, Shadow Warrior 2 is a slick and satisfying FPS that delivers engaging combat at a blistering pace unlike anything else on the market.

This is actually a relatively enjoyable and well designed point & click adventure game... for an hour or so. Any enjoyment had in that first hour is ruined by a story development that is insultingly obvious in its Christian intent. The game doesn't tell you it's designed by Christians, and doesn't actually use the word "Christian" or make any reference to religion at all, but the narrative message (and the existential "moral" of the story that you're supposed to feel some sort of emotional connection to) is so blatantly Christian that it feels like a patronising attempt at emotional manipulation. I don't want to spoil the story, but believe me: this isn't Christian in the sense that stories about being kind or caring or turning the other cheek or whatever are (vaguely) Christian - this is Christian in a very unpleasant, proselytising sense. The game wants you to spread the "light" to others and show them how much better you've become since it was given to you. Seriously. That is basically the main bulk of the story.
If the developers had been honest and said this was a Christian game then it wouldn't feel so insulting. I probably still wouldn't have enjoyed it, but I wouldn't have been annoyed. This is the main issue really: my anger towards this game has nothing to do with disrespect for religion (I honestly don't care what religion anyone follows), but is entirely due to the obvious attempt to mislead and manipulate through the story.

Obligatory header to the review: I focus on four primary areas whenever I review a game: gameplay, story, graphics, and sound/audio/general things that go into your earholes. Gameplay and Story get a rating scale from 1 to 10, and the AV stuff gets a rating from 1 to 5. My philosophy on this is that there are some instances in which a game may not necessarily have that much in the way of gameplay (take Amnesia for example), but the story/atmosphere/whatever it may be is reason enough to pick it up. Also, take the cumulative score with a grain of salt; it's just a numerical feeling about the game as a whole. That's part of why I do these subscores. Also, keep in mind that I'm not going off of school grade based rankings. A 5/10 denotes what I feel to be an average game. Likewise, 7/10 is a game that I think is pretty cool, and something that gets a 2/10 is near-abomination level. Pinning scores to an even further obfuscated rating scale is kinda senseless, but for the sake of my backloggery, I'll repeat again that 1.0-2.7 is a one-star game, 3.0-4.7 is a two-star game, 5.0-6.7, 7.0-8.7, and 9.0-10 are three, four, and five stars, respectively.
Gameplay: For all intents and purposes, I should absolutely love this game. Many people make the comparison between this and Legend of Zelda, and I am certainly in that camp. Why I say that I should absolutely love this game is because my biggest beef with the 3D Zelda games has been the combat. It's not bad, but it certainly could be a lot better. This game does have better combat than the 3D Zelda games. So why don't I like it as much as I should? Here's a few reasons why.
One of the reasons why I'm not too keen on this game is the combat itself. Yes, it is much better than the Zelda games, but it's just too clean. I'm not talking about violence or anything; there's plenty of that. Rather, the combat just feels really light and floaty; there's no weight to it. Admittedly, games like Dark Souls may have spoiled me on weighty combat, but Darksiders just feels sterile to me; you don't feel like you're there hacking up enemies. Mechanically, the combat is very sound, but it just lacks the feel I think a hack-and-slash game should have. Boss fights are a bit of a mixed bunch; no bosses are terrible, but some of them are just kinda meh.
In fact, "meh" kinda gets to the point of why I don't like this game as much as I probably should. The whole journey just feels like a "been there, done that" sort of adventure. It's not the easiest thing to describe in words, but this game just feels soulless to me. There are some inspired bits here and there, but they only account for about 20% of the game's running time. The biggest mark against this game has to be the dungeon where you get what is basically the Portal Gun. I can't help but feel that the game design meeting for this section went along the lines of, "Hey, you know what's popular? Portal. Let's do a Portal section." Again, there are a few clever uses of the Portal gadget, but it just reeks of the designers giving up.
Despite these three paragraphs of negativity toward the game, I can recommend it if you're looking for a Zelda-like game that has better combat than Zelda. Just don't go into it with too high of standards. I would use the phrase "Diamonds in the rough" to describe the good bits in this game, but I feel that's a bit too harsh of a comparison. Rather, I think "Garnets in the Styrofoam Peanut Pile" is a good comparison. There's good sections and bosses in there. You just gotta wade through a lot of mediocre stuff to get to them. 6/10.
Story: The story is actually mildly inspired by the Biblical story of the Apocalypse and the coming of the Horsemen. By this I mean that there is some other original stuff added to it so that it's not a complete carbon copy, much like a lot of the game is anyways. However, this game just tries way too hard in my opinion to be cool. Also, "Creator" and "Destroyer"? What's so bad about God/Jehovah/YHWH/whatever you wanna call him vs. Lucifer? I get that hiding the identity of the "Destroyer" is actually relevant to the plot, but the story is
inspired by the story in Revelations (New Testament stuff, so no crossover with Judaism), so why not just call the character God? I'm making petty complaints, though. It's alright, but the writer really needed to lay off with the angst, especially with some of War's dialogue. 6/10.
Graphics: The art style isn't actually half bad in this game. I dug some of the enemy designs, even if they were repeated quite a bit with "color palette switcheroo"-esque changes. Plus, many of the areas have a very "big" feeling to them, a feeling that I love seeing in areas in video games. Some people say that War's character design could've been a lot better, and while I agree, I don't think it's that abysmal. After all, Square Enix has had MUCH worse character designs than War. Now, on the technical side of things, there unfortunately isn't very much in the way of graphical fidelity control. There's no option for Anti-Aliasing or Anisotropic Filtering, which is quite disappointing for a game released in 2010. There's also no option for windowed mode, so if you're a person who likes playing game in windowed mode, you're kinda stuck. Fortunately, the game does run at 1080p, which it does run fairly well and fairly cool on my GTX 760 with all the settings that I could max out maxed out. However, I again suspect that the reason why it does run cool is because they never implemented the high-end features. 3/5.
Music: The game does come with the OST, but like many orchestral soundtracks, none of the songs really left an impression on me. It's not like Dark Souls (and this is the last comparison I'll make to Dark Souls for this review; I swear) where each track is anthemic to some area. It basically comes down to a multipurpose battle theme and a multipurpose boss theme. The final bosses' theme wasn't bad, but I'd be hard pressed to remember it if you played it back to me without telling me what it was from. The voiceacting, much like the story, is very try-hard to be cool. You can hear the angst dripping off of War's lines, and it's actually kinda funny listening to the game try to be hard. Again, this may be because the VAs didn't have much to really work with, but the voiceacting is forgettable at best and absolute ham at worst. 2/5.
Overall score of 6/6/3/2; 5.7/10. To refrain what I said in the intro, a 5 isn't awful in my perspective; it's just average, and that's what this game feels like to me: average. Your mileage may vary; in fact, one of my friends thought this game was worthy of a five star rating. To me, though, it's just a slightly above average hack and slash game. This is probably my all-time favorite Isometric loot Pinata Action RPG (i.e "Diablo clone" - you can see now why most people prefer that term).   Set in a huge, beautiful Elder Scrolls-like open world, it is immediately set apart from its contemporaries in other ways as well - some good, some bad, some simply arbitrary.
The Good - The character customization/development is second to none compared to others in the genre, the loot/gear is extensive (the armor sets look incredible for the most part) and the art style is impeccable.  The world is varied and interesting, really a joy to explore as it is handcrafted with all kinds of cool side areas and vignettes waiting to be discovered.
As far as I know this is the only game in its genre to have mounts, and they are badass.  Starting off, every class has access to various types of horse, but soon can acquire unique class mounts (like the Seraphim's Tiger or the Dryad's Lizard) and later several advanced horse-types (flaming horse, unicorn, war horse) to ride and fight on.  Did I say fight on? Yes - this game has mounted combat and it's really not much different from the usual bipedal mob-mowing method. In fact, my shadow warrior fights exclusively on his Hellhound (while in the overworld, at least - in dungeons and other subterranean locales you have to hoof it the old fashioned way)

The Bad - It suffers in a few areas that may matter more to others than myself - such as the writing - and although many quests are genuinely interesting, no one reads text any more. The actual "plot" is fairly abysmal and sparse but hey, this is a Diablo clone - we just want to click and kill and get loot.  Many game mechanics are not explained properly in-game so research or an experienced friend are recommended.
The "Could go Either Way" - While the classes are, as always, unique and cool - they are still gender locked (as Sacred 1 was).  I personally hate this approach to class design but I put up with it because these games are so damned great.  The classes aren't as appealing to me as Sacred's were (where's the vampiress? she was awesome)  Also the voice work is inconsistent - but that is merely a minor complaint.  The game is a bit "old school" with a lack of respec and the ability to totally bork your character development, so lots of rerolls are in store for a new player.
The usual Diablo-type mechanics are also thrown a bit on their heads in some cases, which may discomfort those taking the 'clone' portion of the genre name for granted.  There are no skill trees, but a set of skills you can learn from a pool (and put points into every level, up to 200 or so i think) that provide passive bonuses.  This is the open-ended aspect of character development here, taking a cue from the elder scrolls series; which skills you select and level shape your toon's flavor.
The "active' skills, called Combat Arts or CAs; come as runes, loot that drops from enemies that you can 'eat' to improve each one's power. They can range from healing spells to gap closers to AOE attacks, etc. All the usual abilities we are accustomed to in ARPGs.  Like sacred 1, eating lots of runes increases not only their power but their cooldown time as well (which can be countered in many ways including the aforementioned skills) so there is a balancing game with power vs spammability.  Path of Exile took a version of this concept for use in their gem-based skill system, highlighting Sacred's influence and innovation.
The Lowdown - Although the multiplayer servers were shut down, one can still play through a tunnelling service such as hamachi or Tunngle and I suggest someone try to utilize these as I'm looking for people to play with!  Despite its age I still feel like the graphics are among best in class for the Diablo Clone/loot ARPG genre.  The soundtrack (done by the band Blind Guardian) is a bit different for the genre - a power metal vibe to it, also giving you gentle pastoral pieces that help keep the fantasy cohesion intact.  Also each character class has its own flavor of battle music!  There are so many little details- evidence of the developer love that was put into this game - that it breaks my heart it never caught on as much as some other, less-deserving titles have.
Also to note - for some reason, the screenshots in the steam store page are all stretched-out looking and strange.  The game looks way better than that in motion lol.  I recommend the community patch (now v.0105 or something) and the camera mod if that is not already included, but otherwise I use no other mods.

I picked this game up yesterday, because it's only 4 bucks, and I liked Minecraft quite a bit. I was hoping Anthony's review was a bit of an exaggeration, but even after dozens of hours playing Minecraft, I was pretty lost after about a half hour playing this game.
There were birds flying around that I couldn't kill, with text attached to them about crafting (Not sure if this is a bug or one of many confusing features), and even with tutorial screen at the beginning, I was still clueless. It kind of feel like it was written for someone who already has a lot of experience playing this game.
I think I was supposed to find my crashed ship, but when I went to the area where it seemed to have gone down, there was just some "power thing" floating well above where I could reach it. I was able to mine a few rocks and trees, but couldn't seem to craft anything with them but torches. Even after chopping down trees, I saw no way to turn those into planks, or construct anything.
Survival mode in Minecraft starts you with nothing, and no endless menu of things you could eventually build, which eases you into what eventually becomes a very complex game. I'm not sure how much more complex this game is supposed to be, but it's almost impossible to get into a game when I don't have the slightest clue what I'm doing.
I'll try watching a Youtube tutorial on how to get through the first few days, but since this is still Early Access, I'd really recommend to the developers that they consider a very basic, starting from scratch, survival mode, and slowly introduce new features. I usually don't need my hand held figuring out games, but this one almost requires it. Assume the people playing your game have never even heard of a game like this before, and teach them how to play it. Right now, a 6 page tutorial on topics that make no sense to a beginner, isn't helping.
I think I could really get into this game, but right now it's almost impossible, even if I wanted to. Please consider a more basic starting point for beginners, Devs, and teach as we go, rather than bombarding us with a bunch of information and features from the get go.
But all in all, I'm going to recommend this game because it is Early Access, and the Devs do seem dedicated to making improvements.
TL;DR: Survival mode is incredibly difficult to figure out, even if you've played Minecraft, but at this price point, this game is still worth picking up.

Short version:
FortressCraft is basically a Minecraft + tech mod clone, minus Minecraft's charm. With a side of difficuilt and awkward to use interface. Plus an extra helping of bugs (even for early access). Not recommended.
Longer version:
On startup Fortresscraft greets you with possibly the most detailed and intricate menu ever. This turned out to be a bad omen though as it's also possibly the most difficuilt to use menu ever. Difficuilt to the point of needing a tutorial to navigate. However after much random mouse button mashing I managed to overcome this hurdle and start a new survival world. Alas, I was one of the lucky few. We should spare a moment of thought for all those poor souls who failed to navigate the main menu, and instead flocked to Steam's forum for a solution... on how to use the main menu.
Once the world had loaded and the ringing in my ears caused by the really LOUD crashing ship passed I came to another hurdle, the help screen. I quickly browsed over the help text and tried taking in as many hotkeys as I could. There are a number of them as the only way to select a tool is with a hotkey. Which you can't rebind.
After skimming the help screen I tried to close it by pressing escape, nothing. Tried clicking on stuff, nothing. Only after rolling my face across the keyboard, not once, but twice! Was I finally rid of the cursed help screen. (edit: The escape key sort of works in the latest version)
With arch-villan help screen defeated I was finally able to take in the world, the very bland world. This is where the clone shows through. Even the block's textures have that familiar MInecraft look, albeit high resolution. All other voxel games have moved away from cubes into their own form of voxels, and all of those new voxel games feel nice and fresh.  So coming back to a cube game can feel a bit underwhelming. Made worse by a world that has nothing going on. It's just snow and the occassional tree. Totally lacking in features that convince you this is an alien world.
The actual game, in it's current state, is centered around building an automated mining network similar to many Minecraft tech mods where you have mining machines that feed a conveyor of some sort. You then need a power network to run those machines etc.  So far the stuff in game is similar to stuff I've seen in mods. Which isn't a bad thing. Expanding on these ideas could lead to somewhere interesting. But.
And it's a big but. This game has a lot strange design features that either take away player agency or are there to♥♥♥♥♥♥you off. Like the decision to go against the convention of every other game in this genre, and reverse the block breaking and block placing mouse buttons. Those buttons are so ingrained now that I'm constantly wrecking my machines or digging holes when I meant to place a machine, infuriating. Then there is the bizarre inventory mechanic where you can't choose what you put into a machine. The game decides for you and it's pretty much always the wrong choice. So you have to wait around for the machine to finish then hope it chooses the correct material next go around.
Finally the inventory or lack of. The inventory is just for show it lets you know how much of each block you are carrying and that's it. Since it's non-interactive you can't organise it or anything you can usually do with an inventory. The only thing it lets you do is spew blocks everywhere via another hotkey. A number of those blocks will often get lost because of physics bugs. Spewing is the only way to get stuff from your inventory into a storage container. The problem being another container in the vicinity will suck up your block spew. Meaning you need to empty that container then try again. As you imagine can this becomes a real chore, real quick.
This game is the game for you if you like blood and gore  it also has a good selection of weapons

review of 1.9 EA
OK, it has blocks, crafting, and mining. That's where the similarities end really.
My daughter plays Minecraft, she plays it for hours. However, whenever I sit down to have a go, I get bored after about 20 minutes. You dig. You build. You dig. zzzz
FortressCraft is much more immediate than that. Your power is running out, you're going to freeze to death, so you need to organise. This forces you to think stategically, about power, about distance, about supply lines (and presumably, in the future, defending them from other players). It kind-of feels more like a RTS, but with blocks.
If you're used to other Mine games, this one IS even more complicated. But part of that is due to a very alpha GUI, things aren't as obvious as they could or should be. This will be fixed!
for example, bringing up your inventory, you have a bunch of blocks. What are they? no idea, a mouse-over tooltip would be nice :)
Also, I'd rather you only had things in  your toolbar that you actually owned, it's too confusing with *every possible thing* being shown, yet you can't use 90% of it. Again, early access, these things are to be expected.
One thing that is immediately "wrong" with the game - shelter. If you build a "house" over your base equipment, put a torchfire or two in there, surely it should be warm enough inside that you don't freeze? What's the point of building a "Fortress" if it doesn't have any benefits lol :)
I absolutely recommend this, if you're a fan of Voxel miners or even RTS games. I see a bright future for this game, because unlike others, there is actually a game to be played, a point to it all. (you can, of course, go into creative mode and just build pretty stuff, but I kind-of don't see the point of that unless you can then turn the world into a survival one for you and your friends. No doubt that's coming too eventually).
Buy it, try it. If you don't get on with it, try it again the next update. and the next. It's going to be a good one :)

Ultimate General Gettysburg, is a large scale American Civil War strategy game. I hesitate to use the term RTS as many of the usual tropes associated with them, such as basebuilding, and diplomacy are noticeably vacant. Instead the game focuses on a well built and historically accurate ORBAT, with persistent troops throughout the campaign. For Example if the Unions Iron Brigade had single handedly held Devils den against a full division of confederates, and lost most of its men. Then in your next battle they will be just as weak and quite likely exhausted and low on morale.

This gives a feeling of importance to each and every brigade you have, and infact I personally found myself favoring certain brigades, or even hating some (Damnit Baxter! Your supposed to hold Devils den! Why did you advance!?!?). You see, each unit has its own AI Commander who will make choices on their own unless told not too. This includes retreating and advancing to some degree, but mostly focuses on shifting their flanks to face the enemy proper. More than once, a Brigadier Generals advance or retreat has completely changed the way the battle plays, and what was initially my biggest issue with the game has now become one of its strengths.

Its not just the individual AI either, ingame the enemy AI itself is brilliant, coordinating attacks on certain positions. If your playing as the union, the second battle of day one is going to be a difficult one, as the AI completely outmaneuvers you. (I'll avoid spoilers here).

Now, despite all of this, the actual ingame UI and gameplay is shockingly simple. Its drag and release the mouse. Thats it, ocassionaly you might rotate a units facing, or check the heights of hills with the terrain map. But these are still incredibly simple things to do.

There are a few flaws with the game, the brilliant AI sometimes wants to misbehave, and doesn't always take risks. IE: In the last battle of the confederate campaign, the union soldiers outnumbered me by 9000 men, they were exhausted however and the AI decided to let them rest. By the time they had recovered, the battle was nearly over and they didn't have time to push the Victory Point. Small issues like this exist, but for the most part the game is amazingly polished, infact it feels more finished than many games I've played that aren't in early access.

In conclusion, I gotta say, if you like strategy games and like games with muskets in them, this is the game to buy. Don't hesitate, this price point and the replayability (I've completed the campaign 8 times now)  means it is a must have in your library.

Game started out great, with a great story hook and great art. An hour and a half  later, I was no longer playing Alum, but rather 'Jesus, Your Lord and Savior - the Bejesusing'.
Don't get me wrong, I'm a Christian myself and am not bashing because I'm an antheist hipster. Just the way the overbearing Christian narrative is pushed in your face, without much subtlety or any game-specific adaptation and meaningful changes, feels very hamfisted. I understand the devs wanted to make a story about God and the way faith works but playing this feels exactly like being indoctrinated into some branch of protestantism and I don't feel this has a place in a point-and-click adventure game, especially one that advertises itself as something completely different.
It does the game a disservice, as the pixel art is indeed superb and the puzzles are enjoyable for the most part, without being too easy or too silly and frustrating. The theme could have been handled much more gracefully but the way it is, it feels forced and cringey, which largely ruins the fun.

Alum is clearly an indie game put together by a small team, as is shown by the quality of its presentation. The graphics are pixelated a bit more than a lot of retro stuff, but if you're an old school adventure gamer, that shouldn't bother you too much. The audio is fine for what it is, but the voice acting is... not good. In fact, it's pretty lousy. You can tell most, if not all, of the voice actors are amateurs or first-timers. Still, the puzzles aren't bad, although after the first chapter, they've been bordering on too easy. The story, however, is where the game shines. It's something of a dystopia futuristic city setting, but there are enough odd elements to make it feel a bit fresher than average. There have been a few weird twists so far that have kept me guessing too, trying to figure out exactly what the heck is going on. I'm willing to put up with the games other weaknesses just because I'm so intrigued by the story. And for five bucks, it's not too painful of a purchase. Alum is a mixed bag, but on balance, it's decent enough to recommend.

This is a gem of a game. A basic Point & Click Adventure game that has a amazing story that keeps you wanting to continue through the entire game in one sitting if you have the time to. There aren't that many flaws in this game that I came across but there are still a few things that I would suggestion changing slightly.
This game is amazing. I'm not normally for one with point and click games but this one is a exception, it has a very intriguing story (Don't worry no spoilers here) that gets you hooked in and wanting play through the entire game (I didn't because I suck at puzzle type games). Obviously, with each Point & Click come with puzzles. Let me start off by saying that the tutorial actually blends in with the story and game play, which is really good because you normally have to go through a few text boxes before you can even start playing. This game tells you how to do things then you use it at that moment. Really good idea. I found the first chapter puzzles to be pretty self-explanatory then it started to get a bit over my head and got a bit more complex. Some of the puzzles are a bit to obscure to really know that, that was what you where suppose to do. Unless you hovered your mouse of it you wouldn't of found out how to do it. There was a few occasions this happened to me while playing this game, maybe that's just because I am bad at puzzles games. There is a hint one the options page that will help you if you understand what that means. If not then you will be walking around, hovering your mouse over every area of each place. None the less this is still a amazing game, it has some witty jokes inside and doesn't go over board when it uses them.  Each chapter of the game sets a atmosphere, or a question that you don't know the answer to. That really hooked me into each chapter that I played, this combine with some really intense moments in the game really sets it up to be a brilliant atmospheric game! The small cut scenes in this game look really good, you get the feel that you really are this person and you want to help them. Again, setting a terrific atmosphere which just made me want to play it more. The pacing in this game is very well done, it starts off slow with a few questions to the game, then by the end of chapter 1 (Took me about 30 minutes) it's then faced paced! A nice little element of the game that they added that I don't see often in other Point & Click games is the ability to show where all the exits are. This really does help you because sometimes you are unsure where they are, they aren't always obvious. The writing of the story and the voices of all the characters is very nice, the story is structured really well and the words they use just grab you into the game. I found that it's structured very well right at the beginning of the game.
You can see the type of graphics that are on the game through the trailer, it has nice pixel graphics that fit the game really well. Everything looks really nice and polished for pixel graphics. I feel like this game works really well with these graphics, and the whole atmosphere you keep with you through the entire game.
In my opinion the music and sounds make the whole game how atmospheric it really is. There is very soft background music at times and every sound that you would expect to hear you would hear it, the songs that are played really suit the situations that you are in as well. It really makes you feel like you are in the game, and then when it gets to the emotional parts the music and sounds set in just right to get the most of out the game. Although I would like to hear a little more variation for the background music but that's just a little thing.
This is what a Point & Click game should be. Very atmospheric, with all the music and the sounds, nicely crafted puzzles that (in my opinion) get a bit too hard as you went along the game and the graphics set the game up to be really good, and well fitting with the music.

Alum is a point and click adventure with heavy religious themes, but is not a very good game.  I got it for $1 off of Indie Game Stand, and I wouldn't recommend it for much more than that.  As always, it is important to note that this game DOES have failstates, but checkpoints you immediately before them.
The religious element of the story is essentially christianity, with a rename on most elements and a lot of the themes still present.  This isn't prima facie bad, and it could actually be a very interesting setting for a game... if it was well written, and this game wasn't.  I would expound on this further, but as it turns out
All you have are usual christian cliches of faith, persecution, redemption, forgiveness, and so forth.  The game is neither robust nor well made enough to make up for its lack of original content.  Even if we give a huge benefit of the doubt to the game and its developers in assuming that this story isn't some sort of subtle preaching and take the game at face value, the face value is pretty empty.
"This game is dedicated to all of our friends and family who have gone ahead to be with the true and living Unfeigned Altruist (Jesus Christ)" is displayed at the end of the credits.  I can't help but feel that this game was written specifically for a christian audience, a story full of good values and affirmation of your beliefs so that you were supposed to nod your head along to the religious elements with a warm fuzzy feeling inside.  It wasn't written to be original.  It was written to preach.
Story aside, the rest of the game isn't much good either.  The puzzles aren't particularly interesting or clever.  The characters have no charm or personality to make you feel for them, and their voice acting is mediocre and almost always lacks the right emotion for the scenes (even taking into account the game's plot point of The Vague influencing this).  Locales are not particuarly interesting nor does any of the art draw much wonder, but the music is fairly passable.
Its probably best to say that the game just isn't good.  Its not abysmal in any of these categories I critique it for (voice acting being the worst of the set), but I didn't at any point crack a smile or feel like I was enjoying myself and I did give this game a fair shake.  The game is about 8.5 hours long.  Just pass, there's plenty of other point-and-click adventure games with much better content from Daedelic and Wadjet Eye you'd be much better off playing.

Dear god the crashes!  I can even replicate them at will.  Steam really lowered the bar on aplha.... WHAT? IT'S BEEN FULLY OUT SINCE MARCH?  I guess they decided to skip all the testing and QA phases.
Read below or pretty much any of the other reviews that aren't obvious shills and you'll see.  With bugs like these this game should be considered a Beta right now at best, and it doesn't look like the dev's are still working on it.
STEAM, PLEASE PULL THIS GAME UNTIL IT IS NOT BROKEN.
When the game works, it plays a lot like Empire At War and has command weapons ala Red Alert 3.  The bots are smart and the board-game style galaxy conquest, although not unique, adds some replayability.
There is no actual campaign other than the galactic conquest.
Multiplayer has no public matches option (either that or shows no matches by default and you can't search for "").
If the game worked and had real multiplayer and a campaign it could be a really polished title.  However, even getting passed the crashes, the game is a mess.  Here's a few reasons why:
- AI goes from retard to genius between Easy and Medium.
- Badly designed load screens (press to continue after match loads will press itself after a few seconds)
- Unbalanced species
- Bulky and poorly laid out UI (keyboard shortcuts suck by default too)
- Important messages disappear quickly and/or get replaced by useless information (like letting you know your division is under attack during this firefight that's been going on for the last 5 minutes rather than the volcano is about to erupt)
- No save game option during matches (so, when it crashes at the end of a match, which it will, you have to start that part of the conquest over again)
Overall there isn't really anything unique about the gameplay itself.  Between command and conquer, starcraft, empire at war and supreme commander, it's all been done before and better.  The only originality I see is in the galactic conquest - kind of like the EAW version only with trading cards and no space battles.  If you see me playing this in the next 3 days (free), it's because I want to finish ONE conquest before I uninstall it forever (right now certain territories crash after I beat them so it's a mini-game in itself.)
DO NOT SPEND MONEY ON THIS. - INSTALL FOR THE FREE WEEK ONLY IF YOU WANT TO BE FRUSTRATED

Rather than a game, this should be called a prologue. It sets the stage for a good and interesting game, and then it ends. I guess that the idea is that this will be episodic, but all it does now is get you hyped up and leave you with blue balls. It's a demo for an experience that doesn't exist yet.
What does exist isn't bad, though. The art is quite solid and the story, while nothing too special so far, isn't bad and shows promise to get better.
Besides shortness, the game is hindered by technological weakness and a lack of options, as it doesn't let you set text speed or to review previously displayed text, which together make this bit of a hassle to proceed through, and I found myself also missing skipping, as I wound up going back to a quicksave and hurrying through to read a bit of text I missed, by using mouse clicks to hurry the printing along, a few different times.
The writing occassionally drops into artsy bits that, to me, come across more as pretentious than deep, and the pacing feels rushed, but overall it's an engaging style and the storyline was effective at grabbing my interest. I would like to read more from the author, if only this author did add more to his story. I think that when/if there's some manner of "Invisible Apartment: Complete" released, with the full story completed and packaged together in a single, more professionally composed program, and when the story has had some good editing work done, this has the potential to be an excellent VN and perhaps one of the best on Steam.
This release is nothing more than a tease for a product that doesn't yet exist, though. My real recommendation is "wait" but the closest option Steam provides is "don't recommend", to be ammended later.

Coins act as your way of attack mainly, but also are a sort of secondary health and currency in the game forcing you to use them wisely as running out of them is game over. The alternate characters in this game also change the way it's played entirely, such as making you use all the coins in your hand to do a lot more damage but also risk running out of coins faster, or removing the main way to get coins and replaces it with more coin drops from enemies. The game isn't too difficult for the most part, most of the potential challenge comes from the alternate characters abilities as mentioned. The overall game is pretty simple and my only compaints are that sometimes coin descriptions could be better and I'm not the biggest fan of the art style at times.

reminds me of my impressions of
When a teenager, I was quite excited about the series until I read some critics. Then my reaction was like, "What?! This wonderful lion, Aslan, is no more than old boring Jesus? Oh no!" However,
's creators aren't as subtle as C. S. Lewis; their approach is more like that of
You play as a member of religiously driven anarcho-primitivist gang of those who use terror as a way to convince people and would destroy the city's central heating system just to make people "think out of a box" and "understand things wider" (?!). The Rogations (that's their name, but it probably should be The Rogues) blame their contemporaries (modern people) that they live in industrialized society and can no longer be guided by "faith" as it were in the Middle Ages; if so, Middle Ages should be returned artificially. Does it remind you some, so to say, not very good people (from the real world)?!
They are not even Trotskyists, they are just ordinary fanatics. Let us believe that Kosmos is really "oppressive totalitarian state." But the Rogations themselves are no better. Just see how they demonize their political and ideological enemies, how they tend to idolize their leader, how they give reason for their activity using just theological "arguments." Actually,
is a rare case when my sympathies are entirely on the antagonist's side.
Of course, the game is pretty linear and has only one possible ending. Actually, there are some other endings, but the player isn't encouraged to get them: there are no corresponding achievements, and they look more like another way to say "game over." I felt pity when I get a perfect ending to my tastes
, and they said just like, "Okay, now load and do it as we need you to do." You feel constantly driven by the hand (checkpoints, strong recommendations to save, various reminders etc.), and this affects even puzzles: I am no good at adventure games, but almost the entire game were walked through by me with no hints or guide. (But it could be a virtue of the game in terms of puzzles' consistency, I don't know.)
Also, the name of the studio is completely justified: it takes a great mumbo-jumbo to launch the game and especially to make it work via Steam.
That said, I can't help but note the positive side of the game: adorable graphics, pleasant soundtrack, satisfactory voice acting, complete length and pretty logical (mostly) puzzles. So, if you don't mind all of the said above, you are welcome to buy this game and enjoy it.

If you can get this for the early access price of $9.99, go for it.  Otherwise, stay away... it has some aggravating issues.
The propaganda says "no more babysitting your units", untrue.  I found that I absolutely have to micromanage because the AI does such a poor job of handling my units.  Some examples:
I've found units with their backs to the enemy (and not facing another enemy unit, nor had I previously issued any facing instructions to this unit).  One time, I watched one of these units to see how long it would remain facing away; it did so until it routed.
Sometimes units will go into what I call "Night Rider" mode where they constantly change their facing, thus never actually firing on any nearby enemies.
I have ordered artillary to fire on units which are in range and in LOS, only to have the artillary advance toward the enemy unit, rather than firing from its current position.
I have found artillary firing at distant skirmishers in cover, rather than a nice juicy unit in line formation begging for a dose of cannister.
Bottom line, if you can get it cheap, do it.  Otherwise, wait to see if they fix some of these vexing issues.

Short, sweet, and loads of fun! Crush the dastardly Yankees at Gettysburg and secure victory for the Southern people!

An RTS, Ultimate General: Gettysburg is a really well made game. Players are given predetermined troops who must seize certain objectives on the battlefield. The landscape is beautifully rendered in a clean, vibrant style. At the end of the battle's time limit (which may be delayed for certain reseans), scores are tallied to determine the victor. Casulties (I believe) are carried over into the next battle. The Iron Brigade was crushed in the first battle and practically ceased to exist (take that Lincolnites!). Before the next battle, the player is given two option to choose from on the overall goal of the next battle (seize Seminary Ridge, hold Culp's Hill, etc). Even as such a short game, this creates a lot of replayability. First time I played (Dixians of course) I narrowly lost. Second time round was an epic victory with 37,000 Yankee casulties to the South's 25,000. "Field promotions all around! President Davis will be most pleased."
I really hope this same system spawns sequels. Ultimate General: Sharpsburg, Ultimate General: Atlanta Campaigns, and Ultimate General: Spanish Fort and Fort Blakely would not only be epic but extrordinarily unique!
