While this game is no longer in Early Access, some of it still feels very much "beta".  This is not a bad thing, at least not in this instance.  For example, the graphics settings are very basic.  You'll be forced to live with Jar Jar Abrams due to any light source emitting massive amounts of bloom.  So your options are going to be darkness, one light, or blinding nova of brightness.
"So what?" That's pretty much what I mean by still feeling "beta".  Don't like music?  Better also not like other sounds, it's all one slider: Volume.  Some other GUI issues pop up, like no exit to menu.  You must always head to your desktop, and since the game has stringent survival mechanics and no pause...well it's either full exit or no bathing.
"Just GUI issues?" So far, that's about it.  I mean there is a lack of content (trees that grow, plants that grow, a sun/moon/sky/weather) But these, to me, are fluff.  The base game is there, the mechanics are sound.  It just needs the finishing polish to make it a full game.
"Lack of Documentation" There is still a big issue with information in game.  You need to craft item "Thing" which is made up of items "A" "B" "C" and "D".  Item "A" is made up of "B","C", and "E".  Item "B" is made up of "E".  Item "C" is made up of "F".  And item "D" is made up of "E","F" and "G".  Confused?  The help menu helps, but it's just a start.  (Back to feeling beta...)
Lastly, I feel the AI is just not there.  I see some slugs, and other minor mobs.  But nothing that screams "life".  The planet (always snow, nothing else...) you land on is a dead husk, with aimless monsters.  Again, the mechanics are there they just seem under utilized.
No modding that I can find, can't even change textures.  Might need to use a fancy program to edit files though.
Anyway, do I recommend the game?  It's hard to say, I really enjoy playing it.  Would enjoy it more if modding was there, or at least information as to how to mod.  Until then, it has plenty of hours worth of content to keep you busy, if you're after a crafting/building game with really bright lights.  So I give it a green thumb, though with my track record with plants it might as well be red.

Keep in mind that this is an early access game, so there are bound to be bugs, crashes and weird behaviour, but overall; I highly recommend it to anyone interested in a challenging historical wargame.

Positive:  From the man that brought you Darthmod Rome, Medieval (II), Empire, Napoleon and Shogun, comes an independant title that is sure to please any fans of the strategy genre. This game provides the deep tactical gameplay you would come to expect playing a Darthmod title. It is also worth mentioning that the graphics themselves give the game a nice flavour. Lastly the AI... It is a true challenge to defeat the computer in a battle, which is refreshing in itself. The computer will respond to your tactics in realistic ways, this makes exploiting the AI very difficult to do. However, being that this is an early access game I have only been able to face the AI in one of the scenarios. I have no idea how it will act in later battles, if it is anything like the first battle though you will be in for a challenging yet enjoyable experience.
Negatives:  The game is very solid, even in its early stages. However, there are a couple of things I found lacking in it. First of all is the controls. The buttons on the bottom right seem to work fine, but the way you must move your troops does take a bit of getting used to. You must click on the unit and then drag it to the place  you want them to move to. This doesn't sound like a very big deal until you realize that there is no way to order your troops to stand in a specific spot or line up in a specific way. It really negatively affected the gameplay in my opinion. The only other issue I found was your own troops AI... I say this because, your own troops will auto adjust their lines according to enemy positioning. This usually is very affective at cutting down the amount of micro-managing you would expect in a game like this. Although in certain situations your troops will auto adjust even when told not to. I've even run into situations where my men will just turn around when fired upon only to expose their back to the hot lead volley of musket fire that ensues. These are things that really take you out of the experience.
Final Verdict:  My final opinion on this game is an 8/10. It is truly worth picking up if you're a fan of strategy games or a casual player.
DISCLAIMER: This game is still early access. ALL issues that have been listed above are able to be changed.

- Good volume of realism, armies rout and react to surprise attacks and battlefield conditions.

- Squalor mechanic is slightly broken meaning that cities become more rebellious despite good quality living standards.
- Diplomacy is next to pointless other than for trade agreements, alliances very rarely offer any military benefits.
Overall this is a great game and its only minor things that prevent this game from being perfect.

So a friend recommended this game to me while, by chance, he noticed it was 80% off. Never bought a better 5$ game. I am not, or have ever been, a big fan of Diablo style games. I just kind of missed that train. But this game broke my pre-concieved ideas about it in just the first few hours.
The world is pretty rich and just when I thought I was making progress on the map, I discovered I had only uncovered a dot of it. Every level, while comes slower than my personal taste, gives back benefits you can see each time, rather than a ton of levels all the time with hardly anything to show for each one. Another one of the games strong points is customization. Oh man the customization. It's not as intimidating as 'Path of Exile' (a Diablo-style game I tried), though a tad confusing at first. Even with reading up I still had that "trash first character" with my points being in places that were less than helpful. The 'runes' you get to increase your skills are pretty abundant as well, but not always with the ones you need, which can be solved by trading in 1-4 runes of any kind to pick the one you want, increasing your power at a good pace (for a small fee). Combine all that with a rich world, much like Skyrim, open and with entirely too much to do, with so much exploring to do, and you've got a game that will have your style of play, with the story and pacing that you want.
However the game's not perfect. Some annoying things like having to drop items and pick them back up to stack them, certain moves having a hard time targeting an enemy making you dance in place until you find that sweet spot, and not having a very clear chart of where your stats are coming from (though it does list which ones you have, just not if it's on your gear, temporary effect, etc). But if you aren't terribly anal about little bumps in the road, it's a great game to buy.

Say hello to one of the most noteworthy recent horror games. Looking at an early access top down procedurally generated rogue-like, you'd be forgiven for thinking this is just like every other game currently on steam. But, Coin Crypt has an original twist that adds strategy, and enough polish to elevate it above most of the dross early access throws at people now-a-days.
In this game, your battle moves are tied to coins. Once you use that coin on attacking, healing or any other move, it disappears. Every coin also has a monetary value that can be used to trade at a variety of points throughout the game. What all of this means is that you always need something, keeping every game exciting. If either side runs out of coins in battle, they lose, but if you defeat an enemy before they run out, you get all of the coins they haven't used. So you always have to becareful with your choices in and out of battle. You might end up with a bag full with attacks just when you're hanging on 3 hp and desparately need a heal, or a bag full of heal coins that limit your attack options significantly and leaves you to wait for the enemy to run out of coins, but then you don't get any attacks from the enemy at the end of battles!
But most of the coins don't come from enemies, but from chests. You can only pick a limited number of coins from chests, giving you more choices to make. As the game goes on, more coins of different types get introduced with the enemies and chests, altering your deck to have more coin diversity.
Naturally for rogue-likes, you will die quite a bit. When you die or win a run you get to spend the coins you got throughout the run into unlocking new characters. Every character plays differently but most if not all of them aren't objectively better than others. You unlock your first classes quite quickly to experiment with but the more you unlock, the more expensive they get. This is the game's way to give a purpose to each playthrough, some people will like it, and some will want a more substantial meta game. There are over 14 classes so to those who do care it will take quite a bit of play to unlock all of them!
This is what early access should be, Coin Crypt was already functional from the first time it arrived on steam and has only improved ever since.
So, yeah, this is worth a buy!

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is what I would like to call "the revival of horror." Amnesia is a beautiful and deliciously horrifying game.
You play as Daniel who wakes up in a castle with no recollection of how he got there or what he was doing there. Upon searching deeper into the castle, he learns from a note from himself that he has amnesia and that he is to kill a man named Alexander. He also learns that something only refered to as "The Shadow" is stalking him and seeks to kill him. From here, the true descent into madness begins.
The game is played in a first person perspective. In games such as F.E.A.R. or Condemnded, one can defend themselves using combat. In Amnesia, however, combat is not an option due to the lack of it. This further increases the tension felt in this game because all you can do is run and hide. Players can hide in dark corners or inside wardrobes. Players can go as far as to grab any items in a room and barracade a door (though sometimes not recommended). The game forces a player to use their wits to out maneuver the horrors that you run into along your descent. Another mechanic is sanity. Sanity can affect your gameplay by warping your vision and increases the breathing of a character. Once sanity has been drained, the character gives in to an episode of insanity that can give away the player's position while hiding. Sanity is decreased from the characters phobia of dark places which can be fixed by holding up your lantern or lighting candles, but doing this can also give yourself away. Another way it decreases is by looking at the horrors that are constantly hunting you, similar to Call of Cthulu: Dark Corners of the Earth. Sanity can be restored by lights and solving puzzles.
The music in this game does wonders to set the mood and tone of the game. The scores range from forboding dark ambeince to intense orchestras for chases and to a relaxing tone when in a safe place.
The story is delivered via file pick-ups. Main story files are fully voiced while minor pick-ups aren't.
All-in all, Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a wonderful horror game that is guaranteed to scare you.

What do you get, when you have a multiplayer focused game, terrible marketing and therefore almost no awareness of your game, coupled with a low-budget approach?
The answer is Etherium.
The gameplay itself is solid and an experience, that focuses on the main things you'd expect from a strategy title:
- rock/paper/scissors mechanics
- multiple tech tiers
- focus on map/ressource control
- base building and defense
It takes all of this and breaks it down to the bare essentials:
- Counter mechanics are straith forward and most units are hardcounters to others.
- Unit production is almost instant.
- The map is controlled via sectors with a capture point in each.
- Base buildings are limited to pre-defined locations in the sectors and can only be upgraded however you see fit (with the exception of defenses, which are limited by number in each sector).
All that makes the game a very streamlined experience, which is not necessarily a bad thing. You can focus on making decision. And having only a limited set of options makes every choice count.
So it doesn't sound to bad, right? HOWEVER as I initially stated Etherium is obviously built with Multiplayer in mind. You have only a lackluster "skirmish vs AI" - campaign mode, your "rank" is displayed in the main menu aswell as a button to enlist in matchmaking... If only pressing that button would do anything!
Because YES, Etherium is dead already. I strongly advice to look it up on
, should you have any willingness to buy it left in you. With a peak of around 15 (!) players per day this is a multiplayer title with no one to play with.
It should come as no suprise to the devs, that people will not pick up their game, if they fail so hard at raising awareness. Etherium is yet another failed attempt to create a low-budget title that stands on multiplayer alone, but just doesn't have the content, quality and appeal to get enough people to actually play it.
Conclusion: Steer clear of this game and save yourself the money. Neither the Singleplayer nor Multiplayer are worth the price tag.

Have you played an RTS within the past 10 years? Then you probably have seen everything worth seeing in Etherium already. The biggest issue with RTS games nowadays (and other "dead genres" being "revived" lately) is that they try to get away with being just "good enough". There is nothing groundbreaking, nothing creative or inventive, no new game design ideas present here and, despite having its release pushed back multiple times, feels like instant bargain bin fodder during a genre drought.
Outside of the mandatory multiplayer, you have a campaign with convoluted rules (with each side having their own secondary victory conditions) and a skirmish mode. The campaign is very frustrating because of simple oversights, like not being able to save during your opponent's turns and a star system UI that doesn't provide enough information. I spent easily almost two hours defending my territories during opponent's turns simply because quitting the game meant restarting the opponent's turn. This is of course on top of all the issues present in the actual gameplay...
...of which there is little to mention. The main objective (and single game mode) is to either destroy the other player's main base or deplete their tickets by bombarding their mothership with turrets high in the tech tree. Regions of territory are strictly defined and can have only one base inside for adding upgrades onto. The problem with the territories having a fixed size is that smaller territories only allow smaller bases. This creates claustrophobic maps, with clearly defined chokepoints that force you down a corridor to your opponent's base. Most of my campaign victories were from converting the neutral factions on the map and attack-moving them into the enemy's main base.
The absolute bare minimum went into Etherium's factions and their unit design. Units for each race have creative names like Standard Infantry, Siege Vehicle, and Bomber. Races share all the same units (!) with each having only 4 unique units. This might be acceptable in a turn-based strategy game where you have 20+ factions or dozens of units, but here you only have about 6 different units for each unit type. Each race also shares 3 of their 6 faction skills, similar to Dawn of War's faction ability system. Everything about the races just feels very cut-and-pasted and bland and makes me wonder why this game's release was pushed back multiple times.
I am ashamed to have fallen for the hype for this game. If you are thirsty for a good (or great or amazing, whatever) RTS, then revisit an old one instead of wasting money on this. This game couldn't be any blander or generic if it tried. If a monkey hitting keys at random on a typewriter could eventually type out the complete works of William Shakespeare, then this game is proof that they can code a video game too.

What a great story. The graphics, the music, the storyline, it all pulls you in and makes you feel like part of the plot. Some may be able to easily relate to Bunny (The protagonist). The choices you make draw you in, make you feel the happiness of a good decision, the sadness and fear of a bad decision, and the excitement of what is yet to come, and what you have mixed yourself up with in the story. The music was a key factor, I feel. I always wanted to make soundtracks for my stories, and the creators have found a perfect way to do it. There are some tracks that loop a little much, but a few clicks down the rabbit hole and you are into a beautiful song, or an entrancing melody that holds you and wraps you in what the character is feeling as they fight to figure out their life. I'm sure many people can relate to the struggle of not knowing where you are going, or if what you are doing is the right choice, and this visual novel is by far one of the most interesting stories I have ever read and related to on such a profound label. It isn't too wordy to put off a more common reader, or younger eyes, but it isn't dumbed down like some stories out there. You need to pay attention, and learn more about the world and people in it, and once you do, you will be glad you did. I recommend this game for anyone that enjoys a cyberpunk plot and feel, a deeply written and profound story, and if you can relate to a life of struggles and bad choices, then this is definitely for you.
On a personal note, I really hope the creator comes up with more. It is a little bit of a shame that this one is free, but Invisible Apartment Zero is a bit of money spent, though I am sure it is money well spent, and I'll gladly help crowd fund this endeavor. Also, this is the first time I am writing a review for something on Steam. Even out of my favorite games to play, and ones that I have played that Steam has, but that I had played on different consoles or independantly, this is the one that inspired me to leave a positive review. This creator is heading in a good direction, and whether or not they need support, they have it from at the very least, one die hard fan. I can't wait to learn more about the characters and be even more a part of their lives. As silly as I can be with life, I take some things very seriously, and this story had me at the feels.

This game is a wonderful game as I played it for +300 hours. The classic servers are there if you want to play the real deal of many gamemodes varying to team death match, capturing points, capture the case (CTF), to holiday events holding boss battles or objectives based tasks, to many favorites of man vs machine which most people can understand as "Zombies" In addition to that, there are also community servers where you can have fun flying around or playing on all crit servers.
Classes:
There are tons of classes to choose from of three catagories: Assualt, Defense, and Support
In the assualt we have:
Scout - Agile and uses shotguns and pistols
Pyro - Flame based weapons
Soldier - Rockets and shotguns
In the Defense we have:
Demoman - Gernade launcher or melee focused
Engineer - Builds turrents, dispensers (ammo and health), and teleporters as well as using shotguns
Heavy - The "tank" has lots of health, but slow and uses a chaingun and shotguns
In the support we have:
Medic - Heals
Sniper - Snipes and can also have an SMG
Spy - Disquises, turns invisible, saps engi buildings, and assassinates also uses revolvers
-All classes are balanced to counter each other such as the spy kills the sniper and saps engi buildings where the pyro can easily eliminate the spy threat
-You can maximize the potential of each class on which items and weapons you assign them.
-You can develop your own play style from each class such as the case with the demoman where you can purely use gernade launchers, gernade jump and fly around and melee, or just heavely focus on melee which are dubbed "Demoknights"
-There are lots to customize for each class from custmetics to stats of each weapon or item.
Maps:
-All maps are configured in the right way depending on how you and or your team take avantage on placement, environment, and strategy
-I think all maps are well designed and we all have our own favorite and hated maps of course, but they are well designed.
Community:
This game is heavily community based depending on how you do things such as trading, doing events, community servers, and more

At this point of EA Galactology is good fun for 10-20 hours, after which somewhat shallow mechanics start to annoy. It's quite free from bugs and plays really well from begining to the end. Updates come regularly and add nicely to the gameplay. Developer is active and communicative about plans for the game.
So, Galactology is a base builder with fun comic graphics. It's easy to get into and understand the mechanics. Economics simulation is quite non existant (but being currently improved upon), you always strike profit. If you quickly build stuff that you just reasearched you run into shortages, but there really isn't much need for that. Biggest problem on base building/management is ability to get overall view of demand as there is no queueing and people reserve a "spot" accross the map and walk there, thus everything seems quite empty on a large base.
Planet exploration is all about harvesting materials from new planets. It's essential part to the game. It's part of the game mechanics that at this point doesn't offer much - you pop bulding's and leave, but isn't especially boring either. Materials are carried back to the base by your autopiloted ships.
Galactology is quite possible the best light base builder at the moment. To be a gem it will need more humor (now it's just "funny" graphics), little bit improved economics system and some special thing to make it "unique". It might might be able to pull it of.
4/5 stars for EA.

I really dislike the way this game was designed.  Initially nothing is clear on what your stats mean and do, the power of the 5 gems, how to attack or interact with the map, the fact that the rooms loop Pac-Man style across the borders, which I only figured out on accident several attempts in, or what you're really trying to accomplish.  There is a general explanation on the store page here about all of that, but whenever I get a new game on here I expect the game itself to explain those simple features.
Regardless, even after you figure that out you realize how horribly unfair and unbalanced the game is when a few minutes of rethinking design features could easily remedy it.  Whenever you start the game you begin with absolutely nothing, surrounded in a field of 36 rooms with question marks scattered around.  Your equipment is a joke and you have no spending money or flares.  The flares, when activated, allow you to see what all of the question marks immediately around you are.  Whether it be an empty room, stairs up/down a floor, a treasure chest, enemy, and so on.  Starting off with none of them means you just have to blindly walk around and see what comes your way.  In one attempt, my very first move led me directly to the final boss!  Since the game has 6 floors I don't see why the enemies don't level up accordingly.  Even if that didn't change, having a better beginning equipment payload would give you some feeling of control and capability, a chance and a choice on whether you hold onto those flares for a while or use them early.
From the rounds I played, most of what you're able to find is either worthless or invaluable.  The 5 powerful items are useful, but they don't actually grant you abilities like you would typically think of in a game like this.  Instead their function is to ward off or counter the negative status effects you can get from reading books or opening chests.  That's their stupendous power.  No wonder the final boss wants them so bad; if he can't leave the castle he probably doesn't want to be afflicted with those status effects from walking around the same 6 levels over and over again.  Several books and chests will either have no effect whatsoever or curse you; some grant rewards but there's never any way to tell which it'll be until you activate it.  Very surprised there's no item that gives that as an ability because it'd be very useful.  You would think better weapons would be paramount, but it's much better to just run from fights than to engage so they aren't that valuable.  That makes the armor very useful as you'll likely get hit by something eventually in all but the best of runs.  There's one item called the sign that wards off almost every negative status, making me wonder why the 5 items are needed if that is so much more powerful than the others individually.  Sadly the absolute best item in the whole game is the lamp.  Once you get it, if it spawns in your run that is, it acts as a permanent flare, making it so you always know what is around you, meaning you can farm out the precious items before opening chests and reading books to protect yourself while avoiding all enemy fights entirely.  It totally changes the way the game plays and is undoubtedly broken.  A regular lamp should not be that much better than mystical artifacts.
I think the worst part of the entire game, though there are other contending features for that dishonor, is how the stats work.  You begin with very low stats, and unless you choose the warrior, are so vulnerable it's unreal.  Sure, with how this games works, any attempt only lasts for a few minutes (or seconds in some cases), but it's no fun dying through no fault of your own because you got a bad round of RNG.  There's no skill or planning, you just push a direction and hope you come across something good early instead of a blight that immediately ends the run.  Oops, bumped into a strong enemy in the first 5 turns; there goes half my health as I tried to run away!  Regardless, what really sucks is that as weak as you are it's possible to increase your stats and be a greater force to be reckoned with.  However, there are maximum limits on how high you can level them.  Why?  It's really unlikely you'll do so well to get to that point anyways, but considering how overpowered the final boss is already, why hinder the player more when they're already working against a stacked deck?
Here's the kicker that makes this absolutely atrocious though.  Enemies have separate stats for their health, attack, and intellect.  If you whale on an enemy it obviously lowers their HP and leaves their attack alone, like any other game.  However, you aren't granted that same luxury back.  Your HP and attack power are linked together.  If an enemy hits you, your attack power dwindles; it's a total double whammy.  Not only are you closer to dying you're now less viable in combat, making it so that even weak enemies are incredibly hazardous because they'll drain your attack.  They don't give you anything worth a darn so it's absolutely not worth the risk.  I've played several games and this has to be the first time where a well-equipped person avoids fighting a puny rat they can kill in one shot because doing so could weaken them and ruin their chances of victory.  Ridiculous.
The way the magic spells work is just as bad.  Casting a stun spell costs 1 point of intellect and a fireball takes 2 points; each time you use a spell you'll lower the strength of your ability to cast spells.  At least the warrior's attack goes down when he's injured, but if you want to be a mage you'll get weaker each time you attack!  There is a spell that makes it so that if your IQ is higher than your enemies they die instantly without you losing any magic and for a while I thought that was the winning strategy.  However it's worthless against the final boss who is working with 99 against your max of 40, meaning you'll die if you do it.  Plus, with that max of 40, I came across a random orc of all things with a stat of 41.  Talk about insulting and punishing.
Throughout my attempts I have been able to get all of the items and get to the final boss, but I haven't succeeded in killing him and frankly I'm not going to spend anymore time trying.  I'm sure it's possible to beat the final boss, but from the description below it suggests there's no reason to.  That you won't even get an ending or anything because ultimately you can't get out of the castle.  For such a basic, short, unfair, and overall pointless arcade-style game I would expect it to be free or pocket change at the most.  Even if it cost under a buck though, in my opinion this isn't worth picking up regardless.  Escape while you still can and avoid this game altogether.

While all four storyline arcs can easily be completed in a total time of under two hours, this game offers a good combination of intriguing storyline, catchy music and consistently high quality artwork. It manages to throw an almost endless barrage of (often intentionally bad) puns at you without it becoming tiresome, and even offers a plot-twist or two to try and keep you off the track of the real perp. While the character cast is small and predictable at first, they are very thoroughly worked out and run deeper than they seem, making the story feel complete without becoming too crowded.
In short: an excellent game, as long as you don't expect to get more than a few hours of gameplay out of it.

I'm not going to give this game a number score because its early access and that makes the entire game very hard to judge till we see the final product. I will say I recommend it and its absolutely something to look at. My frustration with Total War games has always been the absolute poor lack of scale of the size of battles fought. I mean major Napoleonic battles with armies of 5k on each. side is laughable. I guess they wanted to show off the blood of the fighting man on the ground or to zoom and see each and every dude you put down but it means that they sacrificed the actual use of tactics of that age. Napoleon you didn't just hold one hill with your entire army and wait for the enemy to meander his way up you held that hill, the ravine between, the next hill over till you hit river or something defendable enough to anchor your line, and this game gets it. You don't want to just stretch your line as far as possible to get that flanking bonus like in TW you actually want a reserve. Also the entire battle doesn't play out in a day. You get to watch in your first engagement with Hill turns from a skirmish of a couple thousand men to the almost claustrophobic panic of engagements of 20k on each side contantsly jostle and throwing themselves and testing than falling back. Also the movement system is a really good idea. Instead of just pressing on the terrain where you want your units to go you glide you plot their movement with a swipe of your mouse its quick and effective.
EDIT:
Alot of the bad stuff in my orginal review has been corrected with the positive stuff staying intact. So I'll say what's still wrong with the game at this point. The map while being very carefully and lovingly designed is still a pain and worse I fear that they have no intention of making it a 3d map. While the artillary and it's strange line of sight issues has been fixed the 2d map makes it impossible to perfectly realize the idea they had with line of sight and artillary and such. Judging if one hill is taller than the next hill over is harder than it should be. The town of Gettysburg itself as well suffers from this since it isn't as much of a obstacle as it should be in the heat of a battle, beyond again Line of sight issues. Units that are sent though the town should have to either break up their lines and become ineffective or avoid going through the town entirely, instead they simply glide through as if there are no buildings in the way and even get a significant cover. I still don't know and don't think that walls or the railroad ditch (which should function as a trench) adds to your cover and if it infact doesn't than it REALLY should.
I've been noticing some people are complaining about the lack of complexity to the game and I honestly don't think  that should be a issue. Complexity and Depth are not the same thing after all and this game is truly deep. The first engagement I've played many times from both sides and its never the same engagement twice. As the Union i've held my line before and even took the objectives of the confederates while other times I've almost been dislodged from my primary objective and taken more of a whipping on the defensive than I dished out. This isn't to say its because theres a random unfair factor, its simply because same approaches have different results against different AI opponents. Archers 1200 man brigades internal numbers don't change just how the AI uses him. I in turn have to change my tactics because of this. I will have to pause the game consider that if I weaken my quiet but already battered left flank to support the center turning to the enemys saliant on my right can I break through it before my battered but quiet left gets routed which in turn makes my center turned in the opposite direction open to 2 or more entire volleys being shot in their rear and opens my artillary up as well which is a disaster. That's depth and that situation will not be the same twice. Are the game mechanics complex that made that situation possible, not really but what complexity is there is enough to be used in so many different ways to make a wide varity of different decisions possible with the same tools and thats depth. In contrast a rube goldburg machine is complex but its not deep because after all its bells, whistles and moving parts it still only cracks a single egg and thats all it can ever do.

I am sorry to have to write this for a game with over 99% positive reviews but the truth must be told.
First off, I must acknowldege that this is a early access version of the game and so there is always hope that the game will improve, but for me there are significant short commings in the version that leave this version far short of what would make this a great Strategy game.
Having studied the strategy and tactics of real 19th century warefare I was hoping this game would be a good way to expereince and explore those tactics.  I recognize that no game, no matter how well written would be able to capture 100% the reality of that, but this game lacks all of those elements and for me fails on so many levels and makes the game unable to hold my interests.
The game does offer much as a strategy game and I do acknowledge the many good things about this game which the vast majority of reviewers have already pointed out, but I must provide a negative review in order to provide balance to others considering purchasing the game.
The game touts itself a a simulation of Gettysburg and as such I would expect it to use as much of the real commands and tactics as possible for a game, a goal that Sid Meier's Gettysburg better achieved, although that game had many short comings as well.
To make this an effective civil war startegy game I should be able to issue commands to units that real commanders would issue.  There is too much automation in the way the troops behave and act.  It seems that the only thing I can tell the troops is where to go.  I can not make a decision on how to form, single battle line, double  battle line, etc.  These were critical decisions a commander would make deciding where he needed strength (double line) and where he needed to guard the flanks (single line)  I might even want to order a unit to "dig in"  I really only have once choice for forming my units and they are made for me,
If I have a brigade arriving to the rear, I might want to position them in a certain location to be ready to reinforce my line, but as soon as I do that they move from colomn formation to a line formation.  In fact, if I even order a unit to halt, they will move from column to battle line.  This denies me the tactical decision to leave a brigade in the faster moving column formation until I decide to move them into a battle line.  I can't order my calvary to mount or dismount,  Gamble's skirmishers remain skirmishers.  In reality, once the infantry arrived, I would order them to mount up and guard the flanks or scout the north or west, but  I can't do that again denying me important tactical decisions.  I can't order my artillary to limber up or un-limber and the artillary seems to move the same regardless taking away another important decision that can make or break a battle.     When I order a unit to "Fall Back" an experience unit would accept this to mean a slow withdrawl while fighting a delaying action an orderly process to tactically reposition the troops.  Instead it looks more like a retreat, even with high morale units.
All too often, units  are automatically moving to "face the enemy" again denying me the tactical decision to maintain my line unless I specifically remember to tell them to hold.  In reallity they should hold the line unless they are told to skirmish.  A unit in real life would never make a move like that.  This often creates units with their flanks in the air when my intentions was to have their flanks anchored by other units or natural obstacles.   It seems I have a whole army of Dan Sickles.
Looking in the release notes I see there is work pending on group commands and obliques but not sure if these pending additions will significantly improve these limitations.   I also wished there was more granularity in the units as primarily I can only control at the brigade level.  It would be nice if I could issue orders at either the regimental or brigade level.  For civil war history buffs the role of regiments is of high interest and a good civil war game that fails to recognize the regiment falls short of satisfying a civil war enthusist.  Players should be able to control both the regimental and brigade level units.  For example, order a brigade to form a double battle line, but during the battle, order a specific regiment in that line to move to a single battle line at the end of the brigade to guard the flank.  I should be able to order a single regiment for form a skirmish line in front of the brigade or order the regiment at the end of the brigade to wheel right or left to avoid having my flank in the air.  While having division and corps commanders in the game adds historical interest and recognizes these hostoric figures I agree that the way the are implented in the game is correct.  Since these roles were more strategic and administative there is not need for tactical commands at the division or corps level.  I do look forward to the addition of divisional commander characters to add depth to the game.  But the lack of regimental/brigade level tactical commands is a big dissapointment.  Ideally, I should be able to issue commands to those units like a real commander would and they would react based on how experienced and well drilled they are.  For example. ordering a unit to form a double battle line might be done quickly and smartly for a well drilled and experienced unit but a little slower for a new unit.  To me it appears that the developers lack a deep understanding of civil war tactics and army procedures.  Even little things like the fact that I issue a "run" command instead of a "double time" command.  Nitpicking for sure and an easy fix, but perhaps a symptom of how far off this game is from being a true civil war strategy and tactics game.
So bottom line, a lot of hard work went into this game.  The map is beatiful and the game is playable as a basic, simple, strategy game, but as a game claiming to be a civil war strategy game, it lacks sufficient depth at this time to be a rich and satisfying game of civil war strategy and tactics.  In a toss up between this game and Sid Meir's Gettysburg, Sid would win.  While I hope there is substantial improvement between the early access and final release I can not recommend the game at this time.  However, at the early access price of only $9.99 it is worth a look by any strategy game fan and I hope that our early support and honest feedback will encourage the developers to improve on the game and help it to rise to the level of one of the best civil war strategy games ever.
Good luck.

Pros:
- Faction and Unit Diversity, muliple unique infantry units, eveything has an intended use and purpose.
- Large scale conflicts.
- Unit count for each faction: approx: 30+ per faction and several turrets each.
- Airdropped supply and resupply is cool.
- Another RTS type of game, has been and always will be my favorite genre.
- Interesting and unique strategy possibility with sub-factions - you and the AI can use them against each other.
- AI is fairly capable, it will befriend sub-factions and build an array of units to assault you later in the game.
- Two colossals for each side, nice surprise.
-Weather system is a lot of fun, seeing a hurricane come when you in the middle of an air assault is great.
- Overall, I'm really enjoying this game, the uniqueness of each faction is really nice, totally enjoy the Vectides look and feel.
- Stable, no game breaking bugs noted.
- Ability to upscale image in game, pick higher resolution than your monitor and then have it downscaled to fit your monitor, no this is not AMD VSR or Nvidia DSR - it's within the game itself, I'm using Nvidia 770m.
Cons:
Intar just looks as if each unit were comprised of about 50 polygons (being somewhat generous here). Whoever did the graphics for this faction needs to SERIOUSLY take a moment to reflect on their overall level of effort. Quality wise, it's Vectides>>>>>Consortium>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>Intar
- No articulated parts on tanks and many other vehicles, i.e., tracks that don't move, units that literally glide over the terrain = painful to watch.
- Units do not emit any type of munitions, for example a multiple rocket launcher - never truly fires a rocket, everything is supposed, no rockets ever leave the tube.
- Maps, horrible looking, think red, red, red - everything, the one world where it's supposed to look somewhat similar to earth, more red. Everything is flat, meaning there are minimal shards of vegetation, you'll see things that look like grass, though they are lifeless, as are the planets themselves. They have a low resolution cell-shaded appearance.
- Sound has static throughout at random times.
- No way currently to offset teams, 2 vs 1 etc. everything has to be equal.
- No save game function in skirmish mode.
- No advanced movements, formations etc.
- Units will not engage often unless directly forced to, your base can be under assault and your units unless they are directly in the enemies line of sight will not engage.
That said, I really like this game a lot, would love to see a fourth faction via DLC and some more maps offered.

Developed by Tindalos Interactive (known for Stellar Impact) and published by Focus Home Interactive (Cities XL Series, Trine 2, Farming Simulator), Etherium is a daring new multiplayer RTS game looking to pump fresh energy into a slumbersome genre. Not since Starcraft 2 has there been such a relevant sci-fi entry for a 4X multiplayer game. Tindalos is a small, independent studio so much credit is deserving for even attempting such a monumental task.
In Etherium players will choose one of three different factions, each with their own unique abilities. These factions battle across multiple maps for control of a precious resource called etherium either against other players in multiplayer games or against AI players in single player skirmish mode and conquest mode. There are a multitude of units and upgrades available and units can level up through combat. Aside from the main factions, some maps also include a neutral faction which can advantageously be swayed into aiding your cause and be a nuisance for your opponents. The maps offer a variety of terrain features and can be used to your advantage as well. Additionally, Etherium contains a weather element based on terrain that can greatly impact battles and strategies.
Etherium gameplay will be similar to most other RTS games of the genre and easy for veteran gamers to become familiar with early on (there is a tutorial included for newcomers), but in a much more direct approach. Instead of expansive base-building elements, Etherium introduces the idea of dividing the maps into zones with a central node where players can build a multi-functional "control structure" to gain control of that particular region. Each of these structures have a variety of upgrades and expansions available, offering a lot of flexibility in your strategic approach. This stream-lining concept allows for more focus on the combat element of the game while still offering a full compliment of benefits and options for your faction.
While the graphics aren't going to leave players with that "Wow!" feeling, they are solid and more than get the job done. Zooming in will show some greater detail but is wasted since a game like this requires players to have a broader visibility of the map. There is a good soundtrack and the cut-scenes offer up a back story of sorts, which is good since (for unknown reasons) the developers chose not to include a lengthy single player campaign. The different factions are well-balanced, which is important for a mutiplayer combat game. This game has low system requirements and runs smoothly on most systems even using the highest visual settings. The AI is very intelligent and the combat is very direct so players can fully expect to be challenged even in single player skirmishes.
While Etherium doesn't reach its full potential and may fall short in comparison with some of the most renown 4X Space RTS games of our generation, it is still a solid game and offers many hours of entertaining gameplay. Everything this game does, it does well and could be the building block for a successful series with a few tweaks and additional improvements. Time will tell, but for RTS fans who have been neglected by the genre for a long time, this game is one you definitely want to get your hands on. I thoroughly enjoyed it.

It must suck to be a chicken, you lay eggs and people eat them, you don't lay enough eggs and people eat you.
It's little wonder that chickens have a nervous disposition, If I were a chicken, I'd be a chicken too.
There are plenty of other less tasty creatures that lay eggs, most of which have some sort of strategy to keep them safe until they hatch.
Turtles will bury their eggs in the sand, penguins will shuffle about with their eggs balancing on their feet (Happy Feet was a great film wasn't it!) and Xenomorphs will lay their eggs in the chests of Colonial Marines.
Now there's another creature, the Madrith (some sort of giant inter-dimensional chicken), which has a unique strategy to keep its eggs safe, it lays them in another dimension where I assume it hopes that they'll be safe from their natural predators.
Unfortunately this strategy doesn't really work out too well for the Madrith as the dimension it has chosen to be its safety blanket is ours.
Well, from our perspective, that's an easy one. The egg, it's always the egg, there's a perfectly good planet floating around minding its own business when "Boom" a ruddy great egg appears on its surface, no sign of the Madrith, just the egg, it's always just the tasty, tasty egg.
These particular giant eggs are far too valuable to be left alone whilst nature takes its course,  they're so valuable in fact, that when they start appearing once every thousand years or so, the whole galaxy gears up to fight over them.
You see, these eggs contain a unique and amazing resource, a minute quantity of which can produce enough energy to power a large colony and enable vast vessels to travel through space at the speed of light.
This eggy gas is so valuable that the three dominant races of the galaxy, in anticipation of a visit from the extra-dimensional Easter bunny, build up their forces and the millennial "Egg Wars" begin.
Luckily for us, the  Madrith are creatures of habit, they always lay their eggs on six "deposit" planets, each with their own varied environments, ranging from" Hoth-like" Ice Worlds to "Tatooine-like" desert globes, each environment provides its own challenges, it's own weather events (which is a nice touch) and each will require a different strategic approach.
To get to these planets you're going to need to construct fleets and park them in orbit, from there you can clear out any enemy fleets before sending the troops down for the ground war
Don't expect a "Distant Worlds" or "Sins of a Solar Empire" type experience here though, this is a simplistic "space layer" used primarily to select which planet to fight on next with a little espionage and research mixed in for good measure.
When you've selected your battleground of choice, you'll be treated  to a cut scene showing the seed of your first colony drop down from space and establish your initial base.
You'll quickly want to sniff out some eggy goodness and start gathering its Etherium, this will be the resource you'll be using to build units and structures in the game.
Each planet is divided up into territories with each territory having a monolith which you need to take control of.
This is achieved by building a "Comms Infantry" which you can send out to establish an outpost at the monolith site.
These outposts can then be expanded with a choice of extensions, each of which will provide a bonus regarding Etherium production, research, number of units you can control, etc.
You can also build a limited number of turrets to help defend your interests in each territory. There are a few different types to choose from, each with their own particular strengths and weaknesses.
They say that attack is the best form of defence and that certainly holds true in Etherium.
You're going to need an effective war machine to remove any unwanted intruders from the map and there are plenty of units for you to construct, providing you've had chance to research them, the command points to control them and the Etherium to pay for their construction.
This research mechanic does  make the initial combat encounters of the game a slightly shallow affair as you'll only be churning out basic infantry until you've managed to build up a few research points to unlock the more interesting units.
In addition to the three dominant powers in the game you also encounter three minor races.
You can steam roller over these and wipe them out or if you want to be a little more subtle, you can try and bring them round to your side, this is achieved by converting some of your Etherium refinery improvements in to a black-market service which will gain the minor factions favour, you might even benefit from a unique unit or two if you take the time to play nice with the little guys.
There are also a bunch of special abilities you can utilise to give you an edge on the battlefield, these range from temporarily dispelling the fog of war in a certain place on the map to blasting the hell out of an area with an orbital cannon (which is hugely satisfying!).
There is also a political card mechanic which you can play in the space layer of the game between battles, these could help you ally with one of the previously mentioned "little races" or maybe even force an enemy to miss a turn. This is a welcome addition to add a little more depth to the game.
Like a Faberge egg, Etherium can be quite pleasing to look at initially, holding the right mouse button down lets you look around the landscape, you can even look up to the sky where you'll see ships in orbit taking pot shots at each other.
However, the more you look  at a Faberge Egg, the more you realise it's just a glittery egg, the same can be said of Etheriums graphics, once the novelty of the right click free cam wears off, the graphics themselves begin to look a little mundane, not awful, just not as special as you'd initially hoped.
Don't go into this game expecting rich cut scenes and a detailed narrative thread interwoven between the battles or you'll be disappointed, the fight for the eggs premise is about as deep as the plot gets, which is a little disappointing, I've always viewed little narrative cut scenes in RTS titles to be a reward for winning the preceding battle.
Etherium also really wants to be a multiplayer title, which is fine and probably explains the lack of narrative, but online play does seem a little on the quiet side, especially for such a new game, that's not to say that by the time you read this a healthy community won't have built up around the multiplayer experience....  I hope so because it's needed to increase the longevity of the games appeal.
However, the single player campaign and skirmish modes whilst not dazzling  are perfectly entertaining in their own right and the AI seems competent which is always a huge plus for an RTS title.
Etherium is a competent RTS and it ticks a lot of the right boxes, if your looking for a straight forward no nonsense experience you could do a lot worse, the downside is that whilst its a perfectly playable RTS it doesn't really bring anything new to the breakfast table.
It's like an egg, it's nice, you know what to expect, if you're in the mood for it then you'll probably enjoy it, but sometimes you want something more than an egg for breakfast.

Invisible Apartment is a short visual novel that took a painstakingly long time for me to finish. Thirty minutes of gameplay should be a breeze to get done in one session -- especially for bingers like myself -- but I just couldn't bring myself to do so this time around. In an attempt to judge the game as unbiasedly as possible, I ended up "leaving" and coming back to it three separate times. Unfortunately, these breaks didn't make the story (or the characters) any less of a hassle to sit through. I personally found the MC and the cast to be a group of bland, stock characters with very little dynamic and very little room to grow. The writing and general flow of information seemed inconsistent and the relationships between the characters were lacking, if not completely dull.
For what it's worth, the artwork and the music of Invisible Apartment aren't half-bad; they're definitely the strong suits of the game. Everything else, however, just comes off as "rough draft" material rather than "finished product" material. Despite it being free and short, this is one VN on Steam I wouldn't really recommend.

This is one of those games where you wish you could leave a review without saying Yes or No to recommending it. Because I do feel like there is value to the game, but on the other hand the bugs and some of the game mechanics make the game very frustrating. The tutorial is very basic, and not very fleshed out. It is helpful when you first start out, but there is a lot missing from it. Once you're on your own, there are a lot of issues.
The first thing I encountered was not being to move items. The developer has stated that this a core mechanic of the game. If you build something in the wrong place, you have to destroy it and then rebuild it elsewhere. This would probably be fine, if you could get your people to get onto that pronto. But here we have the next issue I encountered. There doesn't seem to be a way to prioritise tasks. If all your people are busy doing other things, the object you want dismantled will sit there waiting for minutes and minutes. This is also an issue when it comes to crafting items - especially cooking food.
For example, I had almost 30 people in my small colony at the time of writing this review and they were almost all starving. Not because I didn't have any food, because I had plenty of raw ingredients. No, because no one would cook it! I had every single person set to cooking. In the global settings for kitchens I had it set to maintain a minimum of 100 basic meals, and I set the kitchen to make 100 basic meals. And then.... nothing. Occasionally someone who finished a different task, would wander over and make themselves one meal. And then... go back to doing something else. Not cooking. Not making soap. (Everyone was feeling dirty, but no one was making soap either.)
And then, everyone started losing their minds. They would stop working, and started attacking other people. Nothing I would do would restore their mental health. But there wasn't a whole lot I could do because everything that could help was locked behind advanced research and after 7 hours or so of playing I still had not unlocked the items that would help. There were other more important things that needed to be researched first.
And then there were building issues. If you want to expand a room, you have to remove the wall which of course, means that the items in your room won't work because they need an enclosed room to work. And if the wall is external then the objects start degrading because they are exposed to the outside air and by the time your people get the wall removed and rebuilt everything is fritzing and exploding and
when things explode, no one puts the fire out even though everyone is set to firefighter. I mean, jeeze. It just got so very frustrating.
I really wanted to like this game, and I think given time, it could be great. But right now there is too much that feels like it needs to be fixed. Buy the game if it goes on special for cheapy cheap but otherwise wait and see how it progresses. (Though you may be waiting a while. The game has been out for a year, and its still in Early Access!)

NOTE: This review only covers Shovel of Hope.
The Nintendo Entertainment System was, to say the very least, a console which had its fair share of platformenrs in its library. As such, for many the platformer genre has a certain measure of nostalgia to it. Shovel Knight: Treasure Trove is thus intended to be a tribute to platformers of the NES era, and serves that purpose pretty damn well. The developers, Yacht Club Games, are made up of former members of WayForward Technologies, who as we can tell from their release history are very, very good at making platformers, a trend which if critics are to be believed seems to be continuing here, with almost unanimous acclaim from all four corners of the Internet. So why's that? Well, let's have a look, shall we?
Yacht Club Games said themselves on their own website that Shovel Knight's design brief was essentially "What if development for the NES never stopped" and "How would an 8-bit game feel and play if developed today?" So understandably they broke a good few rules of the NES when making this game, but retained the 8-bit graphical aesthetic, and in my opinion this was a very good move. It makes it feel like a modern game in a retro game's clothing; it retains the nostalgic charm of the "retro" platformer whilst simultaneously not being dragged down and made stale by any self-imposed technological limitations.

It does still draw on some old NES traditions, however - for instance, much like many NES games with the faintest shred of story, the plot is touched upon at the beginning in the form of a slideshow. It tells of how Shovel Knight and Shield Knight, once famed adventurers, were separated in an accident whilst exploring the Tower of Fate, with Shield Knight apparently dying. Shovel Knight eventually returns from a long exile, during which time the evil Enchantress and her Order of No Quarter have claimed dominion over the land; it is now up to Shovel Knight, adamant that Shield Knight is still alive, to defeat them. Interestingly enough though, unlike the games that so heavily inspired it Shovel Knight's plot is not just a frame for the gameplay; what would otherwise be an inconsequential excuse plot is expanded on to great lengths. Just for instance bits of every character's personality and the game's lore are revealed through dream sequences between some levels, conversations between Shovel Knight and the Order of No Quarter as he meets and fights them as well as the people he encounters in the towns, all of whom have something either funny, useful or lore-related to say, oftentimes all three. In addition to that, especially near the end, the story sometimes gets really, really emotional, more so than you'd expect from a game of its type. It manages to maintain an almost perfect balance between keeping you sated with the gameplay and pondering the questions that appear as you follow Shovel Knight in his quest. And I might also say, very rarely do I find myself actually trying to talk to everyone in a game just for the giggles that they may elicit from me.
The 8-bit inspiration is also very apparent in the gameplay, with many, many elements harking back to some memorable classics. At its core it's standard platforming fare in sort of Zelda 2 crossed with Mega Man vein, you can swing your shovel to attack enemies, do a DuckTales-esque stomp attack, pick up treasure and items from fallen enemies and, well, since your main weapon is a shovel; it stands to reason that you can also dig up piles of dirt with it.  There are also hidden areas to be found, where you can obtain extra Gold, Music Sheets with which you can unlock tracks from the game's soundtrack to listen to later on, and in some cases hidden merchants who will sell you Relics - special items with a variety of effects, for instance the Wand which lets you shoot fireballs, the Phase Locket which gives you a few seconds of invulnerability, Troupple Chalices which let you store Troupple Ichor, a magical liquid with 3 variants, each with their own effect, and a fishing rod which... lets you fish for things. In towns you can also purchase items which increase your maximum health and Magic, as well as later in the game, upgrades for your shovel and armour which give you various different special abilities (or sometimes not).
The levels are all connected via a map screen which could not be any more of a reference to Mario Bros 3 if it tried, complete with bonus levels and extra bosses to fight. Some of these were added in by Kickstarter backers and thus have their own unique style too. And as for the levels themselves, they all have a recognisable visual design styled after the Knight of the Order of No Quarter they serve as home to, right down to the enemies and even the hazards you can run into. This gives each level a veritable bucketload of personality, serving as more than just levels but almost like extensions of the Knights' personalities and chaeracters, and in the case of King Knight perhaps his ego too. These levels can, however, especially late in the game, get very difficult and at times a bit irritating, so it's perhaps a good thing that the traditional lives system is done away with, and instead when you die you lose some of your accumulated Gold. If you then return to the spot where you died you're given an opportunity to retrieve it. Alternatively if you like a challenge, the checkpoints which can be found throughout the leve;s can be broken for extra Gold, something which I find really quite ingenious.
The soundtrack is absolutely spectacular, perhaps unsurprisingly as it was created by none other than Jake "Virt" Kaufman -already well known for the Shantae series and ghere he shows his prowess yet again. Each track fits its respective level like a glove, and to boot, 8-bit aesthetic of the music, in keeping with the game's general theme, is more than just an aesthetic. The soundtrack was created using a program called FamiTracker, a program which directly emulates the NES's sound chip. As a result, every track can be made to play on official Nintendo hardware - well, alright, provided you have a special sound chip that was only used in a handful of Konami games in Japan, most notably the Japanese version of Castlevania 3, but even so that is pretty mindblowing when you think about it.
In summary, if you were looking for a retro-style game which really feels like a modern one, then look no further than Shovel Knight. The gameplay harks gracefully back to its NES forefathers whilst still at the same time being innovative and fresh, the 8-bit soundtrack is nothing short of fantastic and even the plot is surprisingly good, balancing itself almost perfectly with the gameplay. It's the very definition of a modern classic and a game that should not under any circumstances be passed up. In the UK the price ranges from £10.99 to £12.99 depending on the version you buy, and as far as I can tell in the USA it's £14.99 across all platforms, and I would honestly say that at that price, Shovel Knight is most certainly worth a buy.

I uhh... love this game immensely.
Until the evening of my writing this, I've been looking at this game in the indie marketplace time and time again, over and over, always wondering why it mystified me.
Admitedly I impulse bought it to finally scratch that itch (An activity I honestly hate doing on Steam these days)
It was truely love at first playthrough, if you'll excuse my gushyness.  This game was made for me down to a science.
There are a ton of systems going on in this gem of a Rogue-like (A word I am using to skip over the obvious about the level generation/enemy layouts/item drops/yada yada).
`Real time pillar crawling/evasive maneuvers to avoid combat sequences and a very effective fog of war that makes crawling a tenative and fun as hell experience
`Combat sequences that have you use randomly drawn coins to the best of your abilities.  Each selection has serious ramifications for the rest of your playthrough (for soooo many reasons)  You will need to familiarize yourself with the coins you carry, because the enemies aren't going to stand around watching you decide what your best move is all night long.  Moving fast is the name of the game... right?
`The coins used in combat also serve as your currency on passive-boost items, healing station fodder, ect.
`For those who are familiar with deck building games, the coins in your inventory can be discarded and/or traded to Gods for coins of lesser value (or none, for the sake of removing dead weight)
`Let's call it stressful fun, trying to not spend enough so that you can feel safe moving down to harder depths, whilst being tempted by shopkeepers with shiny treasures, and shortly afterwards feeling remorse when you don't have any coins for combat purposes.  Or perhaps just the wrong coins.
`Don't leave yourself without any attack coins, or you're ♥♥♥♥ed.  Don't leave yourself without any heal coins or you're ♥♥♥♥ed.  Don't dilude your inventory with too many conflicting ideas amongst your coins, or you're ♥♥♥♥ed.
`You're ♥♥♥♥ed.
`Coins you carry through to the end of the game (Be it your trumph or demise) are used to spend on unlocking additional classees with different play styles.  Characters have their own unique benefits and drawbacks.
There's a lot more to be said, but what I would like to put out there is this:
This game is seriously impressive and I ♥♥♥♥ing love it

So far the game is a bit simple, but it's still very fun. One of the most unique things about this game is that there are 9 total difficult levels with varying levels of aggressiveness and skill. For example, you can set the AI to be aggressive but not skilled, and vice versa. Or you can set it to be both aggressive and skilled if you enjoy losing. But even on the least skilled and least aggressive setting (which I call the McClellan AI) it still puts up a considerable fight, which is unique in an era where it's not uncommon to be able to steamroll a game's AI even at the highest setting.
The gameplay is still in early development, but one of my favorite features is the ability to easily draw your own unit routes. In many strategy games, the only way to get your units to follow a specific route is to set various waypoints, which can be time-consuming and tough for the path-finding AI to deal with. In this game, you just drag the mouse where you want the unit to go and it will follow that path. It's a great tool that makes it easier to flank your enemies and increases the mobility of your army.
Even though this game is still in early access, it's well worth the 10 dollars. Even though it only covers one battle, the game offers many ways to fight that battle from either side, which makes it highly replayable and very fun.

Challenging AI, unique game-play.
The game is very well done for its reasonable asking price of $10.
Compared to the Total War series this game relies more so on unit morale than annihalting the enemy units. This brings a much more historically accurate gameplay experience. You will slowly advance and try to flank and out flank the enemy to capture key "Victory Points" on the map. However, it won't be easy. The AI is very well done and will react to your moves.
The game reminds me of an early 2000's game called "Austerlitz, Napoleon's Greatest Victory" except much more polished because of the victory point system.
Depending on how well you do in a scenario you will unlock a set of strategies for the next part of the battle. Will you try to keep Oak Hill or fall back?
Keep in mind this game is in early access mode. That means the game is unfinished and some of the text unwritten. The worst complaint I have so far is the clunky artillery controls. Is it going to stay and fire or run head first into the enemy lines? However I do believe the dev team in Ukraine will address this issue and the other issues. Don't let this turn you off from purchasing. I had to really knit-pick this complaint.
If you enjoyed Empire Total War or Napoleon Total War battles and want a more realistic battle experience this game is for you.

This game has really great atmosphere. It is a real expierience. I wont lie to you part of the reason I love this game is because of the way the developers set this up. As you solve puzzles and find your way, your mind is focused on the puzzles. So once the Amnesia monster pops up you are caught completely off guard and you have to react fast. It is a real different take on the horror genre. Granted Amnesia is more atmospheric than scary. But the way the developers set up the appearance of the monster, makes it a horror expierince. Best part is, I can't fight back. All I can do is I hide in the darkness and wait or make a run for it.
I can't stop playing it. I love it. I waited long enough. I've only had the game for about 3 days. I just can't stop looking for custom stories and going through the main story. I feel like I am playing "Dead Space 2"- my first enjoyable horror expierience- for the first time all over again. It is like the first time I stumbled upon a great story and can't stop reading. I may know the story of "Amnesia" but I can't get enough. I am completely blown away. I would reccomend the game to anyone. If I applaud "Amnesia" for one thing, it is the atmosphere. The music when your being chased, the sounds, the lighting... Everything is beautiful and perfect. It all flows in so perfectly, it is almost like the game has a mind set to totally immerse you in its world.
I truly feel like I have been missing out. Amnesia has been out for four years. I am currently thinking to myself "Why did I put off getting Amnesia? Especially when it is this good." I feel like a fool. I mean there are times when I am being chased by the Grunt- The main monster in Amnesia- and I have to quickly open a pull door. I get real tense knowing that it is right behind me, and that makes it all the more urgent. When I do open it I run through and quickly turn around to shut the door. I know that the grunt will stop and strike the door three times before the door breaks. When I Can't close it and I know the Grunt is only mere feet from me, I just book it. I may not know where I am going, but as long as it is away from the Grunt, I will be happy... and maybe make it out alive. I never quite get the kind of rush I get from "Amnesia" from any other horror game. With the Immersion factor set to 10, the developers at Frictional Games really made a gem... no art... "Amnesia" is a perfect example of video games being classified as art.
I classify "Amnesia: The Dark Descent" as "Atmospheric Horror". Others may Classify the game as a Thriller. I completely understand why. The story and setting is a thrill, when you get chased it is a thrill, and it has a good amount of suspense. Not too much to where you eventually get bored, not to little to the over all pay off to what the suspense was building up to fails, but just enough to where you really feel that uneasyness and dispare that you know something is going to happen you just do not know when. Usually when I start thinking Something is going to happen, I never get to the I just don't know when part. It is not like other games and I really enjoy the gameplay and style. It is no wonder Amnesia has won so many awards.
If you are considering buying this game, DO NOT hesitate to do so.

As of this review (05/01/2017), the game version is 0.942 hotfix. That's right, a game not in Early Access, yet officially is in the beta of development. Overall Score: 4/10 Not awful, but too luck dependant and shallow to recommend.
It's an arena shooter with the special power of teleporting to the opposite side of the screen when the player attempts to move off screen. You get a single shot weapon that upgrades to a three directional cone shot and finally a one shot laser with a much slower firing rate than the base gun. After that, you get the chance of randomly getting non-homing missiles and that is all for your gear.
The problem with the game is the balance. The random power ups are life and death past the first boss thanks to the laser beam losing the entire purpose of the first gun; the ability to bounce targets away from the player and create distance. Without that perk, the enemy will swarm the screen and you will die unless you get lucky and get the tri shot power up to increase your threat range. Took 20 minutes and 18 attempts to reach 1,000+ points.
My only real beef is creating DLC locked achievements. It's fine to have a game not worth playing past achievements, but the base game doesn't have enough content to begin with, yet it needs DLC? Rhetorical question aside, it's not worth buying even if easy to 100%, and it is easy by luck.
Fun, Fast paced, hardcore game, its definitly worth the money in my opinion for a semi casual game to play whenever you got the time.

Zack Lightman glances out his classroom window and spots a UFO that resembles a ship from a video game that he plays every night, a hugely popular online air combat simulator called Alien Attack In Space, in which gamers protect Earth from alien invaders.

He is very skilled at the game, having placed in the top ten among millions of users, however in real life, he is just a high school senior with a reputation of having a short fuse and getting into trouble, having fought a bully student Douglas Knotcher in junior high.

After getting into a confrontation with Knotcher, Zack leaves school and returns to his home where he looks at some of his late father Xavier's notebook about a conspiracy theory involving pop culture films (Star Wars, Flight of the Navigator, The Last Starfighter), novels (Ender's Game), and video games about alien invasions and military simulations.

He works part-time at a video game shop where his boss Ray surprises him with a fancy new controller for Alien Attack In Space as an early graduation gift. He tries it out on one of the new special missions on Alien Attack In Space that involves attacking the home planet of the aliens but the Earth team fails.
A really fun game, and it's fun to progress and unlock new characters. It's a really cool concept!
