Ok first things first, most of the negative reviews are based on undeserved critisism. The game is critisized in places in shouldn't be, and isn't in places it should be.
Campaign: Plot
In terms of the campaign, it is, for the most part, historically accurate. Each of the missions are realistic in the sense that what did happen was not over the top in terms of what could have actually happened during the second world war. From landing on normandy to the battle of the bulge, it sticks strictly to realism.
Now, whether or not one likes the cinematic movie style feel, which is what they were going for, is a subjective and honest opinion. One shouldn't parade it as fact just because they like or don't like this game style. It's call of duty, if you expected it to be different, play 0.3 hours on record then come to complain in the reviews, what are you doing with your life?
Campaign: Content/mechanics
This is where people can justifiably critisize the campaign. Or so I thought. This is where the alleged historical inaccuracies began to show. On Normandy there were a few guns which didn't make too much sense such as the PPSH. FOR SOME REASON, people writing reviews thought that countries ONLY used guns that they created. THIS IS NOT TRUE. Germans used italian, Russian, British, and American styled guns during the war. America used German, British, and so on guns during the war. Same with the British and every other country during the war. So to those crying wolf at the Germans using Soviet guns, this is NOT historically inaccurate. I implore these people to do even some basic research on this.
The Nazi officer uniforms were a tad off though. But overall, these were minor historical discrepencies in terms of hindering from the plot and accuracy of the campaign plotwise.
The user also starts off with a standard 1911 pistol as well as the m1 garand in most cases, sticking to reality. The user also relies on his allies to heal or supply him with extra ammo, amongst other things, shying away from the self regeneration rambo styled player from the other call of duty games. American soldiers have and drop exclusively American guns, while the German soldiers have and drop exclusively German guns.
One last thing I didn't like was with the Germans. The Germans sound cliche from what an American thinks they sound like, but they don't sound like a German German. The American soldier speaking German with the accent is fine though, I have no issue with that. Additionally, there is a huge difference between the Wehrmacht and the SS, one being the army and the other the deathsquad of the Nazi's who committed countless warcrimes and were brutal killers. Although there are few areas where this is blurred, it should not be blurred at all.
Multiplayer
THIS IS WHERE MOST ACTUAL DESERVED CRITISISM  IS VALID
Hackers and cheaters suck. I personally have not encountered many, but a lot of other people in the review section have. If mutliplayer is a huge aspect of the game for you and you can't deal with hackers, TAKE THIS INTO ACCOUNT BEFORE YOU PURCHASE THE GAME. Weigh this as a pro and con against the campaign and nazi zombies.
Now, in terms of other complains about it, some are justified and some aren't. To everyone wondering why there are black female germans on the axis, let alone male black germans, or those who were so mortified their hands began to tremble with fear, the creators of the game said they wanted to allow people to create a character that represents who they are and what they want their FICTIONAL character to be, regardless of if it is STRICTLY historically accurate. EVERY game like this, such as Battlefield 1, sacrifice SOME aspects of reality to add their own touch to the game. In World War One, trenchwarfare was the main style of warfare yet you run around in mutliplayer with a submachien gun (which were no where near as popular/available) as if its call of duty. THERE IS NOTHING WRONG WITH EITHER OF THESE. It's just the creative direction the creators took to stick to their own unique style of game as well as making it more enticing to people.
The guns, uniforms, and kill streaks are also grounded in reality, but again have their own call of duty esque twist to it.
Nazi Zombies
Zombies is a key component of call of duty, I can't complain much here. You either like it or not, and to all the negative reviews, there are countless other call of duty games with zombies, you knew full well what to expect. Stop hating for the sake of hating saying it's "recycled" when you played less than an hour of the game just to write a review where you allegedly have enough experience in campaign, multiplayer, and zombies to offer valid and justified critisism.
If you want to challenge my review, PLEASE PLEASE PLEASE do so. BUT, make sure, when applicable, you have a DEEP understanding and not just a quick wikipedia search, of historical events. Or if it pertains to the German aspect, that you speak the language.

Do you want to be a bear? Do you want to wander around exploring, hunting, fishing, scavenging, eating, and climbing around on things? Do you want to sniff around and find out where other animals have been, and what they've been up to? Do you want to uncover spooky ancient mysteries? Well this is the bear game for you!
I've played this now for quite a few hours, plus some more time with the kickstarter preview, and I have to say this is everything I'd hoped it would be. The graphics are better than I expected and quite good for a one-man development team. Few games live up to the hype, but Bear Simulator absolutely delivered. Beware of negative reviews with very little playtime. Those people have surely not even discovered a fraction of what this game has to offer.
Based on my rate of progress, I'd expect this game will take me at least 40 hours to just explore and find everything, eat everything, and complete the game. Not a bad entertainment/price ratio at $15. Anyone who says it'll take less than that has clearly not found any of the hidden zones yet and isn't playing this game to its fullest. There's a lot of secret stuff to discover, and the world is a bigger place than it first appears.
Are there bugs? Sure. Nothing game-breaking though. The game is difficult at times but I've caught, killed, and eaten ducks, successfully fought and killed some other predators, and gotten over or around various barriers that seemed too challenging at first. Sometimes you just need better bear stats before you attempt things, or need to get better at the game. Take your time, really investigate your environment fully, and then only move on when you're absolutely sure you've finished an area. Chances are high you'll still need to come back though, and don't forget that there's different challenges at night, and the weather changes things too.
This game is not for everyone. If you've got no sense of humor, no sense of direction, no attention span, or are obsessed with graphics above all else, you'll probably hate this game. If you like adventure, like exploring every nook-and-cranny of a huge and fascinating world, and don't take things too seriously, you'll have a blast. The game does start slow, and at first doesn't appear very deep. Give it some time, explore a bit, both in daytime and nighttime, and you'll really discover all that this game has to offer. This is not a game that can be judged in a 15 minute let's play.

I kickstarted this game for $30 and I don’t regret it.  It’s exactly what I expected.  A silly, fun, little bear game.  You walk around, beat up animals to eat, and harvest bugs, berries and mushrooms.
Dev doesn’t communicate?  He posted 46 different updates to kickstarter.  He did fine.  The game runs exceptionally well on ultimate graphics settings for me.  I’ve gotten stuck on the map twice, but saving and loading shifts your position, so no big deal.
Yes, you can lose to a fox.  The point of gathering berries, bugs and eating other animals is to improve your stats, such as damage and health.  It’s called progression.  Something too tough?  Gather more things first.  Not sure why everyone is making such a big deal out of such a simple game.
The game is incredibly in depth for a one man project, especially his first project.  Don’t listen to the kickstarter hype.  I’m satisfied with my backing.  Honestly I’d say this is almost fit to be a children’s game.  If you’re looking for a serious game, then move on.  This is just a little silly fun.
To get this game via Kickstarter was only $15.  Same price as it is now.
There were 17 different updates emailed out by Kickstarter to backers in 2015 alone between March and September. 45 updates since backing.  The Dev wasn't silent.
It had an
release of Nov. 2014.  Pretty good for a one man show's first time.

Before you play this game you need to wash out your expectations for a AAA game. This isn't that, don't come in expecting that. This game was made entirely by one person, and it was made with the purpose of having fun, and that's it, but having said that.
I have enjoyed every second of this game. It gives you exactly everything that you'd ask for in a BEAR simulator. You're a bear, so have fun. The game itself is very soothing to me--akin to something of Viscera clean-up but in a collect-a-thon way. It's not the prettiest game, but that isn't the focus. It's being a bear, and doing bear things.
This game is a wonderful experience, and although it might not be for everyone with its quirky humor and playful gameplay, I've had a blast playing it, and it was worth every cent.
On another note, supposively due to the bad reviews(although few, currently It's at 30 negative to 120+ positive) has incited the game dev to stop developing the game. I hope he continues to make it, there is a lot of promise here, and I really want to see this game at its fully-fledged beartential. Having said that, the game is still well-worth the price.
And Game dev, if you see this, thank you so much for making this game! I love it so much, and you shouldn't let the opinions of the few outweigh the many! We understand you, we understand what Bear Simulator is supposed to be, and we love it even for what it is! So don't let the negativity drag you down! Thank you for an amazing game, and I hope you reconsider developing it a bit more.

Okay. Where to begin? First of all, this game is scary. VERY scary. But not the sort of scary that you see in modern horror like when you turn around and the monster's appeared right behind you and a loud noise plays sort of scary. It relies more on stealth, and the fear comes from the anticipation of being found by the monster(s). Also, add in that if you hide in the darkness too long you start going mad and hallucinating all sorts of awful things, it becomes just that much more tense. Second of all, the story is AMAZING. It's not like the sort of story where you walk down straight corridors and it's explained to you in cutscenes. Oh no. You have to look around the castle for notes that explain the story, but not in order. You will find one note that explains the nature of your friendship with Alexander in Castle Brenenburg, then you will find a note some levels afterward that explains why you went to castle Brenenburg in the first place. Oh, and if you avoid hunting down the notes, you will be very confused towards the end. And as incentive to hunt down these notes, they restore the player's sanity (if I remember correctly). Thirdly, the graphics. While they may not be the highest resolution or highest poly, the castle and everything in it looks damn good. The best part of all was the lighting. The devs clearly knew how different forms of lighting affects the human mind, making a simple shower room look like a gateway into hell. That is, until you bring up your lantern or use a tinderbox. All in all, this is probably the best horror game. Ever. Better than F.E.A.R., or Slender: The Eight Pages, or any of those countless horror flash games on the web. While in those games, you simply walk from point A to B and watch jumpscares happen in cutscenes, in Amnesia, you will feel like you are Daniel, and you will understand his motivations and his many flaws, and you will feel in peril during the entire game. 10/10

I'll give you the TL:DR right up front here; This game is worth every penny. Buy it!
Shovel Knight is an amazing game. It is definitely a throwback to the olden days of gaming, but you definitely do not need that nostalgia to enjoy it.
If you wish for me to go more in depth, read on.
Gameplay:
Shovel Knight has very fun gameplay. Sure, it's a platformer, with many combat elements, so there will be some challenging points, but it is generally very forgiving.
For example, there are no "lives", and the only punishment for death, is losing some of your money, which you could scoop back up when you get back to your death point.
They also are making additional campaigns, (There is one so far, they are working on at least two more.) where you play as other characters, (with their own storylines) with their own unique movesets, which can mix up the gameplay quite a bit.
And, before you ask, no. It does not get dull at all playing it again and again. Sure, playing a game blind has it's qualities, but the gameplay is just very fun. I have already beaten the original campaign FOUR times, and I'm approaching my second time beating the second campaign.
(My play time on Steam doesn't exactly reflect this, as I have this game on the 3DS, and Wii U as well.)
Music:
The music is very very nice. It is very good at setting the mood for each level, and is just very nice to listen to in general.
(And I don't often listen to music.)
Each stage has unique music, as well, and each boss has music that reflects, but is different from, their corresponding stage.
Graphics:
First of all, I must say that, if you think super nice HD graphics, super high res textures, etc. make a game, then you need to wake up.
Obviously, this game has little pixel graphics, and a very limited color pallette, but it is strangely easy on the eyes. Never eye-bleeding. And, at times the scenery can be quite beautiful.
They also did a pretty good job with the sprites, too.
Story:
Yes, this game has a story. A story, which I shall not spoil for you. :)
Though I will say, it is very simple at first glance, but there is actually quite a bit it you look a little deeper.
Additionally, the developers of this game have already released a second campaign for this game, FOR FREE!
It allows you to play as another one of the characters of this game, in what seems to be a re-imagining of the story.
AND THEY'RE MAKING MORE!
Seriously, the people at Yacht Club Games are amazing, and definitely deserve the support. They have made a game that is truly amazing, and they continue to add more to it.
Get this game.

First and foremost, if you're thinking of buying a Civ game, and think Civ 5 is better than Civ 4, you might be wrong.
Civ 4 has a great deal of game play depth, offering multiple ways to achieve victory (culture, domination, conquest, space race, diplomatic) whilst also being accessible to the casual gamer who wants to play a no-stress peaceful game, to the best of strategists who play on the hardest difficulty, defending their lands from relentless barbarians and aggressive AI whilst trying to maintain stable relations and expand to dominate the world.
You can be a peaceful nation, focussing on culture or speeding through research. You can also focus on expansion, setting up as many cities as possible to own as much landmass and resources. You can be a nation of great military prowess, devoting production and research to improving your armies, which you can then use to defend your cities or dominate your enemies. You can decide to care about diplomacy, forging friends with the AI, and eventually, winning the diplomatic victory at the U.N.
World wonders are a fun feature. I always build the Stonehenge, and from then on build as many as possible. The culture and great person points they give are powerful. The game is also fairly educational on wonders of the world that actually exist or existed.
10/10 would recommend.

Starlite: Astronaut Rescue is a 2002 tech demo for... oh wait. Nevermind. It's a "mini-adventure", sporting "Unity Terrain Mars Environment and Shadows, Futuristic advanced rover setting, advanced biosuit space suits, professional voice acting, realistic physics, original story and dialogue; and advanced robotic navigation".
Every single one of the aforementioned features are over-exaggerated. This
game
is what you'd expect from one of those 100 Games on 1 Disc compilations for Windows 95. It's truly awful, but luckily it lasts only 15 minutes.
My single positive for this title is that I encountered zero bugs/issues with my short experience. But, bugs/glitches are directly proportional to content, and so this is expected.
In your short experience you'll control a rover and a human character. The looking action is awful, and movement is just as bad thanks to really terrible mouse acceleration. Avoid.

The #1 Diablo clone in my opinion. But Sacred 2 is so much more than a Diablo knockoff. It has a HUGE persistent world. Walking a bee-line from main quest to main quest will let you see less than 10% of the game's content. The meat of the game is the ~500 or so side-quests this monster has. Ascaron really broke themselves making a deep, massive world full of stuff to do. It really feels like you're walking around in an MMORPG.
Sadly they ruined it a bit with the level scaling system: monsters will always be your level or a little above, no matter where you go. I can only presume they did this because balancing such a huge world would be next to impossible. Despite this, Sacred 2 is still an AWESOME game. You feel epic and godly, just like you should, and there's always improvements to be made to your character.
Multiplayer is STILL AROUND, even though Steam says it's not. The online servers are gone forever, but you can still play in LAN mode with Hamachi. So if you want to play with friends, you can with a little leg-work.
The build system is very different from other Diablo clones. You spend less time focusing on your spells (which are called Combat Arts) and more time focusing on passive buffs that power specific components of your character (called Skills). You can cast any spell, but it's the skills that define what you're good at. There's thousands of combinations, and room for experimentation galore.

Even as a huge Serious Sam fan, I simply can't recommend this game.
For starters, there's a HUGE game-breaking bug with the XXL version that causes the game to crash on start-up after you play it for the first time. Restarting your computer, even uninstalling and reinstalling the game, none of it works, and even after 3 years the dev team hasn't been able to fix it.
Besides that, the whole gun stacking mechanic sounds interesting on paper, but in practice you just end up wielding a bunch of shotguns and rifles together and the magic quickly wears off. Explosives are even more dangerous here than they are in the 3D games, because you have an extremely limited line of sight meaning that usually by the time you can see an enemy, they're already rushing towards you and using a rocket launcher will just get you caught in the splash damage. The grenade launcher is also useless for this same reason, since it's main use in the 3D games was lobbing a grenade into a horde of advancing enemies.
Melee enemies are also hideously broken. Just one kleer can do a ton of damage, but unlike in the 3D games they can occupy the same space and deal damage simultaneously, meaning you can have about 6-7 kleer running and lunging around beneath you, and if you end up dropping down (probably while you're distracted with another horde of enemies) you might as well have fallen into a pit of instant death spikes.
Serious Sam's trademark of having massive hordes of strong enemies rushing you simply doesn't translate well into a 2D platformer, or if it does, the devs haven't done a very good job of translating it.

As a Kickstarter backer of this game, Bear Simulator is an absolute treat that I have played hours on end. As expected, you play as a bear doing bear things like hunting, scavenging, exploring, wearing silly hats, and discovering ancient bear temples. Bear Simulator is a sort of Sandbox/Action & Adventure game with a hint of plot behind it. It should be noted that Bear Simulator is not just a game you can relatively finish and find everything within an hour. In fact, I've played over 18 hours of this game and I still have not seen everything. Most of the fun from Bear Simulator comes from finding and collecting things and exploring the land. So if you enjoy games that center around collecting and adventure, this is the game for you.
With all of that said there are some problems with the game any potential buyer should know about. There are a lot (and I mean A LOT) of places you can get literally stuck in with saving and respawning at your den or whatnot being your only saving grace. Also, the hitboxes for some of the animals can be quite wonky and there are a few platforming segments that can be absolutely rage inducing. However, it should be noted that the single creator of this game, Farjay, is trying to fix these problems but is having a hard time with some of them as he is a first-time game developer.
In the end I feel as if maybe this game should have been released as early access or backer only until more problems were fixed but as it is its a very fun and unique game to play that I would recomend to anyone who enjoys being the best bear they can be and doesn't mind the bugs.

I have waited for 3-4 years before getting ArmA 3 so that it is polished and now that I finally got it it's worth the patience, that said there are some flaws with the game still.
Pros:
- Great graphics (realistic even, major improvement over A2, gorgeous lighting ambience)
- Good sound.
- Good environment and level of detail for an open world game.
- Improvements, mostly community based (A3 vanilla feels like a soft version of ace and other mods)
- An even better sense of realism, should be great with VR.
- It's ArmA 2, except that it is not if that makes any sense. Simply put it got the ArmA formula but it is very different, feels different. A2 regulars will need some time getting used to it, for me it took 2 days tho.
Cons:
- Terrible netcode issue, ie the game is resource hungry. It is really up to luck if you can find a server that can handle it, some maps work good some don't. This may be the biggest issue with the game which have put off so many players from playing it with mods. Perhaps this is not game's fault but that servers simply lack the power to host it. Most coop servers run with a very small amount of AI which is sad.
- PvP arcade community syndrome. PvP games in general have bad playerbase, but it's even worse in a sandbox that is meant for coop not for pvp due to netcode, physics etc. Yet there are many vanilla pvp servers and very few tactical servers to play on.
- There are more servers on A2 than on A3 (or at least feels like it) which is very sad. When A2 launched, there were over 500 coop servers to play tactical missions on and even nearly 10 years on you can still dig up around 50 vanilla and 10 ace ones, in A3 with a lot of effort you can find only up to 10 with and without ACE RHS and TFAR, that is for year 2017 though maybe things will change.
- Price is too high, while the game is worth it and even more this puts away many players. Tactical games like ArmA cannot take a risk and gamble with it's playerbase like arcade pvp shooters can. If it was lower many would buy it and I do hope that with time this will change so A3 will see a rebirth.
So what can I say?
This is ArmA, a step forward. If you have a PC that can handle it and if you get through all the hassle with mods then find a server to play on tactically this is a game for you. If you are easily annoyed by stuttering due to server performance or lack of options this is not a game for you. To those who play from OFP I recommend it, just make sure you get a decent PC and to find tactical servers to play on.
P.S. Campaign is putrid garbage, avoid it unless you're a pleb.
P.P.S. Even though they are super rare and hard to find, hardcore A3 servers still exist.

TL;DR:  While I cannot speak for the multiplayer of the game, Arma 3 provides a solid framework for the single-player experience.  Vanilla controls and mechanics can be clunky at times, but, with some tweaking, Arma 3 can provide excellent gameplay with high replayability.  With its emphasis on thinking before shooting and situational awareness, Arma 3 can be considered the apex of a long line of tactical shooter games.
I have been a long-time fan of tactical shooters.  The very first game in this genre I can remember playing was Ghost Recon 2.  A few years ago, I took a dive into history playing the original Ghost Recon and Rainbow Six, followed by BIS’s own Operation Flashpoint:  Cold War Crisis.  Thus, my Arma adventure had begun.
Arma 3 is an open-world, tactical, combined-arms shooter, throwing aside the on-rails formula many shooters today follow.  It emphasizes thought before action, teamwork, and smart gunplay to achieve objectives within the game.  “Lone wolf” mentality and action-movie shooting result in a very, very quick end to the game.
It is hard to pick a spot to begin to talk about, so I’ll start with the soldier, the core component to combat in the game.  Characters in the game fall into several preset classes, such as auto-rifleman or pilot, and all their equipment can be customized to a high degree.  This equipment includes weapons, gear, helmets, uniforms, even what sort of glasses you want them to wear.  But this is just the tip of the iceberg.
Alongside the numerous classes are the weapons you have access to.  Rifles are the most extensive of the weapons and that is not including DLC rifles.  Pistols and light-machine guns are fewer but still have a good variety, and sniper rifles are limited to two or three per faction.  Again, this is not including weapons that come with the Marksman or Apex DLC.  All of these weapons can be customized with sights, lasers, bipods, you name it.  These weapons are accurately simulated with recoil, bullet drop, and accuracy based on the type and caliber of the weapon.
Vehicles give the combined-arms element to the game.  Several different tanks, cars, boats, helicopters, and planes allow you to take combat to the land, sea, or sky of the two maps that come with the game:  Altis and Stratis.  These maps are massive, so don’t worry about running into an invisible wall or the like; both maps are open-world and you are not restricted in how you approach the combat zone.  Like the weapons, these vehicles fall under the simulation of the game, being affected by bullet holes, flat tires, wind, and so on.
The mechanics of the game gives the simulation feel:  Wounds will affect how your soldier shoots or moves, wind will cause you to miss your shot if not accounted for, and so on.  This gives the game a level of realism that most other games can barely scratch the surface of.  This makes Arma 3 and other games in the series have a steep learning curve and very punishing to play.
Of course, Arma 3 is not without flaws.  For a game that has been around for a few years, it is very unstable sometimes, often crashing or giving low framerates for no apparent reason.  The hardware requirements are steep and often have no effect on the performance of the game.  The AI are known to be notoriously buggy and playing custom missions can often make or break the game depending on the source.  The poor design or lack thereof certain mechanics can also be very frustrating.  But Arma 3 has a good mod community who often takes these concerns into their own hands and shares their content via Steam Workshop or Armaholic.  Arma even gives you the tools to do it yourself with the Editor, Zeus, and the Arma 3 Tools program if you are willing to learn how to use them.  Mission-making alone is a very rewarding process, and beginners can set up missions within an hour once they know how.
Multiplayer is not an aspect I will be touching anytime soon.  It is not that I do not want to, rather I am satisfied with the single-player component.  Plenty of content is there for single-player and as stated the tools are there to expand upon it.
Overall, Arma 3, despite its flaws, is an excellent game for those who want to take their tactical gameplay to the next level.  This game, to be blunt, can be a pain in the ***, but by the same token it is also very rewarding to play once you figure it out.  You won’t regret buying it.
This has probably been my longest review yet, so if you made it this far, thank you for your time.  GG and Good Hunting.

Montaro is exactly what you see. It's a cute endless runner/platformer game filled with memes. You play as Montaro, a doge, walking down the street collecting dogecoins and pantsu. The dogecoins are the currency you collect in game which you can use to purchase costumes for Montaro, and the panties are collecting by jumping while walking under school girls. The game is really dividied into two levels. The lower level contains school girls, obstacles like open man holes, dumpsters, and bicycles, and things that will allow you to jump to the higher level, like vending machines, dumpsters, or stairs. The higher level contains the coins, but also its own set of obstacles like crows, and the ever so fearsome chickens and pigeons.  The game provides points the longer your walk lasts, the more panties you collect, and the more dogecoins you collect. However, you'll find yourself less concerned about your score and more worried about your coins until you unlock every costume. The game also features several fairly easy achievements. Most you unlock just by playing the game, but some are secret, although easily unlocked if you're curious enough to navigate the game in its entirety. For such a low price, I'd say this is a must have. It's a simple and relaxing game that you can always return to for some fun.

Quick Summary: A side-scrolling Serious Sam game with tons of guns, secrets, and enemies running at you. The game’s graphics are dated and the resolution is such that you’d think you should be playing it in windowed mode, but don’t do that or you’ll keep clicking off the edge of the screen during frantic battles.
You play the title character ‘Serious’ Sam Stone, a badass soldier battling the alien hordes of the warlord Mental throughout Earth’s history. Sam’s only companions are Netrisca, a computer program that for some reason now looks like a woman (think Cortana from Halo), and a large assortment of guns for mowing down aliens. I’m not sure when this game takes place in the Serious Sam game series, but since there’s time travel involved it doesn’t really matter. Just kill everyone who charges at you.
Since the game is a side scroller, your character will always be in the center of the screen, which means enemies only need to travel ½ screen to reach you. Like other Serious Sam games, a lot of the enemies have just enough life that it takes a little focus fire to bring them down. This is only a problem in the beginning of the game though, because of a new feature of this game: gun stacking. Using “connectors” that you find throughout the game, you can “stack” up to 6 guns together so you’re actually wielding all 6 at the same time and firing them all with a press of the button. Each weapon has 4 versions available, so by the end of the game you could be simultaneously firing 4 laser canons and 2 rocket launchers, shredding aliens as you go. Each gun still needs ammo though, so save your most powerful stuff for the game’s various bosses. You’ll be encountering a bunch of familiar enemies from other Serious Sam games, like the headless bombers, bio mechanoids, and kleers, along with a few new ones.
Pros:
+Simplistic shoot’em up game with the ability to increase your firepower as the game goes on, all the way to “golden guns” (2x damage + infinite ammo) after you beat the game.
+Small download size, but it will still take you about 7 hours to beat Serious Sam Double D.
+When you start the game you can choose Classic or the XXL version which has improved graphics and some voice acting, rather than just text dialogue.
Cons:
-The game has a lot of secret guns/connectors to be found (many of which you will NEVER find on your own), and one of them glitched out for me. I found the “secret area” but there was nothing in it so I couldn’t 100% clear the game without completely restarting.
-There isn’t much of a story to this game, just some short dialogues where Sam is wisecracking with Netrisca, or the big bad General Crabface talking with his goons. That’s not really his name, I just don’t remember what it was, and honestly it doesn’t matter.
All told, Serious Sam Double D is a decent game if you’re bored and looking to kill some aliens. It’s a mix of casual and bullet hell game (kind of), and if you’re having a hard time, you can actually choose to lower the game’s speed to give you more reaction time. Try it out, and if you don’t like it, the game is less than 1 gb to download so don’t sweat it.

Shovel Knight is a must play game, not only for platformer lovers but for everyone. It offers about 20 hours of gameplay after free DLC (Plague of Shadows) and these 20 hours are spent only during campaign while the game offers more. For those who don't want to read the whole review, I'll try to catch it in few words. The game is really fun, amusing and replayable. Also it offers many challenges and unlocks, so if you are still wondering if you should buy it, JUST BUY IT!
For those carrying on, let's talk about GAMEPLAY
In Shovel Knight you can play campaign and after finishing it, a new game+ can be started (enemies hit harder, there are less check points and food platters will spawn a bomb instead of regenerating health). The game offers 2 playable characters : Shovel Knight and Plague Knight (obtained after finishing the game with Shovel Knight). It takes 8-12 hours, to complete the campaign with one of those characters, depending on how good player you are. Playing as Plague Knight feels like totally diffrent game (the whole gameplay mechanics is changed). All levels differ from each other. Once you' ll land between cold mountains and suddenly you'll be in a middle of volcano. Besides splendid campaign, developers added optional challenge mode which introduces player to another level of insanity. Freaking 26 levels created just to make your life harder, all of them completely irritating. You can play with controller or keyboard. Both options work flawlessly.
Now it's time for in-game STORY
I'm not going to lie about it. The story is just really simple, but the simplicity makes it even better. It's hard to not spoil the story talking about it, so I'll say that playing with diffrent characters makes the story diffrent. Whenever you meet someone and start a dialogue, you will be amused and surprised how funny the conversations are.
Eventually we came to a point where glorious PC gaming master race takes place. GRAPHICS
The graphics looks beaufitul, the colors are bright, there are many details. Every single detail is well-made and matches with the rest of the level. For those who want to play the game in 4K resolution, ultra settings etc. etc. etc. there will be small disappointment... IT'S ALL PIXELS and no matter what you do, no diffrence will be seen on any 4K monitor or any other. I mean the game will look lovely no matter what.
SOUNDTRACKS
I'm not a music lover so I'll just say that it's just great. Music varies from slow, atmospheric songs to faster and lively ones.
At the end comes REPLAY-VALUE
So not much to say..... YES THIS GAME IS SO SO SO REPLAYABLE. Every second spent in this game will be enjoyed by kids, teenagers and adults, no matter how many times they complete it. You will want to replay some maps just to get more collectibles, unlock some achievements or just to challenge yourself.
Summarising all upper things, there is only one thing to say : This game is perfect platformer for everyone. Developers made a 2D game with retro graphic and soundtrack and they made it well. Shovel Knight's got everyghint it has to have : good gameplay and good replayability. There is nothing more needed for a game to have and I would recommend this game to everyone.
Thanks for reading my review! It was fun to write it for you all. I hope it's helped at least few of you! :D

Starlite: Astronaut Rescue Review from Episode 149 of Steam Shots
Starlite: Astronaut Rescue is sort of an educational title. It was made with the support of NASA and the Bill and Melinda Gates foundation, along with a few other supporters. The title is also really short, like 20 minutes short. It feels like a tablet game in the interactive section of a museum. Moving the camera was difficult, and felt more like I should be dragging my finger around, not pointing a mouse. It doesn’t help the cursor wouldn’t stay in my main monitor either, so I couldn’t get it back in the middle to click on things. The gameplay involves doing basic tasks, like go here, click on this and then it explains stuff to you in a really neat way. It also had you do a math problem that I just couldn’t figure out. Thank god I review games, not build rockets. This short title is a neat thing, and it’s still in early access, with a promised multiplayer mode coming out soon along with some more content once they get it all worked out. Hopefully it isn’t like the Mars Mission and set for a timely 2025 release.

A fun little Free-2-Play PvP-FPS... featuring Terrorists vs Counter-Terrorists. Typical F2P system; with some interesting dynamic environments; like the high-rise office building you can repel down from, an airport terminal complete with aircraft, and a variety of indoor/outdoor settings.
The environments are a little larger than your typical arena-FPS, therefore teams which stick together actually seem to do better. However, respawn location is random; there are no spawn rooms, spawn zones, etc. When you die you will respawn at a random location on the map... which means, from time to time, you will respawn in the midst of enemies (or they will spawn right behind you), and they will slaughter you immedeately. Get used to it; it happens.
Oh, and because there's no POV control, if you're anything like me, you'll be getting caught on the environment... alot. Every little table-leg and door-frame will catch your foot, if you're not careful.
Also, team level-balancing is entirely voluntary, so don't be surprised when all the higher level players stack up on one side.

This game is a very simulation focused game that has a community of very commited players that want to make the word "simulation" a very well defined word.
While I have a limited number of hours compared to much of the dedicated community, I have only scratched the surface of this Bohemouth of a game, I feel that I can describe the experience of a new player entering this franchise for the first time.
When beginning the first game of your experience, it can be quite daunting and you will be looked down upon by a portion of the community that like to take things seriously, there is no room for screwing around in many of the games servers with the mods kicking people for what would be seen as trivial within other games e.g firing within the base. You must follow a protocol such as joining a squad, using tactical language, listening to your squad leader, following orders and the like. Quite often you will then be transported to the section on the map that the objective is focused within, which you will then complete and return to base.
Deaths are common and can happen without seeing the enemy in many cases which can force you to respawn into an empty base and have to wait for a squad which is quite fraustrating if there are not many deaths, and getting transport to the obective can sometimes be difficult or drawn out.
There are other gamemodes such as Altis Life but I haven't experienced those so cannot comment on them, but they change the dynamic in the game into something more casual with an entirely different style of gameplay
7/10 Would reccomend If you like ultra realistic simulations, the army and/or drawn out gameplay.

The game looks and sounds great, and has solid core gameplay. On paper, it should be fantastic. However, the execution is much more flawed. The game tries to tie the gameplay of God of War/DmC and the Legend of Zelda together, but instead of focusing on one and borrowing flavor from the other, it tries to mash them together in such a way that is detrimental to the game as a whole.
The game was not fun to play, which is by far its biggest issue. While it seems more like a Zelda-esque game toward the beginning, there is almost a clear line where they switched the focus to a more Devil May Cry-like/God of War experience. This was noticable after the first dungeon, which is by far the most complex. After the Twilight Cathedral, every dungeon turns into "grab item > complete secondary objective > kill boss", and some don't even have the secondary objective.
Unfortunately, the bosses in this game lack the complexity and challenges of the bosses in Devil May Cry, or the fun of the boss fights in the Legend of Zelda. They boil down to using the item you received in that dungeon, stunning the boss, and then clicking like a madman in order to defeat the boss, which is neither challenging nor fun.
The rest of the game is padded to hell and back with
which disappear halfway through the game and seem like a remnant from early in the development cycle. Most of the areas leading up to the dungeons are just as dull as the dungeons themselves. The
is where I called it quits.
It's very obvious the developers just threw a bunch of stuff at the wall and hoped that some of it would stick. There is a lot of variation in the challenges you have to complete, but none of them are fun. The environments look great, the music and voice acting are alright, and the story is ok. The gameplay just isn't fun. Try at your own risk, I guess.

Serious Sam Double D XXL is a 2D shoot'em'up, one of the games that were part of Indie series of Serious Sam franchise, made by non-Croteam developers. Main feature of this shoot'em'up is ability to stack guns on top of each other. It was made by Mommy's Best Games in 2011, only to come out on XBLA in 2013 as XXL edition and then get Steam version updated to XXL as well. You can choose to play both Double D or DD XXL edition.
It also came out on Xbox 360 through Xbox Live Arcade, but there isn't any reason to prefer it over PC version.
Multiplayer is local only. So don't expect to play online.
The first thing you see is selection between Double D and Double D XXL edition. I suggest you to go after XXL edition immeditly. Double D has no vehicle levels, no coop and no special upgrades for weapons. Without special upgrades for weapons it just doesn't make you think much, you just open gunstacker menu anytime and put weapons into single stack for highest DPS and that's it. And thinking about choosing weapon is important aspect of Serious Sam so it's dissapointing. Other difference is saving anytime, editing gunstack anytime, your own explosions harm you and golden guns which are just lazy direct upgrades you get after beating game.
I also can't help but to recommend a gamepad for this one. Well, it's XInput only, so preferably Xbox 360 one. Aiming with mouse really feels bad in this one.
And indeed, at first it seems like an average twin-stick 2D shoot'em'up. It's not very hot. Art style is that ugly sloppy Flash style that scream comedy Indie. Music is also not good, either being annoying ambient or somewhat cool yet generic fight music.
Then after some time of playing you will collect some guns and finally a wrench which is Gunstacker Connector. Trademark. Copyright. Awesomeright. You have a few stacks and you can put up to 6 weapons on top of each other in each one of them. This feature by itself wouldn't do much by itself, but thankfully they also implented Shop and Special Upgrades in XXL update. Pistol that allows you to hover in air while shooting, thompson that splits into two bullets after the first target it hits, shotgun that slows down target. That, and being able to edit gunstack only at checkpoints makes sure that you will create different stacks for each situation that you think of. Mind it, it has just enough depth only for lenght of this short game, but that's fine too.
It's just a shame that more of core gameplay is pretty unrefined. It does have some occasional puzzles and dynamics, but it also has some silly stuff, like when enemies spawn right in your face or just drag on.
It also has a bit more to it, with jumppad that you can throw anywhere. It's mostly used as the second jump. But sometimes you can use it to either reflect bullets nicely, though it's rare, or make enemies jump over you. But mostly, you use it to cheese challenge levels that you can unlock. Plus, vehicle stages are good fun. That unicycle.
You also unlock Serious difficulty and the second character in single-player after you beat the game. Character is same one as the second player, only some dialog changes.
It also has 2-player local multiplayer. As it's local I didn't get to try it. But it should be fun. There is cooperative where the second player can drop in and drop out in campaign anytime. And you can unlock arenas where you can shoot at each other, I think. So, coop and competetive. Yey.
But it's a pretty fine. Unrefined game with interesting idea that it goes with. Pretty good for a single walkthrough.

Some things to note on this one:
It's not a story with 'choices' or 'multiple endings,' it's just a simple read-through, just so you know.
There are two stories here, the 1st is the original story, and the 2nd is a prequel.  It is recommended (by the author) to read the 2nd first, but I didn't catch that until after I read the first one.  Either way works... I thought the 2nd was better than the first, if that matters somehow.
Not that I care too much about it, but the art could be seen as lacking.
The music seemed to fit in pretty well.
And then we get to the story and characters... This will be tough.
The characters are... not that interesting.  They are bland, to me anyway.  And this usually would be a criticism, but when you go through the story, it makes sense why they are that way.  So, I don't know how to... review this part.  I thought they were boring, and the interactions for the first 90% of the (1st) game are almost cringe-worthy... but I understand why it's that way.  I know this may not make much sense, but take it as you will.  The 2nd story is better with this: some of those characters are pretty interesting (interactions are still a bit weak).
The story is a big 'feels trip,' if you can put yourself in the situations described and imagine it, you will feel strongly about the story, and this is what pretty much makes up for.... everything.  A lot of people praise this, and it certainly made me feel more empathetic at times.  Also, the game is free, so you can give it a few hours of trying it out if you'd like and make a decision as you play.  The story was definitely worth the read.
I, personally, have some issues with the story, but that is of a personal nature: for my review, I'll recommend trying it out and just read above for my 'neutral' take on this.  The rest of what follows is just my personal thoughts/feelings on this.
I felt... that this story 'glorified' or 'romanticized' something that should not be glorified at all.  I know it's a story, and it's expanding one's way of thinking and just a take on things... but I still don't like that at all.  If you read the story, you'll probably guess it rather quickly.
This story also goes into religion somewhat, and presents what I feel is a... one-sided view on things?  I think that's the best way to describe it.  I completely understand why it's included, I know why people feel this way, and I'm sure it's a popular view.  It makes sense with the story. Game: Darksiders
Genre: Action
Developer: Vigil Games / THQ
System: Steam (PC)
Total Score: 80/100
Value Score: 8.0/10
• Story: 8/10
o The Kingdoms of Angels and Demons have been at war for such a long time. However one day a third kingdom was made: The Kingdom of Man. A pact was signed that would stop the fighting in respect of the existence of the third kingdom and the Charred Council was placed to make sure the balance is kept. Representing the Charred Council are the Four Horseman of the Apocalypse. One day one of the seals of the end of the world was broken: War of the 4 horseman was sent out to stop the warring Angels and demons. However he finds out that he was duped into coming into the battlefield. Without his other horseman brethren, his powers drained by the Council and being a enemy to all he must now find who, what, why and how the seal was broken so he could clean his name out of any blame.
• Characters: 8/10
o There are several characters in Darksiders, although at first it may seem like a small cast the cast is quite diverse and more than your average action game. You have War who is the main protagonist, the Charred Council who watch over the balance, the Shadow guard who stalks War while keeping him on a leash, Samael who is neither with the demons or the angels but on his own side willing to help War with a price, the angels and their leaders, and the demons and their leaders. Along with that there are several different enemy types ranging from all sorts of demons and fallen angels and riddled with sometimes machines who will attack you as well. The character roster for Darksiders is nicely done and you'll enjoy the variety which is a rarity not seen in many action games.
• GamePlay: 9/10
o Darksiders uses a wide variety of different types of gameplay. For one thing it is a action game like God of War or Devil May Cry but consists of several elements from adventure platformers such as The Legend of Zelda. Just like in these games you get several different items and power ups which affect your gameplay in battle and out of battle. There are several tools you can find which allow you to reach places you could never before or for a future location so expect to do a lot of back tracking to unlock new paths which lead to treasures which power you up. You have Vulgrim, a merchant who is willing to sell you items and power ups for your equips but with the price of souls which you can collect from enemies. There are three types of souls each which has distinct color and a purpose. Blue souls which are mostly found from enemies and objects being destroyed in the environment serve as the money figure for Vulgrim's shop, green souls replenish health and yellow souls replenish Wrath which is the equivalent of Mana which is needed for special skills. You can assign special skills and weapon swaps through the menu so you can easily swap between whatever you want to use with the touch of a button. You can collect shard pieces for to increase health and wrath - you can also find a health container at the end of every boss battle which will increase your health. There are several puzzles in the game that will test you with timing, item usage, and etc. You can backtrack to older locations and you will get access to far more areas within the old zones once you progress through the game.
• Graphics: 9/10
o Darksiders' visuals are quite nicely done and is like what you would expect in a game of its generation. Great looking environmental effects such as water, plant growth and the detailed designs of the enemies and the characters is very nicely done. However the design of the characters themselves may be a bit too western oriented and bit over done to make the game look more serious than it should be.
• Sound: 9/10
o Darksiders' sound effects are as good as its music OST and as detailed as the visuals. You'll hear different sounds from walking/moving on different environments and is actually noticeable and not repetitive as other games of the same genre. The voice acting although is OK but nothing special or praise worthy except for a few certain characters who have amazing voice acting.
• Music: 7/10
o Darksiders' music is as noticeable as any other action game, you'll be too busy focusing on the sound effects of the enemies and the action upon you. Darksiders' music OST is similar in tone and depth as God of War where there are some soothing tracks when there isnt anything going on and exclusive themes for certain types of enemies and battles.
• Length: 7/10
o Darksiders' playthough should take you no more than 20 hours to complete and that is if you did not go after some of the extra items and power ups which are optional. The game has about over 5 distinct areas which you will explore and focus on along with a few other smaller zone areas which play a part in the game.
• Replay Value: 5/10
o There's not much replay value in the game other than the fact that there are multiple difficulty levels of course only if you are a player who plays normal mode and then a harder difficulty. There's no incentive to replay the game as there are no actual rewards outside of the main game itself like you would expect in another game from the same genre.
• Player Value: 8/10
o Darksiders' storyline is a bit better than most action games and its gameplay is quite detailed with all sorts of ways to travel, fight and explore through the game's world. The game's sound and characters are nicely done and adds a unique feeling to the overall atmosphere along with its amazing visual styles and unique art style to the genre. However the game falls short in terms of its replay value and music which is more unnoticeable than any other OST you would hear from a game. Regardless if you are itching for some action and demon slaying, this is the game for you. If you enjoyed games like God of War and Devil May Cry, this game will be worthy of a purchase especially at the price it goes for on Steam.

A cute little game, where you control a 'doge/shibe/meme creature', and jump around a japanese street fighting kittens, avoiding holes, collecting coins, and stealing underwear from schoolgirls. That is about as far as it goes.
The game lacks quite a lot in depth and skill requirements. Controls are literally one button. Just jump. This creates a serious flaw, wherein you have no means to avoid obstacles that you have no way of predicting will appear. A simple 'cancel jump' button would work. Google's 'no internet dinosaur jump' game is honestly better controlled.
Visually, the game is quite nice to look at. It shows how much the developer worked on this factor, and apart from the whole 'doge' meme, I feel is the main reason people purchase the game. Art style is nice, and nothing feels out of place. Which isn't exactly a good thing in a platformer like this. Objects that you need to avoid or collect become one with the background. Discerning them from everything else is quite a task.
The game also has some servere balance issues. Almost everything one hits you. You have a life counter which is in the form of underpants, which you can collect regularly, but the only thing that takes away your life really is banas, which are all over the ground. Every other obstacle instantly one shots you. The placement of hazards also feels quite random, which it actually indeed is. Its an endless runner game. But randomly generated doesnt need to /feel/ randomly generated. The objects are spaced very close together, and you don't get much time to react to the following hazard. There is no feel of combination between the objects, as in you just have to instantly react, but at times due to the placing, you really dont have time. This is a major flaw. This paired with the difficulty in actually seeing hazards as mentioned in the previous paragraph, can lead to you feeling that you died to nothing quite regularly. It's saddening to see the quality of the visuals brought down by this factor.
For the price, its a fun little time waster. You got a couple minutes waiting for a friend to come online or finish doing something, load this up. It can feel frustrating and unfair at times, but for less than $1 USD, it's not too bad.
If you're looking for a more engaging experience, look elsewhere. I still like tetris more than this.

Team Fortress 2 is easily the best free game I've ever played. The graphics aren't too realistic, but they're not too cartoony, it's a nice balance. Gameplay is super fun. There's 9 classes, 3 of each category. Each one has a fun and unique play style, so If you're getting bored of a class, just switch to another and it's a completely different experience. I've been playing this game for multiple hours pretty much every day for the past few months, and it still hasn't gotten old. This game hasn't really been graphically updated since it released, and considering how it's a 10 year old game, it's still holding up very well. There are microtransactions and community market stuff. It's stuff like weapons, cosmetic items, taunts, etc. However, buying these items doesn't give you any advantage over anyone else. All weapons are available for free through item drops that happen randomly from just playing the game. If you haven't gotten a weapon you want from a drop yet, you can easily buy it from websites like Marketplace.tf for around one cent. There's higher qualities of items, such as strange, professional, unusual, etc., but these do nothing but make the item more valuable. It's good that this game doesn't give an advantage to players who pay more than others. It evens the playing field and makes it so that you're only better than someone else becasue of your experience and strategies. Overall, TF2 is a really fun and great game. It can run on pretty much any PC and it's free, so what more could you ask for. Even after 10 years, it's still recieving updates and hasn't gotten old for me yet. Would highly recommend.

You must follow a protocol such as joining a squad, using tactical language, listening to your squad leader, following orders and the like. Quite often you will then be transported to the section on the map that the objective is focused within, which you will then complete and return to base.
Deaths are common and can happen without seeing the enemy in many cases which can force you to respawn into an empty base and have to wait for a squad which is quite fraustrating if there are not many deaths, and getting transport to the obective can sometimes be difficult or drawn out.
There are other gamemodes such as Altis Life but I haven't experienced those so cannot comment on them, but they change the dynamic in the game into something more casual with an entirely different style of gameplay
7/10 Would reccomend If you like ultra realistic simulations, the army and/or drawn out gameplay.

Rome: Total War is a Grand Strategy game that will peak your interest in Roman Culture and the politics of the Roman Empire. I began to watch Rome Documentaries, read historical accounts and see what lead to the eventual decline and annihilation of the Empire. In the beginning of Rome: Total War you have a choice of which house to represent Rome.  Julii, Brutii,or Scipii. When your orders come in from the senate you are eager to do the biding to further this penisula into an empire. As you progress you are rewarded though the senate with influence in the political wheel. WIth family members and a vested interest in the outcomes of each town with what family member to lead it. Which is easy to determine through the very easy to learn UI. Now the Graphics are dated however its brushed aside as you gain fame and conquest through lower Europe.
There are many reviews and great aclaim for this Total War Masterpiece. Problems did arise with my own gameplay but they are not with the game persay. You have to forget the world in which we know and put yourself in the culture and politics of the era. This alone will start to forge your understanding of what these men and women endured daily. Military  victories and winning against 3-1 odds are awesome. Learning battlefield strategy is learned quickly as there is a vast amount of information in game you can utilize to win the day. But its not all about conquering your enemies abroad but at home. In game you will start to to see beyond the game into why each house is not only doing the Senates will also to further the house they represent.
I would also recommend all the DLC as it increases the immersion of the era and offers many more hours of gameplay.
Also there are Historical Battles to play. And if your like me and study the battle before you play it, your immersion will be 10 fold when you may know the outcome however when it really has happened...exciting.
I recommend this title its well worth it.

I'm usually not posting any review but this needs to be said.
TL;DR: Devs are just mocking us. Lack of interest.
A game who had a great potential as a multiplayer survival horror. But at this point it is more like one of those "early access" grab the money and run. Let me explain.
While the game has an interesting gameplay, it obviously lacks a lot of content, but it's still ok though because of how early it is. Well, it would be if devs actually managed to do useful updates. At the moment I'm writing this review, there has been one "update" within over a month, which added 2 "new" gamemodes.
To quote their post about it they "worked hard" to release those gamemodes "highly asked" by the community. In fact, it is just the 2 basic gamemodes with 3 ♥♥♥♥ing variables modified, not kiding. I am myself a developer and could only laugh at this, they took 3 weeks to release a gamemode copying the first one with just a greater speed and more protection, nothing actually new.
Oh and of course the community never asked for these.
There are also a lot of unbalances and exploits in the game that the community asks to be fixed (which would also take less than an hour to tweak)
Also, they could have released dedicated servers to make the game much more playable but instead left it to be peer-to-peer which gives insane ping, regionlock and a small playerbase.
So now you have an idea on how the game is being handled. The lack of content could also be fixed by a workshop since it's only a matter of gamemode/maps/models.
To sum up, this game is doomed unless they release dedicated servers and workshop which is, at this state, rather unlikely.

Let me first off by saying that I love this concept. I bought into damned back when that first started kicking around for two reasons. First there were not many successful game studios in that part of the world and this seemed like a good start for an alpha stage, secondly because I wanted to see this mechanic done right. Sadly, as so often is the case when risking money on an alpha the production of content slowed to a crawl and game-breaking bugs lingered and stagnated; eventually destroying the very supportive playerbase.
At the time my reaction was "I wish a better run, more solid studio would take this idea and run with it", "I wish this game was more attractive, had atmosphere and solid performance", "this game would be great if it didnt constantly disconnect or lose party members". etc. etc.
Well not long after I had given up on the idea out pops the shiny, polished and rounded Dead Realm. Marvellous game with a good bit of content, fantastically atmospheric maps and lots of little details that just tie the whole experience together; such as taunting as a monster and the use of sound to help you survive.
The great thing about this game is there isnt really any game breaking bugs, the game itself is solid as a rock! Now, before the community have got to the point of asking, the developers have leapt into creating new maps, modes and tweaking the game for an improved experience. It is for the magnificent game and the effort of the developers to ensure their consumers are happy that I recommend this game. 100%

It's a bit buggy, and as of this writing it only contains one mission that is 20 minutes long, but it seems the developers are hard at work adding a multiplayer level and more stuff to do. The game is rough in a lot of ways. Graphically it's sub-par, flat textures, stiff and/or missing animations, very low-poly models; this may make the game run better on a wider variety of hardware, but it makes it look rough, even for an indie game. The controls are floaty and slow, though that may be by design given the lighter gravity of Mars. The gameplay consists mostly of "walk here and press E/LMB", so it's not the most intense or involved game, and although you're on a resuce mission to save a pilot running out of oxygen... there is never a real sense of urgency.
Still, all that said, it's somehow charming. And it's cool to see a non-violent, science-based video game, even if it's just a rough-edged 20 minute sampler of what the developers have planned. If it were more expensive, I might judge it more harshley, but for the price, I think it's still worth it even given all the issues mentioned above. If nothing else, to see where the developers take it.
But be warned, if you don't like unpolished games, you should probably stay away.

I have been playing Civ 4 for a while now, and I have to say that it's a great game to pass the time. It is also a good game to play if you want to end up ruling the world and are unsure of how to do it - um, did you just read that?
So anyway, first of all there's a bunch of empires all with their own technologies, pros, cons and so on. And for each empire you get at least one leader. Each empire comes with a unique unit which can alter gameplay, such as the English redcoat, the French musketeer or the German Panzer Tank.
That brings me to the next great part - the units in the game. You start off with one city, and from there you can choose to make/train anything you have the technologies and resources to make/train. For example, you can train a warrior to fight, a scout to explore the map, a settler to find a new city, and later in the game (literally almost at the end), if you have the right stuff, you can make nukes!
The real icing on the cake is the fact that it is all so - well, real. You make contact with a new country, you make peace with them, you trade with them, you give them stuff - and then they can turn on you. Honestly Germany, why did you? You beat me, and I had grenadiers, war elephants and artillery; all you had were a few archers and a single catapult!
And last but not least, there's the winning. You can win by lots of ways: getting the most points by 2050, getting to Alpha Centauri first (space victory), controlling at least half the world, killing all other civilizations etc. All this great stuff turns the game into a real life simulation that is addictive and super fun. 10/10

I began to watch Rome Documentaries, read historical accounts and see what lead to the eventual decline and annihilation of the Empire. In the beginning of Rome: Total War you have a choice of which house to represent Rome.  Julii, Brutii,or Scipii. When your orders come in from the senate you are eager to do the biding to further this penisula into an empire. As you progress you are rewarded though the senate with influence in the political wheel. WIth family members and a vested interest in the outcomes of each town with what family member to lead it. Which is easy to determine through the very easy to learn UI. Now the Graphics are dated however its brushed aside as you gain fame and conquest through lower Europe.
There are many reviews and great aclaim for this Total War Masterpiece. Problems did arise with my own gameplay but they are not with the game persay. You have to forget the world in which we know and put yourself in the culture and politics of the era. This alone will start to forge your understanding of what these men and women endured daily. Military  victories and winning against 3-1 odds are awesome. Learning battlefield strategy is learned quickly as there is a vast amount of information in game you can utilize to win the day. But its not all about conquering your enemies abroad but at home. In game you will start to to see beyond the game into why each house is not only doing the Senates will also to further the house they represent.
I would also recommend all the DLC as it increases the immersion of the era and offers many more hours of gameplay.
Also there are Historical Battles to play. And if your like me and study the battle before you play it, your immersion will be 10 fold when you may know the outcome however when it really has happened...exciting.
I recommend this title its well worth it.

Deceit is an Asymitrical horror survival game, where you will take the role of a Survivor or an infected. At the start of the match the survivors will be collection items before the blackout occurs, as with the infected they will be collecting the same items, or they will be consuming blood bags so they can't transform. Infected start out as normal survivor, and have to consume blood bags so they can transform into monsters, and they can execute the survivors. Once a survivor had been killed they can not respawn, as with the infected they can respawn, except their terror gauge goes down a bit because of being killed. The game emphasizes on Teamwork, communication, and deception. At times the game can get a bit rowdy or chaotic, because of all the bluffing going on, so beware. I highly recommend this game to anyon who's a fan of asymmetrical horror games, or a fan of Fps games. I would rate this game 9/10 because of the concept, and it's overall gameplay. I'm not such a big fan of it's perk tree, since you can only pick a certain side of the perks, but still the perk tree is balanced.

I'm trying to understand why people are so upset about this game (the negative reviews, at least). Many of the funders knew that (1) this is a bear simulator (2) this was Farjay's first real game and (3) the game was more than 3x overfunded, which is not a good thing. You couldn't go into this expecting a 100k game made by an indie professional, and if your negative review is negative because it isn't a game you'd normally pay ~$20 for, then you came in expecting the wrong thing. This game is called Bear Simulator, and it is exactly that.
We start off waking up from hibernation (by that I mean the extra year of development the game took, much of which was without any updates - which I am not using to affect this review) in a bear den. You explore the world, which is surprisingly large and detailed, looking for food. There are a lot of random things to find (e.g. boards that have Bear Facts on them, random signs that have been graffitied), and I've enjoyed reading pretty much everything. Farjay's humor was what originally drew me into the game (other than my love for bears), and the game is rife with it. I personally quickly found myself acting like a bear - all I cared about was finding food. Everything is pretty much about eating in this game, which is pretty much realistic for a bear coming out of hibernation. Granted, the game effectively becomes a big ol' collectaphon, but I've enjoyed the constant need to stuff my bear stomach. Food gives you stat bonuses, and these bonuses help you in your exploration (and subsequently adding more interesting foods to your culinary repertoire. It's fun, it's silly, and it's very bear-like.
Unfortunately, the game does suffer from a few issues:
These were my biggest issues with the game. Otherwise, this is really just a bear simulator with some bonus things in it. It isn’t much like Goat simulator, which many people seem to have expected it to be.

I backed this game as soon as the kickstarter was released, and I've been watching the progress ever since. Now that I've been able to experience the final product I can say without a doubt that it perfectly does the two things it always set out to do: being about exploration.... and also being a bear.
As I said before, it's about exploration. There's plenty of places to explore, and plenty of things to find. Plus, you get the added bonus of doing all this as a bear. There are of course added bear attributes, such as having a den and hunting for food.
The game can be a bit buggy with hitboxes and getting stuck (I've gotten stuck inbetween rocks a lot, and once in a floor of an area that required me to crawl). However, the hitbox part only seemed to be a real problem with the Mean Wolves. I would certainly look into getting stuck though. I also think the intelligence levels needed to eat some foods is a bit high.
Over all, I think the game is amazing at what it is supposed to be. It's not for everyone of course, but I can 100% recommend it if you like collecting things, good basic humor, and just generally exploring. Unfortunately, I think $15 is just a tad bit too expensive for just this... perhaps $10 would be a better base price. Still... if you have the money and you want it go for it.

Well, first... let me just explain my surprise and what grey areas there are in calling something a "Visual Novel".
I know that, as far as credibility among gamers go, visual novels are among the lowest, most "casual" rung in reputations. However, there are some games I enjoy very much which are often referred to as visual novels.
.
. To an extent,
, though it is more commonly referred to as something along the lines of an "interactive movie". Even some rpgmaker games, such as the line of games:
,
, and, I assume, the coming sequel
.
But the thing is... these "visual novels" normally come with some kind of interactivity. Moving around, examing objects, quick-time events, dialogue options, even some mini-games. They gain the title of "visual novel" from the intense focus on story and that, at times, all you can do to advance the story is to continuously press the button to move to the next line. But they have other features.
, on the other hand, does not.
That is what surprised me about
... That there was literally no gameplay and you just clicked your way through all portions of the story. I'm not going to hold this against the game. It was clearly tagged as such under "visual novel". I'm simply used to, I guess, games that are in the same realm as visual novels, but not quite. So I had a hard time maintaining interest. That, however, does not mean I regret reading through the story.
I found exceptionally compelling. The thoughts of life and death are rather similar to my own. The tedium from inaction at the thought of wasting away in a hospital, terminally ill. The unbreakable spirit in doing what you want in life and dying on your own terms. Every person's right to die when they want or feel they need to die. I found myself to be rather fond of Setsumi's perspective.
wasn't a bad expansion upon the characters, but it is longer and I didn't feel as interested. However, the epilogue ties things up nicely.
I kind of liked this story, and I loved the sentiment behind it. As long as you know ahead of time that this is a true Visual Novel, then there would be no reason not to enjoy it. And if you're the emotional type, bring some tissues.

marks a departure for the series from semi-serious to absurd, particularly with
edition.  Don't go into it expecting the grittiness of the
franchise; just sit back, suspend your disbelief and enjoy the ride.  There are a myriad of missions, collectables, achievements, upgrades, buffs, and customizations galore.  This is not a game for the squeamish, prudish, or easily offended; in fact, it goes out of its way, at times
!  It is not for the kiddies.
The game begins with what is likely the most complete, versatile, and involved character avatar generation system of any game I had come across before.  (Download and run the free
demo to see what I mean.)  It then plunks you down into the game as the ostensible new leader of the "Third Street Saints" street  gang, which had enjoyed success, celebrity and pop culture commercialization, but has been targeted and taken down some notches not only by the criminal "Syndicate" but also by rival gangs, the police, the military, aliens, and... zombies.  The plot is to take back control of the city of Steelport from the various gang factions by doing missions and fulfilling contracts, or just robbing, to get the money to buy up businesses that grant you control, area by area.  Gameplay involves a wild mix of outlandish activities that are accomplished on foot, in cars, trucks, streetsweepers, motorcycles, boats, jetskis, airplanes, helicopters, etc., with a goodly mix of upgradeable weapons ranging from clubs to guns to rocket launchers to tanks.  There's also a built-in system to pimp your rides!  As you progress, a variety of abilities and buffs become available to advance your player-character.
The game is a blast to play, its sandbox missions, contracts, and activities are varied and will keep one entertained for a long time -- as long as you can accept the absurdities of the game world and not be too offended.  You can even play it, co-op, with a friend in multiplayer mode.
SR3 is not without its faults and bugs.  While the game is pretty gorgeous (in Dx10 mode), its graphics are pretty demanding and there
many graphical glitches and problems.  These are more numerous and serious with AMD or Intel graphics.  All
games are console ports after all.  I never experienced any game-breaking bugs, but then I'm still running Win 7 (64-bit) with an Nvidia card, and have no experience with the game on Win 10.  Overall, I would rate the game at 8.5 out of 10.  It remains one of my top ten favorite games.
