I was really into the game. At home alone with a headset, being immersed and scared. But unfortunately I had to realize  quickly, that the game is very shallow.
+ very interesting premise
+ at the beginning I was legitimately scared, way more than in any other horror game recently
+ the limited movement was a great choice
+ some of the websites are scary and could pass off as legitimate darknet websites, similar to real ones
+ its a rogue-like game, meaning there is replayability each time you boot up the game
+ each time you get different websites
+ codes that you have to search are always at a different location
+ you only have 30 ingame days, getting hacked adds to your day counter, its a challenge to make it in time
+ the goal to reach a red room, is surprisingly keeping you searching, you really wanna know how it looks like
+ the game can use your microphone, so you have to be still in some situations, very cool idea
+ the atmosphere is chilling, you hear a bump or footsteps in your home is really creepy
+ having to turn off the light and wait in the darkness is scary
+ the game is cheap
- the creepy atmosphere is pretty much gone after you encounter the first scary event, you know what to expect the next time you play
- the hacking mini games just get annyoing after a while, especially the one where you have to type in a code, was it really necessary to type in 2 lines of code?
- most of the websites dont work at all or just at specific times of the day, which is just frustrating and annoying to figure out
- some things are impossible to figure out on your own and need to be read in a guide
- most websites are very tame, pictures of dead people are so incredibly fake that you just laugh instead of get scared
- its almost a simulator for not-having-internet, as most websites are dead and you are constantly refreshing the page
- sometimes you get links shown and immediately I thought I could go there, but nope, they are not online
- finding the codes sometimes is a chore, you have to click on impossible locations to reveal them, meaning that its a wild guess, having to scan the entire webpage with your mouse to see if something is clickable, which is just stupid
- its all about playing the game a lot of times to know which sites according to which time are online or not, making it a chore to play and not scary at all when you are for the 50th time on a scary webpage
- sometimes if you go on a webpage it generates a txt file on the desktop with a clue or code, with no indication (other times there is an audio cue) you have to close the browser and look at your desktop....this can be missed so easily
- the ending
- once you finish the game there is no replayability, nothing will keep you coming back
- I thought the DLC is horrible, even for 1 buck, its terrible to ask people to pay for essentially a never ending hacking-minigame-marathon for points. The same minigames from the main game, just endlessly in a row......with no leaderboards  making the entire thing pointless. And the DLC probably took 5 minutes to put together, as its using the minigames from the maingame.....
I so wanted to love this game, I really did. I played it again and again to finish it. It lost its (at first really good) creepy atmosphere so fast and the disappointment about the ending hit me so hard. Having to go through all of the boring gameplay was just not rewarding, fun or even scary in the end. Its hard to not recommend it, because its so cheap, but with the lazy DLC I definitely would say dont get it. If you are curious about it though, 2 bucks wont hurt to find out for yourself.

[Description]
Tom Clancy's Rainbow Six Siege is a first-person multiplayer shooter that borrows from Counter Strike and hero shooters, mixing it together into a tactical, objective-based shootout where movement is slow and combat is fast. The game features asymmetrical gameplay where the teams are not always balanced in their abilities. Heavy emphasis is put on procedural environmental destruction allowing players to break certain structures by planting explosives, or shooting walls to make bullet holes or even larger ones to climb through.
[Pros]
+ Over 30 operators to choose from, based on real life counter terrorism units, each with their own unique weapons and gadgets.
+ No match will be the same thanks to the diverse cast of characters which is still getting expanded by Ubisoft, even 1.5 years after the game’s release.
+ Precise procedural destruction of most of the games floors and walls resulting in a tactical shooter like no other; simply running and gunning will only get you so far
+ Customization options for guns which also impact the way they operate. From a simple silencer to four different sights and weapon grips or fore grips, everything will change weapon behavior.
+ Pleasing graphics that look great and don’t require a monster PC to push 60 FPS or higher.
+ A fair use of micro-transactions where you can only buy skins and operators with real money but you can also unlock them through in-game currency.
+ You just can’t buy anything that gives you an advantage over other players.
+ Season pass owners get 1 week early access to new operators and all new operators in that year for free along with other skins and small benefits.
+ Maps are free for everyone, it doesn’t matter if you bought the season pass or not, everyone can play together.
+ Incredible sound engine that lets you hear precise enemy movement, like them walking into glass on the floor and other surfaces, or the exact direction where the steps are coming from. This is making good use of 5.1 surround sound or just good stereo headphones.
+ Music is fitting the game’s tone very well you just don’t hear much of it since it is only playing at the beginning and at the end of rounds which in turn is making you not really care for it all.
[Cons]
- Lag compensation, netcode and tickrate is still broken and you sometimes die out of nowhere while your enemy could clearly see you. (This is being worked on and hopefully fixed in the near future)
- Multiplayer against other players or against AI are the only two modes, there is no campaign which I think is a missed opportunity.
- Steep learning curve that can be very frustrating for beginners since regular players of the game will know exactly what walls can be shot through, what angles work best and how to quickly peek corners to make the best use of the sometimes broken netcode.
- Unlocking operators with in-game currency can take a long time based on your willingness to spend time with the game and how good you are. Just stay away from the starter edition or the game will be even more grindy since each base operators cost much much more than they normally would and you will be unable to upgrade to the standard edition once you bought the starter.
[Conclusion]
While this iteration of the series is vastly different than it’s predecessors, I think it’s a solid addition to the series. Rainbow Six Siege is very unique in what it does and we have yet to see a game like it. I recommend it to fans of SWAT 4, Insurgency, and generally anyone who enjoys or is interested in tactical first person games where you have to be cautious of your surroundings, be aware of your enemies abilities, and a strong emphasis on teamwork.

I could see this being frustrating when not playing in a full group of 6 but it's a really fun game that keeps everyone paranoid and trying to keep an eye on everyone, think about how they're behaving all while trying to get objectives done. If you like games like Trouble in Terrorist Town or Town of Salem, this'll be a game you love. Worth taking a look if you like games like The Hidden or Dead By Daylight too.
The main downside I'd say is the game is tough for people to pick up so for a while, there's a lot of trying to figure things out and attempting to explain stuff as best you can when you've only started to figure things out yourself. There is a tutorial video which opens up YouTube in your browser but there is no in game tutorial to give people a hands on introduction which it could really do with alongside maybe a few challenge modes/maps for both the survivors and infected against AI. It's pretty hit and miss in general whether people want to tab out and watch a tutorial, personally that does nothing for me.
That aside, the game itself is really cool. Trying to figure out who's infected is pretty difficult since sometimes people will unintentionally act suspicious, throw accusations around, go quiet and since there's always 2 infected, you can never be sure if being in a group is safe or not. There's a huge play on trust here that ends up being quite tense
As an infected, you always know who the other infected is and because of how the game works, teamwork gets really interesting. You need to work together to increase your chances but to do that, you'll need to subtly increase suspicion in survivors, not arise much suspicion yourself sometimes for the best result, you'll need to call out the other infected and put some attention on them for a bit so people don't know you're working together. You can't lean too heavily on it though or you'll likely get them killed or make people suspicious.
Probably my two favourite things is that first, you can't just go shooting everyone either as you'll either make everyone suspicious or likely just end up giving the infected less people to kill. Secondly, you can kill both of the infected and not know. When all the infected die, the objectives still have to be completed and survivors need to make it all the way to the final exit. Since you don't know, you'll still be suspicious of people and it becomes a weird game of paranoia in which the survivors can end up all killing each other and losing the match all on their own.
The game is free so it's definitely worth a go if you have a group of people to play it with. There's a bunch of content and cosmetics to unlock through playing and leveling up, and at the time of writing there's even a christmas event that lets you earn stuff for both survivors and the infected. It even looks pretty nice which was surprising. It can take a while to pick up and may not be for everyone but it's definitely worth checking out.

Okay, so you see this game, and you're like, "What? What's so interesting about this stupid looking bear game?" Well, I don't know. This game is exactly what you'd expect it to be like, but as you play it, you start to realize that it's very different than you expected. Yes, you play as a bear. You beat down some lesser-being chumps and forage berries, mushrooms, and such to increase your stats and restore life/stamina. You explore and run around a lot. But let's break this down:
PROS:
- Best Bear Simulator on the market.
- Notable sense of progression.
- A storyline with some lore, surprisingly.
- Plenty of humor as long as you don't take this game seriously.
- Hidden stuff to find.
- Pretty impressive since it was a one-man studio making his first game.
- Achievements and trading cards.
- You can find decorations, pets/friends, and other things to put in your den.
Cons:
-No clear sense of direction.
- You get stuck pretty easily, but learn quickly how to avoid it.
- Food/animals don't respawn, so getting health back can be kind of a pain.
- Textures can be hit or miss. I would assume they're just bought from somewhere, since this was, as previously stated, made by one guy.
- Initially searching for things to increase your stats (specifically intelligence) can be a bit annoying, since you need higher intelligence to eat most foods.
- The hitbox detection for fighting is awful. Don't even try to kite around something, they can hit you when you're behind them and you won't hit them half the time.
You'll mostly like this game if you want something simple, fun, and exploratory. Don't take this game seriously, and you'll enoy it. A good, fairly mindless time sink. (I wouldn't recommend buying this at $15, though.)
*Edited to add hitboxes as a con.
May 5th, 2016 edit: The Dev has fixed many of the issues, by giving you a checklist of what to do, fixing hitboxes, removing a lot of the intelligence barriers on food, and adding quick travel.

Serious Sam Double D is what many other Contra clones strive to be: lots of action, great level design with several secrets to explore, simple but enjoyable story, decent humour, and a weapon system that is so ridiculous it is actually awesome.
In 2011, CroTeam allowed some indie developers to freely expand upon the Serious Sam franchise. Serious Sam Double D was probably the best result: a 2D sidescrolling shooter/platformer, where your shoot, jump, shoot, use a jump pad to jump higher, and shoot some more. This game likes shooting.
This game likes shooting so much that it implemented probably the stupidest, yet coolest weapon handling system in gaming history: you can find wrench-shaped connectors that let you stack any weapon on top of each other. Want to fire a shotgun, plasma rifle, rocket launcher, grenade launcher, flamethrower, and assault rifle with a single trigger? Now you can do it.
The XXL update also added a shop system, where you can buy additional weapon mods to enhance your guns with a variety of abilities. As a drawback, this introduced money grinding.
The plot is the funny kind of stupid, taking you all over the world (the series-defining ancient Egypt, the Jurassic era, and Pompeii) battling Mental’s forces, including new enemies like kamikaze kittens or rocket-legged monkeys. (The story mode in the base game is voiceless, but the XXL edition is fully voiced now.) It’s not much, naturally, but this game is more about the fun action, just like the original series.

A very underrated game. Yes it's kind of buggy, from constant crashing on some machine's configurations, voice desync on some cutscenes, random low FPS, bad gamepad support - basically it hates dinput, to bugged achievements. But hey, it's a good game nonetheless.
Darksiders 1 is a prequel of Darksiders 2 which both are available on Steam. It's best to play Darksiders 1 prior to 2 so you can fully understand the story.
As an action adventure game, the game gives quite big world and enemies to play with. Ranging from the Corrupted City to Ashland/Desert, to fighting mere zombies to the fearsome Demon Lord. I'd say I'm quite content with how they design the whole world and the enemies. Storyline is also an important element. If you want that 'end of the world' feeling, playing the game and watching how the story progresses would be an enjoyable experience. The writer did a good job designing the plot of how Heaven and Hell battle to how our protagonist War acts until the end of the game.
Voice actors are a plus also. Instead of silent protagonist and game overall like other games that's starting to irk me since there's a sense of laziness, Darksiders gives you full voice actors throughout the game. And they've done well on this aspect.
If you intend to feel the true difficulty, start with Apocalyptic difficulty from the start - enemies are getting tougher that way - since normal doesn't pose much challenge aside of puzzles. What you need is to learn how to block and evade, that's it. Once you master the timing and enemies/bosses' attack patterns, it becomes absurdly easy.
Gameplay is the main point of the game, and it does well. The combat is quite smooth and enemy isn't stupid standing there while you slashing them. You can use auto assist to help you better (yes gamepad is recommended for the game) and use different weapons that can be swapped real time using hotkeys to overwhelm your enemies. There are also combos you can mix in together like dual slashes from sword and then finish it with your flying scythe. Not on par with DmC Devil May Cry 2013 though, but it's still ok than some... awkward fighting adventure game out there.
Moreso we have bunch of hidden items scattered throughout the big world of Darksiders. See if you can complete the Legendary Armor and wrath shards without walkthrough.
Some puzzles are annoying and Vulgrim's waypoints are easily missable if you're not careful enough (although none is missable forever) causing you to backtrack all the way. Strong observation, of which I don't have, is required.
Then the achievements problem, sad to say that it's never going to be fixed. THQ went bye bye and the new IP owner isn't interested in fixing anything. You can use Steam Achievement Manager to fix it though. Basically the achievements aren't going to unlock, and as a workaround you'd need to repeatedly complete the achievement requirement or SAM. There's an achievement in Darksiders 2 that require you to have certain achievement in Darksiders 1, so yeah.... I'm still in rage I didn't get credited for completing the game on Apocalyptic difficulty.
Overall, this is a recommended game and I personally am willing to give 80/100. Would be much higher if it weren't for broken mess/bugs that aren't going to be fixed. Since it's been bundled, as far as I know of, two times, I'm sure you can get it cheaper elsewhere (Steam activation key) than on Steam directly.

Amnesia is the epitome of the survival-horror genre, shying away from how action-oriented it tends to be and focusing much more on the scary defenseless side of things. You are unarmed for the entire game, and your only defense is finding somewhere (or some way) to hide in your immediate surroundings, and failing that, running for your life. I do have a few issues with it (like how running for your life is terribly impractible and its success hinges largely on your luck of whether the creature forgets where you are) but it is still a very good way to handle the genre and definitely ramps up the scare factor to 11. The monster appearances get sort of predictable towards the end of the game due to the complete lack of random enemies, but regardless they still keep you on your toes for the first run. Multiple playthroughs were not fun to me at all, as everything is 100% the same and I knew more of less how it was going to play out, taking away a lot of the atmosphere. In spite of these flaws, however, Amnesia manages to create a fantastic scary game that you should DEFINITELY try out. ...Unless you prone to expelling your bowels every time an invisible water monster tries to murder you.

Are you Serious enough? Serious Sam: Double D successfully translates Croteam's signature chaotic FPS action into a two-dimensional format. Perpetual growler "Serious" Sam Stone once again goes rip-roaring through time, slaughtering Mental's alien hordes en-masse, once more in Egypt but also in the Jurassic and to Pompeii, circa the infamous Vesuvius eruption. Netricsa, the snarky AI in Sam's head, is once again audible as seen in Serious Sam II, providing running banter. The game has very tight controls for a platformer and mouse aiming in the vein of Abuse and other 2d PC shooters. Double D's signature gimmick is a nifty item known as a "gun stacker". Gather enough of them and you can stack any six weapons on top of one another and fire them all at once. It's exactly as ridiculous as it sounds, and twice as entertaining. As Sam himself says, "double your gun, double your fun", so why not keep going? There are four copies of each weapon to be found in the game, including series staples such as the repeating laser cannon, chainsaw and rocket launcher, as well as a newcomer in the flamethrower. Each can also be upgraded into one of four specialist types, such as adding a prism to the laser that splits its beam into three. Sam also can use a redeployable jump pad that sticks to virtually any surface. Combining this with a particular upgrade to the basic machine pistol that allows Sam to glide is necessary to access many secret areas. Series regular enemies appear, including gnaars, biomechanoids and of course, the headless kamikazes, but several new, even more ridiculous enemies appear, including animate stacks of carnivorous pancakes, monkeys with axes for hands and jet thrusters for feet, and lava men riding pogo sticks. I can't make this♥♥♥♥♥♥up. Overall the game's difficulty is significantly lower then its parent series, possibly due to the ability to wield six guns at once, but its no less a zany and entertaining experience. This "Double Extra Large" version features 2 player coop local or online. In addition to the campaign, several standalone challenge levels are available, as are versus arenas, but these must first be unlocked in the campaign. This is a game that I can keep coming back to, which is exactly what I want in a good Roguelike.
Each level is a star system with randomized planets, and just the fact that I'm warping around the galaxy and traveling between planets makes the game feel bigger than it really is. It even shows you a map of the galaxy you're currently in, which is different each time you play.
Fighting whilst circling around planets is great fun and also makes gameplay interesting when you get abilities that are affected by the size of the planet you're on. Moonstrider has an interesting system for navigating levels; You have to use 1 fuel to jump between planets, and since you generally only collect 2 fuel at a time you have to plan out your jumps if you want to thoroughly explore a system.
I really like that there is a secret area you can get to, although I have yet to find out what lies in wait if you complete said areas. They add this sense of mystery that I don't get from a lot of games.
The game even has 6 unlockable characters, and they all have a good balance of pros and cons, and some of them have very unique gameplay. When I first played the melee character, Nadia, I thought they were far too difficult to use, but after getting some practice runs in I learned how to use their crazy bomb-and-dodge-jump and they became my favorite character. I love Nadia's risky, in-your-face, high DPS style.
The boss battles are a lot of fun as well, and they even have expert mode variations if you encounter the same boss later in the game.
Overall, it's a very polished game with an impressive amount of content to explore and excellent replayability. I hope it continues to get updates well into the future.

This game does an awful lot right, it has one of the best currency systems I have seen in any game, the fuel system serves it's purpose well, bosses are reasonably difficult, this game is just what you would expect from an indie rouguelike. Now, pros and cons.
Pros:
+ Currency system is the best I have seen in a very long time. Enemies drop the in game currency (gems) when killed, they drop like 4-5 in my experience, which is very little since each planet as on average around 2-3 enemies and items cost upwards of 40 gems, if you are only getting money from killing, you won't be able to buy everything. Likely not even if you kill every enemy in the level. You can instead refine ore into gems, BUT, now you have to choose. Some useful thing, or money. Usually fuel or max energy increase or health or a 30 second powerup. All of which are worth taking.
+ The random occurences in each level are very fun (think curses in Binding of Isaac, but implemented better) I have seen solar flares, which are bright flashes of light which (I think) damage you if you are on a side of the planet exposed to the sun (I never took chances) Not only do solar flares look beautiful, but they take advantage of the core concept of the game (planetoid roguelike). The others are cool as well, and I wish there were more, but none are nearly as memorable as the solar flare.
+ Fuel. The fuel system is one of my favorite elements of the game. Most of the time, you have to choose between fuel and health. The two most important stats. You can dig up the Bright red ore and choose between one exra max health and one extra fuel. If you run out of fuel you have to sacrifice life for being so careless. It is something that is always on my mind, as I like it to be full, yet (excluding each levels starting planet) you can never arrive on a planet with max fuel.
Cons:
- Energy. I feel like the Energy recharge delay could do with a decrease. I don't think the recharge RATE needs increasing. There is items for that. But the default delay is too much, and makes fighting a less fluid experience.
- Characters. I have not unlocked all of the characters, but I never use the ones I have unlocked. The dodge roll is simply too much better than the other characters dodges. My suggestion is that every character have a dodge roll, and a special ability. Like the 180 degree teleport. Maybe make the explode yourself backward could launch UP a similar height to jumping, and damage things around the liftoff point.
- Difficulty. The difficulty curve is a little wonky. The first level I can often get through with full health, but the second level I often die on, and the third level I often die in certain parts, while other parts are easy. A more steady curve would benefit the game. Sadly I can't give suggestions on difficulty, it's too hard to guage an average difficulty.
Conclusion:
This is a game that has some amazing gameplay mechanics, like the fuel system and the currency, but not only are they good, but they are implemented well. The games bosses aren't too creative, but their movesets are hinted at on similar enemies throughout the level. The game has some fundemental flaws, but none severe enough to make me angry, just sometimes disappointed.
Overall score: 9/10

I played this game at a playtest at UNM and enjoyed it immensely. I didn't want to share the controller with anyone else there, but then I found out it was available to purchase on Steam! I got it and have been recommending it to my friends, too.
This game is an old school style of pixel art, which is well designed, colorful, and fun. The sound design is also fun, with appropriate space noises, creatures, music, everything. The entire art aspects alone should be a reason to invest time in the game.
The flow of the game and controls are a bit confusing at first, but then you get into it and the controls become second nature. The way the game forces you to choose how to manage resources and to strategize is clever and has you constantly thinking about what decision you'll make. And the difficulty of a roguelike is definitely present in this. You are certain to die a few times (or several times in my case) before you begin to figure out how things work. For example, learning enemy patterns through each playthrough helps you to make it further and further in the game. And the further you progress, you notice different environmental hazards, such as flytraps and acid pits, and then more extreme, galaxy spanning hazards, like solar flares and ion bursts. Equipment gathered is helpful for different situations, and the more gathered, the better. They can be used in conjunction to increase survivability and effectiveness against enemies. I get excited each time I find a different piece I can add to make my character more deadly.
All in all, I highly recommend this game to anyone who likes space themed shooters, pixelated artwork, and arcade style action with roguelike difficulty.

Better than CS:GO
Edit: Adding this just to clarify some things, since some people don't seem to understand why I continue to play CS:GO, so that they don't have to discuss it on my profile page.
Unlike CS:GO, R6Siege is a game that truly feels competitive even outside "ranked" mode and requires a lot more tactical thinking and teamwork, whereas in CS:GO you can just jump alone into matchmaking where winning or losing doesn't really impact your future gameplay too much, as most players in MM are the same throughout Legendary Eagle to Global Elite ranks and you'll easily reach the rank you want if you're good enough alone. Sure, you'll lose a lot of matches, but you'll certainly win enough to reach Global Elite in no time if you can play properly, exploit imbalanced weapons or you are lucky in general.
Which brings me to the point where someone starts abusing handicapo weapons like AWP, which is basically a pinpoint accurate, slightly heavier MAG7 that works at all ranges and pierces walls, or Five-SeveN, which is a hybrid of AUG and P90, being able to kill in 1 headshot at close range and dealing immense amounts of damage at long range whilst having the same concept of spraying that P90 has, except more accurately, and it's a secondary weapon with high fire rate. Valve could easily fix this by, for example, making AWP work similarly to the "R8" revolver, with charged accurate shots and scarce ammo capacity, but they never will, as long as the game's community continues to be trash that wants to exploit that crap, which it will.
Being the kind of a person that prefers challenge and improvement over easy victory, I don't want to use that kind of stuff, unless I'm forced to by circumstances like those where I have no alternative options. I'd rather use "weak" weapons the way they won't used efficiently by any generic player and try to master everything the game offers, which isn't always enjoyable if the opponent that exploits has a massive upper hand and almost nobody realizes it. Being forced to exploit imbalanced weapons because others do so in order to win affects my opinion of the game, a lot.
Sure, R6Siege might not be perfect, and Ubisoft is probably the worst kind of well-funded company when it gets to having a reliable network within the game, but if you compare the issues that both games have, CS:GO's cluster♥♥♥♥ outweighs the opposite.
It's only logical to say that R6Siege is better. The developers are semi-actively updating the game and bringing new decent content each time. On the other hand, Valve only ever added more money-soaking trash to CS:GO throughout the past years, giving us only 2 extra weapons that were initially overpowered and still failing to balance out the existing ones. Communities are about equally dull in general, but from my experience you're much more likely to meet mature people in casual mode for R6Siege than you would in CS:GO Competitive at high ranks.
And that's not even mentioning how R6Siege content is made by developers, while Valve are sucking the money out of their game through community's efforts. The only kind of effort they put into CS:GO lately is just trying to find new ways to get extra easy money from their Frankenstein of a game. I'd never think ~5 years ago that I would say "Valve are more pathetic than GamersFirst", but here I am.
CS:GO used to be a great game with amazing potential, but that potential went into nothing positive as I see it right now and have been throughout the ongoing years since the point where they ditched development and went straight into grinding money. However, it still remains somewhat unique because of it's mechanics, so it still drags me back from time to time. My situation with CS:GO is pretty much similar to the concept of "Stockholm syndrome".

Along with the poor scripting, the controls are horrible. Play it with a controller or don't bother. The mouse mode doesn't even trap the cursor, so get used to accidentally clicking away from the game window while trying to turn.
The only point of hope I see here for the continuing Starlite project is the visual design. While not AAA-level, the designs are interesting and engaging. And if the robots look a little cartoony... well, real space assistant robot design is headed that way anyway, if Japan has anything to say about it.
Bottom line, even as a sneak preview, this should never have been released on its own. And certainly not for purchase. As part of a much larger game, this would simply be a poorly-designed tutorial, and could mostly be ignored. On its own, there's little to balance out the horrible.

I wanted to like this game. I really did. I know there's a COD hate bandwagon but I assure you, I'm not part of that. I've played every COD released to date and I enjoy the series for what it is, but the past several years have led to not much but disappointment and a lot of people agree on that point.
Now, I did appreciate the atmosphere, but I found it kind of hard to appreciate much more of the game. The campaign felt like a cheap and unoriginal movie rip-off and it lacked heart. I don't know who did the screenwriting for this one, but it was pretty bad. The animations, especially for the weapons were atrocious. The weapons as a whole were pretty bad. I mean, come on... The campaign has the Nazis running around with PPSh-42's! Why? I understand the need to take liberties and that's ok, but they seemed to not care about the campaign much at all and it was probably the biggest disappointment for me.
The zombies mode is not even appealing to me anymore. I didn't spend more than 5 mins in the mode since I'm so burned out on zombies. They've introduced some pretty cool stuff with that like class based gameplay for zombies along with objectives - I think. If you're a big zombie enthusiast or you like the COD zombies series, it's probably your bread and butter. I didn't really care either way.
And lastly there's multiplayer. This is probably what matters least to me since I was never good at the multiplayer in COD anyways and now with this one it doesn't seem like I can stand for more than 3 seconds without dying, so there's that. I know there have been huge numbers of complaints concerning cheaters, but I'm probably just that bad. So don't come to me for that. I really don't know. The multiplayer on this pc port is like lightning fast and I can't keep up with it cause it's not really my thing.
Anywho, I tried to distance myself as far as I could from the COD hate train. Take it or leave it, this is what is probably the unpopular opinion on the game, but I agree with it and I was so disappointed in a game I really looking forward to.

TL;DR
Teamwork is required in this game when playing either side. The game kind've has the same issue that League of Legends does, is it worth playing 10 crappy games where one side steamrolls the other just to get the ONE game where you feel that the sides are balanced, the gameplay is fun and thrilling, and even if you do lose you WANT to stick around and watch?
The Longer Version
The game can be fun, but can be ruined so many ways when playing infested or innocents.
In General
- AFK players, has happened a number of times, both on infested and innocent sides.
- Play with headset and microphone, get earraped by some idiot spamming his microphone. Yes you can mute them, but when your ears are ringing from the start of the match it doesn't make for a good match (especially when hearing is important in this game)
- Playing without microphone, you have to stop and type to talk. An obvious inconvenience
- Non english speakers in the English channel. You need teamwork to play this game, having a language barrier is no fun
- This has happened a number of times... When an infested transforms into a terror, but gets downed by the innocents, the infested respawns. However, sometimes there is a split second flash where the infested's non-terror form gets flashed and then anyone who was looking knows who it was. Unsure whether it's lag or some glitch, but I've been on the giving and receiving end of this and it's can make or break a game.
Innocents
- When you are downed and not revived, you lose all of your items. So you can get teammates just dicking around, knifing everyone, and downing people. If someone doesn't rez you, you lose all your items, but if you kill the player knifing, you're down one innocent (more often than not it is an innocent, not infested...)
- Similar to the above, is another one of the seven sins of gaming: Gluttony... People can be jerks and just hoard items, you can activate a puzzle and have someone else steal the reward from you, but again, if you down them for stealing your items, all of those items are now lost (and you've lost bullets as well)
- You get what you get when you play solo, this isn't a game where one innocent can go HAM and win it all by themselves (at least, if the infested aren't brain-dead) so you HAVE to have teamwork to win. The game basically gets decided by whichever side has the better teamwork. I've had teammates give 100%, working together, perpetually stunning a terror until the lights turn back on, then voting that person out, and I've also had teammates who MIGHT have given 10% where nobody is doing the objectives, nobody is sticking together, and the whole team just gets annihilated.
Infested
- Some people just want to level up (played during the Christmas event, so there is Naughty and Nice points you acquire, Naughty is when you gain xp while infested, Nice is innocent xp) and will say that they are infested, and name the other infested just so they can farm xp points. Obviously makes the game very boring and actually makes there be NO GAME but if you quit the match, you can't join another one until that one has completed.
Gameplay past level 15
- Better memorize all the text popups if you don't want to be detected as infested. Past level 15, people start asking "what is the 10th letter of your objective" or "walk up to this bloodbag and tell me the 8th letter." While it isn't that hard to memorize the few lines they can use, it's a boring fourth wall break that is just no fun (similar problem that Salem has)
- As mentioned in many other negative reviews, premade groups are a thing, as well as people using discord instead of the ingame chat. For a game that requires teamwork, when the team is divided into their group and everyone else, and their group isn't talking, it ruins the game.
- Mostly already mentioned, but the game basically gets decided on whether or not the innocents have any semblance of teamwork and if they don't, whether or not the infested are even slightly competent. If the innocents stay in a group and complete the objectives together, they are basically guaranteed to win unless the infested play perfectly as well. The innocents may lose 1 or 2 people, but will still be able to have some reach freedom, making the infested lose.

Empire building strategy game where you conquer provinces and conduct battles. Lead your family/nation to greatness. Turn based strategy for the overall city production and troop movement. When armies meet, you can have the game calculate the battle automatically or you can control all your troops in a RTS battlefield.

Anyone unfamiliar with this series of games must have been living under a rock for the last 20 years.  Each new version is an improvement on an already good original, adding new refinements and fresh idea's to enhance the game play.  The diplomatic options have come on in leaps and bounds, eliminating one of the few flaws in the first version.  The variety of ways the game can be won, and the option to have a new map every time, ensures each game is different to the last.  The number of Nations that can be played is excellent, and each Nation and it's leaders bring their own skills to the table.  As a result, you can persue a victory based on your Nation's strengths if you wish, or just unleash your Army regardless and go for the hard kill.  A number of difficulty levels change the challenge to match your experience, and the huge customization available gives you the chance to make things as you wish for a specific play.  As an example, if you want a huge Navy select a world type based on islands with a world surface heavy on the water, select a Nation with a nautical skill or Special Unit and get it on.
I played the original back in the 90's, and loved it.  The modern version, with all the extra wonder's and so on, blows it's socks off and steals it's dinner money.  For those seeking a stratergy game, you just found a hard game to beat.

It's rather simple, but quite addictive (at least for me) walking simulator.
I've backed its kickstarter campaign a while ago, yet I didn't expect much - especially knowing that it would be developed by a single, not that experienced developer. And given that fact, it turned out to be nicely done - audiovisuals are well done (not AAA level, but indie level of course), pieces of story come together at times, "character development" seems rewarding.
What I find the most entertaing here is this game is quite nostalgic - it gives you hardly any hints what to do, what is going on and what is your purpose, there is no minimap or objective list, yet the learning curve is well planned, hence you quickly discover everything yourself and feel much rewarded for that - just like in 90's games.
The only things I see that should be fixed are flickering shadows and tendencies to getting stuck and being unable to move - however I'm sure these will get patched soon.
And, well... I wouldn't mind finding a map sometime in later part of the game, just to put pieces of own knowledge together :)

This game has a great atmosphere to it, and the monsters can be pretty terrifying at times. The whole closet-like hiding places have been resolved, the ghost count has greatly increased, but I still want to see this grow even more. What do I mean by this? Well, I'd like to see not only new gamemodes, but at least one ghost with a different mechanic for catching humans. Here's an example of what I mean:
-The Mannequin (or whatever monster you'd like) can only move when a human isn't looking, but beware! Having this said, the Mannequin can vanish into a thick black smoke-burst, making him undetectable for a short period. However, the Mannequin cannot reap anyone while in this state of being vanished. Humans will have a higher chance of being reaped if they stare for too long, or stay near the ghost. Humans will slow down when they're looking at the Mannequin, and if they're near it, they'll begin to whimper or have an increased heart rate, increasing the chance of them being reaped. The Mannequin, unlike the other ghosts, can move incredibly fast when vanished or crawling, and jump higher too... at the cost of speed when running or walking normally.
It's a mere example, but yeah. You get the point; a different way to play would be nice.
Overall, I still believe this is a good game that can go a long way (if they fix some things), and you should check it out ONLY IF YOU WANT TO PLAY TEST IT. DO NOT EXCEED TWO HOURS UNLESS YOU'RE SURE YOU WANT THIS...and end caps lock there.
By the way, despite the "EARLY ACCESS REVIEW", I've seen Vanoss play this with the new monsters and such, so it's all good. ;)

This game has its fun moments. The battle animations are cool and I always love to see games with strong art direction. Darksiders has been compared to Zelda and I would say that for the most part, that's a decent comparison. There are temples with puzzles and new weapons to collect and a big boss to fight at the end. It's a good formula.
But my problem with this game is that it's gratuitous. After slogging through one too many arena-style battles featuring wave after wave of enemies... it got old. I just wanted it to end. The level of violence in this game is pretty gruesome, and going into this game, I knew it was a stretch for me. Maybe some people get a thrill out of splitting enemies in half or ripping the wings off of angels, but again, this got tiresome and trite pretty quickly.
It also doesn't help that virtually every character in this game is some gravel-voiced dude whose character motivations, if they even exist, are hidden behind in-game fantasy jargon. It's been a while since I've played, but from what I remember, they have special names for all kinds of eternal creatures or gods or places, and after a while, I started forgetting who was who and why I should care. Most of the cutscenes could be summed up with "listen to this deep-voiced guy say cool words." If it wasn't that, it was "watch this super muscular guy graphically slice up some enemies."
So if this what a Westernized version of Zelda looks like... I'll stick with the original, thanks.

All my life I've identified as a demi shovel.
When I was a young lad all the other boys played with trucks or soldiers, but I just wanted to play with a shovel. Every year on my birthday and christmas I would ask for a shovel. It didn't even have to be that nice, a 99 cent plastic one would do, but no. My parents would not allow me to carry out my forbidden love.
Later on as a teenager I made a deal with a friend. I went to his house and gave him all of my tooth fairy money in exchange for his shovel. In that moment... I was euphoric. No more longing. No more begging. I had everything I ever wanted right there in my hands. I felt an overwhelming series of emotions: pride, guilt, happiness, worry.
I thought I could hide my precious.
I tried everywhere: the yard, my closet, the neighbors yard, but my parents found it. They found it and they broke it and burned it in front of me. IN FRONT OF ME.
Those were the bitterest tears I've ever wept.
I was grounded for 3 months but I didn't care anymore. My spirit was broken. It was that night I realized I could go on no longer. I ran away, and started dancing for tips on street corners. Sleeping with thugs, jumping from town to town. It was a horrible life, but eventually I gained enough money to buy my own shovel, and I started my own hole digging service. I didn't care if I was dirt poor (no pun intended).... I was happy.
Well the years flew by, and eventually I found a woman, started a family, and got a nice job. But there was a severe price to being a father. I just couldn't keep up my shovel obsession at that point. My wife threatened to kick me out of the house, because the kids were so so scared of my shovel collection and how much time I spent with it. They accused me of not even knowing their names.
I sold them. 600 dollars worth of shovels.
That was 5 years ago, and I'm over it now, after months of therapy. But the other day, my 10 year old asked me to buy him a game on steam.
"Another call of battlefield piece of crap", I muttered to myself.
I saw shovel in the title and passed out.
I woke up 3 days later, staring at the hospital ceiling. It was night, and I was alone. I didn't know who I was, or where I was. I looked over and saw a picture of a small child. I wondered why it was there for a while until I realized he was my son. As I started remembering everything and everyone, one thought became dominant in my mind: shovel knight.
I jumped out of bed and started looking for a way out. I realized I was only a few stories up, so I made a rope out of the sheets and climbed out. I hitched a ride back to my house, not caring who was driving or what would happen, desperate to lay my hands on that shovel game once and for all.
As soon as I got home I bought the game and began playing it, and I just want to thank the developers for this masterpiece. I can't express my gratitude to them. Sure, the gameplay is fun, the music is great, the characters and enemies interesting... but what sells the game is that iconic blue shovel. I can know slay dragons with a shovel. I can defeat evil bosses and conquer obstacles. I know live in a world that revolves around shovels. This game has empowered me as a demi shovel in a way that nothing ever has before.
10/10

I'll explain here everything the game explains you in the first 2 minutes.
Your objective is to find a webpage called "Redroom" within 30 days . You will be attacked by hackers and there is 3 different kind of attacks. Two of them will give you a puzzle to solve. In the third one you have to copy a few lines of code to block the attack and the time limit is pretty tight for a slow typer like me. Also using EU layout has an impact because the signs used are used in programming and programmers do not use your every day Facebook chat layout. You will also be attacked by 2 different nutcases at random times and you will be given warnings when they are approaching.
All that been said... Concept is awesome and the game it self would be great, but there are a few things that bother me. The game feels like a lottery machine. The 2 enemies can attack you at the same time and you can only dodge one of  them resulting in a game over.  The indications for approaching enemies have a chance to be completely meaningless, making you only lose time. You can also be attacked by hackers at the same time as you have to dodge either of the psychos resulting in a game over or you losing 2-6days time. You have to look for what you need by clicking on parts of certain images. The webpages appear in different order in every playthrough and the information you find from the pages depends when they appear during your progress. If you fail to defend your self from a hacker you have a chance to lose all your notes.
Combining all the random factors in all of your playthroughs it makes finishing the game almost impossible. It's more like playing a 58-card memory game where you have to mark the back of the card because the card will be flipped over and scrambled even if you find the pair for it. You will eventually win by a chance or because you were a true hero and took notes IRL about everything you find on any page at any given time during your progress.

I have sunk over 200 hours of my life into this game, and guess what? Every last one was enjoyable. RTW is my favorite title by Creative Assembly, and my favorite real time strategy game as a direct result. The main thing most people sink hours into is the Imperial Campaign, which can last an upwards of 20 hours per campaign if drawn out. Your goal is simple, conquer 50 territories in the known world, and of course, Rome. The most focus in this mode has obviously been given to the Romans, as they have unique mechanics in the campaign, such as the ever hostile senate, the Civil War, the reforms of Gaius Marius, and so on. This isnt to say the other possible factions are any less far to play, far from it in fact. Playing as Carthage, you have access to mighty war elephants, the Greeks get their Spartans, the Germanians get Bezerkers, everyone has a unique element that mixes up gameplay in a way that forces you to adapt different strategy for each campaign. The AI for battles can either be brilliant, or mind numbingly awful, depending upon the difficulty you set it to. However if you want a real challenge, you are going to have to take your skills online. Despite being a very old title, there still is a good chunk of people playing this online. Most of them are experienced veterans, so dont be too upset if they wipe the floor with you the first couple of battles. The nostalgia runs deep in this game, and for those of you who have never played a Total War game, its probably the best game you can start with. It was GOTY worthy when it came out back then, and compared to RTW2, its a gem every collector should have in their library.

In 1979 I was serving as a park ranger in the northwestern quadrant of Yellowstone Park. My partner Steve was sick with typhoid fever, and I was serving my shifts alone. I got a call in the morning that some campers (who were camping ILLEGALLY) had spotted a grizzly bear within 100 feet of their campground. As a devoted ranger, it was my RESPONSIBILITY to protect these people. When I responded to the call, I came upon a campground painted with the blood and guts of these park visitors. I almost VOMITED in pure disgust. Little did I know, the grizzly bear that had committed this atrocious act of violence was still lurking amidst the trees only meters away from where I stood. He must have smelled the peanut butter sandwich I held in my pants pocket. He charged at me, tackling me to the ground with a level of force unrivaled by any earthly creature. Luckily, I had a .44 in my ankle holster, which I used to shoot the bear in the neck, as he snacked on my delicious sandwich (later I learned this bear was allergic to peanut butter anyway). Did I flinch or hesitate to destroy this animal? No, because I had to do it to save my own skin. If I had a scud missile I would've used it. Maybe it was perverse of me to open this game, expecting to play this kind-of encounter out from the other side, but regardless, I didn't get to experience any scenario close to the TERROR of my own. Although later I learned that bear was a golden retriever. I lost my job that day, but I could've lost my life. Instead, all I got were childish memes, clearly picked from the mind of a CHILD, not seasoned by the horrors and sights of what MEN like myself have seen within national parks. You grass men seem to think creatures like these are JOKES. They aren't. A bear killed my brother in '92.
The American Grizzly Bear is one of the most formidable animals in any given forest. Its power is unmatched. One strike from its muscular limbs could leave a man dead.
If you're giving a game in which I step into the body of a BEAR, THEN I'D EXPECT TO FEEL STRONG. I'd EXPECT to overpower any fellow animal, much like that giant golden retriever overpowered me. Nature is NOT a joke. People lose their lives. It's not a little virtual playground for grassmen to make jokes about frogs. Liliputian homunculi.
So next time you think about make a game with bears, please depict them with some goddamn accuracy. LIfe isn't a meme. Men lose their lives. Golden retrievers (unfortunately) get shot in the throat.
I give this game a 7/10 (I have to admit the frogs were quite humorous).
- Ranger Charles

IN-DEPTH REVIEW BELOW!
Okay. So. This is basically a parkour map of hide & seek.
Here's what basically happens.
Launch the game
Start the game
Enter a lobby
Start the game
Run like hell before the seeker is released
Hide
Remain calm
Then get the♥♥♥♥♥♥scared out of your eyeball.
Did I mention the seeker is a ghost and WHEN he finds you and IF he catches you, he will jumpscare you?
There are 2 game modes. seek & reap or Bounty.
This is for Seek & Reap
Basically you're either a human/hider or a ghost/seeker.
There's 3 ghost characters you can choose from. baby William, Wolfman, Or The Butcher. The human, if right clicks, has a radar. The radar can detect if the ghost is near. Humans also have the "G" button which, when pressed, summons a duplicate of that human that stands still and cannot be ran through. It is a decoy to trick the ghost, you only have 2 decoys, place carefully. The humans also have the "R" button. When pressed, the "R" button summons a giant bubble. The bubble is a force field. When placed, nor humans or ghosts and go through it. So place these very carefully, example: a Doorway if being chased. You have 3 force feilds.
As for the ghost, The ghost has one thing. When right clicks, humans appear red and can be seen through walls, kinda like a radar that see through walls. This is why it's not okay to hide in 1 spot for a long time unless you have skill and got to a nearly impossbile spot for the ghost to reach you, like I said, these are parkour maps. Reaped humans then become spirits which are basically another ghost. The spirit has double jump. I forget if the ghost does too. The spirit needs to help the ghost find the rest or the humans and reap them before time runs out.
Bounty
Bounty is basically the same concept except humans can't use decoys or bubbles.
Also, the ghost cannot see humans on their "radar" although, humans can still keep and use their radar.
The rules, however are different. Humans need to go search for 10 pocket watches, not hide. Once the pocket watches are finally found, a portal will open. The humans then will need to locate the portal, which can be seen if right clicked the portal appears through the wall. Once the humans enter the portal, the ghost cannot reap them.
The ghost will need to reap all the humans before the 10 pocket watches are found, if they are found then the ghost needs to reap as many humans as he can before they enter the portal. The portal is only open for 90 seconds and if time is run out then the humans will lose. Also, reaped humans becomes HARMLESS spirts, basically you're a spectator. You can mess with doors and buttons however. ALSO, although the ghost cannot use his radar, he can press his own "G" button which summons a banshee. He has 3 of these and when he places then they stay there until a human runs into it. If/When a human runs into it, the banshee will scream, alerting the ghost and showing up on the ghost's radar as a red orb, and it will also slow down the human a lot. Also, if humans sprint, they will show up on the ghost's radar.
This game is amazingly fun. Better than Gmod's Hide & Seek in my opinion. It gets your heart pumping and it's a very intense and scary game. not that scary unless you get caught.

Now then, on all accounts, I couldn't call this a game. There are no choices that you can make, and there is only one ending to these stories. However, this is certainly worth your time if you like Visual Novels. A must read.
The voice actors and actresses are excellent. Their performances often drove me to tears. Not just one time, but again and again. That's pretty rare for a Visual Novel to really hit home with me. Almost all of the characters feel like real people instead of cookie-cutter tropes.
I find it to be an interesting stylistic choice to have the images usually taking up less than half the screen, and have hardly any images of the characters show up. Despite the fact that I have played a great number of games and Visual Novels, I don't think I've ever seen that before. I think it helps to add to that feeling of being trapped or having no choice, which is what all of the main characters expirence.
Even the little details of the game itself help to drive the point home. From the fact that, when this Visual Novel has been windowed, it measures exactly 15 centimeters. That is the widest the windows on the seventh floor can be opened. It gives the feeling of an outsider looking in or an insider looking out. I think it symbolizes both.
Art: 7/10 (This might be a weird thing to say, but the characters sometimes look to damn adorable to fit the mood of the story. It sometimes distracted me from being properly sad.)
Characterization: 8/10
Concept: 8/10
Music: 6/10 (Lots of songs were reused in Narcissu 1&2, and they have a tendency to loop over and over again)
Originality: 7/10
Plot: 8/10
Replay Value: 2/10 (Maybe if you want to cry some more or look into the stories that are mentioned in the Visual Novel to get a better understanding, but otherwise...)
Voice Acting: 9/10
Overall: 7/10
Would Recommend To: Anyone who likes Visual Novels and sad stories

Shovel Knight is, at its core, a platformer directly influenced by the NES era and its great games like the Megaman series, Castlevania and the Super Mario Brothers series. It has the fun platforming, the great music and of course like most games of this genre, its fair bit of difficult sections that have you on the verge of throwing the controller.
It's pretty easy to recommend this game if you're a fan of the NES era but what if you're not? Should you still play this game? I honestly think so. The game has a great sound track, it's very easy to pick up and play in the same way that Super Mario Bros and Megaman are since you literally just jump and attack, and despite there being some harder areas, the check point system and the fact that there isn't a limited number of lives makes the game feel a lot more fair than games from the NES era feel if you go back and play them now. This game also has a free DLC patch that adds an entirely new campaign with a new character for free, so I mean.. yeah, you get free stuff with your game that adds replay-ability (is that even a word) to it and it has a new game+ as well.
The only way I couldn't recommend it is if you don't enjoy platformers, you don't enjoy games that can be challenging at times or if you're just sick of the whole retro-styled game explosion on Steam where everybody and their mothers are mainly releasing retro-looking games, and even then, this game has a lot more going on beyond being another retro-styled platformer.

Playing ARMA 3, I kept thinking of Falcon 4.0, the 1998 flight simulator. Like the ARMA series, the Falcon simulators claim to fame was their incredibly realistic fidelity. "Falcon 4.0" aimed to improve on this with the addition of a dynamic campaign; rather than simply flying pre-determined missions, it dropped you into a virtual warzone that reacted to the player's actions. It never worked quite as well as the pre-release hype promised but - considering it came out in a time when computer speed was measured in Megahertz and RAM in Megabytes - it was still an impressive attempt.
I mention Falcon 4.0 because the addition of a similar virtual warzone seems a perfect fit for the ARMA series, and ARMA 3 in particular. Older games of the franchise were still playing around with the underlying technology and gameplay, but neither of these areas received significant advancement in ARMA 3; in many ways, this game feels like a re-skin of ARMA 2. The addition of a reactive campaign would have been a logical iteration. Instead, we got its rushed single-player campaign.
Now, I know "ARMA 3" was intended to be played in multiplayer, with large groups of like-minded people role-playing war-game fantasies in player-made battles. Its single-player mode feels like a technology demo; a sampling of what the mission-creator - and game-engine - can do rather than a real attempt to craft a strong story or gameplay. But that campaign was so rough and unfulfilling that it did more to turn me off the series than want to further explore the game's capabilities. The missions were short - one of the earlier missions is little more than you driving down a road for a few minutes - and too frequently interrupted by badly scripted cut-scenes.
The actual gameplay isn't very fulfilling; although arguably realistic, getting sniped by a 'bot hiding in the forest a mile away that you don't even know is there until you fall over dead isn't much fun. Too much of the game has me blindly the following friendly AI, where I was more intent on watching where they were going than keeping an eye out for enemies. It's also a fragile game; don't do what the game expects and the scripting breaks, forcing a mission restart. It's unsatisfying and restrictive; exactly the opposite of what I'd expect from a game with such a huge open world. And don't even get me started on its awful control scheme...
The underlying technology of the ARMA games is incredibly impressive; I just hope that one day they manage to make an entertaining game with it.

At first glance one instantly asks: "Does it deliver?". You'd decide to set yourself some low expectations. You'd say that it looks nice, it's cheap, there's no harm in trying it. Truth to be told, this game amazes me. Before I tell you the rest, let me clear something up.
, the effect is the same; you could know the sites like the back of your hand and
.
As a horror game, it gets pretty much all factors right, without trying hard. You're in a nice place, sitting across a computer. You go in, you find out the challange and the tempation: explore the side of the web that you can't access with a normal browser and look for a myth: the Red Room, the place where torture and murder is streamed. You can get hacked while looking for it, but you'll learn how to fight them. You're going to be warned that there are absurd twisted killers/kidnappers that are going to come for you. You don't turn back. Not because you're brave, but because you've barely played the game for 3 minutes. After the tutorial ends, it's time to play.
The websites work in different game times, though many work no matter what. Like you'd expect, there are horrifying stories, some will tie knots in your neck, other will just make a big "WTF?!" wave in your head. It's all freaky, disturbing and the black hat hacker sites will give you reasons for paranoia. From time to time you'll see the screen glitch away and realize you're hacked. There are three mini games, puzzle like, one simple and one less simple, the third being a typing one, which should be a piece of cake for writers, coders, programmers, people that can type fast without errors. Resetting the modem from time to time is also effective, since it will make a new IP adress. If you get hacked, you might lose the notes and game time will progress by days, making some achievements unachievable from the affected playthrough.
What makes the formula strong is the sound. The envirenment is simple, turn light on and off. But it's the sounds that build the tension. You'll hear noises. Strange ones, like a window moving, a foot step, or any other indistinguishable ones. They will make you turn off the lights and sit in darkness. You will go by the door and see there's no one there. You'll get back to see which people are listed to kill, or which drugs are available for order, or the doll maker(you think it's a cliche in there, but  for most, it's something extremeley disturbing and for the desensitized it's something that's hard to ignore).
If I were to sum up the game, I'd talk about this experience: At some point the caller who would breath loudly stopped. Sometime later I heard a footstep. I browsed some more, I knew I was done, it was clearly a footstep.Coppied a code from the steroid queen's website. The testicle mutilater had one as well, but I read through the main page twice. Disturbing things are made of points of interest after all. I've been to the other sites, and some unexplored ones are still unavailable at the time. So I pulled back from the computer and looked to one side, but nothing. Huh. I turned back to turn off and the lights and DAAAAMN! The kidnapper was waiting at my back, his model not making any effort to escape the Uncanny Valley. I was not prepared to be creeped out like that. Also, game over, I'm dead. Feels like a relief.
Dead Space, Resident Evil, Outlast, I liked them all for their ambiance, their allure. But
. I would describe it as
: what you'll see on the web-pages will keep you tensed&disturbed, the hacks will keep the adrenaline pumping and the sounds will turn out to be maddening, with the game over being made of some good old(but gold) jumpscares.
There are three endings: one being what you're looking for, the second a mind-f*ck and the third something mind-blowing.
If you've been looking for the horror game that keeps you on edge and eventually does it's job on scaring you, this might be the one for you. If any horror does it's job, well, you know what you're signing up for anyway.

For a little context, this was a game sucessfully Kickstarted
ago for something to the tune of $100k.  The KS itself was something of a mess but we aren't here to review a KS campaign.  We're here to review a game and chew bubblegum.  And I'm all outta bubblegum.  ...Wait no, I still have some!
Bear Simulator is yet another one of
kinds of "Simulator" games that are to actual simulations what mockumentaries are to documentaries.  In Bear Simulator you are (duh) a Bear.  Although there
a plot, there is little to no narration or introduction as to what your motivation for getting up and out of the den in the morning should be.  Most of the gameplay consists of wandering around the environment to find hidden bits of food and/or animals to eat.  Eating causes your stats to go up which in turn allows you to access more areas, read more hints, and eat better items.  90% of the game is this, a sort of exploratory collect-a-thon.
There is a story to unfold and other objectives to complete as well, but completing these objectives basically consists of having stats high enough to get into a certain area/being methodical enough to find whatever hidden thing you need.  This process is made that much more laborious by the fact that the game world, which is quite large actually, has
You'll need to simply memorize where everything is and this ends up resulting in a lot of needless backtracking.
The environments themselves range from reasonably pretty to absolutely hideous.  Some areas were made with a bit of care whilst others suffer from terrible texture stretching/shimmering.  Still, it is a bit of chill-paced fun to explore areas, eat stuff, and examine some of the funny notes/items and such scattered about the world.  That world feels rather barren, however, with really not much to do other than eat things, and all food/animals are finite so once you've eaten them it makes everything feel even more like a ghost town.
There is also "combat" to be had.  It is extremely awkward and imprecise and often it's better to run away from that scary frog rather than fight it.  There is a charge attack you can unlock but since it is really quite hard to hit enemies it is sometimes better to simply spam your claw swipe and hope you don't get too jacked up.  It definitely did not make me feel like a mighty bear.  More like an oversized teddy bear.
As you get more powerful/capable, you will be able to venture further out from the starting hub-like zone and discover a lot of strange happenings and mysteries.  It's interesting as passive story-telling but doesn't grip you like a bear-hug should.
Although I'm actually getting a little bit of enjoyment out of being a bear, I can't, at this point in time, recommend it to anyone else (particularly at this price point).  I've already encountered far too many bugs and the first time you see some of the hokey AI and animation you are going to laugh for sure...  For all the wrong reasons.  I'm really hoping that the developer continues to work on the game's
.  If he does, this wouldn't actually be a bad quirky little adventure game.  Would I come back to update my review in the face of future updates?

In short, this game is a collectathon that is fun and whimsical at times, but overall wanted me yearning for more.
As a bear enthusiast, I really wanted to enjoy this game, but I can't. The charm wears off extremely fast due to poor gameplay mechanics that feel like they should be included. Basic things that feel like they should be included: A map, and some form of skill/stat chart. When certain things require for me to have X stat, it's frustrating having to look around to find things that make me smarter or stronger, uncertain of how many I need to eat.
As for the map, this game feels so directionless, and I easily lose track of where I've been, because the general blandness of the map. I feel constantly lost, and end up going in circles, to occasionally rediscover a landmark or two. Maybe something of a radar, a bear-dar if you will, would help greatly. Just something that says "Food is nearby" or "An item is nearby".
Two other gripes I have are the hitboxes, which feel nonexistant, especially when every creature is fast moving, except frogs. Having a massive bear claw swing, it feels like I should be doing something when I hit a location that isn't the center of being.
My last major complaint is that I'm not sure what is poor level design, and what is 'secrets off the beating path'. I'll often be reminded of Skyrim and Fallout, jumping and holding W as I traverse a mountain, only to find a flat surface, with nothing on it. Yet, I still feel obligated to climb up these mountains, in the event there is something hidden, since there is no real other way to know otherwise. Also, on at least two occasions, I felt like I skipped part of the map, just by climbing on things until I was able to jump over whatever barrier was preventing me. Again, not sure if I was supposed to or not, becuase there is practically no explaniation of this is game design of exploiting Dev's errors.
I want to end on a positive note, though. This game is still salvagable. A few features and fixes could make this game fun.  I think that part of what makes this fun is the Steam's stream ability, which allows me to privately have a group of friends watch, and experience the jokes and laugh along with the jokes that are scattered through the game. Honestly, its' the only way I can continue through it at it's current state.
4/10, I am honestly sad that this game turned out the way it did.

I have sunk over 200 hours of my life into this game, and guess what? Every last one was enjoyable. RTW is my favorite title by Creative Assembly, and my favorite real time strategy game as a direct result. The main thing most people sink hours into is the Imperial Campaign, which can last an upwards of 20 hours per campaign if drawn out. Your goal is simple, conquer 50 territories in the known world, and of course, Rome. The most focus in this mode has obviously been given to the Romans, as they have unique mechanics in the campaign, such as the ever hostile senate, the Civil War, the reforms of Gaius Marius, and so on. This isnt to say the other possible factions are any less far to play, far from it in fact. Playing as Carthage, you have access to mighty war elephants, the Greeks get their Spartans, the Germanians get Bezerkers, everyone has a unique element that mixes up gameplay in a way that forces you to adapt different strategy for each campaign. The AI for battles can either be brilliant, or mind numbingly awful, depending upon the difficulty you set it to. However if you want a real challenge, you are going to have to take your skills online. Despite being a very old title, there still is a good chunk of people playing this online. Most of them are experienced veterans, so dont be too upset if they wipe the floor with you the first couple of battles. The nostalgia runs deep in this game, and for those of you who have never played a Total War game, its probably the best game you can start with. It was GOTY worthy when it came out back then, and compared to RTW2, its a gem every collector should have in their library.

This has to be the most poorly designed game I have played in a while. and I hate the fact that I have to hate this game, because the premise is fun and the dev sense of humour is great, and also I backed this game in Kickstarter, but I can't recommend it to anybody.
I love exploring in this kind of titles, but the Stamine system ruins the whole fun of running around and discovering new things, because absolutely everything you do uses stamine and if you run out of it you start getting hurt just by running, something that shouldn't happen in an open game. This wouldn't be a problem because you cain regain health and stamine by eating food, mushrooms and defeating enemies, but what is even the point if those things rarely appear in the game?
In the same vein, the "Intelligence" system is so frustrating. I'm so happy to find something new to eat to level up my character, just to discover that I'm so stupid that I can't even touch it. There's absolutely nothing to point me towards how getting more intelligence, and even if it were, there is NOTHING in this huge overworld for me to gain more XP or Intelligence. Is painfully frustrating discovering great stuff that you can't even read or grab.
And I know this is a "joke game", but what is wrong with the animals balance? How in the bloody hell a freaking RAT obliterated me? I'M A BEAR.
As I said, I really wanted to like and love this game, but I'm not masochist enough to be running around the same places over and over again with no stamina, no strenght and no intelligence, and no elements to get more of those anywhere to be seen. I guess I'll try to fight enemies with my valves or eating off my hats to not starve to death. Hopefully this things will get patched out in the near future, and if so, then I would gladly rejoin the adventure of exploring and recommend it to some friends, but in the state that is right now, yeah, it's playable, but absolutely not enjoyable.

I have just started a few days ago and have played for about ten hours. It was released somewhere in 2015 and it is now the end of 2017 that I am trying it. Thus there shouldnt be any 'teething' issues.
It is indeed very realistic, with graphics that range from fastest, fast, simple, beautiful, fantastic etc. There are many tackles, baits and lures, as well as many different combinations for the different situations. For example there is night fishing, catching bottom dwelling fish, as well as fishing from a kayak that I have not tried before.
For the bad points, I would say that the tutorials may not be enough to introduce the players to the different compatibilities of the rod and reels, as well as the lures and baits. For example a spinner type rod may not be able to be paired with some reels, as well as use lures. For a first time player, I nearly bought higher level equipment without realising that it might not be compatible with the equipment I am using. This is can leave players financially strapped which is explained in the next point.
Travelling expenses are also very expensive. It is normal for a game to tempt you into buying their premium benefits using real money, but they also should leave some breathing space for beginners to try out. Travelling to a next map costs 2k, and it took many hours to catch fishes worth a total of at least 1k. Without the rewards of about 1k+ after every level, there will definitely be no profit for better baits and equipment. Higher level players may be stuck in the first map too.
Overall the the gameplay is definitely intriguing and realistic. But if you do not want to spend real money, be prepared to spend hours planning your fishing properly as the licenses and travel expenses will require even more hours of fishing for your expenses to be recouped.

It has the fun platforming, the great music and of course like most games of this genre, its fair bit of difficult sections that have you on the verge of throwing the controller.
It's pretty easy to recommend this game if you're a fan of the NES era but what if you're not? Should you still play this game? I honestly think so. The game has a great sound track, it's very easy to pick up and play in the same way that Super Mario Bros and Megaman are since you literally just jump and attack, and despite there being some harder areas, the check point system and the fact that there isn't a limited number of lives makes the game feel a lot more fair than games from the NES era feel if you go back and play them now. This game also has a free DLC patch that adds an entirely new campaign with a new character for free, so I mean.. yeah, you get free stuff with your game that adds replay-ability (is that even a word) to it and it has a new game+ as well.
The only way I couldn't recommend it is if you don't enjoy platformers, you don't enjoy games that can be challenging at times or if you're just sick of the whole retro-styled game explosion on Steam where everybody and their mothers are mainly releasing retro-looking games, and even then, this game has a lot more going on beyond being another retro-styled platformer.
