I wasn't expecting much from this after the crappy attempt at cashing in on the faux-roguelike fad that was The Random Encounter. But my doubts were fixed pretty quickly. This game may even be better than the main series in many ways. Now before you call for my hanging let me explain. Besides the gun stacking thing (which is very cool and highly appropriate for the series) this goes way past 11 in the ridiculous scale. For example, you build bridges and ladders out of the bodies of the monsters you kill and you ride around on such contraptions as a dynamite powered unicycle.
The game is also just plain surreal in some ways. Moreso than the "kill all the things that spawned in ancient egypt because time travel" thing. It would appear that Mental's army was taken over by a freakishly tall (but somehow still having tiny legs)... Thing that resembles a combination of prawn and human. The designs of the monsters are pretty weird even by Serious Sam standards. The other art like that of weapons and NPCs is pretty good too despite being a little disconcerting due to the proportions. Which is intentional I'm guessing.
and yes, there are also secrets. Many of which are weirder than the main series'. There is also a notification icon that appears when you're in proximity to one. Something I really wish Serious Sam proper had. Some may argue that it defeats the point of a secret to have an icon. But those people are silly. Also you can disable it.

Personally, I am a fan of survival horror. However, contrary to mainstream belief, I'm not a fan of this game. It must be said, the atmosphere is fantastic, and the music is great, but it the game just didn't do it for me. The monsters look ridiculous, and walk around in a comical way, which ruins the pacing, and creates many laughable moments. The puzzles themselves I found tedious and boring, ruining the atmosphere as nothing happened for around 20 minutes before the monsters came along. I was too bored  to play the rest of the game. Potentially gets better towards the end? I don't know, I just never had that urge to survive. When I died, I felt more like, 'Oh, okay.' And whilst comparing this game to Dead Space 1 seems strange, I'd like to point out that in Dead Space 1, I felt obliged to fend off the necromorphs, constantly checking my ammo and finding the necromorphs more terryifing, than the quite comical monsters in this game. However, to give the community credit, there are some great custom stories out there, which do make the game a lot better. Consequently, it is up to the player whether they want to buy this game or not, this is just my personal opinion, but from my point of view maybe a 4/10 for the game itself, but more 6/10 or maybe 7/10 with the custom stories. Tl;dr the game falls short in the survival aspect as the monsters are too comical to be afraid of.

Deceit offers an interesting and unique experience that is shared by few other titles, and while its mechanics can seem unintuitive to begin with, once the player has learned the basics of the game it plays surprisingly smoothly, working on a simple enough premise with the layers of complexity being introduced gently as the player gets better at it. The progression system is a nice touch, with the unlockable perks and cosmetics providing an incentive to keep playing. I can't speak for Ranked mode yet as I haven't unlocked it but I was pleasantly surprised that it was offered at all. The "horror" aspect of the game is quickly lost as the player comes to terms with how matches generally play out, but the online nature of the experience means that each round is unpredictable and offers new experiences. The game runs very well and looks good, with pleasing visuals, a clean UI layout and subtle post-processing along with a host of customisable graphics options. The audio compliments the ambience well and the maps are interesting and atmospheric- though I would like to see more added in the coming months. For a free-to-play, microtransactions are pleasantly non-intrusive with no pay-to-win systems, and the under-the-cup lootbox system has proven to be a surprisingly enjoyable mini-game which adds some skill to the luck. Overall, Deceit is a fun, unique and rewarding experience with smooth gameplay, a simple yet cunning set of mechanics, and a clean audiovisual exterior, and I wish it all the best in expanding its playerbase and adding new content in the near future.

Soul Reaver 1 ended with a cliffhanger, so the second game continues after a remastered final scene. Graphics are much nicer, a lot more details, improved animation etc. Also, there's mouse support, so it's much easier to navigate around, but still a bit annoying, especially while swimming, and Raziel decides to take a vertical dive, when you actually wanted to jump out of the water/blood. It's also a bit repetitive, cause you're gonna be going up and down the same path quite a few times, in different seasons albeit. Places where you can save are sometimes too long apart. But all those little complaints aren't really important, because
- the same voice actors for the main characters are still there
- dialogues and monologues are very well written, and sometime pretty long
- puzzles are still great, and they now kinda replace boss battles
- story continues to follow Raziel on his path to change his and the faith of Nosgoth
- many cutscenes convey very well the reason behind Raziel's actions, and his choices, or lack there of
- there are actual hints for what you need to do, and what you can't do yet, so it's easier than the first game
As second part of the Legacy Of Kain series, it revealed a lot of crucial story elements, that will resonate in the remaining two games. It explains the deceitful and strained relations between Raziel, Kain, Moebius and others. It shows the lengths they're willing to go and risks they take to acomplish their goal. It's all part of an epic saga that spans across centuries. A fight to cleanse the Pillars Of Nosgoth of corruption, and thus restore the balance in the decaying land.

Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver 2 takes place right after Soul Reaver 1.
Like literally, right after.
In pursuit of Kain, Raziel is pulled from the time stream by Mobius, the world's worst liar. Mobius tries to convince Raziel that they're on the same side, but Raziel doesn't believe him. Even so, Mobius reveals to Raziel that Kain is currently at the pillars of Nosgoth, a landmark that maintains balance in the world.
After not being convinced of anything, Raziel talks mad smack against Mobius before leaving the time chamber in search for Kain, so that he can stab him and say more mean things about him. But is this all part of Mobius' plan? Probably, he's not really subtle about it.
As stated before, Soul Reaver 2 continues right after the cliffhanger of Soul Reaver 1. It plays like it's supposed to be played back to back with the first game, which is great for me but was probably absolute murder on fans back in 1999, since the game didn't see the light of day until 2001.
Playing the games back to back made me appreciate SR2 as a sequel, though. Going from the jaggedy, emotionless polygons of the first Soul Reaver to these brand spanking new Playstation 2 graphics was quite the treat. Characters emote outside of per-rendered cut scenes now, and to a pretty impressive degree. Their mouths sync up with every word almost perfectly
and they show degrees of emotion ranging from anger, to fear, to confusion, to that look you give someone when they keep using words you don't understand.
Like aberration. Or restraining order.
The cut scenes are also much longer now, like, much much longer. It actually feels like they're giving Metal Gear a run for it's money some times. This isn't bad, really, since it serves mostly to build onto the world of Nosgoth and the Legacy of Kain lore. Except for the fact that you can't skip them. That's a nightmare if the game crashes.
Combat isn't much different from the first Soul Reaver, except now you have a block and a heavy attack button! So it's completely different!
Your most common enemy in the game now are regular old humans, though other kinds of critters pop up from time to time as well. Because your enemy are mostly human, you don't have to worry about the methods of murder like you did in Soul Reaver 1, since they're not vampires. Once you kill a human, they stay dead even if you don't eat their soul, that goes the same for any kind of monster you run into.
It feels more basic because of this, even if the whole “Get rid of the vampire” thing of the last game didn't make it all that complicated or difficult in the first place.
I ended up using my claws or a staff weapon more than not when I wasn't blowing fools up with the Wraith Blade. These have to be the most unsatisfying swords I have ever used in a video game in a long time, they work more like clubs than swords. When you hit someone with a sword you expect to get like, a big slicey sound or something, instead you get this meaty whack. You're better off just using any other weapon, if not just your bare hands, considering how awkward they feel to use.
My other big gripe with the combat is how it seems to be used as filler now than an actual part of the game. Going from place to place on the map is more like an endurance run than an actual journey, especially late game where they just throw wave after wave of enemies at you.
I much preferred it in the last game where you would only find some enemies every now and then, though that was more because of hardware limitations and the fact it was trying to maintain that rotting empire motif.
At the very least they manage to mix the puzzles up a little bit, they're only slightly more complicated than the last game, though. At this point I would have preferred more varied puzzles than more combat encounters.
But this all being said, would I still recommend the game?
Well, yes. With all my complaints, I at least stuck around because of the performance and story. The combat isn't bad, it just needed to be toned down a bit, and maybe make the puzzle dungeons a bit smaller? I don't mean less puzzles, just make the maps more compact I guess. You spend a lot of time just running back and forth doing nothing, I would have preferred if there was at least a bit of cut out between destinations.
Soul Reaver 2 is available on both the PC and the Playstation 2. I somehow remember there being a Dreamcast version of the game, though I've been proven wrong in some of my research.
Its still a decently fun game to play, though it can get a bit tiresome at times. The controls are much better this time around, however, I even managed to play the game with a controller without the use of third party programs.
Also the dialogue, oh man that sweet, sweet dialogue. I could just sit around and listen to Kain and Raziel banter all day. Someone make that, Legacy of Kain ASMR, I'd actually pay for that.

This is definitely one of the freshest yet at the same time most nostalgic platform experiences I have played in the recent years, I do wholly recommend this game for those who are in for 5/6 hours filled by tears, blood, swears and genuine fun!
I'm sure I haven't done a positive review in months and luckily, thanks to this year's summer sales, this outrageously bad trend came to an end as soon as i digged into this game.
Truth be told, I have always been a hardcore platform games fan and when one of my friends talked about this game I was fairly excited to finally play once more one of this kind of games after years and years of trying out new genres and, heck, sticking with online multiplayer games (I'm looking at you, Smite and Team Fortress 2!)
So, where to begin? The moment you start the game, you'll be instantly brought to a simpler era, where all that was needed were a controller and free time. The story is told through an old fashioned images medley, and, despite it sounding like something "already seen", in my opinion it adds to the general nostalgic value of the game.
Alright, I hope I don't need to point this out, but yes, your character does indeed use a shovel instead of the stereotyped usual medieval sword, but worry not! It is a really useful tool that will not only help you kill enemies as you continue exploring, but will also get you gold and gems hidden into... I guess... piles of rocks? Yeah!
And these, uh, "goldies" are important in the game, for you will, after finishing the very first level, get to the village where you can saltuarly go to to buy health upgrades, mana upgrades and much more!
You'll also be able to use several spells that grant you powers/invincibility/andwhatnot for a few seconds, and that's a nice touch too.
As a final note for this first part of the review, the game has an astonishingly good soundtrack!
I personally listen to my own metal music whenever I play singleplayer games, but for a few hours I decided to make an exception because the musics in this game are really well made, I might even listen to them one of these days on their own while playing totally different games.
Alright, now that we're done with the praisin', the time has come for the criticizin', shall we begin?!?
Well, I personally haven't found major flaws in this game yet, although there might be a few elements that could possibly make some of you not enjoy the game thoroughly.
First off, this game is straigt up HARD. You're not looking at your average platform game whose difficulty level isn't that high, if you buy this game and decide to play it you WILL swear and insult your nearest deity, albeit the learning curve won't be too unforgiving.
What will be unforviging, however, are the bloody SPIKES. No matter what you'll do, no matter what you'll be handing, there's no escaping from the spikes. You touch them, you die. You don't (and won't) simply escape from the spikes.

Welcome, stranger!
Honestly, I never would have sought out "Serious Sam Double D" on my own. But since the "Serious Sam" bundle was so stupid cheap not too long ago (Oct. '14), I installed it just to see what it was about.
What I found was a glorious hybrid of "Contra" and "Borderlands". The gun stacking mechanic can be as ludicorus as you want... provided you've found enough weapons and connectors, and purchased the mods. Gameplay is not at all complex, though there are a few physics puzzles that will challenge you. Old school gamers who know when to run left, jumper high, or look for hidden paths will be rewarded.
"Double D" is even more over the top than the regular Sam games, and is genuinely funny. Especially on a second playthrough after you unlock Huff. After a few hours of Sam Stone's ultra-serious machoism, you get to experience the whole thing again with Huff's ultra-redneck belligerance. Really, the plot is non-sensical and non-existant. The characters are cartoonish, and the worlds full of in-jokes and Internet memes. So yeah, a lot of "Borderlands" flavor, only you're not stuck with just one gun at a time.
I highly recommend a second playthrough with Huff on higher difficulty. You'll have all the mechanics down pat (and all your upgrades), and will need to be challenged. Plus, Huff's dialogue and cutscenes are great fun, even if you're blasting the same enemies. There're just more of them.
Controller support is just fine, so it makes a great pick-up and play game. The graphics have a hand-painted look that hold up very well in HD. I haven't tried local co-op, but it's a shame there's no online feature. Not a dealbreaker by any means, though. Good value for under $10, a steal at anything less. Don't hesitate to pick it up on sale for yourself or gift to a friend. Seriously!

Playing ARMA 3, I kept thinking of Falcon 4.0, the 1998 flight simulator. Like the ARMA series, the Falcon simulators claim to fame was their incredibly realistic fidelity. "Falcon 4.0" aimed to improve on this with the addition of a dynamic campaign; rather than simply flying pre-determined missions, it dropped you into a virtual warzone that reacted to the player's actions. It never worked quite as well as the pre-release hype promised but - considering it came out in a time when computer speed was measured in Megahertz and RAM in Megabytes - it was still an impressive attempt.
I mention Falcon 4.0 because the addition of a similar virtual warzone seems a perfect fit for the ARMA series, and ARMA 3 in particular. Older games of the franchise were still playing around with the underlying technology and gameplay, but neither of these areas received significant advancement in ARMA 3; in many ways, this game feels like a re-skin of ARMA 2. The addition of a reactive campaign would have been a logical iteration. Instead, we got its rushed single-player campaign.
Now, I know "ARMA 3" was intended to be played in multiplayer, with large groups of like-minded people role-playing war-game fantasies in player-made battles. Its single-player mode feels like a technology demo; a sampling of what the mission-creator - and game-engine - can do rather than a real attempt to craft a strong story or gameplay. But that campaign was so rough and unfulfilling that it did more to turn me off the series than want to further explore the game's capabilities. The missions were short - one of the earlier missions is little more than you driving down a road for a few minutes - and too frequently interrupted by badly scripted cut-scenes.
The actual gameplay isn't very fulfilling; although arguably realistic, getting sniped by a 'bot hiding in the forest a mile away that you don't even know is there until you fall over dead isn't much fun. Too much of the game has me blindly the following friendly AI, where I was more intent on watching where they were going than keeping an eye out for enemies. It's also a fragile game; don't do what the game expects and the scripting breaks, forcing a mission restart. It's unsatisfying and restrictive; exactly the opposite of what I'd expect from a game with such a huge open world. And don't even get me started on its awful control scheme...
The underlying technology of the ARMA games is incredibly impressive; I just hope that one day they manage to make an entertaining game with it.

If you don't know what this game is about, you play as someone who is trying to access something called a "Red Room" on the Deep Web. A Red Room is a site where you can watch or participate in live, interactive torture and murder. As you go through your search for the pieces of the URL to the Red Room, you are in danger of being hacked, located and kindapped, or killed. With each scenario, there is a way to prevent it from happening, whether that be typing in the text that is displayed, pointing in the right direction for a path to follow, or even blocking the front door of your house to keep the maniac outside your house.
This game, first off, is extremely well done. It is easy to say that this is truly one of the best games of 2016. The graphics are fairly good, the atmosphere is extremely well-done, and the gameplay is horrifyingly realistic. I often find myself in such a state of fear that I am literally having trouble breathing and even though there is an option to turn off the mic if a kidnapper is outside, I still find myself trying to stay as quiet as possible for as long as I can. This game causes stress like it's supposed to, it is achieving it's goal of being realistic, and overall, it's extremel nerve-racking most of the time.
Overall, I'd give Welcome to the Game a 98/100. This game is truly fantastic and it's worth far more than it's $2 price tag. Fantastic job, Reflect Studios.

If I had to describe this game in one word, I'd say it's "Cute." If I had to describe it in five, I'd say it's "Cute, but a real mess."
As a well-known lover of bears, I followed and backed the Kickstarter. I was curious to see what it was going to be like, and was interested in the developer's sense of humor. The dry and inoffensive humor is the game's shining feature, as each example of writing in the game has a sort of cute and casual cadence to it that actually had me looking forward to the next item description or animal smell. It's such a shame that the actually interesting things to look at are hidden behind [long stretches of incredibly ugly textures and] (note: this is no longer an issue) z-fighting shadows (even on the highest graphics settings), very difficult "enemies" with incredibly small hitboxes, wonky platforming, and [obnoxious stat barriers] (note: this is no longer as big an issue). I found a door in a place called Nido Valley (A Dark Souls reference?) that required 777 in a certain stat and something called Bear Courage, [and even eating mushrooms would require you to have a high enough Intelligence stat] (note: this is no longer an issue). Also, and I don't really know how to describe this, but the trees wobble. I think that the trees react to your view bob differently depending on how far away they are. Bizarre. (note: I have been informed that this is an engine limitation. It's still weird, though)
As a developer's first game, it's a nice little prototype/practice for what could possibly be described as a "real" game sometime in the future. I'd be interested in reading a wiki for this game, but I absolutely do not have the patience to write it. Maybe pick this up if you really love bears and simple jokes, and have a lot of time to waste and don't mind walking simulators.
Edit: As of March 3rd, Farjay released a patch upgrading the texture qualities and removing the stat requirements on food. Although there is still a significant amount of Z fighting on shadows (Z fighting is where two textures that occupy the same space overlap each other and fight to be seen), these updates fixed the two biggest problems I had with this game. The game is actually pretty good looking now! I am now upgrading this to an uniornic recommendation.

I never considered myself one interested in experimental games. I've played Loneliness by Jordan Magnusson and I find it brilliant for its minimalistic design and the possibilities of creating one's own story without making any direct choices. But there you go, this is likely the only experimental game I've tried or at least the only one that caught my attention enough for me to remember it. So while I was a little interested in seeing what is Memoir En Code, I was far from being enthusiastic about it.
Store page told me to expect 40 minutes of play time on my first attempt to beat the game. So after I finished it in around 15 minutes, I got confused. I had this terrible feeling that I must have missed something, or even a lot of somethings, but honestly, at this point I didn't really want to try again. The game felt chaotic, being a mishmash of various scenes, with each of them having entirely different rules of gameplay, and even some of them having very little gameplay. That said, I'm not one to get angry over a game being short or confusing, so after a while I gave it another go. And this time I spent around 1 hour exploring the game, replaying some sections trying to get a different outcomes and reading the dev commentary. And this time this was a pleasant and most warming experience.
Overall this game is something very new to me, so perhaps this is the reason I eventually found it interesting and entertaining. Autobiography seems truly an unexplored theme in games and I find it most impressive that someone managed to gamify one good bit of his life. As I mentioned before, there are of course some scenes which are not much a game but even those scenes are entertaining. There is a part when you're a little child and you're being told a story - and just as a child would, you get to interrupt and ask questions, sometimes almost unrelated to the story (e.g. "... the boy lived with his mother in a small cabin" "Did he have a dad?"). And on the other hand there is a part that's almost a time management game as you try to prepare yourself to an exam and you need to find a good spot where you can learn efficiently and where no one will bother you.
I really enjoyed discovering this game. To make it short, the more you give yourself to the game, the more you get out of it. Almost every scene might end in one of a few different ways, depending on your actions and it's fun to discover the possibilities. Although sometimes it feels disappointing when even though you perform better than the last time, you still don't get a better result (using the example of the exam mentioned before, I couldn't get a score higher than 80/100). But well, that's life I guess, so it's good the game is disappointing the same way.
I'm a bit concerned about the price tag. This seems to be a case where players pay for the developer's effort rather than the final product they get, but as I have received the game as a gift, I cannot complain about this.
Even if I consider the price too high, it doesn't change my opinion on the game - this is a well made title showing a very personal story. It's innovative and you just gotta appreciate that. I'm absolutely sure that this is not a game that everyone will enjoy but in case you're not sure about yourself, check out the "Should I buy this game?" section on the store page - I find it accurate, honest and very helpful.

I felt like Darksiders did some things right but the main components of the game felt wrong. There are 2 aspects of the game which I think Vigil did right, and that is the sound (voice acting and music) and the art design. Both are well polished and interesting. War looks like a real badass and sounds like one too.
But this game is a 'hack and slash' so the combat should be the main focus, and this is where I felt the game fell short. It felt clunky and slow to put it bluntly. Blocking is extremely awkwards because the put the same button to block as they did dash when you're moving in a direction. So when trying to block you more often than not dash, which can result in you getting hit. And I hate getting hit. Juggling also ties into blocking with how enemies behave. Small things like a certain grunt enemy (which are plentyful) do a ground bash that somehow also hits you in the air, which it honestly shouldn't (I mean, it is a ground attack), causing you to lose your juggle as well as being unblockable. The lock-on system and free aim systems are both awful. When locking on it changes your camera angle so you frequently can't see what is behind you and it is also awkward trying to change between targets. Free aiming is exponentially worse. It is difficult to describe in words, but the aiming is slow, clunky, awkward, and so frequently used it makes for a terrible gaming experience. What's more is that parts when you have to hit something with your projectile weapons is made that much harder because the game forces you to use the free aim controls, instead of just locking on to what you need to hit. I think this is unecessary to the overall experience of platforming.
Manouvering the game world is also a chore in my opinion. Darksiders is a hack and slash, and world design in such games needs so be concise and straight forward, or in other words somewhat linear. Backtracking or having an open level design is fine, exemplified in Devil May Cry 4 for example. But Darksiders has a world designed more like and RPG than the traditional hack and slash and it is painful trying to navigate it. War moves rediculously slow, especially when you're just trying to move from A to B in a big, open space. Moving from area to area is more bearable with a quicktravel system, but that involves War walking from one portal to another in some ethereal space. It takes 2 minutes but it is rediculously tedious. There is absolutely no need for it.
My verdict is that if you can pick up both Darksiders I and II for 10 bucks or less, you can do worse for your money. But small nuances in the gameplay degrade the overall experience too much, and I believe if you want a better hack and slash game you should play Devil May Cry 4 or earlier (not DMC).

The game may show a large amount of mechanical similarity to God of War, that is really where the comparison ends. Darksiders drops you into a post apocalyptic nightmare of a world that is an amazingly organic blend of Heaven, Hell, and the modern world. The game contains many beautifully designed levels that have you running down city streets one moment, and fighting in a Hell spawned cesspool the next, with one flowing beautifully into the other. Character and monster design leave nothing to be desired either, with wonderfully detailed nightmares and angelic warriors coming at you from all sides. This game definitely has the eye candy taken care of.
As far as the mechanics go, as I said, think God of War and you've pretty well got the idea. You're going to collect souls in order to level up. You'll learn new skills, get new toys, and those toys will need to be leveled as well. You'll run around unique, artistic maps solving complex puzzles. Combat is largely combo based versus multiple opponents, with multiple weapons to choose from. One of the amusing additions to combat is the ability to use just about anything in the environment as an improvised weapon. Street signs, street lamps, cars, you can use them all as either projectiles or beating implements. When the boss fights come up, you'll be working to beat them down to a context specific cut scene finale. If you enjoyed the GoW's gameplay style, you'll feel right at home here. And honestly, there is something to be said for that. The familiar mechanics mean that there's no time wasted figuring out how the game works, and more time spent actually playing the game.
Darksiders can be challenging at times, particularly some of the boss battles but the best advice as always is to persevere and you will find the solution. If you can overcome those minor issues then Darksiders has much to offer with a good storyline, many hours of gameplay, and some of the best action sequences you are likely to see.
Though influences from other games are clear to see, Darksiders still manages to excel on its own merits. If you're looking for an action/adventure that will keep you busy for hours then there is no need to look further.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent is game that almost everyone has heard of. It is infamous for its terrifying gameplay and very dark scenes. But is the game beneath all of the horror stories people tell of it worth a play through? To put it simply, yes.
In Amnesia, you assume the role of Daniel, who wakes up with Amnesia in the summer of 1839 in the Brennenburg Castle, located in Prussia. He can only recall his name and that something is trying to kill him.  Your task is simple. Get to the Inner Sanctum of the Castle and kill Alexander, the Baron of Brennenburg Castle.  Throughout the game you will find notes that were written by you before acquiring amnesia as well as witness flashbacks of your time with the Baron.  The story is good enough to get you from point A to point B, but overall it falls flat.
Amnesia is not about the story though, it is about the truly terrifying gameplay and scares that will haunt you from the beginning to the end. Whereas most survival horror games in the past few years have heavily relied on jump scares, Amnesia relies on the pure terror of something unknown waiting in the shadows for you and chasing you throughout the castle walls. The amount of times I found my heart racing as I threw tables and chairs up against the door and praying that the monstrosities wouldn’t be able to get in almost ruined my health long after I completed the game.
The mechanics of the game are very simple. You are not able to fight back the monsters of the game, you can only run or hide. A lantern will light your way around the castle, but it will drain the oil as you keep it lit as well as attract any monsters in the area to your position. Sitting in the dark will decrease your sanity, causing you to hallucinate and have blurred vision. Completing puzzles and making progress will increase your sanity. Everything that can be interacted with is incredibly well done as far as the amount of control you have over the item. You click the mouse to grab the object or door, control it how you wish, and release the mouse button to let go.
The puzzles in the game can be slightly frustrating. There were a few times where I sat trying to figure out what I needed to do for what felt like an eternity, only to finally find a missing piece and wonder either how I missed it or how the ever expected any sane person to figure out how to do it, let alone with the possibility of a monster slipping out of the corner and chasing me until I am lost. That being said, every puzzle at least seems logical once it is completed and it does give you a great feeling of accomplishment.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a very special game. It brings a style of horror that not many other games are able to pull off today. Rarely did I jump while playing this game, but I had a feeling of constant dread every time I had to enter a new room, turn a corner, or heard any kind of noise. If you are looking for a survival horror game that will truly put fear in your soul, Amnesia comes highly recommended.

I can think of no free-to-play game I've played more enjoyable than Deceit. It feels more like a paid game rather than F2P. The matchmaking is quick, the gameplay is original and fun, and the majority of players are merits to the community. This game is great to play with friends or strangers, so long as everyone has a microphone and understands the gameplay. The learning curve is short, allowing new players to get the hang of the game within a few rounds. Groups communicating outside the game (i.e. Discord, Skype, etc.) can ruin the round by telling each other who is infected, but generally players are solo and do not undermine the spirit of the game design. Microtransactions are present, as expected on a F2P game, but almost exclusively for cosmetic items. All pertinent game content is available without spending any real money if you choose not to. Deceit does have a few small bugs, but nothing gamebreaking.
The game does have a competitive ranked mode; for what purpose, I'll never know.
I wholly recommend at least trying out a handful of rounds each as infected and innocent to see if you like the game. After all, you don't have anything to lose.

I strolled by my recommended list on YouTube and found somebody's gameplay of Welcome To The Game. Normally, the junk YouTube suggests is NOT eye-catching to me, but this game in particular... sincerely interested me. I watched the gameplay, got sucked into the scenery and couldn't stop watching it. Believe it or not, this all happened yesterday.
The objective of the game is fun and exciting. The game's concept is intriguing and it captures the horrifying reality of the internet by digging into its pit of disturbing and inappropriate websites. Frantically you hunt codes for access to the Red Room (which, just to say, is for anyone with a twisted liking for torture). The mechanics and puzzles are neat. Being able to fight for your life and do the best you can to avoid the antagonists is so challenging, but that's what makes it exciting and intense. The first stage is hearing little sounds, then you'll reach closer to coming face-to-face with some... visitors. You'll be paranoid, I'll tell you that much.
If you know me personally, you know that I love villains, psychopaths, and monsters. The moment I saw the Russian kidnapper and The Breather, I was instantly glued to the game. I'm so into those uniquely insane and creepy characters that I want to be provided with backstories for each of them. I want to know their motives, thinking, and maybe something from their pasts that impacted their nutty behavior. They're super cool characters; just the way they're designed (appearance and personality wise) is great.
Overall, the game is creative, awesome, and spine-tingling. It's so scary and its atmosphere is well set. Your heart will pound and you'll have a blast facing the felons while surfing the Deep Web. As someone with a big thing for horror games, I like it so much and I'm glad I got to learn about it!

My initial review, below, was posted about a day after release, and is no longer very accurate. I still recommend this game though. It's nothing like Goat Simulator and nor does it try to be, it's an actual Bear Simulator. BEAR that in mind.
------------------------------------------------------
This is a game about being a bear. If you love bears as much as I do, this is a dream come true.... almost. There are some teething issues that hopefully will get resolved before long (no invert mouse option makes this near-unplayable for me), but the most important thing here is that this game captures the spirit of being a bear. You wander around hitting anything that moves or that you don't understand, and eating everything. Other people have done pros/cons so here goes:
Pros:
You are a bear
Map seems HUGE
Graphics are decent
I don't want the pros list to seem small, but you must understand, being a bear is amazing
Cons:
NO INVERT MOUSE OPTION (please fix this ASAP)
Typos everywhere
Very limited resolution options (no 1920X1200)
Steam overlay ghosts at top and bottom of screen (maybe resolution-related?)
Very occasional graphics flicker
Have found no way of locating your den once you've gone exploring, making stamina a real problem
Being too dumb to eat stuff (makes little sense, maybe too dumb to know the effects would work better?)
Yes I still recommend this game, being a bear is awesome and the next best thing to my ultimate dream - owning a pet bear.
Final Score - Bear/10

Being a huge fan of the first Soul Reaver game and the whole Legacy of Kain series I have mixed feelings about this title.
The game has a lot of pros:
- The story is awesome. It seamlessly continues the previous game and fills the gaps of the Blood Omen storyline.
- The cinematics and the cutscenes are well directed and spectacular.
- The voice acting is awesome.
- The character design is brilliant.
However, this game is awfully broken in many aspects:
- It has good cutscenes, but it also has too much unskippable cutscenes that will interrupt you every 20-30 minutes of the gameplay.
- Platforming and 3rd person camera are as bad as they were in Soul Reaver 1. This, and a ton of swimming sections can be infuriating.
- Battles are frustrating: the challenge is achieved by making enemies enormous damage sponges. Moreover, they are simply annoying: most of the time enemies will flee from you / block you / charge-stun you. There are a lot of battles but you will feel the urge to avoid them. Oh, and the enemies are tend to re-spawn just behind your back.
- Environments are dull, long and boring corridors. No exploration and no secrets. Not being such a big deal story-wise, they were the things that made the first Soul Reaver and the original Blood Omen one of the most exciting games.
- The backtracking in this game has no meaning at all, but its amount is just brutal.
- Yay, block-pushing puzzles from the first game are gone! Nay, mirror-rotating-and-pushing puzzles took their place...
tl;dr: Will recommend only to die-hard fans of Legacy of Kain franchise.

A very appreciated Gem of the 2000s Gaming Age. Now don't go in thinking that it has alot to offer like collectibles or anything extra. This is a textbook "Linear" game that is all about it's story and a damn good one.
Soul Reaver 2 picks back up on the journey of Raziel, Kain's former top vampire lieutenant who had been condemned to a painful demise and reborn as a soul devouring phantasm. Unbound by the will of his master, Raziel had embarked on a quest of redemption and vengeance throughout Nosgoth, now rendered into an inhospitable wasteland due to Kain's selfish and parasitic ambitions. Hunting down his vampire brethren and claiming their corrupted souls, Raziel confronts Kain within the Chronoplast, a chamber built by Moebius The Timestreamer.
Armed with nothing left but rage and his Wraith Blade, Raziel chases after Kain through one of The Chronoplast's portals, hurled through time into one of Nosgoth's earlier centuries of history and greeted by the TimeStreamer himself, Moebius.
-However, While the game and it's story are incredible to play, this PC/Steam port version of the game is anything but stable unless you have a good card or program to run it.
-Opening FMV will run black and voices sped up
- Game will freeze within minutes and not respond
-Raziel's Shift between the Spectral and Material realms won't function properly, which can be bad with certain puzzles needed for progression.
-Swimming is very buggy as you constantly bounce up and down
There are discussions to get pass this, and if you do, then I recommend this game for anyone looking for a great story and a simple good game worth finishing.

The graphics have aged but the game still looks decent and let us face it - the game has always been about gameplay first. Multiplayer is fun but the single-player campaign is what this game excels at. A huge map with three roman factions to choose from initially, later each defeated nation is unlocked as playable in the campaign. The gameplay is divided into 3 parts - cities management, sea battles and land battles. The last one is what this game is about and what makes it truly great. All the units, even siege engines, are nicely done and serve a purpose. The fighting is tactical and fair, although sometimes hard. But nothing beats the feeling of  a victory when you are outnumbered 4 to 1, or more! The AI has some problems but that can be forgiven in this case because it does not break the game at all. On top of all this are the mods, the lovely awesome mods. There are so many it would be hard to write all the good ones but MY personal favourites are Europa Babarorum, Lord of the Rings - Total War & Rome Total Realism. Seriously this game is worth your money if you like RTS games so I quite happily recommend it!

Good things in general:
+Parkour
+Beautiful scenery
+Plenty of extra content
Good things compared to the previous game:
+Ability to replay missions without needing to start over.
+Each mission now has some bonus objective for those looking for an extra challenge. It does make some missions more interesting.
+Addition of killstreaks that allow you to instakill people if you manage to maintain your streak. Quite fun when you get surrounded by tons of guards from all sides.
+Cristina's story
+Ability to hotkey the weapons/items you use the most.
+The pistol targets faster, making it actually useful.
+Getting to ride a horse in town and battling on horseback was a nice addition.
+It's nice to be able to summon assassin backup mid-battle.
+Eagle Vision would mark any collectibles on the map. Nice when you're in the middle of a mission and don't want to take a detour. And you can buy a map if you don't want to spend too much time on hunting down the hundred flags.
+Melee weapons are now paired with ranged weapons.
+Crossbow and poison darts added some tactical options for some form of stealth in the game. Especially useful in memories where you had to avoid detection.
+Addition of lifts as a quick way to get on a roof.
+Some things to do in the present day as well, albeit not too much.
Some things I didn't like:
-The story is shorter and interested me less than the previous game
-The numerous Borgia towers you had to destroy to unlock shops in the city were more of a repetitive nuisance than an interesting activity. Each tower was basically the same thing - find a specific character, kill him, and climb a tower to light it. Once or twice is fine, but twelve was a bit much. Especially since most of the viewpoints in this game were those very towers.
-You can select your fast travel destination through the map on the fast travel window. Instead, you have to go through a list of place names until the location you want to travel to lights up. Kinda unnecessarily annoying.
-No ability to replay from checkpoint. If you screw up with the optional objective for a mission, you have to restart the entire thing from scratch. It may not be a problem for most missions, but some require going through some annoying cinematics and other time wasting segments.
-Purchasing landmarks. I'm honestly not sure what point that serves. The pay from landmarks is very negligible (especially compared to how much you invest in them) and it doesn't change anything about the landmark. I'd understand if the payment would restore the landmark to some extent or something, but as it is, it's just something you can dump your extra money on.
-The store investment. I'd understand if you could invest as much money as you liked in as many stores as you wanted, but you can only invest in one store at a time (until you receive income from the stores you renovated) and could only invest a designated amount of money. So, not much you can do with it.
-You can loot some random stuff from bodies and chests, but there's nothing really you can do with the stuff, other than completing a couple of shop quests or just selling the stuff off. Kind of an underused system.
To be honest, while Brotherhood was a nice game, I didn't feel as into it as ACII. I'd still recommend playing it, but I'm not sure if I'd personally be ineterested in replaying it one day.

I'm not usually a fan of games that are difficult. I hate it when I die multiple times in a game, especially by the same enemy, and ESPECIALLY when it's in the same area each time that I just can't get past. I'm that wuss that plays games on easy because I don't want to get frustrated because a game is too difficult. Shovel Knight is surprisingly the exception. Shovel Knight is a tough game, I've died many times and very often during a level. Despite yelling profanities and getting more and more frustrated with each death, I've yet rage quit. Maybe it's because there's no saves within the level, so if you quit you have to start over, but there's something about it that makes me come back each time I die. I don't get just annoyed, I get determined and improve my technique. I last longer in each battle after I die, and there are areas of the level that despite being too difficult to surpass at one point, I've now figured out. It's really refreshing, and I wish other games were able to achieve this level of fun and frustrating. Overall, I was not at all disappointed by Shovel Knight. Really enthralling, old-school, and loads of fun.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent, is a game that, from the very beginning, is intended to be a classic horror title. Whether it be the intriguing story of Daniel, the haunting environments of Brennenburg castle, or the insatiable horror wrought from viewing the hideous monsters that stalk you throughout the game.
In titles such as Dead Space, F.E.A.R., Aliens VS Predator and Condemned: Criminal Origins, you are armed with a vast arsenal of weaponry to combat the horrors that surround you, the occasional jump scare taking you off guard and giving you a rush of pulse-pounding adrenaline that only a horror game can deliver. Amnesia, however, is a new kind of horror. You have no weapons, no tools, not even the slightest rock that you can throw to distract or fight off your enemies. All you can do is think fast and hid in the darkest corner of the room, and hope beyond hope that you'll survive the next couple minutes.
Brennenburg Castle ranks among the best horror game environments ever devised. Where we've grown used to the rusted, boodied halls of the USG Ishumura, the rocky environments of LV426, and the underground railroads of Boston, Brennenburg Castle delivers a diverse, beautiful area to explore.
Survival in this game is key. Your lantern will quickly run out of oil and you have a finite amount of tinderboxes to light sporadically placed torches and candles (which can be blown out by randomized gusts of wind). While it's not quite an RPG like The Elder Scrolls and S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and you don't need to eat anything to keep up your health, your greatest ally is light, and that'll keep you alive.
If you are without light, your sanity will begin to rapidly dwindle. The castle will begin to warp and twist around you, bugs and rats crawling round you. When your sanity is gone, you can consider yourself dead and you might as well huddle in a corner and cry until you work up the courage to turn off the game.
There are downsides, but very few. Some of the environments can be repetitive and boring. The puzzles increase in difficulty as you progress, and some appear to be unfairly placed and you feel more frustrated by the fact that you can't figure out how to turn on a machine to turn on an elevator or how to get through a hole in the floor that the horror aspect loses its focus. Also, this game isn't for everyone. If you're not in to slow paced games that have absolutely no action whatsoever, then you're going to be hard-pressed to enjoy this game. You can't fight, you have to solve countless puzzles that increase in ridiculous difficulty, and you're only abilities are to sprint, jump, and hide. If you play action games religiously, then steer clear of this one.
Amnesia: The Dark Descent is one of the best horror games I've ever played. Though not perfect, it is clearly destined for to be on the list of the top classic horror gamse of all time. It's specifications are not particularly high and can be run smoothly on maximum settings. If you like a good, terrifying horror title, then Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a must buy.

My issues with the game:
TL;DR:

3. Turning of the light does absolutely nothing. You may think "Oh, if I turn the light off, then maybe the kidnapper will stop bothering me", but no, it basically has no effect on you or him what so ever.
4. The loading between the webpages. I understand that they were trying to put a bit of realism in the game, but personally I really hate the page loading, as it isn't like most peoples PC are underspecced to run this game. I would just like an option to toggle this loading.
5. The FPS when not looking at the monitor are terrible. It says it drops down to about 45 FPS (I even tested this game on my friends rig which has a i7 and a GTX 1070 in it, and it still dropped, regardless of the settings), but it is more realistically about 20 FPS.

The last time a COD game has made me emotionally invested was the Modern Warfare campaigns. And this one takes the cake and then some as I couldn’t wait for every character interaction and cutscene not just because they look so good but it was just another way to pull me in and prepare me for the next mission. Being thrown with a group of random people at the start and quickly caring for them not to long after, I’d even find myself screaming irl for Zussman when I needed a medkit. Cause the plot wasn’t just “Hey there are Nazis, kill them.” it was also riding the rollercoaster with the characters whether it’s Zussman making you laugh or Pierson screaming in your face.
I do think having the mechanic to where each character in your group does something different like Stiles giving you grenades or Turner giving ammo when you need it, it makes you want to stick by your men instead of runin n’ gunning giving them a useful purpose. Plus it’s not op because it’s a form of killstreak, the more Nazis you kill the closer you get to some more health or even a mortar fire. I’d always try and play COD campaigns and for me Black Ops 1 and 2 for example didn’t pull me in, I didn’t care to keep playing and have never felt I should go back and play them, but the Modern Warfare series I’ve stayed up all night playing through them one after another. And I always try to enjoy single player games and invest myself into them regardless of how many times I’ve died over and over cause if it’s a good game then it is worth it to me to get through it and this game does not fail on that. I even forced myself to take breaks so I wouldn’t finish it to fast, and would get so scared when I thought I was about to be over and I’d think I knew that something would happen to a specific character and then surprise me when I wasn’t even close. It wasn’t too predictable so my critic side of me couldn’t ruin it for me.
I will say that care and work went into this game and wasn’t another copy and paste “COD: NOW WITH EVEN MORE ROBO SUITS!” It might be the fact I prefer real situations and actually events being portrayed in games but I still believe this was well well worth my money, time and was a great game.

"Here, Raziel. Every-thing is decided here. You cannot comprehend the magnitude, the rapture or the tragedy of this moment. And yet you must; if Nosgoth is to be dragged from the wreckage of it's damnation."
As stated elsewhere in these reviews, Soul Reaver 2 has the quality of story and voice acting that is God-tier.  It's epicness has been unrivavled, in my estimation, since it's inception several years ago. No story in video-games holds such weight that that of the Legacy of Kain series. This, imo, is the pinnacle of the story-telling in this series, from beginning to end. The twists and turns along with revelatory epiphonies that follow Raziel in his quest for the Truth are in no way, in any sense of the imagination, trivial.
History and time-travel also make their appearance here in a way that you've likely not fathomed possible, given the "Back to the Future" esque sense of time-travel most of modern media is inundated with. History, in particular, is a character in the story that can and will take action in the need to preserve continuity, a stunning inclusion and narrative-defining element. I'll not spoil the details here but the rules this universe are bound by are unique and very concievable, lending credence to the overal arc of this tale.
The voice acting is a remarkable feat in this game. Most games have solitary actors being cued up for their lines, leaving much to be desired in the natural ebb and flow of a genuine conversation; often stilted and jarring given that actors simply have to pretend they are talking with someone else when giving their lines. Not here. Every scene of dialogue has actors standing side-by-side in a sound booth, bouncing line after line off one another in such a way you would beleive these characters to be rea not only in their solidity but also in their convictions. Truly an example of a byegone era of voice acting. Unparralleled. A treat to be savored, for sure.
If you've never experienced the joy of Soul Reaver, I would implore you to either buy the game and play it (though the combat and platforming are a little dated by todays standards, the puzzles are fun though) or watch the movies of them online, starting with either the first soul reaver or the first legacy of Kain entry. It's hard to wrap your head around at first because there is much context to the story but once you get to this entry you are simply hooked.
There's nothing like this entry in all of the video games that I've ever played. Do yourself a favor and sink your teeth into it. You won't be disappointed

I bought this when it was first released for Mac. My opinion of AC2 Brotherhood is tinged by the technical issues I've had with the game and with some gameplay issues.
Technical first - starting with the longstanding issues. When I bought the game it locked me out of AC2 which would fail at launching uplay - an issue Ubi support swore blind wasn't caused by Uplay DRM. I eventually gave up contacting them after around 4 months or so as it started to seem more like busywork rather than actually resolving the issue. Eventually a patch came out after a few years which magically (and silently) resolved the issue.
I have always had to launch the game multiple times so the game will accept keyboard input.
Multiplayer never really worked on OSX - and it seems Ubisoft decided it wasn't worth the hassle of fixing  hence the large notice saying MP isn't supported on mac.
The combination of the above led me to never buy any Ubisoft game since.
Newer issues (which I expect will get no fixes from the devs due to the game's age and lack of interest in the platform) - the uplay app has an opaque white overlay, essentially obscuring the single means of launching the game.
It's still functional - you just have to memorise the button positions as the overlay flickers to life or launch the game from MP which bypasses Uplay altogether. This latter is actually faster than going through Uplay - which underlines how important tethering the game to Uplay actually is for user experience.
Finally on OSX 10.13.1 the game freezes for reasons I've yet to figure out. So if you are contemplating buying the game for the first time - be aware you may only get to play it in bursts of 5-10 minutes.
As to gameplay, at its best its enormously fun. While combat is kind of reliant on block and counter and the kill streaks have always given me a Dance Dance Revolution meets QTE vibe which I never quite liked, there is some variety there if you look for it.
My niggles with the gameplay though:
With hindsight taking the route of collectables/feathers/flags to pad any claims of "XX hours of playtime" trend started with AC but I gather it is a staple of Ubisoft open world games. The biggest AC2 B peeve however the control schemes are messed around to make things more difficult in certain, non skippable, timer critical, missions. This is something that gets hammered into budding game devs as a major no-no - don't spend time encouraging and rewarding players for using your control system, then whip the rug out from under them unless you really want to♥♥♥♥♥♥them off. This isn't a "git gud" issue, I completed the missions but I despised and resented the game for punishing me for being good at the game's, up to then, control system.

I like this a lot more than Ninja Storm 3 Full Burst. The Story doesn't feel like monotonous rehashed story elements from the manga, and much of the gameplay is in the tournament mode anyways which feels more like an pseudo-open-world environment. You can pretty much explore the tournament-mode map at your own leisure and help out other characters whom will then become available to support you in the battles ahead. You can also do some side missions for more money or explore the map and get items from things like floating balloons or stacks of mushrooms. Travel time is a bit tedious but there are NPCs to fast-travel between locations which helps alleviate it.
There are tons of items to collect, both cosmetic and otherwise, and despite some cosmetic items being restricted on whom can wear them, it'd also be pretty silly having things like the Two-Tails Tail on Rock Lee or something so it's not like it doesn't make sense. There are also hundreds of items to customize your online profile that are super collectable.
Albeit not a huge amount of new characters from the prior title, there are only so many characters that could be added from the series as after a point you're just creating movesets for characters that had a very small impact on the plotline and some others wouldn't make much sense as they've been dead for so long. Every character that someone would really want to play that I can forsee is included that were known at release. And some that people might want as characters are indirectly available as transformations (the tailed beasts).
The gameplay itself is pretty cool too. The tournament-mode capture the most orbs style allows you to give it your all and it's not over until the timer ends, In the multi-round tournaments, you can also come back from a huge loss in the prior round just by playing better on your current round character, which is nice. This is quite unlike prior 4-man gamemodes where if you ran out of health you're out, which is no fun at all. It does reward ranged large-aoe attacks more, but a small price to pay for a more varied and less punishing gamemode. In the case that you want more normal matches where you remove your foes health to win, most of the game outside of the tournaments is like that.
The only aspects I'd like more is some other ways to unlock characters than simply stockpiling money, and maybe different outfits for some characters that otherwise have none. A more clear difficulty for each recruitment mission before starting it would also be helpful so you know what to expect to an extent and can prepare accordingly, as some of them can be pretty challenging for a new player.
I'd give the game an 9/10 overall. The issues I have with it are trivial and it fulfills my expectations of an anime-based fighting game in almost every way.

My actual playtime of FFXI is something like 2.5 years. (That's total in-game time. Though I did AFK a lot trying to get NM death times, but 2.5 years is not far off.) I started at PS2 release and played off-and-on til the Level 80 expansion. I was not on board with the rapid update schedule they had lined up. It simply didn't make sense to continue to play, I thought, until the dust had settled. Coupled with my Linkshell losing members for different reasons and life changes, I stopped playing for a very long time.
Recently, my brother and I were talking about it in nostalgic terms and I decided to repurchase the game and start playing it again. I cannot stress how much different the game is now. But, they truly improved it in many different ways. I actually have like giddy JRPG type fun when playing it. It feels like a Final Fantasy game in a way it never did before. I don't know how much the enjoyment will last, but I've been leveling jobs to 99, unlocking AI companions (called trusts), and completing the questlines (while actually reading/enjoying the dialogue). And, remarkably, I am doing it solo and having a blast. If my brother wants to play, we team up, but it's never a big deal if we are not aligned together to do things.
I admit, I have not delved into the new end game content at all. I also greatly dislike the 'item level' system. It seems very silly to add such garish skill/stat increases on items to somehow fudge levels beyond 99. We didn't need 75+ content for years... why did it need 99+ content? But it's a small complaint really.
If you are fan of FF games and you missed FFXI, or you are a bit nostalgic about the game and want to try it again, I really do urge you to do so. There is a lot to do for returning players, and I really think you will have a lot of fun. Also, if you're on the fence about it, keep an eye on the website because there are return to FFXI campaigns rotating all the time and that might convince you. As I write this, there is a bonus exp campaign going on.

Deceit is ONE of the best multiplayer horror survival games to exist. You take on the role of being "Innocent" or "Infected."
Innocent players must activate levers in order to obtain objectives and also need to escape the map.
Infected players must drink blood bags (without being seen) in order to kill the innocent players.
As stated in the game's summary, "Deceit tests your instincts at trust and deception," meaning as an innocent player you have to gain other innocents' "trust," where the same applies to Infected players. Infected players should try their best to lie (where "deception" comes into play) to the other innocent players, so they can gain your trust. Pretty self-explanatory.
During the game, their is something called the "blackout period," where Infected players can transform into "terrors." In the terror form, you are much stronger and faster then the innocent players, you also have the ability to see in the dark. Each terror (Experiment, Yeti, & Werewolf) is unique and has there own ability. It is wise to use these abilities to your advantage.
For innocent players during the blackout period, they must find fuses and put them in the fuse box. Doing this will advance to the next stage and will be one step closer to escaping. However, beware of infected players transforming into their terror form. To avoid these terrors, you must activate levers (which you can before the blackout period; you may also do this during the blackout, but I do not recommend it). The camera is one of the best items to fight terrors, as it slows them down and blinds them, making them easier to take down. Each time you advance to the next stage, objective count is decreased, but more powerful objectives will spawn.
Deceit is extremely fun with friends, I highly recommend you get a partner or others to really have a fun experience. However, if you are solo, be aware of "premade" parties. These premade parties can be very unfun and unfair, as they can tell their party members wheather someone is innocent or infected pretty easily. I personally don't do this when playing with a friend as it just isn't fun and I don't want to ruin someone's experience.
Really the only cons I have with this game are these premade parties, thai players in the wrong servers, and sometimes some stuttering with the recent christmas update (which I hope gets fixed soon).
Overall, this game is extremely fun and I highly recommend you try it out, you won't be disappointed.

Halfway's story reminds me somewhat of space siege (2008) in that there are mishaps on a colonist transport ship and you have to scavenge the ship to get materials to buy upgrades, but set turn based tactics and with pixel art.
You will also have to inventory manage as each squad member generally carries 8 items max and your storage space is limited to 50 items. This requires you to only reload when empty and see how long you can hold off healing for (unlike modern FPS which spoon feed you ammo & health), so may not be for all casual strategy/turnbased RPG players.

The turn mechanics follow one of two methods: 1) no hostiles = unlimited actions; 2) hostiles present = 2 actions per squad member in a turn (includes reloading, healing & changing weapons). You also gain half or whole cover when stood next to hard terrain.
If you are a fan of Templar Battleforce, Hard West, Xcom etc. then this game is likely to float your boat.
The only negative I've experienced is a small but noticeable amount of .exe errors when attempting to start the game, otherwise I can't really fault it having bought it during the sales.

is a game I really
want to like. And I do like it, except the part where you have to play it. The reason I'm giving it a thumbs down is in order to post this where presumably human eyes can see it, I must select a direction for the thumb to point because Lord Gaben won't grant us the audacity to have a nuanced opinion from a glance aka “a sideways thumb”. And I believe that the technical issues with UI and overall gameplay outweigh spending the time of what I'm told and have it on good authority is an eighteen hour campaign.
This is wholeheartedly XCOM inspired, down to having 90% chance shots 2 tiles away and missing. Ammunition, meds and batteries can be synthesized in the safe room of the ship using “energy” you either find or get from extra stuff in your inventory that you decide to recycle. Additionally, the guns all use magazines (or, the ones I found at least.) Meaning, if you reload them before depleting all the rounds you'll lose the ammo you didn't shoot. This can make using an action point to reload sooner in order to take a shot THIS turn rather than the next to save face rather... problematic. Granted, quite strategic still if not nerve racking. Even Darkest Dungeon doesn't make me feel as nervous about supplies. Wasteland 2 either, at least in that you can sell junk to scrap for new ammo. Again, I feel it would have been better as a preparation task rather than just low, always scarce ammo. This is largely due to low energy rewards/high item cost and low backpack storage space.

I found the UI to be a bit claustrophobic. Since each character only has about 8 or 12 slots in their backpack. It would have been a life saver to have been able to sort every ones on the same screen. It works well enough but not anywhere near as well as it could. Switching between them all one at a time and having to select multiple things just to send it to someone else would have been astronomically aided if I could have say, have 2 or more characters inventories up and simply drag and drop the item over.
I think my dissent from liking this game as much I could have also stems from the fact that.. and I'm sorry about this, I don't really care for XCOM. That series has never clicked with me. However, this game is still markedly different than XCOM. There is no XP for only kills or permadeath. It's also much more narratively driven. Rather in Halfway, XP is earned through stim packs that permanently raise stat points. To which over doing it can have adverse effects.

Brotherhood is a direct continuation of AC2, and mostly more of the same in terms of story, gameplay, missions, etc.
One thin this game does that I really liked was that you can run your own assassin's guild, send them on missions, level them up, and make money and gain items by doing so. I had a lot of fun with this, although it's not a very big part of the game.
Although the game is more of the same when looking at AC2, there is definitely quite a lot more of it here. Unlike AC2, I ignored most of the side missions in this game, and just focused on the main story. The reason I skipped most of the side content though, was because there was just so much of it. If you enjoy the side activities in AC games, there's quite a lot to delve into here. However, I never really felt it was all that necessary. I only upgraded my items a few times, and was able to beat the game with low to mid tier equipment. So challenge wise I didn't feel the need to level my stuff up.
There is also a nice mechanic in this game, where you are "rebuilding" Rome by buying and refurbishing businesses, making money off of investments, etc. After a while I could afford anything in the game, but didn't really need to buy anything. Which I think is a problem AC games have in general. Unless you can offer me something really cool, or unless the equipment is really necessary, the in-game economies never make much sense.
On that note, something else the AC series keeps trying to do but never seems to get quite right is the player housing. I love the idea of having an Assassin's base, but there's really no reason to ever go there, and not a lot of customization options either, so I don't really feel like it became my home.
The story feels very much like a middle game, in that it continues the plot from AC2 but you can tell it's just filler before the third installment.
Overall, a solid, enjoyable Assassin's Creed adventure, although much of the same as the previous game in the series.

In 2017 CE I completed AC Brotherhood for the first time.
Brotherhood is the first game in the series that introduced an idea of a 100% synchronization. And let me tell you, I parted with any notion of achieving the sync the way the humanity parts its way with its past - laughing. Basically, I got Don Auditore out of the Room#1 when the timer for the entire dungeon expired.  No need for any eagle vision to see the writing was on the wall: 50% is good enough.
I also was blown away by Ubisoft managing to cram in even more map markers for even more numerous pass-times for those who are intent on squeezing every last second of the purchase of a videogame. In sampler form those missions are not exactly bad, but Ubisoft stretched out something fierce to add Renaissance: The Monopoly  and The Roman Tycoon and Indiana Jones and the Raiders of the Lost Cause in one title. So, yup, I burned a few towers, frollicked througha the Romulas’ dungeons, tried to put the saved citizens to a good use and (sort of) kept up Ezio’s income in-line with his (extravagant) needs.
This time round I said a firm “no” to glyphs and everything else.
Meanwhile, what propelled the game past the AC2 to my second favorite installment in the franchise so far (that’s AC1>AC2:B>AC2 for extra-clarity) was the most cohesive story and absolutely the best villain so far.
Yes, AC2:B regains what AC2 lost - its focus. Granted, it’s not the same focus as in the AC1. The Ancient and Noble Order of the Assassins now reminds Free Masons even more so & Altair still remains as the only qualifying Assassin in the franchise (save for that one secondary character called Mickelotto). But it is a focus nonetheless.
Ubisoft could not have picked a better focus. I doubt that any of the subsequent games beats AC2:B in that respect.
Because it's Cesare Borgia! HELLS YES!
500 years of bad publicity, and the unflattering portrayal in a videogame (that alone would have destroyed any lesser man, I wager) done zip to contain Cesare’s raw appeal and wow factor. The sheer awesomeness of chasing after Cesare smoothed out many cases of having to watch Don Ezio doing idiotic things. Carrying yelling Lucretia all over the Castlo Di Angelo instead of finishing her off and taking the key takes the cake & I guess it was so appealing to Ezio, he had to do it again with a naked guy by Coliseum - by all rights, if Assassins are a force of good, evil deserves to win, ‘cause good is so dumb.
Anyway, yes, yes, yes, they did it right to focus on Cesare and keep showing him throughout the game as Ezio’s nemesis. Loved that!
I found controls in AC2:B the most stubborn and sluggish, and was disappointed that the only solo thing I can do in the MP module is an intro mission. I thought “everything is permitted” extended as far as letting a fool to get into an MP mission on her own and die whenever. But, well, as bare-bones as Intro mission is, playing a girl-assassin was fun!
The modern-day stuff was as bizarre and boring for me as ever despite the injection of parkour - but I know there are good folk out there who serioulsy love Mr.Dull and Miss Lucy, so yeah, the game had some of that too and the modern storyline ended up on a cliffhanger.

Narcissu is a kinetic novel (no choices, just reading) about several young people in a hospice (place for the terminally ill). As such, it is a fairly heavy story with none of the fan service/romance type of themes you might see in typical VNs.
I have to say that when I first started, I did not like the art and felt the game was confusing because you can't tell who is talking. The latter is because there is no sprite that shows up on the screen when someone is talking like in typical VNs. After finishing the game (about 4 hours total play time), those complaints are still there, but I was drawn in by the story. I think it is an interesting take on the philosophy of mortality. Just one of those games where you can think about it afterwards and decide whether it makes sense for you or not.
If you are into VNs I think it is worth a couple hours, especially since it is free.
Tip: When you start a game, it will let you choose between launch screens. It is not obvious that you are actually picking between 1st or 2nd since there is no labeling. You should be playing 1st before 2nd for proper story continuity. You want the left screen for 1st, or right screen for 2nd. If you start the game and it talks about a boy, then you are in 1st. If you start and it takes about a family of girls, you are in 2nd.

One of my favorite games thanks to its time-jumping story and excellent dialogue. The gameplay was the perfect evolution from the original Soul Reaver, bringing the world and gameplay properly into a newer generation. The map difference is nice, being able to go from packed buildings in the commercial district to open grass plains and/or ruins, without ever needing to leave the city walls. Chain kills, a new indestructible armour, a DLC that's all about making up for missed screen time with Da Vinci, achievements that mean nothing, a memory sync meter for unlocking certain secret memories (honestly not worth the extra time to 100% a lot of memories). This game should be played immediately after finishing AC2, but still be aware that it plays significantly differently.
