Rome Total War A great game despite it's age.
Graphics 4 of 10
It's a really old game and the first total war game with 3D units instead of animated 2D sprites so you can't expect much in the way of graphics. and what you expect is what you get.
Learning curve (the lower the number the less learning curve there is) 5 of 10
The tutorials are good and the game is fairly simple to get into. This game has some learning curve for those who have never played any other RTSes but for those who have played other RTSes before they will have no problem getting into this game's controls.
Gameplay (on the battlefield) 7.5 of 10
Pros.
+Siege battles are very fun and challenging without being too hard.
+Land battles are Fun and tactical without being too hard.
+The AI is very good for a game of this age and can keep up with human opponents.
Cons
-some units are a bit over-powered such as elephants.
-some units are completely worthless unless under very specific circumstances such as the incendiary pigs that are only effective against elephants and have a tendency to kill more of your own people then the enemy’s that are killed due to the attack.and they do the same thing that a barrage of fire arrows from your archers could do.
Overall the land battles are very fun to play and are even better if you can find a human opponent to play with (CA recently migrated this game to steam due to the gamespy shutdown.)
Gameplay (Grand campaign) 4.5 of 10
Pros. 
+can be very fun when everything works well in tandem.
Cons
-Very dated
-It is nigh imposable to keep your budget in check when at war.
-diplomacy is clunky
-auto-resolving battles tends to end with your army losing a battle that anyone could win when controlling the units themselves.
Overall the campaign is good at times and really bad at others.
Overall 7 of 10.
Rome Total War is a game of two qualities; on one hand the battles are great and fun to command, on the other side the campaign is clunky, and not all that great at all. The good does outweigh the bad however. I completely recommend this game as custom and historical battles circumvent the horrid campaign and go to what is great about Rome Total War the combat.

You may be wondering I have not recomendded total war.  Well the reason for that is quite simple.  If i had just recomended it, then my review would have been lost among a sea of other reviews that also recomend it.  Hopefully someone somewhere will actually see this because its in a much smaller pool.  Anyway Rome total war is an excellent game, tatics while rather straightforward most of the time are realistic and you need to have a basic understanding of strategy to beat the AI on anything above easy.  Every faction has different unit compositions to use so your tatics will have to change on subsequent playthroughs. Game: 9/10
Developers: 6/10
Community: 9.5/10
After a while I decided to write a review for this production.
This game, is definitly not for some casual players, this is completly diffrent type of the games you will find commonly on the market.
I can't really tell you the cons and pros in this case since this game is very..."special" and "diffrent" but what I can do is give you several fair and real points about it.
First thing first: This game is "officialy" one of few that started from alpha, went through beta and came out as a final product. There are still DLC's comming for this game yet it's almost 4 years past the premiere.
2nd: There is a pretty good and fairly long campaign specialy if you have the DLC but that's something you "MUST HAVE" to really enjoy this game(Maybe skipping the kart DLC)
3rd: The basic multiplayer provided by the developers/producers is "ok" allthrough there is not much uniqe things compared to other games.
4th: Modding. The keyword for this production is "MODS". To be fair, as much as I love this game without mods, it wouldn't be nothing close to what it is with them. The modifications created by the community makes what this game actually is. We can fairly say that this is one huge playground for the modders, just like the GTA/Elder Scrolls or Fallout. It's maybe not that popular but it's one of the most modded games on steam avaliable at this date.
5th: The bugs. This game is clearly made for the patient part of the gaming community. Whenever you want to hunt someone and fire a perfect bullet right into the enemy traveling 2.6KM for several seconds while it's influenced by wind OR starting the game. The amount of bugs in this game is so high that you sometimes have to analyze what really is happening and ask yourself if it's a "feature" or "bug". Most of the bugs are actually funny rather than annoying, but sometimes it might get under your skin if you aren't chilled enough.
6th: Optymalization. There is a lot of talk about the FPS people are getting in this game, and just between you and me, on the singleplayer they are very fine. 60FPS is something pretty easy to get. On some small group/clan servers where there is not much of armagedon happening you should also get pretty fine FPS very close to the smooth 50-60FPS. But there are situations, where you join a server with 40/60/80 or even 100 or more people where there are also many other things running like scripts or mods. Low FPS between 20-30 will be normal, and that's something you will have to get yourself used to. Problem is that there are also random FPS drops and micro lags where the picture is just not smooth. Sure, the game went from 32bit to 64bit but don't you think that the FPS will increase! Sure, we get much higher RAM usage but that't not enough! Atleast with that you might have less random micro lags or even game crashes but that's as much as it offers.
7th: The price. I personally believe that the price is too high(With all the DLC) due to the fact that it's the community building this game not the developers them self. Many people create amazing mods for this game, spend weeks if not months to create something new for us, the players, but they aren't well rewarded. So, if you are new to this, you should consider waiting for some nice sale where the game will be at around 50% of the price.
8th: Hard drive space. If you become an armaholic you will need at least 100GB of free space to really test out the game and the mods which the community offers. What is also very helpfull here is a "SSD" drive. The game loads much faster and so does the textures, so when you are driving or flying somewhere and you have the textures on high you will surely notice diffrence.
9th: CPU and GPU. If you read anything about Arma 3 you will see information about the usage of processor. It's mostly turtlepoop. I have a 6 core I7 CPU and when I play the game the usage is very low, and so ofc. are the temperatures(What is the bright side of the medal). So to actually boost your performance in game, the overclocking of your CPU might be helpfull since the game doesn't use many cores. Getting an e.g. I7 from 3.6 to 4.4-6 GHz might bring you several FPS which might be worth it. Graphics card doesn't really matter here if you have an avarage one or high end SLI/Crossfire setup(Specially on multiplayer-servers) you won't notice that huge diffrence and you will rather cry your self to sleep for thinking that you actually spend a lot of money for a high end machine which can't generate you enough smooth FPS.
I think that's the most important and basic informations which you might need about this game before buying. Overall I am personally happy for buying this game and spending so much time within it. No regrets.

The point of "Welcome to the Game" is somewhat simple: find codes on various websites, put them together, and bam you get to watch some sweet sweet red room action. But, there's one little catch: You also have to avoid hackers, strange deepweb websites, Russian kidnappers, and.. well, pretty much your own ears. The game focuses a whole lot on sound, especially with the microphone option turned on, so make sure you're not using cheap headphones. Every sound is something: Chairs scrapping against your floor, knocking or banging, voices, footsteps, even breathing (that isn't your own of course) are threats to you and your data. When you turn the lights out, and the microphone is on, make sure to shut your trap. Every sound from a nervous half-breath to "oops you accidentally knocked over 10 pounds of your mother's priceless china" can cause the kidnappers to come right on over and do whatever they please. The codes are a bit tricky to find considering most of the websites that contain them only are able to be visited on certain points throughout the day. Plus, some sites with text are VERY long, so some codes are a bit tricky to locate. This game is very immersive, again even when the microphone is on. I personally found out about this game from Markiplier and Jacksepticeye, and even while watching them play it, like a lot of people, I was sp00ked out of my socks. When the lights are on and you begin to hear sounds, every little thing makes you jump up and practically dive for the lightswitch. When the lights are off, and you're holding your breath in order to not make a single sound, the crickets outside the window don't help much. It also immerses you into it by making you actually write down the codes in the notes provided you find instead of just clicking them or something. The game was a bit slow on my laptop, but that's probably only because my laptop isn't very good with games. I just really enjoy the concept of this game and how they executed the idea so very based around noises and such. I recommend this game to anyone who likes horror games that have tough puzzles, invasive mechanics, and just an overall fearful atmosphere to it. I'm surprised it's only two dollars; it's such a wonderful game. If you have an extra two dollars,  recommend you purchase this, or maybe just put it on your wishlist for sometime else.

I played this originally on console and I was completely floored by how much this game surprised me. It's easily one of the best, if not, the best 3D Zelda-style games out there. Although the PC port could use more options in terms of Anti Aliasing, Anisotropic Filtering, detail settings, etc., it will pretty much run smoothly on most modern PCs. Highly recommend a controller to play this game, especially an Xbox 360 controller.
The art style is the work of Joe Madureira, a famed comic book artist who has a very distinct style, usually overgrown, muscular men (and even women). Its got a bit of a comic book and maybe a little cel shaded-ish style. The combat is a mix of Zelda and God of War, a bit simpler compared to God of War, but gets the job done. It is very Zelda in terms of having a hub world to explore and then exploring dungeons to get new weapons and other items necessary for progression. But the game is way more violent and "edgy" in terms of content, such as blood, graphic dismemberment, etc.
Highly recommended, easily one of my favorite games in the last decade.
EDIT: Go for the Warmastered Edition since this version is no longer for sale.

I was surprised Halfway hasn't gotten more attention, what with XCOM and other turn-based squad games being so popular in recent years. The promised sci-fi stylings and tactical combat made it an easy sale purchase for me, despite the lack of buzz around it. Once I made it near the end of the game, though, I think I can understand why it flew under the radar. It definitely deserves more attention than it got for what it accomplishes, but not without a few caveats.
Halfway starts you off in control of Morten Lannis, a space marine-looking dude aboard a junky colony ship called the Goliath. He's come out of cryosleep way too early only to find the ship overrun with some very unfriendly types, and it's up to you to help him survive. The way you do this is very similar to how XCOM or the recent Shadowrun games operate. Outside of combat you can move around freely, talk with people, and loot containers. Combat is turn-based, with each of your characters having two (and only two) action points per turn. These points can move them around the grid maps (distance dependent on their agility stat) to find cover, attack enemies, reload weapons, use items, and so on.
It's a very familiar system with only two real stand-outs, the aiming system and the Retaliate option. Veterans of XCOM will notice that the hit percentages in Halfway are really, really low. Starting out, you're going to see a lot of 40-60% shots even from just a few squares away. The reason for this is that you can add action points to your attack to boost its accuracy. A one-point assault rifle shot may only sit at 50%, but adding your other point might kick it up to 75%. This is less important for shotguns but vitally important for sniper rifles, which have very low base percents but get a huge jump from the second point, simulating the need to set up and aim. As for Retaliate, it replaces the familiar Overwatch response with a sort of revenge, where your character returns fire only if attacked. It's not a bad idea but has very limited functionality in practice, and you're usually better off healing up or reloading if you have an extra action point to spend.
Additional characters will join you as you progress, each with their own stats and special abilities. There's plenty of gear to find, including armor (which uses Halo-style recharging shields), grenades, and stimpaks which can permanently raise character stats. You'll need to use everything you find because enemies in this game do not screw around. The campaign spans about two dozen missions, some optional, some multi-part, and all pretty harrowing. Enemies follow the same rules you do, terrible hit percentages and all, but very quickly the game starts stacking the numerical odds against you. By the mid-game you'll be facing up to a dozen foes at once, with the potential to lose a character in a single turn if you're not careful (dead characters revive at the end of combat).
This is where the game starts to grate because not only is it a long haul through tons of enemies, there's not much variety to the enemies or the combat. For the first 5-6 hours, you're going to be blasting melee dudes and ranged dudes. Only after the halfway point of the game will you start seeing things other than dudes, but this includes standard threats like heavily-armored turrets that only really add to the frustration. Failing a long mission after a bunch of samey combat is incredibly discouraging, and there are some missions in the middle where this is very likely. Missing three 80% shots in a row is very much a thing that can happen, and I definitely went back and forth between enjoying and raging at Halfway for a few nights, I'll admit.
After my last bout of frustration, though, I soon found myself eager to get back to the story. For all the flaws of the combat, the story and atmosphere of Halfway are fantastic. Each of the characters is unique and they all have important relationships that play out through the plot. The banter between them is excellent, with plenty of genuinely funny moments. Even the basic "ship under siege" plot has some interesting twists to explore. All of this is told against a surprisingly deep backdrop of dystopian future society, where people are separated by classes and basic human rights have been reduced to an alarming degree.
The pixel art is top-notch, with smooth animations, cool visual effects, and fantastic little details to find on every map. Sound is up to the task as well, with some really meaty weapon and hit sounds and a somber soundtrack reminiscent of FTL or Risk of Rain. The interface suffers from some bugs, however, making it hard to click on certain option or map elements, and it's bad enough to be distracting. Between that and the combat frustrations I did consider giving up on Halfway a few times, but I'm glad I stuck it out. For the price it's a rich and engaging strategy game that'll last you 15-20 hours, provided you have the patience to push through the rough parts.

A hidden gem type of game. Heavily inspired by the newest Xcom game, it's a turn based strategy game featuring a 2 action point system for shooting, moving, using items, etc. Battles take place in square tile maps.
It features a great style of 2D pixel art, specially the environments, which feature a lot of small, nice details. The sountrack is amazing and heavily inspired by the works of Vangelis in Blade Runner.
The core gameplay is solid and accessible. Veteran TBS  players will find that there isn't that much depth, but it's fun nonetheless. One thing that I missed initially is that there's a stealth component where the AI actually detects your units via sound and line of sight.
You will get access to 8 playable characters, each one with different base stats and unique special abilities. While I think the character could be more unique, they are different enough.
Equipment progression is in my opinion the weakest aspect of the game. It's mostly linear and there isn't much variety. The balance could also be a bit better, with sniper rifles being a bit overpowered and short range weapons being a bit underpowered. It's mostly fine though.
The campaign is mostly linear, with a couple of optional missions. The plot is nothing groundbreaking, but leaves you wanting more, specially after the ending. Looking forward to Halfway 2 if that ever happens. Oh, and after you beat it, I suggest replaying it with the NewGame+ mod. It makes the game significantly harder and fun (to me anyway).
Very recommended game, specially at the low asking price.

I really enjoy the ArmA Series as a concept, but I have a lot of issues with ArmA 3 that really just kill the fun for me. I'll go ahead and talk about what I like and don't like.
What I like:
The open world maps, the wide selection of vehicles and weapons, the ability to create limitless scenarios and the wide modding community. Sadly, I think the game is let down early enough by its level design, and the odd choice of keeping one of the main aspect from the bad platformers of the days of yore: the directional 'pushback on hit' mechanics combined with instadeath pits. It makes enemies uninteresting, and turns them from being a threat to being an annoyance that might, sometimes, precipitate your death to the offscreen void.
The game seems aware of that issue, since it is somewhat generous with its checkpoint system and temporary invulnerability skills a go-go - the main departures from the games Shovel Knight wants to pay tribute to. But this is just a rough patching work to the underlying issue. The game also reserves you some more one-hit kill surprises I won't spoil for you.
Ironically, compared to the dreaded pits and spikes, the boss fights felt like relaxing distractions.
The game also tends to focus on the grabbing of monies, gems, whatever... borrowing in that respect from Western 16bit platforming (think of all those German Amiga ones, with♥♥♥♥♥♥to grab everywhere). But then, the economic model your looting is supposed to support is so weak it makes little sense. Since there is no high score, there is basically no incentive past the halfway point, besides Pokemoniac Compulsive Behaviour, to grab anything.
I guess I am too cranky an old ♥♥♥♥ to be any patient with this kind of gaming experience anymore. Navigating the tedious and somewhat boring levels to get to the enjoyable little distraction of a boss fight and experience the pixel poetry of the inter cutscenes wasn't enough to keep me from grumbling.

I had a lot of anxiety growing up. Perhaps it was the side effect of being an overweight, socially awkward kid without any friends, or part of a larger psychological disorder that was never diagnosed, but either way it made day to day life immensely stressful and difficult. Emotional meltdowns were common, and anything unexpected usually sent me into a downward spiral that sometimes took days to crawl out of. This of course extended to my creative endeavors, which no matter how much time I poured into them I never felt confident they were good enough, or that I could show anyone else for fear of ridicule.
So when Estaban the bull breaks down in tears because to him his art never feels acceptable, I can relate. He might be a cartoon with a simplified version of anxiety, but his lack of confidence in the things he makes is something myself and almost everyone creative I know suffers from, but is rarely brought up in any sort of media. That alone made his journey in Slow Down, Bull to find the perfect decorations for his art, but more importantly to become empowered by it, something meaningful to me, even more so given its kid friendly aesthetic and accessible design.
Here was a game for kids and adults alike letting us know that it’s OK if something doesn’t turn out perfect, and that the stress you feel when sharing it with others is almost always unfounded. It’s the sort of reassurance I’d have greatly appreciated when I was a kid freaking out over what in hindsight was always inconsequential, and that half the royalties go to a children’s charity is just icing on the cake.
Sadly Slow Down, Bull’s narrative is saying one thing, while it’s gameplay is saying another. While it’s design is simple enough for anyone to understand in a minute, utilizing only two buttons and focusing around a straightforward collecting mechanic, its scoring system is far less lenient. I was constantly being punished for small mistakes, having to make extremely precise runs just to pass levels and even then being told it wasn’t good enough and I needed to try again.
So much of Slow Down, Bull feels designed so as to be a game everyone can enjoy, with an encouraging message and easygoing gameplay loop, but despite how many times it told me it’s OK that I’m not perfect its scoring system defiantly stated the opposite. It told me that I had to be exact, to get the best scores, to be absolutely perfect if I even wanted to see the next level, and this in turned made playing Slow Down, Bull incredibly stressful. Suddenly I understood why Esteban was getting so worked up, as his game is almost hostile in how hard it pushes you before you’re allowed to proceed.
I really do love a lot of what Slow Down, Bull is trying to do. I like that Insomniac Games is branching out into new platforms and gameplay styles, that they tried to make something encouraging and entertaining regardless of your age, and they’re giving part of the proceeds to help kids that need it. But I feel like by making the game so needlessly challenging and frustrating, they’ve diluted its purpose and made something that instead of helping relieve stress, only served as yet another source of it.

Introduced to odd-couple Esteban the bull and his brother Mango the cat, you set out to travel the world collecting decorations for your artwork. Stressing out when things are not perfect generally results in tearing his artwork to pieces so the more decorations you can the find, the better.
Slow Down Bull surprised me a lot, while it may seemed aimed at the younger generation by appearance the gameplay itself is both decent and addictive. Spread across 5 uniquely themed zones levels start simply by requiring you to collect art and make it to the end. Gradually they introduce a range of new game mechanics including possums that cling on and double your score but giving mirrored-like control penalties and a Bull-catcher that chases you but can be trapped in ponds. Eventually not even being given enough art per level you are then required to make use of multiplier stacking and general avoidance skills.
Controls are simple though I would recommend a gamepad. Later levels introduced more hazards with greater time restrictions and it become somewhat twitch-based trying to perfect runs. With that said, completing levels is all that was required to make further progress so it's certainly enjoyable for all ages without becoming too frustrated.
Slow Down Bull may not be the game people hoped to see from Insomanic Games but the silver lining is they now have the foot in the door. With half the proceeds going to starlight foundation and much of the game being directly influenced by these youngsters in very unfortunate circumstances, I can easily recommend this game as both fun and a worthy investment. Cheers folks. :)

I like the idea. Freecell with some light RPG elements.
The problem is that it's fundamentally broken. Even before you get to the RPG elements they've added, the game doesn't work as a Freecell game. For unknown reasons I often couldn't move cards, until after moving other, unrelated cards, I suddenly could! Can't move that King into an unoccupied space? Five moves later, now you can!
The RPG elements mostly take form with 'spells', a neat idea, and 'attacks' that are thrown at you mid-match. Essentially, a card with other cards on top of will flash a bit. If you don't uncover that card, you take damage. Problem is, firstly, that Freecell is meant to be a game about thinking and strategy. Rushing the player ruins that. And, perhaps more importantly, the card attacking you is usally one you've stacked other cards onto, meaning that to uncover it, you would literally have to undo your own progress, something that is often impossible anyway due to the nature of Freecell!
In short, it's a neat idea broken at its core by failing to even do Freecell right.

I went back and forth on buying this game but what ultimately decided me was that even the 'negative' reviews (e.g. Destructoid's) stated: "Still I had fun." Well, that's all I'm really looking for.
So I did buy it, and I beat it in one weekend of heavy playing.
The game is an ultra solid tactics/strategy game, basically an indie version of XCOM. While Halfway isn't going to OMG WOW AMAZE you, it's still just plain fun. The RPG elements are minor - item collection & stat increase via stimpacks - but the tactical combat plays smoothly backed up by an intriguing, fresh story. Basically, it explores FTL travel, asking the question: What happens BETWEEN jumps? Hence the title - Halfway.
The characters themselves are nothing spectacular. The protagonist is a marine who's more cool competence than great empathy. Nevertheless, they get the job done. Because each character has a specialty, you get a sense of how they all fit in, even if there are some gaps (Nia anyone?).
Honestly, if you like sci-fi and you like strategy/tactics games, you'll almost certainly like this, even if you're as jaded a gamer as I am. Halfway's a smooth little game that goes down easy, and with no regrets the next morning.
One small note: If you're a tactics/strategy pro ['pro' means you've, e.g. beat XCom on classic ironman or harder], I recommend enabling the difficulty+ mod. I found the game a tad easy without it.

Assassin's Creed: Brotherhood is the third installment in the long-running AC series, and is a direct sequel of Assassin's Creed II, including the return of its protagonist and cast of side characters.
+Globally speaking, while the gameplay of the more recent games of the series is smoother and has a higher degree of visual beauty, this is a solid game that aged relatively well both graphically and gameplay-wise. While the series has evolved a bit since this game came out, it's still a worthy experience.
+The city of Rome is a large, detailed and beautifully rendered open world to explore, and is a really cool setting to play in. While it can be argued that it's annoyingly the only city truly explorable in the whole game, its sheer size and elaborate construction compared to the previous game's locations makes up for it.
+The combat has been graced with a bunch of new animations and (overpowered) mechanics that, while significantly lowering the difficulty of most fights, at the very least makes them entertaining.
+While this can easily be called a filler episode while getting away with it, the plot is still interesting and solid, following Ezio's adventures right from where ACII ended, while also expanding on the present day story as always.
+Good longevity thanks to a decently large amount of main missions (ACII was longer, however), many sidequests and optional tasks and the Monteriggioni management mechanics from the previous game expanded unto the whole city of Rome, which by itself, along with exploration for collectibles, is quite a time-consuming task.
+The game runs right, thankfully, and looks good enough to have aged decently even by today's standards. The Italian voice acting, my main language, is great, but i can't offer an opinion on the english dub.
-While Brotherhood does a great job at cutting out some quirkiness from Assassin's Creed II and improves to some extent in every field, from graphics to gameplay, it's decidedly a "more of the same" game with the same general setting, weapons, combat system and mostly the same cast of characters too. You should not expect anything but a VERY surefire follow-up to a hugely successful game.
-The game feels too easy most of the time. If you combo your instakill follow-up to your first kill, you can easily plow through dozens of enemies near-effortlessly, and the rest of the gameplay isn't much more challenging. It's fun, sure, but if you've played this series (or any third person melee-based game, really) you'll have a really hard time dying.
-The side activities can get repetitive.
-Oh, right, this is the first game in the series to feature multiplayer. But it's dead now and it never was amazing, so whatever.
If you liked Assassin's Creed II you will find this game a good but somewhat lazy sequel that doesn't take absolutely any risks, but rather reprises the successful formula with a few tweaks and minor additions here and there. A literal, and surely well made, more of the same.

Just finished Darksiders tonight, so, here's my little review.
Epic. If there was one word to describe this game, it is that. And I got some varied play out of this title, too. The first 10 minutes are a hack & slash experience, until you hit a cutscene, where you're stripped of your powers and suddenly, it becomes clear. This is a grown up Zelda game!

All of this, plus a♥♥♥♥♥♥ton of blood. It's of the genre, at least. And the story is pretty good. It's fun to watch the cutscenes further the story along.
Overall, it's a helluva game. I picked it up for a fiver and got 22(ish) hours of play on the campaign. Well worth it. Just know that you're in for a longgggg game :P
P.s. If you have 3DVision, treat your eyeballs to some gloriously delicious 3D Darksiders. Some of the best I've experienced, thus far. :)

I really enjoy the ArmA Series as a concept, but I have a lot of issues with ArmA 3 that really just kill the fun for me. I'll go ahead and talk about what I like and don't like.
What I like:
The open world maps, the wide selection of vehicles and weapons, the ability to create limitless scenarios and the wide modding community. All of these factors make for a military sandbox unlike anything else on the market right now. It also has a ton of improvements over older games in the series, which makes it feel more modern. The only games were incredibly clunky and didn't feel so great.
What I don't like:
How many bullets it takes to kill somebody. Its supposed to be a military simulation, but with body armor and helmets it can take upwards of three or four shots to kill an enemy. It becomes really frustrating when you ambush somebody only for them to turn around and kill you after 3 shots in the back, it just feels weird. Maybe its realistc but it doesn't feel like it. I might just accept that I'm bad and play Co-op only, but all the really popular co-op missions drop my frames into the 15s. WIth a GTX 1060, 16gb DDR3 and a i7 4820k I feel like I should manage above 30 at least.
I want to enjoy this game, but I'm either frustrated with some feature of the game design, or just unable to play because of the really poor frames. I even tried to join a Milsim Co-op group, maybe for a more tailored experience rather than just KOTH but the server performance on our missions was terrible.

The game is obviously brilliant. It looks wonderful. The sprites are lively, incredibly animated while not overdoing it. The soundtrack is the best kind of chiptunes you could dream of. The controls are pretty tight: the jumps feel right.
Sadly, I think the game is let down early enough by its level design, and the odd choice of keeping one of the main aspect from the bad platformers of the days of yore: the directional 'pushback on hit' mechanics combined with instadeath pits. It makes enemies uninteresting, and turns them from being a threat to being an annoyance that might, sometimes, precipitate your death to the offscreen void.
The game seems aware of that issue, since it is somewhat generous with its checkpoint system and temporary invulnerability skills a go-go - the main departures from the games Shovel Knight wants to pay tribute to. But this is just a rough patching work to the underlying issue. The game also reserves you some more one-hit kill surprises I won't spoil for you.
Ironically, compared to the dreaded pits and spikes, the boss fights felt like relaxing distractions.
The game also tends to focus on the grabbing of monies, gems, whatever... borrowing in that respect from Western 16bit platforming (think of all those German Amiga ones, with♥♥♥♥♥♥to grab everywhere). But then, the economic model your looting is supposed to support is so weak it makes little sense. Since there is no high score, there is basically no incentive past the halfway point, besides Pokemoniac Compulsive Behaviour, to grab anything.
I guess I am too cranky an old ♥♥♥♥ to be any patient with this kind of gaming experience anymore. Navigating the tedious and somewhat boring levels to get to the enjoyable little distraction of a boss fight and experience the pixel poetry of the inter cutscenes wasn't enough to keep me from grumbling.

This is the kind of old school gameplay that you'd expect from a Mega Man game, but with the kind of conveniences you expect in a modern game. And, for once, those conveniences don't exist solely to make the game EASIER -- they're just there to give you features that the old games would have had if they could.
I'd still only consider Shovel Knight to be about as hard as Mega Man 2, and most of the bosses are easier than that. There are way harder games out there. But while it may not be "Nintendo Hard" it still gives you a good challenge, and the New Game+ ramps things up to full-on platform HELL.

It's a solid piece of work, with decent story and characters, sadly let down by its short length, easy puzzles and VERY dissapointing last boss. In fact the game pretty much gets easier the further you go.
But yeah pretty cool if you like any of the games it rips off.

Story of Narcissu 2nd takes place before Narcissu 1st. A story of another person with the same despairing fate. However, it is a bit lengthy. Assassin's Creed Brotherhood is the sequel to the highly successful 2009 release, Assassin's Creed II. Released in 2011, two years after its predecessor, players once again take on the role of a romantic, yet badass, Italian assassin from the Renaissance era known as Ezio Auditore da Firenze. For those who have never played a game from this franchise, there's absolutely no reason to start on this installment; Assassin's Creed II, Brotherhood, and Revelations are a trilogy that are best played in their original chronological order. That being said, whether you liked or disliked the prior two installments, many elements of the franchise have changed, for the better, with Brotherhood, and gamers who may have disliked the repetitve nature of the last two releases would be well advised to give this title a shot.
When we last left Ezio, he had finished conquering some beautiful, well-known cities in Italy such as Venice and Florence, all the while abolishing the Templar scourge that laid within each one. In the end, his uncle Mario officially inducted him into the Assassin order, and he was last seen capturing the ever elusive Apple of Eden in a highly technologically advanced underground chamber. Assassin's Creed Brotherhood picks up right where the last title ended, and continues onward from there. After a terrible and somewhat unexpected attack on his homestead, Ezio and his family flee from the now ruined Villa Audatorie. With his sister Claudia and mother Maria, Ezio settles in Roma (Rome), where he has the vast city at his disposal, and many exploration opportunities lay in wait; as do the Borgia, the enemy army of this title.
While the last two franchise installments were seen as fairly repetitive, though to a lesser extent with the second game, Brotherhood is anything but repetitous. It's jam-packed with content, though all of it is hurled at the player from nearly the start of the game. If one doesn't feel like tackling the 9 sequence story, there are a multitude of other events to take on; memories of Ezio's first love, Cristina, Borgia towers to scale and burn down, thief missions, assassination contracts, courtesian tasks, Leonardo sequences, and so very much more. Not to mention the plethora of chests, feathers, and Borgia flags that need to be collected. While the main story lasts about 13-15 hours, players can expect a solid 30-50 if they choose to complete everything; there is absolutely no lack of content here.
There are also a number of series changes and franchise firsts in Brotherhood. This is the first Assassin's Creed title to introduce challenges, though they are all faction-themed for the mercenaries, theives, and courtesans. It's also the first to include 100% Synch objectives, where one must attempt to meet the extra criteria per mission to achieve a complete synchronization with Ezio. More virgin elements include the ability to replay any mission, main or not, as well as the Assassin's Guild; a somewhat mini-game where Ezio can send his army of assassins out into the field to level them up with experience points, as well as gain gold and items. Speaking of which, yes, Brotherhood is the debut of actual items that are used to complete shop quests. There are also fast travel points now, and Ezio can spend his hard-earned money rebuilding Roma by reconstructing shops, banks, stables, and purchasing historical landmarks.
Roma is the only map players will be traversing for the entirety of their game time, and while that may sound boring, rest assured that it is not. Roma in and of itself is massive, especially when taking in to account everything that there is to do within it; let's not forget the down right incredible Armor of Romulous that can be earned by finding six scrolls, much akin to earning the Armor of Altair in Assassin's Creed II, but I digress. Gamers will absolutely need a horse to get around, and luckily there are plenty about; another series first, being able to ride a horse in town. This also means there are new, challenging enemies that ride horseback if you spark the guards' interest enough. On the topic of guards, the combat system has been revamped a little bit. Chain kills are much easier to achieve, and Ezio's new executions are as gruesome as they are fascinating.
On the downside, Brotherhood does little in the way of modern-day story telling; not much emphasis is placed on current-era protagonist Desmond Miles, although players are free to exit the Animus at any time before finishing the game. There's very little incentive to do so, aside from collecting a few artifacts, reading a few e-mails, and getting fed some irrelevant, uninteresting dialogue from Lucy and the gang. Where as at the end of Assassin's Creed II, there was at least a sequence to play through as a reward for sitting through the grueling amount of end-game credits, Brotherhood has nothing but a cliffhanger and a 15 minute long, unskippable credit sequence. This title also still has fairly wonky climbing mechanics, although they do seem to be a little improved over its predecessor.
All in all, if you hated the last two releases of the franchise, play Brotherhood; it may very well redeem the series for you with its refreshing plethora of content. If you enjoyed the last two Assassin's Creed titles, then definitely grab this installment. The villains are some of the most memorable in the entire series, the side missions are completely worth spending the time on, and Ezio is just as suave and charismatic as always. Once again, I highly recommend getting The Ezio Trilogy on console if you have one; the remastered set gives breathtaking new life to these old titles with vibrant color, better textures, and upgraded character models.

I just completed this game and I must say – this was one of the rare games that I was eager to see the outcome of.  From start to finish I felt like I was always against the wall – no mission was too easy and all felt like they furthered the plot along.  Let's get to the details!
==Graphics==
They are simple but nothing else is really needed; the characters and enemies are all recognizable and feel unique.  Plasma Fire looks good, the 'dusting' of enemies leaves a satisfying feeling, and the levels made sense.  The medical ward, cafe, apartments – they all felt right.  Little touches were here or there to give the impression of varied life throughout the ship and I really liked the fluff 'medical bay' in the home bases you established to explain how your party recovered life in between missions.
==Sound==
I'm going to sound like a wimp here – but one of the home-base themes always makes me feel sad; like longing for home.  The combat music felt right – helping to keep me on the edge (the final boss music especially, was unlike the rest and definitely 'alien' as it were).  The sounds of the guns firing, screams of the mutants (or your team-mates), doors, platforms; all of these seemed perfect to me.
==Story==
More than any game I've played in the past 3 years I needed to know how this was going to end.  I was really pulling for these survivors to make it through and escape.  I wanted to know how party conflicts were going to resolve themselves and some of the more hinted at details of the survivors.
Unfortunately the game does leave off on kind of a cliff hanger; I feel as if the game story was 'halfway' completed akin to Anachronox if you ever played that game. This need not be a bad thing, but like Anachronox I really want a 2nd part!  ;)
==Gameplay==
The levels feel incredibly fine tuned – which is to say perfectly balanced with the idea of you gaining a grasp on the combat system, and purchasing/using equipment and gear through out the game.  The enemies were strong where they needed to be and frightfully good at gaining a tactical point to blast me with.  Every battle had me on edge – I wasn't sure if I'd pull through.
The game interface is a bit tricky to get used to at first though but it's still simple enough.  A heads up for the would-be purchaser (none of the below are what I would consider 'bad' at all though).
1)- I did not notice it, but I think you can only use medkits/shield-cells on other party members (not on the active character) through the inventory screen as opposed to the radial menu.
2)- There is no 'undo movement' button which resulted in my untimely demise in the very final part of the very final mission.  Thankfully the game saves during each 'stage' of it so I didn't have to redo an hours worth of work.  :)
==Sum Up==
A simply wonderful game.  Tough.  A great story.  Simple but challenging game-play, excellent sound and appreciated graphics.  You've sold me on your product/games Robotality; now make the second part of the story so I can find out what happens!  ;P

Wasn't expecting much when I first started playing it but man, I'm now glad I did! Its basically Zelda with a lot more mature setting and harder difficulty. You'll want to play on Apocalyptic difficulty or you'll be doing yourself a disservice!
The game strikes a good balance between combat, platforming and puzzles. I'll admit it, I was stumped a few times but with enough time and a careful eye you should be able to solve/spot the solutions to the games puzzles. The combat is combo based and requires some precision timing and dodging to do well. You also have various powers and 3 main weapon types that you can weave into the flow.
As for the setting its post-apocalyptic but ORIGINAL style, that is, ANGELS AND DEMONS and not nuclear war - I like angel/demon style better. :D Some truely epic sights to behold like a giant goth cathedral on an island surounded by lava, a giant desert with huge sand worms on the hunt and a truely massive demon tower looming in the background (your ultimate goal is to get into that tower). Its all connected via a HUB zone and you can freely travel back to previous areas to get goodies you may have missed like heart pieces (life shards) and bottles (vessels), haha its pretty Zelda-like but thats not a bad thing.
So, great game. Basically a mature, goth Zelda. Story isn't anything to write home about but it doesn't get in the way and the characters are all pretty awesome. 8.5/10

I have never been so disappointed in a CoD game so much as this game has made me. I never really had high hopes for this title either, since SHG was developing it. I was expecting the game to be mediocre, not downright abysmal. Every single aspect of the game is either mediocre, uninspired, or unfair.
is normally something that players know what to expect from. You're supposed to be a trained soldier, fighting for a personal cause (often associated with honor) with a few badass side-characters that help you along the way. It's a cheesy actionfest that teeters precariously between hilariously simple gunfights and hilariously over-the-top cutscenes and setpieces. That isn't what this CoD is going for, preferring a more character driven story that tries to illustrate the idea that the characters you see in these games are mortal. That's more what SHG said they were going for, but the concept of consistency eludes them. Also, due to the overabundance of elements taken from WW2 media and other CoD games, the campaign for WW2 has almost no identity.
- The story has you in the boots of some boring guy from Texas, accompanied by a Jew, a kinda-racist New Yorker, a nerd, the good cop, and the bad cop. At some point you meet a black guy. You will swap back and forth from Band of Brothers-like cutscenes, to the typical CoD shooting gallery, to some sort of "key" segment where your character becomes a marksman or a Nascar racer, and eventually reverts to the Band of Brothers cosplay. When the story wants to drag in the middle of the gameplay, you're forced into a QTE. The game also attempts to set up the bad cop as an antagonist, but he does nothing other than be a complete jerk for most of the game. There are no discernable character arcs throughout the journey.
- Levels are padded out into three segments, each having a different style of gameplay from the last. The first mission features your character "cinematically" storming the beaches of Normandy, followed by around 10 minutes of shooting Nazis in the face while intermittently stopping yourself to eat a packet of morphine, and finally wraps up with your player dragging a wounded soldier across the field, shooting about 10-15 Germans with your sidearm. This system uses different setpieces and characters to allow for a little variety, but this well ends up drying out due to a lack of any dynamic story elements. You will end up playing that "perched sniper," segment multiple times throughout the campaign, you will end up playing the "stealth" segment around 4-5 times throughout the campaign, and you will be shooting enemies with your sidearm in desperation very many times throughout the game. This results in the campaign being forgotten rather quickly after a single playthrough, with so many levels blending together in the mishmash of stripped down gameplay.
really isn't something I jumped into with any sense of urgency. It's been done numerous times, so I don't care about it as much as I would have around 6 years ago. This part of the game will only ilicit a short review of the new features. That said, there is a prologue that plays as a tutorial of sorts for zombies. Yes, that's right. The Zombies mode has a tutorial. Other new additions include an ability meter, akin to the specialist bonuses from Black Ops 3, that provides the players with a temporary power, such as infinite ammo. The last new thing they did for Zombies was providing an objective list that tells the player what the next main objective is, making easter egg hunting rather easy. By my fourth play, I completed the easter egg with some high-ranked player who complained about me not knowing eveery step in the procedure.
is by far the biggest draw of any CoD game, so the most effort should go into this segment, right? That's what I thought, but the game says otherwise. This is by far the worst entry into CoD's catalogue of multiplayer. The game was released in an unfinished state, which is surprising even for CoD. Even to this day, not all of the issues are ironed out.
- WW2 features 9 regular multiplayer maps, a far cry from the 14-16 maps we would get pre-2013. These maps are all functionally flawed, featuring only 2-4 spawn points, level design cluttered with flank routes and blind spots, making it very difficult to hold any given area that's not a window. Of the 9 maps, 3-4 are almost universally hated by the community (Gustav Cannon, USS Texas, Pointe du Hoc, and Aachen). I personally hate all of them, thanks to their bland design choices and overabundance of blind spots. There were also multiple exploits that were found in WW2, allowing players to escape the map, see enemies through walls, and spawn trap enemies for the entire duration of the match. Some of these issues were eventually fixed, but the overall poor design will stay forever.
- Supply drops are a very touchy subject that have been writhing in our souls for the past 3 years. This time? They're just as bad as most players will say. The "social" system set in place explicitly encourages the opening of supply drops, so you can function as effortless advertisement that will entice more players to try opening, or even purchasing supply drops. The biggest issue with this system is how weapon camoflages function in this game. Your weapon will not feature the full camoflage UNLESS you have equipped a heroic variant of a weapon. If you want to really show off that gold camo, you gotta start opening these crates.
- Gunplay is another issue that seems to have core issues that can't be hammered out with a patch or two. Not only are specific weapons functionally useless (any shotgun, any semi-auto rifle, and any launcher), but there are issues with the overall hit detection. I have played multiple games where one of my bullets will hit, the next phase out of existence, and then the next hits. Also, SHG is going out of their way to not listen to any of the regular CoD community, and seems to act like they know what's wrong with the game and what isn't. In the latest patch, there were multiple buffs to various weapons that didn't necessarily need one (Lewis, Thompson, MG15, and MP40), and there were nerfs on weapons that no one complained about (Auto Pistol, FG42). What people have been asking for is any sort of nerf to the sniper rifles, as they already have multiple aspects that make them much easier to use than other weapons, such as greatly reduced flinch. People also want the health regen to return to the CoD standard of 5 seconds, which will make rushing a possible tactic, but these prayers have gone without answer. Funny, this is the only CoD game that simultaniously punishes rushing AND camping.
- Streaks, streaks, streaks. The biggest appeal of playing a CoD game is reaching a high enough streak where the game will essentially start winning for you. Streaks are the staple of CoD, they are the chocolate chips in your cookies, they help decide whether you'll feel accomplished at the end of the match or not. They suck in WW2. Most high-level streaks require upwards of 12 kills, add another six if you're not playing FFA/TDM, they tend to get around 4-5 kills before petering out, and games tend to end far too quickly for the player to want to put the effort in for them. Take it this way. The firebomb run takes around 10+ kills to earn. The BO1 Napalm Strike takes 5 kills, and arrives with almost no delay. The fire in BO also killed much faster than fire in WW2, while the WW2 firebomb run covered a slightly larger area. They have the same payout. What. The. ♥♥♥♥.
was already stated in the header. After enduring about 80 hours of WW2, a good chunk of which was squatting in the Headquarters, I can't take any more. I don't ever expect to come back to playing this mess of a game, and I pray that Treyarch's next CoD is as good, if not better than BO3.

Amnesia: The Dark Descent. Another game by Frictional games, famous for publishing the Penumbra Series, mostly known Penumbra: Black Plague. Black Plague was notoriously known for being scary as there is no possible way to defend yourself. So it seems that Frictional seems to go by 'Stick with what you know' and what Frictional seems to know is how to make me poo my pants. The same mechanic is in Amnesia: The Dark Descent. You have no means to defend yourself and must hide. However, the mindbending areas combined with your draining insanity making sounds, you have no idea if that loud clang behind you was a monster coming in or just a rock hitting metal. When you stay in the dark, your sanity slowly disipates making your vision blur and starts making you see things that likely are not there. Your only source of light is a lantern(which oil can be hard to find at times) and tinderboxes to light torches and candles. You must be frugal with these precious items. The only way to stop your ever growing insanity, you must stay in the light and try to progress. However, horrible and disfigured creatures likely wait around the corner, so you must decide, stay in the light where they might see you, or stay in the dark and lose your sanity more and more each passing moment. Frictional also understands that a monster stays scary the less you see it, so if you spot a monster, your sanity quickly starts going down, making it so you WANT to see it, but can't if you want to keep your precious sanity. Atmosphere and sound design are the cornerstone items that make a horror game and Amnesia hits it spot on, many of my friends are afraid to play this game. The only criticisms I have about this game is that the monsters can be pretty predictable to spawn(such as picking up a key). Another thing is that the game is not randomly generated. Randomly generated scares could have done so much more. But all in all, if you are a horror fan and want to try something that is not run and gun, and makes your spine tingle, Amnesia is for you. If you want to stand behind some sort of weapon and face the threat head on, go elsewhere because this game is not for you. If your still interested, enter the haunted Castle Brennenburg... if you dare....

Fan favorite Ezio Auditore is back for another episode in his story! AC: Brotherhood takes place RIGHT after the events of Assassin's Creed 2 (So, if you haven't played AC 2, definitely play that first) and Ezio is in search of the Apple of Eden as he attempts to save Roma from Templar control. This game's story is really good and it's a great followup to AC 2, and the twist at the beginning is great!
Since this is a sequel to AC 2, you'll see a lot of familiar faces as you play through. Each character is great and well-written, including the main antagonist, and none of them ever feel boring. They all feel like they belong in the game. Ezio himself, like always, is fantastic. You get the sense that he's matured a lot through is journeys and you get to continue to see him grow as a character.
The setting as well is great and beautiful. The map is rather large, even if you don't really get to go anywhere else besides Rome. There's even flags and treasure to collect, if you're into that sort of thing. The graphics look even better than AC 2, despite there not being much time in between the two. The colors are vivid and the game runs smoothly.
Now, onto the real reason you want this game (Well, besides for the story and Ezio). The combat system in this game is so far one of the best combat systems we've gotten in an AC game. There's not too much of a difference between AC 2's and Brotherhood's combat system, but it's still fun and satisfying (Not very challenging though saddly).
Obviously, you're going to need weapons to go into combat. You'll find a nice variety of weapons in the black smith shops, from light, sharp, and fast swords, to heavy and powerful ones, to the typically one-hit kill wrist pistol, as well as hammers, maces, and even daggers for those quick kills. Of course, you also get two hidden blades (Eventually ;) ) The weapons are all well designed and feel fantastic when using them. Also, you'll find armor in the smithing shops that will boost your resistance to attacks, as well as add more health points to Ezio.
Since you have all of these weapons, it's time for some slicing and dicing (And we're not talking about carrots here). You'll fight an assortment of different enemies, from heavy armored powerful axe/large sword wielding dudes, to light-on-their-feet daggermen, to the basic hammer/sword dudes, pistol dudes (SO annoying), lancemen, and light armored swordsmen. So, yeah, you probably won't run out of things to stab anytime soon. Some of the enemies can be a little challenging, especially when they group up, but they're not all that difficult (And still can't swim! If they just asked Ezio for swimming lessons, maybe he'd do it). They are, however, fun to kill.
Tired of fighting bad guys alone? Well, this is Assassin's Creed BROTHERHOOD, right? Where's the Brotherhood? Well, guess what...you can now rescue civilians and train them to be assassins! Once you save civilians, you'll be able to put them to good use and train them up. You can call your men/ladies into battle and they'll take out soldiers for you. In fact, if there's not too many soldiers, you don't even have to lift a finger! Once you have enough, you can call in an arrow storm to take out some fools! Awesome! You can also send these guys on missions for you in different areas in Europe/Asia (They'll send you postcards, I'm sure of it!). On missions/contracts, they can gain more levels (max level is level 10) and even get you some much needed cash! Once they've leveled up, you can upgrade their armor or weapon, free of charge. This is a great new mechanic and thankfully made it to Revelations.
If you need more people for your Brotherhood, all you have to do is take out 'Borgia Towers'. These are restricted areas that are controlled by Borgia (Templar) Captains. Take out the captain, destroy the tower, and the area's yours (Along with an extra slot for another assassin in your Brotherhood!).
While fighting, you might take a few hits so, you'll need to heal up. For that, you'll need some medicine (Just pop some pills, you'll be fine!). Where are you going to get this medicine though? The back alleyway? Nope. Uncle Mario's meth lab? Definitely not. You'll find different venues all over Rome that will sell you much needed supplies (including a doctor that will get you that medicine). Most of the stores are closed though so, you have to upgrade them so they're open. Doing this gives you a discount. There's a tailor, who can dye your clothes and give you storage upgrades on throwing knives, medicine, and the heavy weapon upgrade. The doctor, of course, gives you heals, medicine, and poison. There's also an art merchant, because who doesn't love some Italian art?
If you're looking for side quests, this game's got it! There's 'shop quests' that allow you to get the best armor (and I believe the best sword) in the game by completing them. All you have to do is find different needed materials around Rome. There's also Leonardo's Machine levels where you help destroy Leonardo's war machines he's been forced to make for the Templars. These are always fun and are usually action packed! (Do all of these and you'll get a reward ;D) There's also some other side quests scattered around, but I'll let you do the exploring. Also, DO THE CRISTINA MISSIONS!!! (BUT MAKE SURE YOU PLAY AC 2 FIRST!!!). If you're stuck on how to get the Cristina missions, they're based off of total sync. Once you reach a certain level of total sync, they will show up on the map (And a message will pop up).
Overall, AC Brotherhood is one of the best editions to the Assassin's Creed franchise. I HIGHLY recommend getting this game, but like I said before, make sure you play Assassin's Creed 2 first! You won't regret it!

I would say this is one of the best horror games out there.
I say that because it messes with you psychologically through carefully setted up scenarios, not cheap jump scares. It's a great game because it knows how to be scary.
You play as Daniel, a character that suffers from amnesia and wakes up in an empty castle during the middle of the night. You don't have any weapons and your only form of defense is to run and hide. This is why the game is scary, it makes sure you are helpless and it's trusting your imagination to fill in the blanks and scare yourself.
Other horror games rely on gore and jump scares to basically gross you out, while Amnesia keeps everything in the dark. The whole environment is very dark and your lamp has limited fuel. You go insane if you spend too much time in the dark and the game makes sure you know there is something out there, but it doesn't quite show you what, and that fear of the unkown eats you from the inside out.

I'm a big fan of turn-based squad tactics games - Xcom, Fallout Tactics, Shadowrun, etc. If you are also a fan of these, you'd probably find something worth liking in Halfway. Overall, it was a challenging, well-written game that I really enjoyed despite a few quirks.
Difficulty
This is not for the faint of heart. You will probably find yourself re-playing some of the missions several times, trying to find the best mix of tactics and team cominations. Especially in later levels, when some very dangerous enemies show up, You'll probably want to (if you don't feel like it's cheating) make a habit of simply restarting the level once you've got an idea of what enemies and level layout you're dealing with. But the flipside is that FINALLY beating a mission is really rewarding.
Variation
Both weapons, armor, and enemies seemed to have the same pattern going on - they're split up into basic "types" and then there's several "levels" within each type. Sniper rifles - Mk1, Mk2, Mk3, etc.. Armor with high shield recharge but low damage resistance...Mk1, Mk2, Mk3, etc.. Enemy with no shield but huge amount of health...easy version, medium version, toughest version. It makes for very clear-cut tactics - you're making definite decisions about what kind of weapon/armor to equip, and then you just keep upgrading it. You see certain enemies, you use specific tactics and abilities. While I do, on a base level, really appreciate that the mechanics of how these all work and fit together has been worked out and clearly signposted for me, I did feel at times that the lack of diversity and "grey area" sometimes made the game feel a bit empty.
Story
I loved the story, hands down. I liked the characters, I enjoyed seeing their interactions, and I was interested in seeing how things would play out and how the story would resolve up through the end. There are NO dialogue trees. You are essentially watching pre-determined dialogue at every "conversation" in the game, but I still enjoyed it, even in places where it was a bit cheesy.
Tactical playstyle
This game takes a page from Xcom and Shadowrun in that there's essentially two "actions" per turn per character. No points or anything like that to manage. You can move and shoot, reload and shoot, move and use an item or ability, take an aimed shot, etc. Very straightforward, very accessible. My one gripe (which I've seen others echo) is that the "retaliation" ability kinda sucks - it's basically "overwatch," but you're essentially holding onto one or both action points to fire at any enemy THAT FIRES AT YOU. Not enemies that become visible, not enemies that walk right up next to you, not enemies that fire on teammates - only the ones that shoot at the specific character who has activated "Retaliation." Be aware - using it properly can actually save a run, but not using it or overrelying on it can be devastating.
No Leveling Up
That's right. No leveling up your guys. You can give them "stims" which will permanently raise one or more stats, but those arerisky to use more than 5 of per character. You also should definitely be upgrading your weapons and armor as you find new stuff to use. But you absolutely, especially in late-game, need to play cautiously. If a tough enemy gets a concentrated burst of fire on you, or if a squadmate gets flanked and fired on by several enemies at once, you could go from "sitting in cover with full shields and health" to "only 2 of 4 squaddies still alive" VERY fast.
Buy this game if:
-You like squad-based tactics games
-You don't want to have to do too much micromanaging in your Squad-tactics game
-You want a game with a sci-fi horror kind of feel to it
-You want a game that's challenging but rewarding
Don't buy this game if:
-You want a game that'll be easy to play through
-You want to micromanage every aspect of your characters' stats or have lots of control over how they develop
-You want to charge into every scenario with guns blazing, ignoring cover
-You want a game with a rich, complicated, branching storyline

There are only three kinds of players in Team Fortress 2: the distracters, the distracted, and those who take advantage of the distracted.
That's how this game works in a nutshell. With so many players allowed in a single match (and maps so big that they're boring without a lot of players), it feels like the end result of matches largely depends on which team overpowers the other in terms of brute force and numbers (and yes, the number of players per team can be, and often are, unbalanced). Sure, there are nine classes, each with its own unique playstyle and application of "skill" which every person will probably find their own preference with practice, but by the end of the day, numbers usually determine the winner (not including AFK players, which I found on my team very, very often).
For the individual player, this means you can often get blindsided by something or someone that you couldn't have hoped to react to in time. If you're playing to win, this can be frustrating, and you may want for a game with a more level playing field. If you're playing casually, however, it's not so bad knowing that your death isn't entirely your fault, usually. There are simply too many players to keep track of! Still, this game desperately needs a better matchmaking system. Uneven teams will prompt the system to ask the bigger team for volunteers to switch, but it's always a by-choice basis and may not be heeded.
What is more agregious, however, is the overall lack of instruction this game gives to new players. There is a tutorial section, but only tutorials for four of the nine classes exist, and while the existing ones are useful, the lack of the other five class tutorials is baffling, especially considering that this game has been out for ten years, with all nine classes having been available since release. Granted, some of the remaining classes, like the Heavy and Scout, don't need a lot of instruction, but the Medic and Pyro definitely do--the Medic because it's not immediately obvious how to do what he's known for and heal people, and the Pyro mostly because of airblasting, a technique that blows away projectiles and bombs, that is pretty invisible and therefore undetectable by other players unless they're paying close attention. If I hadn't watched xlr105's TF2 Interactive videos, I wouldn't even have remembered that airblasting was a thing! This game is all about teaching players to swim by throwing them into the water. Once you're done with the four tutorials, that's it. You can do some offline practice against bots, which I found to be very helpful, but additional instruction would be appreciated.
Unfortunately, it's not just the gameplay that suffers from the game's cryptic nature. Trading items--which you either buy or unlock randomly while playing matches--with friends is all-out impossible unless you pay any amount of money for this game, be it for something in the store or for a clearance pass to one of the game's more competitive modes. There was no sign whatsoever that I needed to pay in order to trade items (or unlock more inventory space, for that matter), and I first thought I was having problems with my connection when none of my items would show up in the trade menu. Once I actually paid and tried again, the trade wouldn't finalize for another 15 days because of some ridiculous precaution that prevents players without a Steam Mobile Authenticator from going through with the trade immediately. The amount of anti-consumerism that plagued my experience was astonishing. And really, how easy would it be for the developers to tack on a little notice on the trading menu that tells non-Premium players that they need a Premium membership in order to trade? Ten years this game has been out for, and nobody thought to fix this? It's as if Valve one day decided that no one other than the players who had already played this game to death were still playing it. Instead of adding new features to the game to keep that playerbase interested, they should really focus on polishing up what's already there.
Speaking of new features, the Contracker system they installed offers some initiative for players to reach certain goals during playtime, but a lot of them are specific to only one weapon, which, like all items, you have to either buy or unlock at random. And you have to complete certain Contracts before you unlock others, so if you don't have the required weapon, you're stalled in place until you get it. For this reason, I can't comment on how rewarding the Contracker system is, as I've barely managed to progress through it.
It's not all bad for Team Fortress 2, however. What the game lacks in user-friendly gameplay, it makes up for with its style and sense of humor. I daresay the lore of the game, if you're willing to look for it, is one of the most entertaining aspects of the franchise, if not THE most entertaining aspect. While I'm not one for the crude humor and the blood and gore, cartoony as it is, Team Fortress 2 is just bursting with personality, which I think is where it really shines. Playing through the game was worth it just to hear the range of laughable quotes the nine classes would give.
All in all, I find Team Fortress 2 to be a clunky, unbalanced, beginner-unfriendly dash of charm that anyone interested in the game from its looks alone should definitely give a try. There are many good elements.  The overall structure will be familiar to anyone who has played the recent XCOM.  It's fun for a few hours, but gets a bit repetitive toward the end.  The final boss fight is somewhat tedious.
Things that would have made this game better:
- A decent tutorial.  If you've played XCOM, you'll understand the basics of movement and firing, but there are many details that aren't apparent.  Case in point: I read a number of reviews that stated sniper rifles are the ultimate weapon, and based on the numbers the game presents, they are.  But if you *try* an assault rifle, you'll discover that the base to-hit is much higher, so you don't have to spend an extra AP aiming.  Which means you can fire it twice in a round and generally hit both times.
(Another example: you'll figure out pretty quickly that every unit MUST have a weapon and armor at all times, so if you sell off the last spare gun or suit you will be unable to swap equipment around.  But it would have been nice for a tutorial or (gasp) manual to warn you to hang on to the spares.)
- A save game feature that recorded more than what level you were on.  I had to leave the game running while away from the computer for a few hours because I didn't want to lose my progress.  Most of the levels aren't terribly long, but it's not obvious where the save points are, and you don't want to re-play some of the drawn-out battles.
- Better indications of cover.  If you're going to steal XCOM's full/half cover system, you should probably steal the part where you show the current cover status of the unit.
Not a great game, but it's sufficiently entertaining to merit a run-through.

For those who are looking for a rich strategy experience, but prefer to take time to plan their steps without being put under the pressure of real time gameplay, this game is for you. Epic in scope and in production values, with multiple play styles, if you've been curious about the Civ series before, this makes an excellent start!

I think the idea behind this game is pretty great: gain experience points and gold to level up and get new gear, respectively, all by playing rounds of FreeCell. You get magic spells that help you "bend" the rules of the game to change card positions and more, and you lose the round if you get damaged too much and run out of hit points.
That last part certainly makes sense from a development standpoint, because otherwise, each round has no feeling of danger. However, in its execution, it can take some players a
of pondering on which cards to move where, and the longer you take, the more times you get hit. I found myself pretty darn stuck on some of the early rounds with all four suits of cards, despite having played lots of FreeCell in my youth on the earliest version of Windows that ever had it. Getting smacked around while trying to solve a difficult card layout doesn't make the game hard; just very annoying.
The spells help out, as you can get one that stops you from receiving damage from the next attack, and you can pull a card one slot down toward the bottom by spending mana, but all of this is simply a distraction from the core of the game: FreeCell. None of the RPG elements were making the game any more enjoyable for me, there are no characters, no personality, no plot, no intriguing world, etc. I certainly don't demand these things be in the game. I just want to like it better than FreeCell, which I think is an alright game and would welcome changes to make it more entertaining. Despite my adoration for hybridizing games by putting fun RPG elements into them, I came to the disappointing realization that,
, FreeCell Quest was less enjoyable than plain old FreeCell from Windows back in the ancient times.
On a final note, leaving personal taste and opinion out entirely, the game does not even function properly as a FreeCell game. Although I'm no expert at FreeCell (not even close to being "decent," really), I know that you can put a single red card on a single black card, if the red card is one number lower than the black card. That's how Solitaire and FreeCell work. I believe I had a red four and a black five, both exposed at the bottom of two columns. I was not trying to move more than one card at all, and I had plenty of free spaces even if I had been. The game absolutely would not let me stack the red four on top of the black five. Furthermore, the game is more finnicky about letting you place cards on other cards in general: don't place it close enough and it doesn't stick. The original FreeCell I played on Windows way back when had better "sticking" than FreeCell Quest. This game needed to work properly as FreeCell before it tried to add more to it, and it did not succeed in this.

An interesting game in the sense that it successfully adds RPG elements to a card game (remember puzzle quest?).
Granted: the quest takes a while to really get going. This if for two reasons:
1) the story aspect is pretty much non-existent: there is this huge map with dots to travel to. Going there means you've got to play freecell to "liberate" the city from...something.
2) the difficulty of the actual games starts out too easy. Just two decks and a whole bunch of lanes. Perhaps someone totally (but TOTALLY) infamiliar with freecell might get stuck for a bit, but I honestly doubt it's even possible at this point.
The first part isn't really improved upon, to be honest. I don't expect epic cutscenes in these kind of experimental indie games, but it's just clear the story is just a means of stringing a bunch of steadily harder freecell games together.
...and that's where freecell quest absolutely shines. The amount of lanes slowly decreases (meaning: more cards stacked upon each other, which means higher difficulty), there are degrees of ways the deck is shuffled and the amount of suits also increases. Luckily, by that time the RPG elements kick in. There are spells that at first seem like cheating (e.g. a random card to the goal stack) but are counteracted by the fact that these uses are limited AND that the cards deal damage to you (it's a decent way to break analysis paralysis, but you shouldn't try to figure out how that's supposed to work :P ). Fights earn you experience (increase of life and mana) and gold, which you use to buy everything needed for later levels. Which brings me to a minor gripe: you start out with nothing equipped. Meaning: I apparently liberated the first country being a naked ninja with an "extra experience" ring worn on...erm...if "I" wore it, it was somewhere NOT on the finger. :P
But in all seriousness: it's incredibly good at what it sets out to do. If you like solitaire games, this one's a pretty good one (better than faerie solitaire, IMHO).
